Title: Chicken burrito bowls
Ingredients:
For the chicken:
- 2 1/2 lb boneless, skinless chicken breasts (about 5 breasts)
- 2 tbsp olive oil
- 2 tsp chili powder
- 2 tsp ground cumin
- 1 1/2 tsp garlic powder
- 1 1/2 tsp smoked paprika
- 2 tsp kosher salt
- 1 tsp black pepper
- Juice of 2 limes

For the cilantro-lime rice:
- 3 cups long-grain white rice, rinsed
- 4 1/2 cups water
- 1 tbsp olive oil
- 1 tsp kosher salt
- 1/2 cup chopped fresh cilantro
- Juice of 2 limes

For the bowls:
- 2 cans (15 oz each) black beans, drained and rinsed
- 2 cups frozen corn kernels, thawed
- 2 bell peppers, any color
- 1 large red onion
- 1 tbsp olive oil
- 1/2 tsp kosher salt
- 3 cups shredded romaine lettuce
- 2 cups halved cherry tomatoes
- 2 ripe avocados
- Extra lime wedges and cilantro, for serving
Steps:
1. Mise en place (do all of this before any heat goes on): Rinse the rice in a fine-mesh strainer until the water runs clear — this washes off surface starch so the grains cook up fluffy, not gummy. Dice means cut into small even cubes, about 1/2 inch: dice the bell peppers and red onion. Mince means chop very fine, almost to a paste: mince nothing yet, but have 2 limes cut in half, cilantro chopped, cherry tomatoes halved, avocados whole (you will cut them at the end so they do not brown). Drain and rinse the black beans. Pat the chicken breasts completely dry with paper towels — dry chicken sears instead of steaming. Measure all spices into one small bowl.
2. Season the chicken: Rub the chicken breasts all over with the 2 tbsp olive oil, then coat evenly with the chili powder, cumin, garlic powder, smoked paprika, salt, and pepper. Squeeze the lime juice over them. Let sit at room temperature 15 minutes while you start the rice (never more than 30 minutes out of the fridge).
3. Start the rice: Combine the rinsed rice, water, 1 tbsp olive oil, and 1 tsp salt in a large pot with a tight lid. Bring to a rolling boil over high heat, stir once, then drop the heat to the lowest setting, cover, and cook 15 minutes. Do not lift the lid — the steam is doing the work. After 15 minutes, turn off the heat and let it stand, still covered, 10 minutes.
4. Cook the peppers and onions: While the rice cooks, heat a large skillet over medium-high heat until a drop of water sizzles and evaporates in 2 seconds. Add 1 tbsp olive oil, then the diced peppers and onion with 1/2 tsp salt. Cook 5-6 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the edges get browned spots and the peppers soften but still have bite. You want char, not mush. Transfer to a bowl.
5. Sear the chicken: In the same skillet over medium-high heat, lay the chicken breasts down — they should sizzle loudly on contact. That sizzle is the sound of a good sear. Cook 5-6 minutes without moving until deep golden brown on the bottom, flip, and cook 5-6 more minutes. The chicken is done when the thickest part reads 165 F on an instant-read thermometer and the juices run clear. Rest the chicken on a cutting board 5 minutes (resting lets the juices redistribute instead of running out onto the board), then slice against the grain into strips.
6. Warm the beans and corn: Add the black beans and corn to the skillet with 1/4 cup water and a pinch of salt. Cook over medium heat 3-4 minutes, stirring, until heated through and the water mostly evaporates. Lightly mash a few beans with the spoon — this makes the mixture creamy.
7. Finish the rice: Fluff the rested rice with a fork (never a spoon — a fork separates grains without crushing them). Fold in the chopped cilantro and lime juice. Taste: it should be bright and lightly salty.
8. Build the bowls: Divide rice among 6 wide bowls. Top with sliced chicken, beans and corn, peppers and onions, romaine, and cherry tomatoes. Slice the avocados just before serving and fan over the top. Serve with lime wedges and extra cilantro.
9. Storage: Keep components separate in the fridge up to 4 days. Reheat chicken, rice, and beans in the microwave with a sprinkle of water, covered, 2 minutes. Add cold toppings fresh. Avocado does not store — cut only what you will eat.

Common mistakes:
- Wet chicken in the pan: if you skip patting dry, the chicken steams and turns gray instead of browning. Paper towels are not optional.
- Lifting the rice lid: every peek lets steam escape and gives you crunchy rice. Set a timer and walk away.
- Overcooking the chicken: pull it at 165 F, not 180. Carryover heat adds a few degrees while it rests.
- Cutting avocado early: it browns in 20 minutes. Cut it last, right before the bowls hit the table.

Title: Chicken stir fry
Ingredients:
For the chicken (velveted):
- 2 lb boneless, skinless chicken breasts, sliced thin
- 1 tbsp soy sauce
- 1 tbsp cornstarch
- 1 tbsp vegetable oil
- 1 egg white

For the stir-fry sauce:
- 1/3 cup low-sodium soy sauce
- 2 tbsp oyster sauce
- 1 tbsp honey
- 2 tsp cornstarch
- 1/2 cup low-sodium chicken broth

For the stir fry:
- 3 cups long-grain white rice, rinsed
- 4 1/2 cups water
- 1 large head broccoli (about 1 1/2 lb)
- 2 bell peppers
- 8 oz snap peas
- 2 medium carrots
- 6 cloves garlic
- 1 piece fresh ginger, about 2 inches
- 3 tbsp vegetable oil, divided
- 1 tsp toasted sesame oil
- 1/2 tsp kosher salt
- Sesame seeds and sliced scallions, for serving
Steps:
1. Mise en place — stir fry moves fast, so everything must be ready before the wok gets hot: Slice the chicken against the grain into thin strips, about 1/4 inch thick (partially freezing the chicken 20 minutes makes thin slicing easy). Cut broccoli into small florets — bite-size pieces with flat sides that sit nicely in the pan. Slice means cut into thin strips: slice the bell peppers into strips. Slice the carrots on a diagonal into thin coins (the diagonal gives more surface area for faster cooking). Mince means chop very fine: mince the garlic and peel and mince the ginger (scrape the skin off with a spoon first — it comes right off). Trim the snap peas. Whisk the sauce ingredients in a bowl. Whisk the velvet marinade (soy sauce, cornstarch, oil, egg white) in another bowl and toss the chicken in it. Start the rice: combine rinsed rice, water, and 1/2 tsp salt in a pot, boil, cover, lowest heat 15 minutes, rest 10 minutes covered.
2. Velvet the chicken: Let the chicken sit in its marinade at room temperature 15 minutes. Velveting is a Chinese restaurant technique — the cornstarch and egg white form a silky coating that keeps the chicken tender even in a screaming-hot wok. Bring a pot of water to a boil, add the chicken, and blanch exactly 45 seconds, until the outside turns opaque but the inside is still pink. Drain immediately. It will finish cooking in the wok.
3. Heat the wok: Place a large wok or the biggest skillet you own over high heat until it just starts to smoke — about 2 minutes. A properly hot wok is the entire secret of stir fry. Add 2 tbsp vegetable oil and swirl. It should shimmer immediately.
4. Sear the chicken: Add the blanched chicken in a single layer. Do not touch it for 90 seconds — let it get browned spots. Then toss and cook 2 more minutes until golden at the edges and cooked through (165 F if you check). Remove to a plate.
5. Cook the vegetables: Add the remaining 1 tbsp oil. Add broccoli and carrots first with 1/4 cup water — the water steams them while the wok heat chars the edges. Cover 2 minutes. Uncover, add bell peppers and snap peas with the salt, and stir-fry 2-3 minutes until bright and crisp-tender. They should still squeak when you bite them.
6. Aromatics: Push the vegetables to the sides, add the garlic and ginger to the center with a drizzle of oil, and stir 30 seconds until fragrant — it will smell sharp and sweet. If the garlic browns past golden, it turns bitter, so keep it moving.
7. Sauce and finish: Return the chicken. Stir the sauce (cornstarch settles) and pour it in. It will bubble and thicken into a glossy glaze in 1-2 minutes — that shine means the cornstarch is cooked. Drizzle with sesame oil and toss. Serve immediately over rice, topped with sesame seeds and scallions.

Common mistakes:
- Crowded wok: too much food at once drops the temperature and everything steams into sogginess. Cook in batches if your pan is small.
- Cold wok: if the oil does not shimmer and the chicken does not sizzle loudly on contact, the pan is not ready. Wait for the smoke wisp.
- Skipping the velvet: unmarinated chicken breast in a hot wok goes dry and chalky fast. The 15-minute marinade is the difference between homemade and takeout.
- Overcooked vegetables: pull them while still bright and crisp. They keep cooking from residual heat.

Title: Turkey chili
Ingredients:
- 2 1/2 lb ground turkey (93% lean)
- 2 tbsp olive oil
- 2 large yellow onions
- 1 large bell pepper, any color
- 6 cloves garlic
- 3 tbsp chili powder
- 2 tbsp ground cumin
- 1 tbsp smoked paprika
- 2 tsp dried oregano
- 1 tsp cocoa powder, unsweetened (optional but recommended)
- 2 tsp kosher salt, plus more to taste
- 1 tsp black pepper
- 2 cans (28 oz each) diced tomatoes
- 2 cans (15 oz each) kidney beans, drained and rinsed
- 2 cups low-sodium chicken broth
- 1 tbsp brown sugar
- Toppings: shredded cheddar, sour cream, sliced scallions, diced avocado
Steps:
1. Mise en place: Dice means cut into small even cubes, about 1/2 inch: dice the onions and bell pepper. Mince means chop very fine: mince the garlic. Measure all the spices into one bowl — chili powder, cumin, smoked paprika, oregano, cocoa, salt, pepper. Open and drain the beans. Open the tomatoes. A note on authenticity: strict Texas chili has no beans and no turkey — it is beef and chiles, period. This is a family-friendly weeknight chili that borrows Texas seasoning logic. If anyone at the table objects, tell them Texas can come fight you.
2. Brown the turkey: Heat the olive oil in a large Dutch oven or heavy pot over medium-high heat until shimmering. Add the ground turkey and break it into small crumbles with a wooden spoon. Let it sit undisturbed 3-4 minutes so it browns — browned meat equals flavor. Then keep breaking and stirring 5-6 more minutes until no pink remains. If the turkey releases a lot of water, let it cook until the water evaporates and the meat starts sizzling again.
3. Soften the vegetables: Push the turkey to the edges, add the diced onion and bell pepper to the center with a pinch of salt. Cook 6-7 minutes, stirring, until the onion turns translucent and soft and the edges start to brown.
4. Bloom the spices: Add the garlic and the whole bowl of spices. Stir constantly 60-90 seconds. Blooming means toasting spices in hot fat — it wakes up their flavor and you will smell the chili powder turn rich and earthy instead of dusty. Do not walk away; burnt spices taste bitter.
5. Build the chili: Pour in the diced tomatoes with their juices, the drained beans, the chicken broth, and the brown sugar. Scrape the bottom of the pot with the spoon to release all the browned bits — that is pure flavor, not burnt food.
6. Simmer: Bring to a boil, then drop to a gentle simmer — a few lazy bubbles breaking the surface, not a rolling boil. Partially cover (lid ajar) and cook 35-40 minutes, stirring every 10 minutes. The chili is done when it thickly coats the spoon and a dragged spoon leaves a trail that slowly fills in. If it is too thin, simmer uncovered 10 more minutes. Too thick, splash in broth.
7. Taste and adjust: This is the most important step. Add salt 1/2 tsp at a time until the flavors pop. If it tastes flat, it needs salt. If it tastes harsh, a pinch more brown sugar rounds it out. If you want heat, add cayenne 1/4 tsp at a time.
8. Serve: Ladle into deep bowls over nothing or over rice. Set out toppings and let everyone build their own.
9. Storage: Chili is better on day 2 — the flavors marry overnight. Fridge 5 days, freezer 3 months. Reheat gently on the stove with a splash of broth.

Common mistakes:
- Boiling instead of simmering: a hard boil makes the turkey tough and the beans mushy. Lazy bubbles only.
- Under-salting: chili needs more salt than you think. Taste, salt, taste again.
- Dumping raw spices into liquid: they stay gritty and dull. The 90-second bloom in fat is non-negotiable.
- Serving immediately: give it 10 minutes off the heat before serving so the texture settles.

Title: Sheet-pan lemon herb chicken and potatoes
Ingredients:
- 3 lb bone-in, skin-on chicken thighs (about 8 thighs)
- 2 lb baby potatoes (about 1 1/2-inch size)
- 1 lb fresh green beans, trimmed
- 1/3 cup olive oil, plus 1 tbsp
- 6 cloves garlic
- 2 large lemons
- 2 tbsp fresh oregano leaves (or 2 tsp dried)
- 1 tbsp fresh thyme leaves (or 1 tsp dried)
- 2 tsp kosher salt, plus more to taste
- 1 tsp black pepper
- 1 tsp paprika
- Lemon wedges, for serving
Steps:
1. Mise en place and oven: Position a rack in the center and heat the oven to 425 F — hot enough to crisp chicken skin and brown potatoes. Line a large rimmed sheet pan (18x13 inch) with foil for easy cleanup. Mince the garlic. Zest means scrape off just the yellow outer skin of the lemon with a grater, stopping before the white pith (pith is bitter): zest both lemons, then cut them in half. Strip the thyme leaves by pinching the stem and sliding your fingers down — the leaves pop right off. Chop the oregano. Halve any potatoes larger than 1 1/2 inches so everything is the same size and cooks evenly. Trim the green beans (snap off the stem ends). Pat the chicken thighs completely dry with paper towels.
2. Season everything: In a large bowl, toss the potatoes with 3 tbsp olive oil, half the garlic, half the herbs, 1 tsp salt, and 1/2 tsp pepper. Spread them on the sheet pan in a single layer with space between them — crowded potatoes steam instead of crisping. Rub the chicken thighs all over with 2 tbsp olive oil, then the remaining garlic, herbs, salt, pepper, paprika, and the lemon zest. Squeeze one lemon half over everything on the pan.
3. Roast the chicken and potatoes: Place the chicken thighs skin-side up on the pan among the potatoes. Roast 30 minutes. The skin should be starting to turn golden and the fat rendering — you will see it glistening.
4. Add the green beans: Pull the pan out, toss the green beans with 1 tbsp olive oil and a pinch of salt, and scatter them around the chicken. Squeeze the remaining lemon halves over everything. Return to the oven 12-15 minutes more.
5. Check doneness: Chicken thighs are done when the skin is deep golden and crisp and an instant-read thermometer in the thickest part (not touching bone) reads 175 F — thighs are better at 175 than 165 because the extra heat melts their connective tissue into tenderness. Potatoes are done when a fork slides in with no resistance and the cut sides are browned. Green beans should be blistered in spots but still bright green.
6. Rest and serve: Rest the chicken 5 minutes on the pan. Serve right off the sheet pan family-style with lemon wedges — squeezing fresh lemon over at the table wakes everything up.

Common mistakes:
- Crowding the pan: if the potatoes touch, they steam. Use two pans rather than one crowded one.
- Pale flabby skin: the chicken must be dry going in, and the oven must be fully preheated. Wet skin never crisps.
- Adding green beans too early: they go in for the last 12-15 minutes only, or they turn army-green and limp.
- Skipping the rest: cutting into chicken immediately lets all the juice run out onto the pan.

Title: Beef and broccoli
Ingredients:
For the beef (velveted):
- 2 lb flank steak
- 1 tbsp soy sauce
- 1 tbsp Shaoxing wine (or dry sherry)
- 2 tsp cornstarch
- 1 tsp vegetable oil

For the sauce:
- 1/3 cup oyster sauce
- 3 tbsp low-sodium soy sauce
- 1 tbsp Shaoxing wine
- 2 tsp sugar
- 2 tsp cornstarch
- 1/2 cup low-sodium beef or chicken broth
- 1 tsp toasted sesame oil

For the stir fry:
- 2 large heads broccoli (about 2 lb), cut into florets
- 5 cloves garlic, thinly sliced
- 1 piece fresh ginger (1 inch), peeled and julienned (julienne means cut into thin matchsticks)
- 3 tbsp vegetable oil, divided
- 3 cups long-grain white rice, rinsed
- 4 1/2 cups water
- Steamed white rice, for serving
Steps:
1. Mise en place: Freeze the flank steak 20 minutes — firm meat slices thin cleanly. Slice against the grain into 1/4-inch strips (look for the lines running through the meat and cut across them; this shortens the fibers so the beef is tender, not chewy). Toss with the velvet marinade (soy, Shaoxing, cornstarch, oil) and set aside 15 minutes. Whisk the sauce ingredients in a bowl. Cut broccoli into bite-size florets. Slice the garlic thin. Julienne the ginger into matchsticks. Start the rice: rinsed rice, water, pinch of salt, boil, cover, lowest heat 15 minutes, rest 10.
2. Blanch the broccoli: Bring a large pot of salted water to a boil. Add the broccoli and cook exactly 90 seconds — it should turn vivid green but still be firm. Drain and immediately run under cold water to stop the cooking (this is called shocking, and it locks in the color). Cantonese beef and broccoli keeps the broccoli bright and crisp, never olive-drab.
3. Sear the beef: Heat a large wok or skillet over high heat until smoking. Add 2 tbsp oil. Add half the beef in a single layer — it should sear, not steam, so do not crowd. Cook 60-90 seconds per side until browned at the edges but still pink inside. Remove. Repeat with the second half.
4. Build the sauce: Lower heat to medium. Add the remaining 1 tbsp oil, the garlic, and ginger. Stir 30 seconds until fragrant and the garlic is just golden. Pour in the sauce mixture — it will bubble. Stir until it thickens into a glossy coat-the-spoon sauce, about 1-2 minutes.
5. Combine: Return the beef and broccoli to the pan. Toss 1 minute until everything is glazed and heated through. The beef finishes cooking in the hot sauce — pull it while a slice still shows a hint of pink inside, because it keeps cooking off the heat.
6. Serve immediately over steamed rice. This dish waits for no one — the sauce tightens as it sits.

Common mistakes:
- Slicing with the grain: long fibers make flank steak chewy no matter how well you cook it. Find the grain lines and cut across them.
- Gray broccoli: overcooking turns it olive and sulfurous. Ninety seconds, then cold water.
- Crowding the wok: beef that steams instead of sears turns gray and tough. Two batches, single layer, screaming heat.
- Overcooking the beef: flank goes from perfect to shoe leather in about 60 seconds. Brown the outside, keep the inside blushing.

Title: Shrimp tacos with lime slaw
Ingredients:
For the shrimp:
- 2 lb large shrimp (21/25 count), peeled and deveined, tails off
- 2 tbsp olive oil
- 2 tsp chili powder
- 1 1/2 tsp ground cumin
- 1 tsp garlic powder
- 1 tsp smoked paprika
- 1 1/2 tsp kosher salt
- 1/2 tsp black pepper
- Juice of 1 lime

For the lime slaw:
- 1 small head green cabbage (about 1 1/2 lb)
- 1/2 small red onion
- 1 cup plain Greek yogurt
- 1/4 cup mayonnaise
- Zest and juice of 2 limes
- 2 tbsp honey
- 1 tsp kosher salt, plus more to taste
- 1/2 cup chopped cilantro

For serving:
- 18 small corn tortillas
- 1/2 cup chopped cilantro
- 1/2 cup diced white onion
- Lime wedges
- Hot sauce
Steps:
1. Mise en place: If the shrimp are frozen, thaw them in a colander under cold running water 10 minutes, then pat very dry — dry shrimp sear, wet shrimp steam. Shred means cut into very thin strips: shred the cabbage thin (a sharp knife, quarter the head, slice across as thin as you can). Dice means small even cubes: dice the red onion fine. Zest the limes (yellow-green outer skin only, no white pith), then juice them. Chop the cilantro. Mix the spice blend in a small bowl.
2. Make the slaw first: Whisk the Greek yogurt, mayonnaise, lime zest and juice, honey, and 1 tsp salt in a large bowl. Taste it — it should be tangy, lightly sweet, and well salted; add more salt 1/4 tsp at a time until it pops. Fold in the shredded cabbage, diced red onion, and cilantro. The slaw needs at least 15 minutes to soften and marry, so make it now and refrigerate. It will release some liquid — that is normal; toss before serving.
3. Season the shrimp: Toss the dry shrimp with the olive oil, then the spice blend and lime juice. Let sit 10 minutes while the slaw rests. Do not marinate shrimp in lime juice longer than 15 minutes — the acid starts to "cook" them (like ceviche) and makes the texture mushy.
4. Warm the tortillas: Heat a dry skillet or griddle over medium-high heat. Warm each tortilla 30-45 seconds per side until soft, pliable, and lightly charred in spots. Stack them in a clean kitchen towel to steam and stay soft. Cold stiff tortillas crack and ruin the taco — this step matters.
5. Sear the shrimp: Heat a large skillet over high heat until a drop of water dances. Add the shrimp in a single layer (work in two batches). Cook 90 seconds per side — no more. Shrimp are done when they curl into a C shape and turn opaque pink with lightly charred edges. A tight O means overcooked and rubbery. Squeeze extra lime over the hot shrimp.
6. Assemble: Two tortillas per taco is traditional for street-style (double tortilla holds juicy fillings without tearing) — or one if you prefer. Fill each with shrimp, a generous mound of slaw, diced onion, cilantro, and hot sauce. Serve immediately with lime wedges.

Common mistakes:
- Overcooking shrimp: 90 seconds a side is real. They go from perfect to rubber in under a minute.
- Soggy slaw timing: dress the slaw at least 15 minutes ahead so it softens, but not hours ahead or it weeps into soup.
- Cold tortillas: the number one taco killer. Warm, charred, and wrapped in a towel.
- Over-marinating in lime: 10 minutes seasons; 30 minutes pickles. Set a timer.

Title: Greek chicken souvlaki bowls
Ingredients:
For the chicken:
- 2 1/2 lb boneless, skinless chicken breasts
- 1/3 cup extra-virgin olive oil
- Juice of 2 lemons
- 6 cloves garlic, minced
- 2 tbsp dried oregano
- 1 tbsp red wine vinegar
- 2 tsp kosher salt
- 1 tsp black pepper

For the tzatziki:
- 2 cups plain Greek yogurt (full-fat)
- 1 large English cucumber
- 3 cloves garlic, minced
- 2 tbsp extra-virgin olive oil
- 1 tbsp red wine vinegar
- 1 tbsp chopped fresh dill (or 1 tsp dried)
- 1 tsp kosher salt, plus more to taste

For the bowls:
- 2 1/2 cups long-grain white rice, rinsed (or 6 pita breads)
- 2 large cucumbers, diced
- 3 cups halved cherry tomatoes
- 1 large red onion, thinly sliced
- 1 cup pitted Kalamata olives
- 6 oz feta cheese, crumbled
- Lemon wedges and fresh oregano, for serving
Steps:
1. Mise en place: Grate the cucumber for the tzatziki on the large holes of a box grater. Mince the garlic (some for chicken, some for tzatziki — keep them separate). Juice the lemons. Chop the dill. Dice the cucumbers for the bowls, halve the cherry tomatoes, and slice the red onion paper-thin (thin slices mellow the bite). Rinse the rice. Pat the chicken dry.
2. Marinate the chicken: Whisk the olive oil, lemon juice, garlic, oregano, red wine vinegar, salt, and pepper in a large bowl or zip-top bag. Add the chicken, turn to coat, and refrigerate at least 30 minutes and up to 4 hours. The acid and oil carry the oregano and garlic into the meat — this is the entire flavor of souvlaki, so do not skip the time. (If using wooden skewers, soak them in water now so they do not burn.)
3. Make the tzatziki: Put the grated cucumber in a clean kitchen towel and wring it out hard over the sink — squeeze until no more water drips. This is the difference between thick tzatziki and watery soup. Stir the squeezed cucumber into the Greek yogurt with the garlic, olive oil, vinegar, dill, and 1 tsp salt. Taste: it should be garlicky, tangy, and well salted. Refrigerate at least 20 minutes so the flavors marry.
4. Cook the rice: Combine rinsed rice with 3 3/4 cups water and 1/2 tsp salt. Boil, cover, lowest heat 15 minutes, rest 10 minutes covered, fluff with a fork.
5. Grill or sear the chicken: Heat a grill to medium-high or a grill pan/skillet over medium-high heat until very hot. Remove chicken from the marinade, letting excess drip off. Grill 6-7 minutes per side without moving (undisturbed contact = char marks), until the thickest part reads 165 F and the outside has golden charred spots. Rest 5 minutes, then slice against the grain.
6. Build the bowls: Rice in the bottom of 6 wide bowls. Arrange sliced souvlaki chicken, diced cucumber, tomatoes, red onion, olives, and crumbled feta in sections — the Greek way is composed, not mixed. Dollop generously with tzatziki. Serve with lemon wedges.

Common mistakes:
- Watery tzatziki: if you do not wring the cucumber dry, the sauce thins out within an hour. Wring it like you mean it.
- Skipping the marinade time: 10 minutes gives you surface flavor; 30+ minutes gives you souvlaki.
- Moving the chicken around the grill: constant flipping prevents browning. Put it down, leave it, flip once.
- Slicing with the grain: cut across the fibers or the chicken eats chewy.

Title: Salmon with roasted asparagus and rice
Ingredients:
- 6 salmon fillets, 5 oz each, skin-on (about 2 lb total)
- 2 lb fresh asparagus
- 3 tbsp olive oil, divided
- 4 cloves garlic, minced
- 2 large lemons (1 zested and juiced, 1 cut into wedges)
- 2 tsp kosher salt, divided
- 1 tsp black pepper
- 1 tsp paprika
- 2 tbsp unsalted butter, melted
- 2 tbsp chopped fresh parsley
- 2 1/2 cups long-grain white rice, rinsed
Steps:
1. Mise en place and oven: Heat the oven to 425 F with a rack in the center. Line a large rimmed sheet pan with foil. Snap the woody ends off the asparagus — hold each spear near the bottom and bend; it naturally breaks where the tough part ends. Pat the salmon fillets completely dry with paper towels, especially the skin — dry skin is what crisps. Mince the garlic. Zest one lemon (outer yellow only), juice it, and cut the second lemon into wedges.
2. Start the rice: Combine the rinsed rice, 3 3/4 cups water, and 1/2 tsp salt in a pot. Bring to a boil, cover, drop to lowest heat, 15 minutes, then rest 10 minutes covered. Fluff with a fork.
3. Season the asparagus: Toss the asparagus on the sheet pan with 1 1/2 tbsp olive oil, half the minced garlic, 1 tsp salt, and 1/2 tsp pepper. Spread in a single layer on one half of the pan.
4. Season the salmon: Rub the fillets all over with the remaining 1 1/2 tbsp olive oil. Season the flesh side with the remaining 1 tsp salt, 1/2 tsp pepper, paprika, lemon zest, and remaining garlic. Place skin-side down on the empty half of the pan, leaving space between fillets.
5. Roast: Roast 12-14 minutes. The salmon is done when the flesh flakes easily with a fork and the thickest part reads 145 F — but pull it at 140 F and let carryover heat finish the job, because salmon keeps cooking for 3-5 minutes off the heat and 145 straight out of the oven eats dry. The asparagus is done when the tips are crisped and browned and the stalks are tender but still bright green.
6. Finish: Drizzle the melted butter and lemon juice over everything on the hot pan — it sizzles and forms a quick pan sauce. Scatter parsley over the top. Serve each fillet over rice with asparagus alongside and lemon wedges.

Common mistakes:
- Wet salmon skin: moisture is the enemy of crisp. Pat dry, then pat dry again.
- Overbaking to 150+: salmon dries out fast past 145. Use the thermometer and trust carryover cooking.
- Crowding the pan: asparagus piled up steams instead of roasting. Single layer with breathing room.
- Forgetting the woody ends: the bottom 1-2 inches of asparagus are fibrous and unpleasant. Snap, do not cut — the spear knows where to break.

Title: Turkey meatballs marinara over spaghetti
Ingredients:
For the meatballs:
- 2 1/2 lb ground turkey (93% lean)
- 1 cup Italian breadcrumbs
- 1/2 cup grated Parmesan cheese, plus more for serving
- 2 large eggs, beaten
- 1/2 cup whole milk
- 6 cloves garlic, minced
- 1/2 cup chopped fresh parsley
- 2 tsp kosher salt
- 1 tsp black pepper
- 1 tsp dried oregano
- 1/2 tsp red pepper flakes

For the marinara:
- 2 tbsp olive oil
- 1 large yellow onion, diced
- 6 cloves garlic, thinly sliced
- 2 cans (28 oz each) crushed tomatoes
- 2 tsp dried oregano
- 1 tsp sugar
- 1 1/2 tsp kosher salt, plus more to taste
- 1/2 tsp black pepper
- 1/2 cup torn fresh basil leaves
- 1 lb spaghetti
- Fresh basil and Parmesan, for serving
Steps:
1. Mise en place: Dice the onion. Mince 6 cloves garlic for the meatballs; slice 6 cloves thin for the sauce (sliced garlic mellows in the sauce, minced garlic distributes through the meat). Chop the parsley. Tear the basil by hand — cutting basil with a knife bruises it black. Beat the eggs. Measure the breadcrumbs, Parmesan, and milk. Line a sheet pan with foil and lightly oil it.
2. Make the panade: Stir the breadcrumbs and milk together in a large bowl and let sit 5 minutes until the crumbs absorb the milk into a thick paste. A panade is the secret to tender meatballs — the soaked crumbs hold moisture so the turkey stays juicy instead of turning into rubber balls.
3. Mix the meatballs: Add the turkey, Parmesan, beaten eggs, minced garlic, parsley, salt, pepper, oregano, and red pepper flakes to the panade. Mix with your hands just until combined — 30 seconds, no more. Overmixing develops the protein and makes meatballs dense and tough. The mixture will feel soft and slightly sticky; that is correct.
4. Shape: Wet your hands with water (prevents sticking) and roll into balls about 1 1/2 inches across — a heaping tablespoon each. You should get about 36. Place on the oiled sheet pan without touching.
5. Brown the meatballs: Heat the oven to 425 F. Bake 18-20 minutes until browned on the outside and 165 F inside. Browning first means they hold their shape in the sauce instead of falling apart.
6. Start the sauce while the meatballs bake: Heat the olive oil in a large Dutch oven over medium heat. Add the diced onion with a pinch of salt and cook 6-7 minutes until soft and translucent. Add the sliced garlic and cook 1 minute until fragrant and just golden. Add the oregano and stir 30 seconds.
7. Simmer the sauce: Pour in the crushed tomatoes, sugar, salt, and pepper. Bring to a gentle simmer and cook 20 minutes, stirring occasionally, until slightly thickened and the raw tomato edge is gone. Taste and add salt until the sauce tastes bright.
8. Combine: Gently nestle the baked meatballs into the sauce. Simmer 10 minutes so they absorb flavor. Stir in the torn basil off the heat.
9. Cook the spaghetti: Boil in well-salted water (it should taste like the sea) until 1 minute shy of the package time — it finishes in the sauce. Reserve 1 cup of pasta water, then drain. Toss the spaghetti with the meatballs and sauce, adding splashes of pasta water until the sauce clings silkily to every strand. The starch in the water is what makes sauce stick instead of slide off.
10. Serve in wide bowls topped with Parmesan and basil.

Common mistakes:
- Overmixing the meat: 30 seconds with your hands, then stop. Dense meatballs come from overworking, not from the turkey.
- Skipping the panade: breadcrumbs straight into meat absorb meat juices and turn gummy. Soak them in milk first.
- Boiling the sauce hard: a rolling boil makes tomato sauce bitter and splatters everywhere. Gentle simmer, lazy bubbles.
- Not salting the pasta water: unsalted water makes bland noodles no sauce can save. Salt it like the sea.

Title: Chicken fajitas
Ingredients:
For the fajita seasoning:
- 2 tbsp chili powder
- 1 tbsp ground cumin
- 1 tbsp smoked paprika
- 2 tsp garlic powder
- 2 tsp dried oregano
- 2 tsp kosher salt
- 1 tsp black pepper
- 1/2 tsp cayenne (optional)

For the fajitas:
- 2 1/2 lb boneless, skinless chicken breasts
- 4 bell peppers (mix of colors)
- 2 large yellow onions
- 1/3 cup olive oil, divided
- Juice of 2 limes
- 12 large flour tortillas (10-inch)

For serving:
- Sour cream, shredded cheddar, guacamole or sliced avocado, pico de gallo or salsa, lime wedges, chopped cilantro
Steps:
1. Mise en place: Slice the chicken breasts against the grain into strips about 1/2 inch thick — uniform strips cook evenly and stay juicy. Slice means long thin cuts: slice the bell peppers into strips and the onions into half-moons (cut the onion in half top to bottom, then slice across). Mix all the fajita seasoning spices in a small bowl. Juice the limes. Have toppings in bowls ready — fajitas are served sizzling and fast.
2. Season the chicken: Toss the chicken strips with 3 tbsp olive oil, the lime juice, and 3 tbsp of the seasoning mix. Let sit 15 minutes at room temperature while the pan heats. The lime juice starts tenderizing and the spices bloom on the meat.
3. Sear the chicken hot and fast: Heat a large cast-iron skillet or griddle over high heat until smoking — fajitas are defined by char. Add 1 tbsp oil, then half the chicken in a single layer. Do not touch for 2 minutes so it chars, then toss and cook 2-3 more minutes until cooked through (165 F) with blackened edges. Remove. Repeat with the second half. Crowding the pan steams the chicken instead of searing it — two batches is mandatory.
4. Char the vegetables: Add the remaining oil to the screaming-hot pan. Add peppers and onions with the remaining seasoning and a pinch of salt. Cook 4-5 minutes, stirring occasionally, until softened with blackened spots but still crisp in the center. Authentic Tex-Mex fajitas have real char — those black spots are flavor, not burnt mistakes. Squeeze extra lime over the vegetables.
5. Warm the tortillas: While the vegetables cook, warm the tortillas directly over a gas flame 10-15 seconds per side (tongs required), or in a dry skillet 30 seconds per side, until soft with charred spots. Stack in a towel.
6. Serve sizzling: Return the chicken to the pan with the vegetables, toss 30 seconds to rewarm, and bring the whole skillet to the table if you want the restaurant drama — it will sizzle all the way there. Serve with tortillas and toppings for everyone to build their own. Two fajitas per person is a serving.

Common mistakes:
- A lukewarm pan: without screaming heat you get gray steamed chicken and limp peppers. Wait for the smoke wisp.
- Crowding: the single biggest fajita killer. Single layer, two batches, every time.
- Overcooking the chicken: thin strips cook in 4-5 minutes total. Pull at 165 F — carryover does the rest.
- Cold tortillas: stiff tortillas crack and spill. Warm them until soft and pliable.

Title: Teriyaki salmon rice bowls
Ingredients:
For the teriyaki sauce:
- 1/2 cup low-sodium soy sauce
- 1/2 cup mirin (Japanese sweet rice wine)
- 1/4 cup sake (or dry sherry)
- 3 tbsp brown sugar
- 1 tsp grated fresh ginger

For the bowls:
- 6 salmon fillets, 5 oz each (about 2 lb total), skin removed if you prefer
- 1 tbsp vegetable oil
- 1 tsp kosher salt
- 1/2 tsp black pepper
- 3 cups short-grain or jasmine rice, rinsed
- 4 1/2 cups water
- 1 1/2 lb broccoli florets (or 3 cups edamame, thawed)
- 1 tbsp toasted sesame seeds
- 4 scallions, thinly sliced
Steps:
1. Mise en place: Rinse the rice. Cut broccoli into bite-size florets. Grate the ginger (a spoon scrapes the skin off easily). Thinly slice the scallions on a diagonal. Pat the salmon very dry — dry fish sears, wet fish steams. Combine the sauce ingredients in a small saucepan and stir to dissolve the sugar.
2. Cook the rice: Combine rinsed rice, water, and 1/2 tsp salt in a pot. Boil, cover, lowest heat 15 minutes, rest 10 minutes covered. Fluff with a fork.
3. Make the teriyaki: Bring the sauce to a boil over medium-high heat, then reduce to a steady simmer. Cook 8-10 minutes, stirring occasionally, until it thickens enough to coat the back of a spoon and looks glossy — it should reduce by about a third. Real Japanese teriyaki is just soy, mirin, sake, and sugar reduced to a glaze; no cornstarch, no pineapple juice. Keep warm on the lowest heat. It thickens more as it cools, so pull it while still slightly loose.
4. Steam the broccoli: While the sauce reduces, steam the broccoli over boiling water 3-4 minutes until bright green and crisp-tender, then season with a pinch of salt. (Or microwave edamame per package directions.)
5. Sear the salmon: Heat the vegetable oil in a large skillet over medium-high heat until shimmering. Season the salmon with salt and pepper. Lay the fillets down away from you (so no oil splashes toward you) and cook 4 minutes without moving until the bottom is golden. Flip and cook 2-3 more minutes. Salmon is done at 140-145 F in the thickest part — the center should still look slightly translucent when you pull it, because carryover heat finishes it to a silky medium.
6. Glaze: In the last minute, spoon 2-3 tbsp of teriyaki over each fillet and let it bubble and lacquer onto the fish for 30-60 seconds. The sugars caramelize into a shiny coat.
7. Build the bowls: Rice in 6 bowls, salmon on top, broccoli alongside. Drizzle each bowl with extra warm teriyaki (reheat it if it thickened too much — a splash of water loosens it). Sprinkle with sesame seeds and scallions.

Common mistakes:
- Cornstarch in the teriyaki: authentic teriyaki thickens by reduction alone. Starch makes it gummy and dull.
- Overcooking the salmon: past 145 F the glaze cannot save it. Pull at 140 and rest 3 minutes.
- Reducing the sauce too far: it goes from glaze to candy quickly at the end. Coat-the-spoon, then stop.
- Wet salmon: moisture prevents the glaze from sticking. Pat dry twice.

Title: Lean beef tacos
Ingredients:
For the beef:
- 2 1/2 lb ground beef (90% lean)
- 2 tbsp chili powder
- 1 tbsp ground cumin
- 2 tsp paprika
- 2 tsp garlic powder
- 1 tsp dried oregano
- 2 tsp kosher salt
- 1 tsp black pepper
- 1/2 cup water or low-sodium beef broth

For serving:
- 18 small corn tortillas
- 3 cups shredded iceberg or romaine lettuce
- 2 cups diced tomatoes
- 1 cup diced white onion
- 1 cup chopped cilantro
- 6 oz shredded Monterey Jack or cheddar cheese
- Lime wedges and your favorite salsa
- Sour cream (optional)
Steps:
1. Mise en place: Dice the tomatoes and onion. Chop the cilantro. Shred the lettuce. Mix the dry spices in a small bowl. Have the cheese, salsa, and lime wedges ready — tacos are assembled hot and eaten immediately.
2. Brown the beef: Heat a large skillet over medium-high heat. Add the ground beef and break into small crumbles. Cook 6-8 minutes, stirring and breaking, until deeply browned with no pink. Do not drain the small amount of fat from 90% lean beef — that fat carries the spice flavor. If you used 80/20, spoon off the excess.
3. Season: Sprinkle the spice mix over the beef and stir 1 minute until fragrant — toasting the spices in the hot fat blooms their flavor. Pour in the water or broth and stir, scraping up the browned bits. Simmer 3-4 minutes until the liquid reduces into a light sauce that clings to the meat. It should look juicy, not soupy and not dry.
4. Warm the tortillas: Corn tortillas must be heated or they crack. Warm them 30-45 seconds per side in a dry skillet over medium-high heat until soft, pliable, and lightly charred in spots. Stack in a clean towel to steam. Work in batches — do all 18 before assembling.
5. Assemble: Fill each tortilla with beef, then lettuce, tomato, onion, cilantro, and cheese. Three tacos per person is a serving. Serve immediately with lime wedges and salsa — a squeeze of lime over the top brightens the rich beef.

Common mistakes:
- Under-seasoning the beef: plain browned beef in a tortilla is sad. The full spice mix plus the simmer in broth is what makes it taste like a taco.
- Cold corn tortillas: they crack and fall apart. Heat is mandatory, not optional.
- Watery beef: simmer until the liquid becomes a glaze that coats the meat. Soup in a tortilla is a mess.
- Overfilling: two heaping tablespoons of beef per taco. Overstuffed tacos break.

Title: Chicken tikka masala
Ingredients:
For the marinade:
- 2 1/2 lb boneless, skinless chicken thighs, cut into 1 1/2-inch pieces
- 1 cup plain whole-milk yogurt
- 2 tbsp lemon juice
- 2 tbsp garam masala, divided
- 1 tbsp ground cumin
- 1 tbsp ground coriander
- 1 tsp turmeric
- 1 tsp paprika
- 1 tsp cayenne (use 1/2 tsp for mild)
- 4 cloves garlic, grated
- 1 tbsp grated fresh ginger
- 2 tsp kosher salt

For the sauce:
- 3 tbsp ghee or unsalted butter
- 1 large yellow onion, finely diced
- 4 cloves garlic, minced
- 1 tbsp grated fresh ginger
- 1 can (28 oz) tomato passata or crushed tomatoes
- 1 tbsp tomato paste
- 1 1/2 cups heavy cream
- 1 tbsp honey or sugar
- 2 tsp garam masala (the reserved half)
- 1 tsp crushed kasuri methi (dried fenugreek leaves) — optional but transformative
- Salt to taste
- Chopped cilantro, for serving
- Cooked basmati rice or warm naan, for serving
Steps:
1. Mise en place and marinade (do this at least 2 hours ahead, ideally in the morning): Cut the chicken into 1 1/2-inch pieces. Grate the garlic and ginger on a microplane or the fine side of a box grater — grated aromatics melt into the marinade instead of sitting in chunks. Whisk the yogurt, lemon juice, 1 tbsp garam masala, cumin, coriander, turmeric, paprika, cayenne, garlic, ginger, and salt in a large bowl. Add the chicken and turn to coat every piece. Cover and refrigerate 2-8 hours. The yogurt's acid tenderizes while the spices penetrate — this marinade is the soul of the dish. A note on the story: this dish was most likely born in Glasgow, Scotland, in a Bangladeshi-run curry house, when a customer complained his chicken tikka was too dry and the chef improvised a creamy tomato sauce. It is British-Indian restaurant food, and that is exactly what we are making.
2. Char the chicken: Position an oven rack 6 inches from the broiler and heat the broiler to high. Line a sheet pan with foil. Shake excess marinade off the chicken (too much marinade steams instead of chars) and spread in a single layer. Broil 8-10 minutes, flipping once, until the edges are blackened in spots. Char equals flavor — those dark edges are what make tikka masala taste like the restaurant version. The chicken does not need to cook through; it finishes in the sauce. Set aside.
3. Build the sauce: Melt the ghee in a large Dutch oven over medium heat. Add the diced onion with a pinch of salt and cook 8-10 minutes, stirring, until soft and golden at the edges. Add the garlic and ginger; cook 1 minute until fragrant.
4. Bloom and tomato: Stir in the tomato paste and cook 2 minutes until it darkens from bright red to brick — this caramelizes the paste and removes the tinny taste. Add the remaining 2 tsp garam masala and stir 30 seconds. Pour in the passata. Simmer 15 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the sauce thickens and the fat starts to glisten at the edges.
5. Blend smooth (optional but recommended): For restaurant-silk sauce, blend with an immersion blender until completely smooth. Be careful with hot liquid — keep the blender head submerged or it will erupt.
6. Finish: Stir in the heavy cream, honey, and kasuri methi, crushing the dried leaves between your fingers as you add them to release their aroma. Add the charred chicken with any juices. Simmer gently 10 minutes — never boil after adding cream or it can split — until the chicken is cooked through (165 F) and tender. Taste and salt until the flavors pop; the sauce should be rich, tangy, lightly sweet, and warming, not aggressively spicy.
7. Serve over basmati rice or with warm naan, scattered with cilantro. The sauce should generously coat everything — this is a saucy dish by design.

Common mistakes:
- Skipping the marinade: unmarinated chicken in sauce is pale and bland. Two hours minimum, eight is better.
- No char on the chicken: the broiler step is what separates homemade from takeout. Do not skip it.
- Boiling the cream sauce: a hard boil splits cream into grainy oil. Gentle simmer only.
- Forgetting the kasuri methi: it is the background note that makes restaurant tikka masala taste like itself. Find it at any Indian grocery.

Title: Pork tenderloin with sweet potatoes and green beans
Ingredients:
- 2 pork tenderloins (about 1 1/4 lb each, 2 1/2 lb total)
- 2 lb sweet potatoes (about 4 medium)
- 1 1/2 lb fresh green beans, trimmed
- 1/4 cup olive oil, divided
- 3 tbsp Dijon mustard
- 4 cloves garlic, minced
- 2 tbsp chopped fresh rosemary (or 2 tsp dried)
- 2 tbsp chopped fresh thyme (or 2 tsp dried)
- 2 tsp kosher salt, divided
- 1 tsp black pepper
- 1 tsp smoked paprika
- 1 tbsp honey
Steps:
1. Mise en place and oven: Heat the oven to 425 F. Line a large rimmed sheet pan with foil. Peel the sweet potatoes and cut into 1-inch cubes — uniform cubes cook evenly; big chunks stay raw inside while small ones burn. Trim the green beans by snapping off the stem ends. Mince the garlic. Chop the rosemary and thyme. Pat the pork tenderloins completely dry. Look for the silverskin — a shiny, tough membrane running along the tenderloin. Slide a thin knife under one end and slice it off; it does not melt during cooking and eats chewy if left on.
2. Season the pork: Rub the tenderloins all over with 2 tbsp olive oil, then the Dijon mustard (the mustard helps the herbs stick and adds tangy depth). Coat with the garlic, rosemary, thyme, 1 1/2 tsp salt, pepper, and smoked paprika. Let sit at room temperature 15 minutes — cold pork straight from the fridge cooks unevenly.
3. Sear for color: Heat a large oven-safe skillet over medium-high heat until shimmering. Sear the tenderloins 2 minutes per side until browned all over — about 8 minutes total. Searing builds the flavorful crust that roasting alone cannot. Transfer to a plate.
4. Roast the vegetables: Toss the sweet potato cubes on the sheet pan with 2 tbsp olive oil, the honey, and 1/2 tsp salt. Spread in a single layer. Roast 15 minutes, then pull the pan, flip the potatoes, add the green beans tossed with the last of the oil and a pinch of salt around the edges, and nestle the seared tenderloins on top.
5. Finish roasting: Roast 15-18 minutes more. The pork is done when an instant-read thermometer in the thickest part reads 145 F — pork tenderloin is safe and at its juiciest at 145, with a hint of blush pink inside. The sweet potatoes are done when a fork slides in easily and the edges caramelize. The green beans should be tender with blistered spots.
6. Rest and slice: Rest the pork 10 minutes on a cutting board — this is non-negotiable; the juices need time to settle back into the meat. Slice into 1/2-inch medallions against the grain. Serve over the roasted vegetables, spooning any pan juices over the top.

Common mistakes:
- Leaving the silverskin on: it shrinks, curls the tenderloin, and chews like rubber. Take 60 seconds to trim it.
- Cooking to 160+: at 145 F pork tenderloin is juicy and safe; at 165 it is dry and gray. Trust the thermometer.
- Skipping the rest: slice too soon and the juices flood the board instead of staying in the meat.
- Uneven sweet potato cubes: size them the same or half will be raw and half burnt.

Title: Korean beef bulgogi bowls
Ingredients:
For the marinade:
- 1 Asian pear (or 1 Bosc pear), peeled and grated
- 1/2 cup low-sodium soy sauce
- 1/4 cup brown sugar
- 3 tbsp toasted sesame oil
- 6 cloves garlic, minced
- 1 tbsp grated fresh ginger
- 1 tsp black pepper

For the bowls:
- 2 1/2 lb ribeye or sirloin steak
- 2 tbsp vegetable oil, divided
- 1 large yellow onion, thinly sliced
- 3 cups jasmine or short-grain rice, rinsed
- 4 1/2 cups water
- 6 scallions, thinly sliced
- 2 tbsp toasted sesame seeds
- Kimchi and lettuce leaves, for serving (optional)
Steps:
1. Mise en place (start 3-4 hours before dinner): Freeze the steak 30 minutes — firm meat slices paper-thin. Slice against the grain into 1/8-inch strips, as thin as you possibly can; thin slices are the whole identity of bulgogi ("fire meat"). Grate the pear on a box grater — the pear's enzymes tenderize the beef and add subtle sweetness, the traditional Korean secret. Mince the garlic, grate the ginger, slice the onion thin, slice the scallions. Whisk the marinade ingredients in a large bowl.
2. Marinate: Add the beef strips to the marinade and massage it in with your hands so every strip is coated. Cover and refrigerate 2-4 hours (no more than 8 — the pear enzymes will turn the meat mushy if left too long). Start the rice when there is 30 minutes left: rinsed rice, water, pinch of salt, boil, cover, lowest heat 15 minutes, rest 10.
3. Sear in batches: Heat a large cast-iron skillet or grill pan over high heat until smoking. Add 1 tbsp vegetable oil. Using tongs, lift beef from the marinade, letting excess drip off, and lay in a single layer — do not crowd. Sear 60-90 seconds per side until caramelized at the edges. Thin bulgogi cooks in about 2 minutes total; it should be browned outside and just cooked through. Remove to a plate. Repeat with remaining beef, adding oil between batches.
4. Cook the onion: In the same hot pan, add the sliced onion with a splash of water to deglaze — scrape up all the browned bits. Cook 2-3 minutes until softened and sweet.
5. Combine and serve: Return all the beef to the pan with the onion and toss 30 seconds to rewarm. The pan juices mixed with the marinade remnants form a light glaze. Serve over rice in 6 bowls, topped with scallions and sesame seeds. Set out kimchi and lettuce leaves — wrapping bites of bulgogi and rice in lettuce with kimchi is the Korean way to eat it.

Common mistakes:
- Thick slices: 1/4-inch beef eats chewy and takes too long. Go as thin as your knife allows — 1/8 inch is the target.
- Marinating overnight: the pear enzyme keeps working and the texture goes mealy. Two to four hours is the sweet spot.
- Crowding the pan: wet, gray, steamed beef instead of caramelized bulgogi. Single layer, multiple batches.
- Skipping the rest after slicing: let the beef sit in the marinade the full time — the flavor needs hours, not minutes.

Title: Chicken Caesar wraps
Ingredients:
For the chicken:
- 2 lb boneless, skinless chicken breasts
- 2 tbsp olive oil
- 2 tsp garlic powder
- 2 tsp kosher salt
- 1 tsp black pepper
- Juice of 1 lemon

For the light Caesar dressing:
- 1 cup plain Greek yogurt
- 1/3 cup grated Parmesan cheese, plus more for serving
- 3 tbsp lemon juice
- 2 tbsp olive oil
- 2 tsp anchovy paste (or 4 anchovy fillets, minced)
- 2 cloves garlic, grated
- 2 tsp Dijon mustard
- 1 tsp Worcestershire sauce
- 1/2 tsp black pepper
- 2-4 tbsp water, to thin

For the wraps:
- 6 large flour tortillas (12-inch burrito size)
- 3 romaine hearts, chopped
- 1 cup croutons (optional)
- Extra Parmesan, for serving
Steps:
1. Mise en place: Chop the romaine hearts into bite-size pieces — wash and spin or pat them completely dry, because wet lettuce repels dressing. Grate the garlic and Parmesan. Juice the lemons. Pound the chicken breasts to even 3/4-inch thickness (place between plastic wrap and whack with a heavy pan) — even thickness means even cooking, no dry thin ends with raw thick middles. Season the chicken with olive oil, garlic powder, salt, pepper, and lemon juice.
2. Make the dressing: Whisk the Greek yogurt, Parmesan, lemon juice, olive oil, anchovy paste, garlic, Dijon, Worcestershire, and pepper in a bowl. The anchovy paste is what makes it taste like Caesar instead of just garlicky yogurt — it melts into the background and adds savory depth, not fishiness. Thin with water 1 tbsp at a time until it drizzles off a spoon. Taste: it should be tangy, salty, and bold. It will seem strong on its own and perfect on lettuce.
3. Grill the chicken: Heat a grill or grill pan over medium-high heat until hot. Grill the chicken 5-6 minutes per side without moving, until charred in spots and 165 F inside. Rest 5 minutes, then slice into strips against the grain.
4. Dress the romaine: In a large bowl, toss the romaine with about 3/4 cup of the dressing — enough to lightly coat every leaf, not drown it. Add more by the spoonful if needed. The lettuce should glisten, not swim.
5. Warm the tortillas: Warm each tortilla 20-30 seconds per side in a dry skillet until soft and pliable. Warm tortillas roll without cracking.
6. Assemble: Lay a tortilla flat. Pile dressed romaine down the center, top with sliced chicken, a few croutons, and extra Parmesan. Fold the sides in, then roll tightly away from you, tucking as you go. Slice in half on a diagonal. Serve with extra dressing for dipping.

Common mistakes:
- Wet romaine: water on the leaves means dressing slides right off. Dry the lettuce thoroughly.
- Skipping the anchovy: without it, the dressing is just seasoned yogurt. The paste is the Caesar identity — be brave.
- Overdressing: start with less than you think. You can always add; you cannot take away.
- Cold tortillas: they crack when rolled. Thirty seconds in a hot pan fixes it.

Title: Shrimp fried rice
Ingredients:
- 4 cups cooked long-grain white rice, day-old and refrigerated (from about 1 1/2 cups dry)
- 1 1/2 lb medium shrimp, peeled and deveined
- 4 large eggs, beaten
- 2 cups frozen peas and carrots, thawed
- 6 scallions
- 4 cloves garlic, minced
- 1 tbsp grated fresh ginger
- 1/4 cup low-sodium soy sauce
- 1 tbsp oyster sauce
- 2 tsp toasted sesame oil
- 1/2 tsp white pepper (or black pepper)
- 4 tbsp vegetable oil, divided
- 1 tsp kosher salt
Steps:
1. Mise en place: This recipe lives or dies on preparation because the wok work takes under 10 minutes. The rice MUST be day-old and cold from the fridge — fresh warm rice is moist and turns to mush; cold rice has firm, separate grains that fry up with chewy texture. Break up any clumps with your hands. Beat the eggs with a pinch of salt. Thinly slice the scallions, keeping whites and greens separate. Mince the garlic, grate the ginger. Mix the soy sauce, oyster sauce, and sesame oil in a small bowl. Pat the shrimp very dry.
2. Scramble the eggs: Heat a wok or the largest skillet you own over high heat until smoking. Add 1 tbsp oil and swirl. Pour in the beaten eggs — they should sizzle and puff immediately. Scramble 30-45 seconds into soft curds, breaking into bite-size pieces. Remove while still slightly glossy (they finish cooking later). Set aside.
3. Sear the shrimp: Add 1 tbsp oil to the screaming-hot wok. Add the shrimp in a single layer with 1/2 tsp salt. Cook 60-90 seconds per side until pink and curled into C shapes. Remove immediately — they will go back in at the end.
4. Fry the rice: Add the remaining 2 tbsp oil. Add the cold rice, breaking up clumps with the spatula. Let it sit undisturbed 1-2 minutes so the bottom grains toast and pick up wok flavor — you want some crispy, golden bits. Then toss and fry 3-4 minutes total, until the grains are hot, separate, and a few are lightly browned. This toasting is where fried rice gets its smoky restaurant taste (wok hei — the "breath of the wok").
5. Vegetables and aromatics: Push the rice to the sides. Add the peas and carrots, scallion whites, garlic, and ginger to the center with the white pepper. Stir-fry 1 minute until fragrant and the vegetables are hot.
6. Sauce and combine: Pour the sauce mixture around the edges of the wok (not directly on the rice — hitting the hot metal first caramelizes the soy slightly). Toss everything 1 minute until the rice is evenly amber and glossy. Return the eggs and shrimp, add the scallion greens, and toss 30 seconds to rewarm. Taste: it should be savory with a whisper of sweetness and sesame. Add a splash more soy if it needs salt.
7. Serve immediately in wide bowls. Fried rice waits for no one — it tightens and dulls as it sits.

Common mistakes:
- Fresh rice: the number one fried rice failure. Cook the rice yesterday, refrigerate uncovered or loosely covered, and use it cold.
- A crowded or cool wok: if the rice steams instead of fries, the pan was too full or not hot enough. High heat, single batch, constant motion.
- Overcooking the shrimp twice: they go in, come out, and go back only to rewarm. Pink C shapes, not tight rubber O's.
- Drowning in soy sauce: too much makes it dark, salty, and soggy. The measured 1/4 cup is enough — the oyster sauce adds depth so you need less soy.

Title: Black bean and sweet potato enchiladas
Ingredients:
For the filling:
- 2 lb sweet potatoes (about 3 large), peeled and cubed
- 2 cans (15 oz each) black beans, drained and rinsed
- 1 large yellow onion, diced
- 4 cloves garlic, minced
- 2 tsp ground cumin
- 1 tsp smoked paprika
- 1 tsp dried oregano
- 2 tsp kosher salt
- 1/2 tsp black pepper
- 2 tbsp olive oil

For the enchilada sauce:
- 3 tbsp vegetable oil
- 3 tbsp all-purpose flour
- 1/4 cup chili powder
- 2 tsp ground cumin
- 1 tsp garlic powder
- 1 tsp dried oregano
- 1 can (15 oz) tomato sauce
- 2 cups vegetable broth
- 1 tsp kosher salt
- 1 tsp sugar

For assembly:
- 18 corn tortillas
- 8 oz Monterey Jack or pepper Jack cheese, shredded
- 1/2 cup chopped cilantro
- Sour cream and lime wedges, for serving
Steps:
1. Mise en place and oven: Heat the oven to 425 F. Peel and cube the sweet potatoes into 3/4-inch pieces — even cubes roast evenly. Dice the onion. Mince the garlic. Shred the cheese from a block (pre-shredded cheese is coated in starch and melts poorly). Measure the sauce spices into one bowl.
2. Roast the sweet potatoes: Toss the cubes with 2 tbsp olive oil, 1 tsp salt, and 1/2 tsp pepper on a sheet pan. Spread in a single layer and roast 25 minutes, flipping once, until tender inside and caramelized at the edges. Roasting concentrates their sweetness — boiled sweet potato would make the filling watery.
3. Make the sauce: While the potatoes roast, heat 3 tbsp oil in a saucepan over medium heat. Whisk in the flour and cook 1 minute — this roux thickens the sauce. Add the chili powder, cumin, garlic powder, and oregano; whisk 30 seconds until fragrant and brick-red. Slowly pour in the tomato sauce and broth, whisking constantly to prevent lumps. Add salt and sugar. Simmer 10 minutes, stirring, until it thickly coats a spoon. Taste: it should be rich, earthy, and lightly tangy. Homemade sauce beats canned by a mile and takes 12 minutes.
4. Make the filling: In a large bowl, combine the roasted sweet potatoes, drained black beans, diced onion, minced garlic, cumin, smoked paprika, oregano, remaining 1 tsp salt, and 1 cup of the shredded cheese. Lightly mash with a fork — you want a chunky mixture that holds together, not baby food.
5. Warm the tortillas: This step prevents cracking. Warm the corn tortillas 30 seconds per side in a dry skillet until soft and pliable, stacking in a towel. Cold corn tortillas split when rolled — every time.
6. Assemble: Spread 1/2 cup sauce in the bottom of a 9x13-inch baking dish. Dip each warm tortilla in the warm sauce (this flavors the tortilla and keeps it supple), fill with about 1/3 cup filling, roll snugly, and place seam-side down. Three enchiladas per person — 18 total. Pour the remaining sauce over the top and sprinkle with the remaining cheese.
7. Bake: Bake at 375 F for 20-25 minutes until the sauce bubbles at the edges and the cheese is melted and lightly browned. Rest 5 minutes before serving so they hold together when lifted. Top with cilantro; serve with sour cream and lime.

Common mistakes:
- Skipping the tortilla warming: cold tortillas crack, the filling spills, and you have enchilada casserole instead of enchiladas. Warm every one.
- Watery filling: if the sweet potatoes are not roasted to caramelized (not steamed), they weep liquid into the dish. Single layer, real browning.
- Too much sauce on top: a generous coat, not a flood. Drowning them makes the tortillas disintegrate.
- Cutting immediately: the 5-minute rest lets the cheese set so servings lift out cleanly.

Title: Thai basil chicken
Ingredients:
- 2 1/2 lb ground chicken (or chicken breast, minced)
- 2 cups packed Thai holy basil leaves (Thai basil works; see note)
- 8-10 Thai bird's eye chiles (use 4-5 for medium heat)
- 8 cloves garlic
- 3 tbsp vegetable oil
- 3 tbsp fish sauce
- 2 tbsp oyster sauce
- 1 tbsp low-sodium soy sauce
- 2 tsp sugar
- 1/4 cup low-sodium chicken broth or water
- 6 large eggs
- 3 cups jasmine rice, rinsed
- Sliced cucumber, for serving
Steps:
1. Mise en place: Rinse the rice and get it cooking first: 3 cups rice, 4 1/2 cups water, pinch of salt, boil, cover, lowest heat 15 minutes, rest 10. Pick the basil leaves off the stems and pack them into the measuring cup — you need a mountain; it wilts to nothing. A note on authenticity: real pad krapow uses holy basil, which is peppery and sharp. Thai basil (the common grocery kind) is sweeter with an anise note — it works and is what most of us can find, but the dish is named for holy basil. Mince the garlic. Thinly slice the chiles — bird's eye chiles are tiny but fierce; wash your hands after handling and do not touch your face. Mix the fish sauce, oyster sauce, soy sauce, and sugar in a small bowl.
2. Pound the aromatics: The traditional move is to pound the garlic and chiles into a rough paste with a mortar and pestle — pounding releases more flavor than chopping. No mortar? Mince them together very fine with a knife. This paste is the flavor base of the whole dish.
3. Fry the eggs first: Heat 2 tbsp oil in a wok or large skillet over medium-high heat until shimmering. Crack in the eggs (work in two batches of three) and fry 2-3 minutes until the edges are lacy and crisp and brown, the whites fully set, and the yolks still runny. Thai-style fried eggs have crispy lace edges — that texture against the rice is essential. Season with a pinch of salt. Set aside and keep warm.
4. Sear the chicken: Add the remaining 1 tbsp oil to the same wok over high heat. Add the ground chicken and let it sit 2 minutes undisturbed to brown, then break it up and cook 4-5 minutes until no pink remains and the edges get crispy brown bits. Do not add the sauce yet — browning first means flavor.
5. Aromatics and sauce: Push the chicken aside, add the garlic-chile paste to the center, and stir-fry 30 seconds until it smells intensely fragrant. Pour in the sauce mixture and the broth. Toss 1-2 minutes until the sauce reduces to a glaze that coats the chicken — pad krapow is not saucy; it should glisten, not swim.
6. Wilt the basil: Turn off the heat. Add all the basil and toss — the residual heat wilts it in 30 seconds. It will smell incredible. The basil goes in last and off the heat so it stays bright and peppery instead of turning black and bitter.
7. Serve: Mound jasmine rice in 6 wide bowls or plates. Spoon the chicken over one side, top each with a crispy fried egg, and add sliced cucumber on the side. The runny yolk mixed into the rice is part of the dish — break it over everything.

Common mistakes:
- Adding the basil too early: it turns black and loses its punch. Off the heat, last 30 seconds, always.
- A watery stir fry: the sauce should reduce to a glaze. If it is pooling, cook 1-2 minutes more before adding basil.
- Fear of the chiles: the heat is the point of pad krapow, but start with 4-5 chiles if you are unsure. You can add heat; you cannot remove it.
- Using dried basil: there is no substitute here. Fresh basil or do not make the dish.

Title: Baked cod with lemon capers and orzo
Ingredients:
- 6 cod fillets, 5 oz each (about 2 lb total), about 1 inch thick
- 1 lb orzo pasta
- 3 tbsp olive oil, divided, plus more for drizzling
- 4 cloves garlic, thinly sliced
- 1 pint cherry tomatoes, halved
- 1/2 cup dry white wine (or chicken broth)
- 3 tbsp capers, drained
- Zest and juice of 2 lemons
- 1 tsp kosher salt, divided, plus more to taste
- 1/2 tsp black pepper
- 1/2 tsp red pepper flakes
- 1/2 cup chopped fresh parsley
- 1/4 cup grated Parmesan cheese
- Lemon wedges, for serving
Steps:
1. Mise en place and oven: Heat the oven to 400 F. Bring a large pot of well-salted water to a boil for the orzo. Slice the garlic thin. Halve the cherry tomatoes. Drain the capers. Zest the lemons (outer yellow only), then juice them. Chop the parsley. Pat the cod fillets very dry — dry fish sears instead of steams. Check for pin bones by running a finger along the fillet; pull any you find with tweezers or clean pliers.
2. Cook the orzo: Boil the orzo until just shy of al dente — 1 minute less than the package says. It will absorb sauce later and keeps cooking. Reserve 1 cup of the starchy pasta water, then drain. Toss the orzo with 1 tbsp olive oil so it does not clump.
3. Build the sauce base: Heat 2 tbsp olive oil in a large oven-safe skillet over medium heat. Add the garlic slices and red pepper flakes; cook 1 minute until the garlic is golden at the edges (not brown — brown garlic is bitter). Add the cherry tomatoes with 1/2 tsp salt and cook 4-5 minutes, stirring, until they slump and release their juices into a light sauce.
4. Deglaze: Pour in the white wine — it will bubble vigorously. Scrape the bottom and let it reduce 2 minutes until the raw alcohol smell cooks off. Stir in the capers, lemon zest, and half the lemon juice. This is a Sicilian-style piccata sauce: briny capers, bright lemon, good olive oil. No cream, no heaviness.
5. Add the fish: Nestle the cod fillets into the sauce. Season the tops with the remaining 1/2 tsp salt and the black pepper. Spoon some sauce over each fillet. Transfer the skillet to the oven.
6. Bake: Bake 10-12 minutes, depending on thickness. Cod is done when it flakes easily with a fork and the thickest part reads 140-145 F — the flesh should be opaque but still moist, separating into large flakes. Overbaked cod goes dry and cottony fast, so check at 10 minutes.
7. Finish the orzo: While the fish bakes, toss the warm orzo with the Parmesan, parsley, remaining lemon juice, a drizzle of olive oil, and splashes of the reserved pasta water until it turns silky and the cheese melts into a light coating. Taste and salt until bright.
8. Serve: Spoon orzo into 6 wide bowls, top each with a cod fillet and a generous spoonful of the tomato-caper sauce from the skillet. Serve with lemon wedges.

Common mistakes:
- Overbaking the cod: it goes from silky to dry in about 3 minutes. Start checking at 10 minutes and trust the thermometer.
- Brown garlic: golden is sweet, brown is bitter. Thirty seconds is the difference — stay at the pan.
- Mushy orzo: pull it a minute early. It drinks up sauce on the plate and keeps softening.
- Forgetting the pasta water: that starchy liquid is what turns the orzo from plain pasta into a silky dish.

Title: Chicken parmesan (lightened)
Ingredients:
For the chicken:
- 2 1/2 lb boneless, skinless chicken breasts (about 5)
- 1 cup panko breadcrumbs
- 1/2 cup grated Parmesan cheese
- 2 tsp Italian seasoning
- 1 tsp garlic powder
- 1 tsp kosher salt
- 1/2 tsp black pepper
- 2 large eggs, beaten
- 1/4 cup all-purpose flour
- Olive oil spray

For assembly:
- 3 cups marinara sauce (homemade or good jarred)
- 8 oz part-skim mozzarella cheese, shredded
- 1/4 cup grated Parmesan, for topping
- 1 lb spaghetti or 6 servings of pasta
- Chopped fresh basil, for serving
Steps:
1. Mise en place and oven: Heat the oven to 425 F. Line a sheet pan with foil and place a wire rack on it if you have one — the rack lets hot air circulate under the chicken so the bottom crisps instead of steaming. Pound each chicken breast to even 1/2-inch thickness between plastic wrap. Even thickness is critical: thin spots dry out while thick spots stay raw. Pat the chicken dry. Set up a breading station in three shallow dishes: flour in the first, beaten eggs in the second, and panko mixed with Parmesan, Italian seasoning, garlic powder, salt, and pepper in the third.
2. Bread the chicken: Working one breast at a time, dredge in flour (shake off excess — a thick flour layer turns gummy), dip in egg (let excess drip off), then press firmly into the panko mixture, coating both sides. Pressing matters — the crumbs need to adhere or they fall off in the oven. Place on the rack.
3. Bake crisp: Spray the tops generously with olive oil spray — this is what browns the panko without deep-frying. Bake 20-22 minutes until the crust is deep golden and the chicken reads 165 F. The lightened version bakes instead of fries, and the panko still delivers real crunch.
4. Sauce and cheese: While the chicken bakes, warm the marinara in a saucepan. Cook the spaghetti in well-salted water until al dente; reserve 1/2 cup pasta water and drain.
5. Melt the cheese: Spoon about 1/3 cup warm marinara over each baked chicken breast, then divide the mozzarella and extra Parmesan over the top. Return to the oven 3-4 minutes until the cheese melts and bubbles in spots. Do not overbake here — the chicken is already done; you are just melting cheese.
6. Serve: Toss the spaghetti with the remaining marinara and splashes of pasta water until silky. Plate pasta, top with a chicken breast, and scatter basil over everything.

Common mistakes:
- Uneven chicken: unpounded breasts cook unevenly — pound to 1/2 inch everywhere.
- Soggy bottom: without a rack (or without flipping halfway), the bottom steams. A wire rack is a five-dollar fix.
- Drowning in sauce before baking: sauce goes on after the crust is crisp, or the breading turns to mush. Crisp first, sauce second.
- Skimpy oil spray: dry panko stays pale and dusty. Spray until the crumbs glisten.

Title: Beef and bean burritos
Ingredients:
- 2 lb ground beef (90% lean)
- 2 cans (15 oz each) black beans, drained and rinsed (or 1 can refried beans + 1 can black beans)
- 3 cups cooked long-grain white rice (from about 1 cup dry)
- 1 large yellow onion, diced
- 4 cloves garlic, minced
- 2 tbsp chili powder
- 1 tbsp ground cumin
- 2 tsp smoked paprika
- 2 tsp dried oregano
- 2 tsp kosher salt
- 1 tsp black pepper
- 1 can (8 oz) tomato sauce
- 6 burrito-size flour tortillas (12-inch)
- 8 oz shredded cheddar or Monterey Jack cheese
- Sour cream, salsa, shredded lettuce, diced tomato, for serving
Steps:
1. Mise en place: Dice the onion. Mince the garlic. Mix the dry spices in a small bowl. Cook the rice if not already cooked (1 cup dry rice, 2 cups water, pinch of salt — boil, cover, lowest heat 15 minutes, rest 10). Shred the cheese from a block for better melting. Have the tortillas at room temperature — cold tortillas crack when rolled.
2. Brown the beef: Heat a large skillet over medium-high heat. Add the ground beef and break into crumbles. Cook 6-8 minutes until deeply browned with no pink. Spoon off excess fat if needed, leaving about 1 tbsp for flavor.
3. Season: Add the diced onion and cook 4 minutes until soft. Add the garlic and the spice mix; stir 1 minute until fragrant. Pour in the tomato sauce and 1/2 cup water. Simmer 5 minutes until thickened into a rich, clinging sauce. Taste and salt until bold — the filling seasons the whole burrito, so it should taste slightly over-seasoned on its own.
4. Warm the beans and tortillas: Warm the black beans in a saucepan with a pinch of salt and a splash of water until hot, then lightly mash a third of them for creaminess. Warm each tortilla 30 seconds per side in a dry skillet until soft and pliable; stack in a towel. Warm tortillas are stretchy; cold ones tear.
5. Fill: Lay a tortilla flat. Down the center, layer about 3/4 cup beef, 1/3 cup beans, 1/2 cup rice, and a handful of cheese. Do not overfill — overfilled burritos burst. About 1 1/2 cups total filling per tortilla.
6. Roll: Fold the sides in over the filling, then pull the bottom edge up and over, tucking tightly as you roll away from you. A tight roll is what holds a burrito together — tuck, roll, tuck, roll. Place seam-side down.
7. Crisp (optional but excellent): Heat a dry skillet over medium heat and place the burritos seam-side down 2-3 minutes until golden and sealed, then flip to crisp the other side. This seals the seam and adds a toasty crunch.
8. Serve: Cut in half on a diagonal and serve with sour cream, salsa, lettuce, and tomato. One packed burrito per person is a full meal.

Common mistakes:
- Overfilling: the number one burrito failure. Less filling, tighter roll, intact burrito.
- Cold tortillas: they tear every time. Warm until soft and steamy.
- Loose rolling: a lazy roll unrolls on the plate. Tuck tightly with each turn.
- Underseasoned filling: bland filling makes a bland burrito no topping can save. Taste the beef before rolling.

Title: Egg roll in a bowl
Ingredients:
- 2 lb ground pork (or ground turkey for lighter)
- 2 bags (14 oz each) coleslaw mix (shredded cabbage and carrots)
- 1 large yellow onion, diced
- 5 cloves garlic, minced
- 1 tbsp grated fresh ginger
- 4 scallions, thinly sliced
- 3 tbsp low-sodium soy sauce
- 1 tbsp oyster sauce
- 1 tbsp rice vinegar
- 2 tsp toasted sesame oil
- 1 tsp sriracha, plus more for serving
- 2 tbsp vegetable oil
- 1 tsp kosher salt
- Sesame seeds, for serving
Steps:
1. Mise en place: Dice the onion. Mince the garlic, grate the ginger. Slice the scallions. Mix the soy sauce, oyster sauce, rice vinegar, sesame oil, and sriracha in a small bowl. Open the coleslaw bags. Everything cooks in under 15 minutes once the pan is hot, so have it all within arm's reach.
2. Brown the pork: Heat the vegetable oil in a large wok or the biggest skillet you own over medium-high heat until shimmering. Add the ground pork and break into small crumbles. Let it sit undisturbed 3 minutes to develop browned, crispy bits, then keep breaking and stirring 5-6 more minutes until cooked through with no pink. Those crispy browned bits are what make this taste like actual egg roll filling instead of plain ground pork.
3. Aromatics: Push the pork to the edges. Add the diced onion to the center with the salt and cook 3-4 minutes until soft. Add the garlic and ginger; stir 30 seconds until fragrant.
4. Wilt the cabbage: Add both bags of coleslaw mix — it will look like a mountain; that is normal. Toss with tongs 4-5 minutes until the cabbage wilts down by half and turns bright. You want it tender-crisp, not mushy — it should still have bite. If your pan is small, add the cabbage in two batches so it stir-fries instead of steams.
5. Sauce: Pour the sauce mixture over everything and toss 1-2 minutes until the liquid evaporates and coats the filling in a light glaze. Taste: it should be savory with a tangy edge. Add more sriracha for heat or a splash more soy for salt.
6. Finish: Turn off the heat and fold in the sliced scallions. Serve in bowls topped with sesame seeds, with extra sriracha on the side. It eats like the inside of an egg roll — all the flavor, none of the deep-frying.

Common mistakes:
- Steaming instead of browning: too much cabbage at once in a small pan drops the temperature. Two batches if needed.
- Mushy cabbage: 4-5 minutes is enough. It keeps softening off the heat, so pull it while still crisp.
- Forgetting the crispy bits: if you stir the pork constantly from the start, it never browns. Let it sit undisturbed first.
- Over-saucing: the sauce should glaze, not pool. Cook until the liquid evaporates.

Title: Chicken noodle soup
Ingredients:
- 2 1/2 lb bone-in, skin-on chicken thighs (or 1 whole 3 1/2-lb chicken)
- 10 cups water
- 3 tbsp olive oil or butter
- 2 large yellow onions, diced
- 4 large carrots, sliced into 1/4-inch coins
- 4 celery stalks, sliced 1/4 inch thick
- 5 cloves garlic, minced
- 2 bay leaves
- 1 tbsp fresh thyme leaves (or 1 tsp dried)
- 8 oz wide egg noodles
- 1/4 cup chopped fresh parsley
- 2 tsp kosher salt, plus more to taste
- 1 tsp black pepper
- Juice of 1/2 lemon
Steps:
1. Mise en place: Dice the onions. Slice the carrots into coins and the celery into half-moons — uniform pieces cook evenly and look like real soup. Mince the garlic. Strip the thyme leaves. Chop the parsley. Pat the chicken dry.
2. Brown the chicken: Heat 1 tbsp oil in a large stockpot or Dutch oven over medium-high heat. Sear the chicken thighs skin-side down 4-5 minutes until golden, flip and sear 3 minutes more. You are not cooking them through — just building the browned flavor base that makes the broth taste like chicken instead of hot water. Remove to a plate.
3. Soften the vegetables: Add the remaining 2 tbsp oil to the pot. Add the onion, carrots, and celery with 1 tsp salt. Cook 8-10 minutes, stirring, until the onion is soft and the vegetables start to take on color. Add the garlic, thyme, and bay leaves; cook 1 minute until fragrant.
4. Simmer the soup: Return the chicken to the pot with any juices. Add the water — it should cover everything by about an inch. Bring to a boil, then immediately drop to a gentle simmer: small bubbles lazily breaking the surface. Skim off any gray foam that rises in the first 10 minutes (that foam is just protein; skimming keeps the broth clear and clean-tasting). Simmer 30 minutes, until the chicken is completely tender and reads 165 F.
5. Shred the chicken: Remove the thighs to a cutting board. When cool enough to handle, pull the meat off the bones and shred into bite-size pieces. Discard the skin and bones (or save the bones for stock). Return the shredded meat to the pot.
6. Cook the noodles separately: This is the pro move — noodles cooked in the soup absorb broth, bloat, and turn the leftovers to mush. Boil the egg noodles in a separate pot of salted water until just tender, drain, and add to bowls, not the pot.
7. Season: Taste the broth — the most important step. Add salt 1/2 tsp at a time until the chicken flavor pops. Add the black pepper and the squeeze of lemon juice, which brightens the whole pot the way salt alone cannot. Stir in the parsley.
8. Serve: Put noodles in each of 6 deep bowls, ladle the hot soup over them, and serve immediately.
9. Storage: Keep noodles and soup separate in the fridge up to 4 days. The soup itself freezes beautifully for 3 months. Reheat gently; add fresh noodles when serving.

Common mistakes:
- Boiling the broth hard: a rolling boil makes cloudy, greasy broth and tough chicken. Gentle simmer, always.
- Cooking noodles in the soup: fine for tonight, mushy by tomorrow. Bowls, not the pot.
- Under-salting: bland broth almost always means not enough salt. Taste and salt in stages.
- Skipping the browning: pale unseared chicken makes pale, thin-tasting broth. The sear is the flavor.

Title: Lentil and sausage soup
Ingredients:
- 1 lb Italian sausage (sweet or hot), casings removed
- 2 cups brown lentils, rinsed and picked over
- 2 tbsp olive oil
- 1 large yellow onion, diced
- 3 large carrots, diced
- 3 celery stalks, diced
- 5 cloves garlic, minced
- 1 can (14 oz) diced tomatoes
- 8 cups low-sodium chicken broth
- 2 bay leaves
- 1 tsp dried thyme
- 1 tsp dried oregano
- 1 Parmesan rind (optional, but a great flavor trick)
- 4 cups baby spinach
- 2 tsp kosher salt, plus more to taste
- 1 tsp black pepper
- Grated Parmesan and crusty bread, for serving
Steps:
1. Mise en place: Rinse the lentils in a strainer and pick out any shriveled ones or tiny stones — lentils sometimes hide a pebble. Dice the onion, carrots, and celery into even 1/2-inch pieces (this trio is called a soffritto in Italian cooking, the flavor base of the soup). Mince the garlic. If your sausage is in casings, squeeze the meat out and discard the casings.
2. Brown the sausage: Heat the olive oil in a large Dutch oven over medium-high heat. Add the sausage and break into small crumbles. Cook 6-8 minutes, letting it sit undisturbed for the first 3 minutes so it develops deep brown crusty bits. Those browned bits are the foundation of the soup's flavor. Remove the sausage with a slotted spoon, leaving the fat in the pot.
3. Build the soffritto: Add the onion, carrots, and celery to the pot with 1 tsp salt. Cook 8-10 minutes, stirring, until soft and the onion turns translucent and sweet-smelling. Add the garlic, thyme, and oregano; cook 1 minute until fragrant.
4. Simmer: Add the lentils, diced tomatoes with their juices, chicken broth, bay leaves, and the Parmesan rind if using (the rind melts slowly into the broth and adds incredible savory depth — save your rinds in the freezer for exactly this). Return the sausage to the pot. Bring to a boil, then reduce to a gentle simmer, partially covered, for 30-35 minutes.
