8. Storage and reheating: Refrigerate kofta, orzo, and sauce separately up to 4 days. Reheat kofta in a 350 F oven 10-12 minutes; reheat orzo in a skillet with a splash of broth over medium heat until creamy again. The yogurt sauce is served cold.

Common mistakes:
- Overworking the meat: Mixing past the point where everything is just combined squeezes out moisture and makes tough kofta. Hands, gentle, done in under a minute.
- Skipping the chill: Warm, soft kofta fall apart in the pan. The 15-minute fridge rest firms them up.
- Walking away from the orzo: Orzo sticks fast. Stir it at least twice during simmering, and keep the heat low enough that it bubbles gently, not hard.
- Overcooking to well-done-plus: Kofta past 160 F dry out quickly. Pull them at 160 F and let them rest — they finish in the resting time.

Title: Beef Parmesan Risotto
Ingredients:
1 3/4 lb beef sirloin or strip steak, cut into 1/2-inch-thick strips
2 cups arborio or carnaroli rice (risotto rice)
6 cups low-sodium beef broth
1 large yellow onion, finely diced
3/4 cup dry white wine
4 oz Parmigiano-Reggiano cheese, finely grated (about 1 1/2 cups)
5 tbsp unsalted butter, divided
4 tbsp olive oil, divided
2 garlic cloves, minced
1 tbsp fresh rosemary, finely chopped
1 1/2 tsp kosher salt, divided
1 tsp freshly ground black pepper
Fresh parsley, chopped (for serving)
Steps:
1. Mise en place: Pour the beef broth into a saucepan and keep it at a bare simmer over low heat — warm broth is essential; cold broth shocks the rice. Dice means small cubes about 1/2 inch: finely dice the onion. Mince means a very fine chop: mince the garlic. Grate the Parmigiano-Reggiano, chop the rosemary and parsley, measure the rice and wine, and slice the beef into 1/2-inch strips across the grain. Pat the beef strips very dry.
2. Start the risotto: heat 2 tbsp of the butter with 2 tbsp of the olive oil in a large heavy pot over medium heat. Add the onion and cook 5-6 minutes until soft and translucent but not browned.
3. Add the rice and stir to coat every grain in the fat. Toast 2 minutes, stirring constantly, until the edges of the grains turn translucent with an opaque white center and they smell faintly nutty. This tostatura keeps the risotto creamy instead of mushy.
4. Pour in the white wine and stir until it is completely absorbed, about 2 minutes — it will hiss and steam. Season with 1 tsp of the salt.
5. Add the warm broth one ladle at a time (about 1/2 cup each), stirring often and letting each addition absorb before adding the next. Keep the risotto at a steady gentle simmer — lazy bubbles. This takes 18-22 minutes. Start tasting at 16 minutes: the rice is done when it is tender with a slight bite at the center (al dente) and the mixture flows slowly like lava, not stiff like oatmeal.
6. While the risotto cooks, sear the beef: heat the remaining 2 tbsp olive oil in a large skillet over high heat until it just starts to smoke. Season the beef strips with the remaining 1/2 tsp salt and the pepper. Sear in a single layer 1 1/2-2 minutes per side until deeply browned but still pink inside (125-130 F for medium-rare). Do it in two batches if crowded. Add the garlic and rosemary in the last 30 seconds, tossing until fragrant. Transfer to a warm plate and rest 5 minutes.
7. Finish the risotto: remove the pot from the heat. Beat in the remaining 3 tbsp cold butter and the grated Parmigiano-Reggiano — this is the mantecatura, the step that makes risotto glossy and rich. Stir vigorously 1 minute until it melts in. Taste and adjust salt.
8. Plate immediately: risotto waits for no one. Spoon generous mounds onto warm plates, arrange the seared beef strips on top, drizzle with the beef pan juices, and scatter with chopped parsley. Serve extra Parmigiano at the table.
9. Storage and reheating: Risotto is best fresh — it thickens as it sits. Refrigerate leftovers up to 3 days. Reheat in a saucepan over low heat with a splash of broth, stirring until creamy again. Leftover risotto also makes excellent pan-fried cakes.

Common mistakes:
- Cold broth: Adding cold liquid to the pot drops the temperature and the rice turns gummy instead of creamy. Keep the broth simmering the whole time.
- Adding all the broth at once: Risotto needs gradual additions so the starch releases slowly. One ladle, absorb, repeat — no shortcuts.
- Overcooking the rice to mush: Start tasting at 16 minutes. Al dente with a creamy wave is the goal; one minute too long turns it to porridge.
- Searing wet beef: Damp beef steams gray instead of browning. Pat the strips dry and get the skillet truly smoking hot before they go in.

Title: Beef Picadillo Rice Bowls
Ingredients:
2 lb ground beef (85/15)
2 cups long-grain white rice
3 1/2 cups water
1 large yellow onion, diced
1 green bell pepper, diced
5 garlic cloves, minced
2 tbsp olive oil
1 can (15 oz) tomato sauce
2 tbsp tomato paste
1/3 cup raisins
2/3 cup pitted green olives, sliced
2 tbsp capers, drained
1 tbsp ground cumin
2 tsp dried oregano
1/2 tsp ground cinnamon
2 bay leaves
1 tbsp apple cider vinegar (or dry white wine)
1 1/2 tsp kosher salt
1/2 tsp freshly ground black pepper
2 tbsp fresh cilantro, chopped (for serving)
Steps:
1. Mise en place: Dice means small cubes about 1/2 inch: dice the onion and green bell pepper. Mince means a very fine chop: mince the garlic. Slice the olives, drain the capers, and measure the tomato sauce, tomato paste, raisins, vinegar, spices, rice, and water. This is your sofrito base — the soul of Cuban picadillo.
2. Cook the rice: combine the rice, 3 1/2 cups water, and 1/2 tsp of the salt in a pot. Bring to a boil, stir once, cover, and reduce to the lowest heat. Cook 15 minutes without lifting the lid. Remove from heat, rest covered 10 minutes, then fluff with a fork.
3. Heat the olive oil in a large deep skillet or Dutch oven over medium heat. Add the onion and bell pepper and cook 5-6 minutes, stirring, until soft and the onion turns translucent. Add the garlic and cook 1 minute more until fragrant — this cooked-down trio is the sofrito.
4. Raise the heat to medium-high, add the ground beef, and break it into fine crumbles. Cook 7-8 minutes until browned and cooked through. Spoon off any excess fat that pools in the pan.
5. Stir in the tomato paste, cumin, oregano, cinnamon, remaining salt, and pepper. Cook 1 minute until the spices smell fragrant and the paste darkens slightly.
6. Add the tomato sauce, bay leaves, raisins, olives, capers, and vinegar. Stir well, bring to a simmer, then reduce the heat to low. Cover and simmer 15 minutes so the flavors meld and the raisins soften. The finished picadillo should be saucy but not soupy — simmer uncovered 5 more minutes if it looks loose.
7. Remove the bay leaves. Taste: it should hit salty, sweet, and briny all at once — the classic Cuban sweet-savory balance. Add a pinch more salt or a splash of vinegar if it tastes flat.
8. Spoon the rice into wide bowls, ladle the picadillo generously over the top, and scatter with chopped cilantro. Fried sweet plantains on the side are traditional if you want them.
9. Storage and reheating: Refrigerate up to 4 days — picadillo tastes even better the next day. Freeze the picadillo (not the rice) up to 3 months. Reheat in a skillet over medium heat with a splash of water, or microwave until steaming.

Common mistakes:
- Skipping the sofrito: Adding the beef before the onion, pepper, and garlic soften leaves you with a flat, one-note sauce. The vegetables must go first.
- Forgetting the sweet-savory balance: Cuban picadillo needs the raisins and olives to taste right. If it tastes plain, you are probably short on one of them — do not skip both.
- Over-saucing: Picadillo should coat the rice, not drown it. If the sauce is thin after simmering, cook uncovered a few more minutes to tighten it.
- Lifting the rice lid: Each peek lets out the steam the rice needs. Timer, lid on, rest covered — no peeking.

Title: Beef Picadinho with Potatoes
Ingredients:
2 lb beef chuck roast, cut into small 3/4-inch cubes
2 lb russet or Yukon Gold potatoes, peeled and cut into 1-inch cubes
2 tbsp olive oil
1 large yellow onion, diced
4 garlic cloves, minced
3 ripe tomatoes, diced (or 1 can / 14.5 oz diced tomatoes)
2 tbsp tomato paste
2 tbsp Worcestershire sauce
2 tsp sweet paprika (colorau)
1 tsp ground cumin
1 bay leaf
3 cups low-sodium beef broth
1 cup frozen green peas
1 1/2 tsp kosher salt
1/2 tsp freshly ground black pepper
1/4 cup fresh parsley, chopped
Cooked white rice, for serving
Steps:
1. Mise en place: Cut the beef into small 3/4-inch cubes — small cubes are the whole point of picadinho ("little chopped"). Dice means small cubes about 1/2 inch: dice the onion. Cut the potatoes into 1-inch cubes and keep them in cold water so they do not brown. Mince means a very fine chop: mince the garlic. Dice the tomatoes, measure the broth, tomato paste, Worcestershire, paprika, cumin, salt, and pepper, and set the peas and parsley ready.
2. Pat the beef cubes very dry with paper towels. Season with 1 tsp of the salt and the pepper. Heat the olive oil in a large heavy pot or Dutch oven over medium-high heat until it shimmers.
3. Brown the beef in two batches, 3-4 minutes per batch, turning to get color on two or three sides. The pieces should sizzle hard and develop golden-brown edges. Set aside on a plate — they will not be cooked through yet.
4. Lower the heat to medium. Add the onion to the pot and cook 4-5 minutes, stirring and scraping up the browned bits, until soft. Add the garlic and cook 1 minute until fragrant. Stir in the tomato paste, paprika, and cumin; cook 1 minute until the paste darkens to brick red.
5. Add the diced tomatoes and Worcestershire sauce and cook 3 minutes, stirring, until the tomatoes soften and release their juices. Return the beef and any juices to the pot, add the bay leaf, and pour in the beef broth. It should nearly cover everything.
6. Bring to a gentle simmer — a few lazy bubbles, not a boil. Cover and cook 25 minutes. Then drain and add the potato cubes, stir, cover, and cook 15-20 minutes more, until the potatoes are fork-tender and a beef cube is tender when bitten. If the sauce is thin, simmer uncovered 5 minutes to thicken.
7. Stir in the frozen peas and cook 3 final minutes — they should stay bright green. Remove the bay leaf. Taste and adjust salt and pepper. The sauce should be savory and lightly tangy from the tomatoes and Worcestershire.
8. Rest 5 minutes. Ladle over white rice in shallow bowls and scatter generously with chopped parsley. In Brazil this is everyday comfort food — rice is the essential partner.
9. Storage and reheating: Refrigerate up to 4 days; it reheats beautifully. Freeze up to 3 months (the potatoes soften slightly). Reheat gently on the stovetop over low heat with a splash of broth or water until steaming.

Common mistakes:
- Cutting the beef too large: 1 1/2-inch stew cubes need hours to tenderize. Small 3/4-inch cubes are tender in about 45 minutes — cut small or plan extra time.
- Boiling hard instead of simmering: A rolling boil keeps the beef chewy no matter how long you cook it. Keep it at the gentlest simmer.
- Adding potatoes at the start: They would turn to mush after 45 minutes. They go in for only the last 15-20 minutes of cooking.
- Skipping the brown: The golden crust on the beef is where the deep flavor comes from. Crowding the pan steams the meat instead — brown in two batches.

Title: Beef Sukiyaki-Style Rice Bowls
Ingredients:
2 lb beef ribeye or sirloin, sliced paper-thin (shabu-shabu / sukiyaki cut)
2 cups Japanese short-grain rice
2 1/4 cups water, plus 1 cup for the sauce
2 large yellow onions, sliced into thin half-moons
8 oz fresh shiitake mushrooms, stemmed and sliced
14 oz firm tofu, cut into 1-inch cubes
For the sukiyaki sauce:
1/2 cup soy sauce (shoyu)
1/4 cup sake
1/4 cup mirin
3 tbsp granulated sugar
1 tsp instant dashi powder dissolved in 1 cup hot water
1 tbsp neutral oil (such as canola)
For serving:
3 scallions, thinly sliced
1/4 cup pickled red ginger (beni shoga), optional
Shichimi togarashi (Japanese seven-spice), optional
Steps:
1. Mise en place: If your beef is not pre-sliced, freeze it 45 minutes until firm but not frozen solid — semi-frozen meat slices paper-thin easily. Slice it as thin as you can, about 1/8 inch, against the grain. Slice means thin, even pieces: slice the onions into half-moons, the shiitakes, and the scallions. Cube the tofu. Measure the soy sauce, sake, mirin, sugar, and dashi water. Rinse the rice in a pot, swirling with your hand, draining, and repeating 2-3 times until the water runs mostly clear.
2. Cook the rice: combine the rinsed rice and 2 1/4 cups water in a pot. Bring to a boil, stir once, cover, and reduce to the lowest heat. Cook 15 minutes, then remove from heat and rest, covered, 10 minutes. Fluff gently with a rice paddle or fork. Short-grain rice should be tender and slightly sticky — do not lift the lid during cooking.
3. Make the sukiyaki sauce: in a bowl, whisk the soy sauce, sake, mirin, sugar, and the 1 cup of dashi water until the sugar dissolves.
4. Heat the oil in a large deep skillet or Dutch oven over medium-high heat. Add the onions and cook 3-4 minutes until they start to soften and turn glossy.
5. Pour the sukiyaki sauce into the pan and bring to a gentle simmer. Add the shiitake mushrooms and tofu, nestling the tofu in gently so it does not break. Simmer 3 minutes.
6. Spread the beef slices over the top in a loose single layer — do not pile them. They will cook in 1-2 minutes; turn them once with tongs as they change from pink to brown. Overcooking makes thin beef tough and chewy, so pull the pan off the heat the moment the last pink disappears. The beef is done in well under 2 minutes.
7. Taste the sauce and adjust: it should be savory-sweet in the classic sukiyaki balance. Add a splash more soy sauce if it tastes flat, or a pinch more sugar if too salty.
8. To serve, scoop hot rice into wide bowls, spoon the beef, vegetables, tofu, and mushrooms over the rice, and ladle some of the sweet-savory sauce over everything. Top with sliced scallions and pickled red ginger, and pass the shichimi togarashi for anyone who wants heat.
9. Storage and reheating: Refrigerate leftovers up to 3 days. Reheat in a saucepan over low heat with a splash of water until steaming — the microwave turns thin beef rubbery. Store any extra sauce in a jar in the fridge up to 2 weeks; it is excellent on other rice bowls too.

Common mistakes:
- Overcooking the thin beef: Paper-thin slices go from perfect to rubbery in under a minute. The second the pink is gone, it is done — take it off the heat.
- Slicing thick or with the grain: Thick, with-the-grain beef chews like jerky. Semi-freeze, slice thin, cut against the grain.
- Salty sauce from long reduction: The sauce concentrates as it simmers. Keep the simmer gentle and brief after the beef goes in, and taste before serving — adjust with water or dashi if it reduces too far.
- Breaking the tofu: Firm tofu still crumbles if stirred hard. Nestle it in and stir gently around it, never through it.

Title: Beef & Zucchini Bolognese
Ingredients:
1 1/2 lb 90% lean ground beef
4 oz pancetta, cut into 1/4-inch cubes (or 4 slices thick-cut bacon, chopped)
2 tbsp olive oil
1 medium yellow onion
1 medium carrot, peeled
1 celery stalk
2 medium zucchini (about 1 lb total)
2 cloves garlic
2 tbsp tomato paste
1 can (28 oz) crushed tomatoes
1 cup dry white wine (something you would drink)
1 cup whole milk
1 lb spaghetti
3/4 cup freshly grated Parmesan cheese, plus more for serving
2 1/2 tsp kosher salt, divided
1 tsp freshly ground black pepper
1/4 tsp ground nutmeg
Steps:
1. Mise en place (everything ready before any heat goes on): Dice means cutting into small even cubes about 1/2 inch. Mince means chopping as fine as you can, into almost a paste. Dice the onion, carrot, and celery into 1/4-inch cubes and pile them together - this mix is called soffritto, the flavor base of a real ragu. Mince the garlic. Cube the pancetta. Grate the zucchini on the large holes of a box grater and squeeze it gently in a clean towel to remove some water. Open the wine and the tomatoes. Measure the tomato paste, milk, salt, pepper, and nutmeg into small bowls. Grate the Parmesan.
2. Put a large heavy pot or Dutch oven over medium heat. Add the pancetta cubes with no oil. Cook, stirring often, 5-7 minutes, until the pieces turn golden and release their fat. You will smell a rich, porky aroma. Remove the pancetta with a slotted spoon and set it aside, leaving the rendered fat in the pot.
3. Add the olive oil to the pot and then the soffritto (onion, carrot, celery) plus 1 teaspoon of the salt. Cook over medium heat, stirring often, 8-10 minutes. The vegetables should soften and turn sweet and translucent, the onion pale gold - not brown. This gentle softening is the soul of bolognese; rushed vegetables taste harsh.
4. Crumble in the ground beef. Break it up with a spoon and cook over medium-high heat 8-10 minutes, stirring and scraping, until no pink remains and the meat makes a lively sizzling sound (the Italian word for this stage is "sfrigola" - it sizzles and spits). Do not sear it dark; authentic ragu is gently browned, never charred.
5. Add the minced garlic and the reserved pancetta. Stir 1 minute until fragrant.
6. Stir in the tomato paste and cook 2 minutes, until it darkens from bright red to a deep brick red. This removes its raw tinny taste.
7. Pour in the white wine and scrape the bottom of the pot to dissolve the browned bits. Let it bubble 3-4 minutes until the sharp wine smell disappears and the liquid mostly evaporates. If the alcohol smell is still strong, give it another minute.
8. Stir in the crushed tomatoes, 1 cup of water, 1 more teaspoon of salt, the black pepper, and the nutmeg. Bring to a gentle bubble, then reduce the heat to the lowest setting so the sauce barely trembles - a slow "blurp" every few seconds. Cover with the lid slightly ajar and simmer 90 minutes, stirring every 15 minutes and adding a splash of water if it ever looks dry or sticks.
9. Stir in the milk a little at a time - about 1/4 cup, let it absorb 5 minutes, then repeat. This is the signature of real bolognese: the milk tames the tomato's acidity and gives the sauce a silky, mellow finish. Then stir in the grated zucchini and simmer 30 minutes more, uncovered, until the sauce is thick enough that a spoon dragged through it leaves a trail that holds for a moment. Total sauce time is about 2 hours.
10. About 20 minutes before the sauce is done, bring a large pot of heavily salted water to a rolling boil (it should taste like the sea). Cook the spaghetti 1 minute less than the package says. Before draining, scoop out 1 cup of the starchy pasta water. Drain the pasta.
11. Add the pasta to the sauce pot with 1/2 cup of the pasta water and the Parmesan. Toss over medium heat 1-2 minutes until every strand is coated and glossy, adding more pasta water a splash at a time if it looks dry. Taste and add the last 1/2 teaspoon of salt if needed.
12. Serve in warm bowls with extra Parmesan on top. Storage: refrigerate the sauce alone (before tossing with pasta, if possible) up to 4 days, or freeze up to 3 months. Reheat gently in a pot with a splash of water, then toss with freshly cooked pasta. Like all ragu, this tastes even better the next day.

Common mistakes:
1. Cranking the heat for a fast sauce. Real bolognese needs low, slow simmering - about 2 hours - for the flavors to marry. A 20-minute sauce will taste like spaghetti with meat, not ragu.
2. Skipping the milk or dumping it in all at once cold. Add it little by little near the end of cooking so it absorbs instead of separating; it is what rounds out the acidity.
3. Adding the zucchini at the start. It will dissolve into mush over 2 hours. Adding it for the last 30 minutes keeps a little texture while still melting into the sauce.

Title: Blackened Trout & Roasted Potatoes
Ingredients:
2 lb baby potatoes (about 24)
3 tbsp olive oil, divided
1 1/2 tsp kosher salt, divided
1 lb fresh green beans
4 tbsp unsalted butter, melted, plus 1 tbsp for the pan
1 1/2 lb trout fillets (about 6 fillets), patted very dry
1 1/2 tbsp sweet paprika
1 tsp garlic powder
1 tsp onion powder
1 tsp dried thyme
1/2 tsp dried oregano
1 tsp cayenne pepper (use 1/2 tsp for mild)
1 tsp freshly ground black pepper
1 lemon, cut into wedges
Steps:
1. Mise en place: Slice means cutting into thin even pieces. Halve the baby potatoes (cut in half through the middle). Trim the green beans (snap or cut off the stem ends). Pat the trout fillets very dry with paper towels - this is essential; wet fish steams instead of searing. In a small bowl, mix the paprika, garlic powder, onion powder, thyme, oregano, cayenne, black pepper, and 1 teaspoon of the salt. This is your blackening spice blend. Melt the butter. Cut the lemon into wedges. Line a rimmed baking sheet with foil and preheat the oven to 425 F.
2. Toss the halved potatoes with 2 tablespoons of the olive oil and 1/2 teaspoon of the salt right on the baking sheet, cut-side down. Spread them in a single layer with space between pieces. Roast 20 minutes. They should be starting to turn golden underneath - peek under one.
3. While the potatoes roast, set a large cast-iron skillet (or other heavy skillet) over high heat with no oil. Let it heat a full 8-10 minutes until it is smoking hot. This extreme heat is the whole point of blackening. Turn on your stove fan and open a window - there will be smoke, and that is correct.
4. Dip each trout fillet in the melted butter, coating both sides, then press the spice blend generously onto both sides. The butter is what creates the black crust: the milk solids in it char on the hot iron, giving the smoky, bitter-sweet shell that defines blackening. Seasoned side up or down does not matter; coat both.
5. Lay the fillets in the screaming-hot dry skillet, leaving space between them. They will sizzle loudly and smoke - do not touch them for 2 minutes. Lift one edge with a spatula: it should be deep reddish-brown to nearly black in spots. Flip carefully and cook 1-2 minutes more on the second side. Trout is done when it flakes easily with a fork and the internal temperature reaches 145 F. Cook in two batches if the pan is crowded; crowding drops the pan temperature and you get gray steamed fish instead of blackened.
6. Meanwhile, after the potatoes have roasted 20 minutes, scatter the green beans onto the same baking sheet, toss them with the remaining 1 tablespoon of olive oil and the last 1/2 teaspoon of salt, and roast 10 more minutes. The potatoes should be crisp-edged and the beans blistered and tender. Total potato time: 30 minutes.
7. Plate a bed of potatoes and beans, lay a trout fillet on top, and finish with a squeeze of lemon. The lemon juice brightens the smoky crust. Serve immediately - blackened fish waits for no one. Storage: refrigerate leftovers up to 2 days. Reheat the fish gently in a 300 F oven for 8-10 minutes (the microwave makes it rubbery) and warm the potatoes in a hot skillet.

Common mistakes:
1. Using a skillet that is only medium-hot. Blackening demands a smoking-hot cast-iron pan; without it you get pale, steamed fish with raw spices. Let the pan heat a full 8-10 minutes.
2. Using oil instead of butter on the fish. The charred butter solids ARE the blackening; oil cannot produce the same crust.
3. Crowding the pan or moving the fish too early. Give each fillet space and let it sit undisturbed so the crust forms - 2 minutes per side, then done.

Title: Black Pepper Beef & Broccoli
Ingredients:
1 1/2 lb flank steak
2 tbsp low-sodium soy sauce, plus 1 tbsp more
2 tbsp cornstarch, divided
1 tbsp Shaoxing rice wine (or dry sherry)
2 tsp sugar
1 tbsp oyster sauce
2 tsp coarsely cracked black pepper (freshly ground is essential)
1 tbsp plus 1 tsp avocado oil or other neutral oil, divided
1 medium yellow onion
4 cloves garlic
1-inch piece fresh ginger
1 1/2 lb broccoli (about 2 large heads), cut into florets
1/2 cup low-sodium chicken broth
1 1/2 cups dry jasmine rice
2 1/4 cups water
Steps:
1. Mise en place: Slice means thin even pieces. First freeze the flank steak 20 minutes - slightly firm meat is much easier to slice thin. Slice the steak AGAINST the grain into 1/4-inch strips. To find the grain, look for the lines running through the meat and cut across them, not along them; cutting against the grain is what keeps stir-fry beef tender instead of chewy. In a bowl, toss the beef with 2 tablespoons soy sauce, 1 tablespoon cornstarch, the Shaoxing wine, and the sugar. This light coating is called velveting - it protects the meat from the wok's heat so it stays silky. Set aside 15 minutes. Meanwhile, cut the broccoli into bite-size florets with short stems (bite-size pieces cook evenly). Slice the onion into 1/2-inch wedges. Mince the garlic. Grate or mince the ginger. In a small bowl, stir together the remaining 1 tablespoon soy sauce, the remaining 1 tablespoon cornstarch, the oyster sauce, the cracked black pepper, and the chicken broth - this is your sauce; the cornstarch settles fast, so stir it again right before use. Rinse the rice under cold water until the water runs mostly clear.
2. Start the rice first: combine the rice and water in a saucepan with a tight lid. Bring to a boil over high heat, stir once, cover, reduce to low, and cook 15 minutes without lifting the lid. Remove from heat and rest, covered, 10 minutes. Fluff with a fork.
3. While the rice cooks, bring a large pot of salted water to a boil. Blanch the broccoli 2 minutes until bright emerald green, then drain and rinse under cold water to stop the cooking. The broccoli should still be crisp - it finishes in the wok.
4. Heat a wok or the largest heavy skillet you own over HIGH heat until it just starts to smoke - about 2 minutes. Add 1 tablespoon of the oil and swirl. Add half the beef in a single layer. Let it sit undisturbed 60-90 seconds until browned on one side, then toss and cook 30 seconds more. Remove to a plate. Repeat with the remaining beef. Working in batches keeps the pan hot enough to sear instead of steam. The beef will not be cooked through yet - that is fine.
5. Lower the heat to medium-high. Add the remaining 1 teaspoon of oil, the onion wedges, garlic, and ginger. Stir-fry 1-2 minutes until fragrant and the onion edges soften.
6. Return the beef and the broccoli to the pan. Stir the sauce bowl again (the cornstarch settles) and pour it in. Toss everything 1-2 minutes until the sauce boils, thickens to a glossy coat, and clings to the beef. Taste: it should be boldly peppery with a savory-sweet balance. If you want more heat, add up to 1/2 teaspoon more black pepper now.
7. Serve immediately over the jasmine rice. The sauce should pool slightly in the bowl - that is the best part. Storage: refrigerate up to 3 days. Reheat in a skillet over medium heat with a splash of water to loosen the sauce; the microwave works but the broccoli softens further.

Common mistakes:
1. Slicing the beef WITH the grain or too thick. Against the grain, 1/4 inch, is non-negotiable for tender stir-fry beef; with-the-grain slices stay chewy no matter how fast you cook them.
2. Crowding all the beef into the pan at once. It steams in its own juices and turns gray and tough. Two fast batches is the fix - 90 seconds each.
3. Forgetting to re-stir the sauce before pouring. The cornstarch sinks to the bottom of the bowl in seconds; unstirred sauce goes in thin and never thickens.

Title: Brazilian Beef, Rice & Peas
Ingredients:
2 tbsp olive oil, divided
1 large yellow onion, finely diced
3 cloves garlic, minced
1 1/2 cups long-grain white rice
3 cups water
1 1/2 tsp kosher salt, divided
1 1/2 lb 93% lean ground beef
1 tbsp sweet paprika (pimentao doce)
1/2 tsp ground cumin
1/2 tsp freshly ground black pepper
2 medium tomatoes, diced
1 cup frozen peas (no need to thaw)
3 tbsp fresh parsley, chopped
Lime wedges and hot sauce, for serving (optional)
Steps:
1. Mise en place: Dice means small even cubes about 1/2 inch. Dice the onion finely (1/4-inch cubes so it melts into the rice). Mince the garlic (very fine chop). Dice the tomatoes into 1/2-inch pieces. Chop the parsley. Measure the rice, water, peas, paprika, cumin, pepper, and salt into bowls so everything is within reach - this dish moves fast once the pan is hot.
2. Heat 1 tablespoon of the olive oil in a large saucepan or pot over medium heat. Add half the diced onion and one minced garlic clove with 1/2 teaspoon of the salt. Cook 3-4 minutes, stirring, until soft and translucent. Do not let it brown - Brazilian rice starts with a gentle refogado, a softening of aromatics, not a sear.
3. Add the dry rice to the pot and stir 1-2 minutes until the grains turn from chalky white to slightly translucent at the edges and smell faintly nutty. This toasting step gives Brazilian-style arroz its distinct flavor and keeps the grains separate.
4. Pour in the 3 cups of water - it will steam and bubble furiously, so stand back. Add 1/2 teaspoon more salt. Bring to a boil, stir once, cover, reduce to the lowest heat, and cook 18 minutes without lifting the lid. Remove from heat and rest, covered, 10 minutes. Fluff with a fork. The grains should be tender and separate, never mushy.
5. While the rice cooks, make the beef: heat the remaining 1 tablespoon of olive oil in a large skillet over medium-high heat. Add the remaining onion and cook 2-3 minutes until softened. Crumble in the ground beef. Cook 8-10 minutes, breaking it up with a spoon, until no pink remains and the meat is lightly browned in spots. Drain off any excess fat if there is more than a tablespoon.
6. Add the remaining garlic, the sweet paprika, cumin, black pepper, and the last 1/2 teaspoon of salt. Stir 1 minute until the spices smell toasty and coat the meat. Sweet paprika (not smoked, not hot) is the signature seasoning of carne moida - it gives the beef its warm red color and gentle sweetness.
7. Stir in the diced tomatoes and cook 3-4 minutes until they break down into a light sauce. Add the frozen peas straight from the freezer and cook 3-4 minutes more, until heated through and bright green. Taste and add salt if needed - the beef should be savory and well seasoned on its own.
8. Fluff the rice into the beef pan (or serve the beef over the rice in bowls) and toss gently. Shower with the chopped parsley. Serve with lime wedges for squeezing and hot sauce on the side - in Brazil, a squeeze of lime over carne moida is nearly mandatory. Storage: refrigerate up to 4 days. Reheat in a skillet over medium heat with a splash of water, or microwave covered.

Common mistakes:
1. Using smoked or hot paprika instead of sweet. Brazilian carne moida relies on sweet paprika's mellow color and gentle flavor; smoked paprika turns it into a different dish entirely.
2. Stirring the rice while it cooks or skipping the rest. Both make gummy rice. Cover, do not touch for 18 minutes, then rest 10 minutes off the heat before fluffing.
3. Under-seasoning the beef. Taste the meat before combining with the rice - bland beef plus plain rice equals a bland dinner. Salt assertively; the peas and tomatoes need it.

Title: Bulgogi Chicken Rice Bowls
Ingredients:
1 3/4 lb boneless, skinless chicken breast
1/2 cup low-sodium soy sauce
1/2 Asian pear, peeled and grated on the fine holes (or 1/2 sweet apple)
2 tbsp packed brown sugar
1 tbsp toasted sesame oil
4 cloves garlic, minced
1 tbsp fresh ginger, grated
1 tbsp rice vinegar
1 tsp freshly ground black pepper
1 1/2 cups dry short-grain rice
2 cups water
1 English cucumber
1 tbsp rice vinegar, plus 1/2 tsp sugar
4 green onions
1 tbsp toasted sesame seeds
1 tbsp neutral oil, for the pan
Steps:
1. Mise en place: Slice means thin even pieces. Slice the chicken breast across the grain into 1/4-inch strips. (Tip: 20 minutes in the freezer firms the chicken and makes thin slicing easy.) Mince means a very fine chop - mince the garlic. Grate the ginger and the pear on the fine holes of a box grater. Slice the green onions thinly on a diagonal. Slice the cucumber into thin half-moons. In a large bowl, whisk together the soy sauce, grated pear, brown sugar, sesame oil, garlic, ginger, 1 tablespoon rice vinegar, and black pepper until the sugar dissolves. This is the bulgogi marinade - the pear is the traditional Korean secret: its natural enzymes tenderize the meat and add a mellow sweetness you cannot get from sugar alone.
2. Add the chicken strips to the marinade and toss to coat every piece. Cover and refrigerate 20-30 minutes. Do not marinate longer than 2 hours - the pear enzymes will turn the chicken mushy past that point. Meanwhile, rinse the short-grain rice under cold water until the water runs mostly clear (this removes excess starch so the rice is sticky but not gummy).
3. Start the rice: combine the rice and 2 cups of water in a saucepan with a tight lid. Bring to a boil over high heat, stir once, cover, reduce to low, and cook 15 minutes without lifting the lid. Rest, covered, 10 minutes off the heat, then fluff. Short-grain rice should be slightly sticky and glossy.
4. While the rice cooks, toss the cucumber half-moons with the second 1 tablespoon of rice vinegar, the 1/2 teaspoon of sugar, and a pinch of salt. Let them sit 10 minutes - this quick pickle gives the bowls a cool, tangy crunch that cuts the rich marinade.
5. Remove the chicken from the fridge and shake off excess marinade (save it). Heat the neutral oil in your largest skillet or wok over HIGH heat until it just starts to smoke - 2 minutes. Add half the chicken in a single layer. Let it sit 2 minutes without touching so the sugars in the marinade caramelize into charred edges, then toss and cook 2-3 minutes more until cooked through. Remove to a plate and repeat with the rest. Crowding the pan steams the chicken and the marinade never caramelizes.
6. Pour the reserved marinade into the empty hot skillet and boil 1 full minute, stirring, until it thickens into a glossy glaze. (It must boil to be safe, since it touched raw chicken.) Return the chicken to the pan and toss to coat. Check a strip: cut the thickest piece - it should be white all the way through with no pink, 165 F internally.
7. Build the bowls: a scoop of rice, a pile of glazed chicken, a tangle of quick-pickled cucumber, a shower of green onions, and a sprinkle of sesame seeds. Storage: refrigerate chicken and rice separately up to 4 days. Reheat the chicken in a skillet over medium heat with a splash of water; microwave the rice covered with a damp paper towel.

Common mistakes:
1. Marinating for hours "for more flavor." The pear's enzymes keep working and the chicken turns mealy. 20-30 minutes is the sweet spot for chicken.
2. Cooking the chicken in a crowded, lukewarm pan. Bulgogi gets its flavor from fast, hot caramelization - sear in batches over high heat so the marinade chars instead of boiling.
3. Serving the reserved marinade uncooked. It touched raw chicken, so it must be boiled at least 1 minute before it goes back on the meat or over the rice.

Title: Caramel Pork with Cucumber Rice
Ingredients:
1 1/2 lb pork tenderloin
3 tbsp brown sugar
2 tbsp water
1 tbsp avocado oil
1 shallot, minced
2 cloves garlic, minced
1 tsp freshly ground black pepper
3 tbsp fish sauce
1 cup coconut water (or plain water)
1 English cucumber
1 tbsp rice vinegar
1/2 tsp sugar
1 1/2 cups dry jasmine rice
2 1/4 cups water
2 green onions, thinly sliced, for serving
Steps:
1. Mise en place: Mince means a very fine chop - mince the shallot and the garlic. Cut the pork tenderloin into 1-inch cubes (bite-size pieces braise evenly). Trim off the silvery skin-like membrane if you see any - slide a thin knife under it and pull it away; it stays tough no matter how long you cook it. Slice the cucumber into thin half-moons and toss with the rice vinegar, the 1/2 teaspoon of sugar, and a pinch of salt; set aside to quick-pickle. Measure the brown sugar, water, fish sauce, coconut water, and black pepper into bowls. Rinse the jasmine rice until the water runs mostly clear.
2. Start the rice: combine the rice and 2 1/4 cups of water in a saucepan with a tight lid. Bring to a boil over high heat, stir once, cover, reduce to low, and cook 15 minutes without lifting the lid. Rest, covered, 10 minutes off the heat, then fluff.
3. Make the caramel (nuoc mau), the heart of thit kho to: put a large heavy skillet or Dutch oven over medium-low heat. Add the brown sugar and the 2 tablespoons of water. Stir once, then leave it alone and watch it closely. In 4-6 minutes the sugar melts, bubbles, and turns from pale gold to deep amber - the color of strong tea or dark honey. The moment it reaches that color, swirl the pan. Do NOT let it go black or smell acrid; burnt caramel is bitter and cannot be fixed. If you see smoke or smell burning, start over - it is only 3 tablespoons of sugar.
4. Immediately add the avocado oil, then the pork cubes, standing back as they sizzle. Stir to coat every piece in the caramel - the pork will turn a glossy amber color at once. Cook 3-4 minutes, stirring, until the outside is no longer pink.
5. Stir in the minced shallot, garlic, and black pepper. Cook 1 minute until fragrant. Add the fish sauce - it will smell strong for a moment, then mellow into deep savoriness - and the coconut water. The coconut water is traditional: it adds a gentle sweetness and keeps the sauce clear and light instead of heavy.
6. Bring to a boil, then reduce to a gentle simmer, partially covered, 25-30 minutes. Stir every 10 minutes and skim any foam that rises. The sauce should reduce to a syrupy glaze that coats the pork; if it gets too thick before the pork is tender, add a splash of water. The pork is done when a piece is tender and the internal temperature reads 145 F. Rest the pork 3 minutes before serving.
7. Serve the caramel pork over jasmine rice with plenty of the glossy sauce spooned over, the quick-pickled cucumber on the side, and green onions scattered on top. The cool cucumber against the sweet-salty pork is the classic balance. Storage: refrigerate up to 4 days - it tastes even better the next day. Reheat gently in a covered skillet with a splash of water.

Common mistakes:
1. Walking away from the caramel. Sugar goes from amber to burnt in under a minute. Stay at the stove, and the instant it smells toasted and looks like dark tea, add the pork.
2. Adding the fish sauce before the caramel is made. The salt and water in the sauce stop the sugar from caramelizing properly - caramel first, seasoning after.
3. Boiling the braise hard the whole time. A rolling boil toughens the pork and clouds the sauce. Keep it at a gentle simmer, partially covered, so the meat turns tender and the sauce turns syrupy.

Title: Chicken Chile Verde Rice Bowls
Ingredients:
1 1/2 lb tomatillos, husks removed and rinsed
3 poblano peppers
1 jalapeno
1 medium yellow onion, half cut into wedges, half diced
3 cloves garlic, unpeeled
2 tbsp neutral oil, divided
1 3/4 lb boneless, skinless chicken breast, cut into 1-inch pieces
1 tsp ground cumin
1 tsp dried Mexican oregano (or regular oregano)
1 cup low-sodium chicken broth
1/2 cup fresh cilantro leaves, roughly chopped, plus more for serving
1 1/2 tsp kosher salt, plus more to taste
1 lime, cut into wedges
1 1/2 cups dry long-grain white rice
2 1/4 cups water
Steps:
1. Mise en place: Move an oven rack to the top position, about 4 inches from the broiler, and turn the broiler to HIGH. Peel the papery husks off the tomatillos and rinse off their sticky coating. Dice means small even cubes - dice half the onion. Cut the other half into wedges. Leave the garlic cloves in their skins (they roast inside and squeeze out sweet and soft). Cut the chicken breast into 1-inch pieces. Chop the cilantro. Line a rimmed baking sheet with foil. Rinse the rice until the water runs mostly clear.
2. Start the rice: combine the rice and 2 1/4 cups of water in a saucepan with a tight lid. Bring to a boil over high heat, stir once, cover, reduce to low, and cook 15 minutes without lifting the lid. Rest, covered, 10 minutes off the heat, then fluff.
3. Arrange the tomatillos (cut-side down), whole poblanos, whole jalapeno, onion wedges, and unpeeled garlic cloves on the foil-lined sheet. Drizzle with 1 tablespoon of the oil and sprinkle with 1/2 teaspoon of the salt. Broil 8-10 minutes, turning the vegetables once halfway, until the skins are blistered and blackened in spots and the tomatillos have softened and released juice. Char equals flavor here - do not be shy.
4. Transfer the hot peppers to a bowl and cover tightly with foil or a plate; let them steam 10 minutes. The steam loosens the skins. Then peel off as much of the blackened skin as comes away easily (a few charred flecks left behind are fine and add smokiness), pull out the stems, and scrape out the seeds from the poblanos and jalapeno. For a milder sauce, remove all the seeds; for heat, leave the jalapeno seeds in.
5. Squeeze the roasted garlic from its skins into a blender. Add the peeled peppers, the tomatillos and ALL their juices from the pan, the raw diced onion, half the cilantro, the cumin, oregano, and the chicken broth. Blend until smooth. It should be vivid green and smell bright and smoky. Season with 1/2 teaspoon of the salt.
6. Heat the remaining 1 tablespoon of oil in a large Dutch oven or deep skillet over medium-high heat. Season the chicken pieces with the remaining 1/2 teaspoon of salt and sear 5-6 minutes, turning, until golden on the outside (they will not be cooked through). Remove to a plate.
7. Pour the green sauce into the same pot - it will sizzle. Scrape up the browned bits. Bring to a simmer and cook 10 minutes, uncovered, until it darkens slightly and thickens enough to coat a spoon. Return the chicken and any juices to the pot. Reduce the heat to low, cover, and simmer 15-20 minutes, until the chicken is tender and reads 165 F inside. Stir in the remaining cilantro and a squeeze of lime. Taste: it should be tangy, smoky, and savory with a gentle heat. Add salt a pinch at a time until it sings.
8. Serve over the rice in bowls, with lime wedges and extra cilantro. The rice soaks up the green sauce - that is the whole point of the bowl. Storage: refrigerate up to 4 days, or freeze up to 3 months. Reheat gently on the stove; the sauce may thicken, so loosen with a splash of broth.

Common mistakes:
1. Skipping the char on the vegetables. Pale, unblistered tomatillos and peppers make a raw-tasting, sour sauce. Broil until genuinely blackened in spots - that char is the chile verde flavor.
2. Adding the cilantro and lime at the start. Both turn dull and bitter with long cooking. Stir them in off the heat at the very end for bright, fresh flavor.
3. Boiling the chicken hard in the sauce. A fierce boil makes chicken breast rubbery. Keep the final simmer gentle and pull the chicken at 165 F - tender, not tough.

Title: Chicken & Chorizo-Style Paella
Ingredients:
4 cups low-sodium chicken broth
1/2 tsp saffron threads (about 1 generous pinch)
1 1/2 lb boneless, skinless chicken thighs, cut into 1 1/2-inch pieces
1 1/2 tsp kosher salt, divided
1/2 tsp freshly ground black pepper
6 oz Spanish cured chorizo, sliced into 1/4-inch coins
3 tbsp olive oil
1 medium yellow onion, finely diced
1 red bell pepper, cut into 1/4-inch strips
3 cloves garlic, minced
2 tsp smoked paprika (pimenton)
1 can (14.5 oz) diced tomatoes, drained
1 1/2 cups bomba rice (or arborio as a substitute)
1 cup frozen peas
1 lemon, cut into wedges
Steps:
1. Mise en place: Slice means thin even pieces - slice the chorizo into 1/4-inch coins and the bell pepper into strips. Dice the onion finely (small 1/4-inch cubes). Mince the garlic. Cut the chicken thighs into 1 1/2-inch pieces. Drain the diced tomatoes. Cut the lemon into wedges. Measure the rice, peas, paprika, salt, and pepper. Pour the broth into a saucepan, crumble in the saffron threads, and warm over low heat until steaming - do NOT boil. Let it steep 10 minutes; the broth will turn golden and smell faintly of hay and honey. Keep it warm the whole time you cook. A wide pan is essential: use a 14-15 inch paella pan, or your widest skillet. Paella needs a thin layer of rice to cook evenly.
2. Heat the olive oil in the paella pan over medium-high heat until shimmering. Season the chicken with 1 teaspoon of the salt and the black pepper. Add the chicken in a single layer and brown 6-7 minutes, turning, until golden on most sides. It will not be cooked through - that happens in the rice. Push the chicken to the edges of the pan.
3. Add the chorizo coins to the center and cook 2 minutes, stirring, until they release their red, paprika-stained fat and crisp at the edges. (Note for purists: chorizo is not in traditional Valencian paella - this is the popular "chorizo-style" weeknight version, and that rendered fat is liquid gold for the rice.)
4. Add the onion and bell pepper to the center. Cook 5 minutes, stirring, until softened. Stir in the garlic and smoked paprika and cook 30 seconds until fragrant - paprika burns fast, so keep it moving. Stir in the drained tomatoes and cook 3-4 minutes until the mixture thickens into a dark, jammy sofrito. This concentrated base is where the paella's depth comes from.
5. Stir in the rice and the remaining 1/2 teaspoon of salt. Toast 2 minutes, stirring, until the grains are coated in the red fat and smell nutty. Now spread the rice into a perfectly even layer across the whole pan - and from this point on, DO NOT STIR. Stirring releases starch and turns paella into risotto.
6. Pour in all the warm saffron broth. It should just cover the rice. Scatter the peas over the top. Bring to a lively simmer over medium-high heat for 5 minutes - you will see the grains dancing. Then reduce to medium-low and cook 15 minutes, uncovered, without touching it. The rice absorbs the broth from the bottom up.
7. Now the socarrat - the prized caramelized crust on the bottom. Listen: when the bubbling sounds change from wet to a faint crackle and you smell a toasty (not burnt) aroma, the bottom is crisping. Give it 2-3 minutes at this stage, then turn off the heat. To check without stirring, slide a thin spatula or spoon gently under one edge of the rice - the bottom should be golden and crisp, not black.
8. Cover the pan with a clean kitchen towel or foil and rest 5 minutes. This lets the last steam finish the grains. Cut the chicken pieces to check: they should read 165 F and the juices run clear; the rice should be tender with a slight bite. Serve straight from the pan with lemon wedges for squeezing - lemon is not traditional in Valencia, but it brightens the rich chorizo beautifully. Storage: refrigerate up to 3 days. Reheat covered in a 350 F oven with a splash of broth; the socarrat will not recrisp, but the flavor holds.

Common mistakes:
1. Stirring after the broth goes in. Every stir breaks grains and releases starch, giving you creamy risotto instead of distinct, separate paella rice. Spread it level once and leave it alone.
2. Using cold broth. Cold liquid shocks the rice and cooks it unevenly. Keep the saffron broth steaming-hot in its saucepan the entire time.
3. Chasing socarrat too hard and burning it. Toasty and crackling is perfect; acrid and black is ruined. When in doubt, pull it off the heat a minute early - a light crust beats a bitter one.

Title: Chicken Dijon Risotto
Ingredients:
1 1/2 lb boneless, skinless chicken breast
1 1/2 tsp kosher salt, divided
1/2 tsp freshly ground black pepper
1 tbsp olive oil
1 large shallot, finely minced
1 1/2 cups arborio rice (do not substitute long-grain rice)
1/2 cup dry white wine
5 cups low-sodium chicken broth
3 tbsp Dijon mustard
1/4 cup heavy cream
3 tbsp cold unsalted butter, cut into small cubes
1/2 cup freshly grated Parmesan cheese
3 tbsp fresh tarragon leaves, chopped (or 1 tbsp fresh thyme leaves)
Steps:
1. Mise en place: Mince means a very fine chop - mince the shallot as fine as you can; it should nearly disappear into the risotto. Cut the cold butter into small cubes and keep it in the fridge until the end - cold butter is what makes the final sauce glossy. Chop the tarragon. Grate the Parmesan. Whisk together the Dijon mustard and heavy cream in a small bowl. Pour the chicken broth into a saucepan and keep it at a bare simmer over low heat for the entire cook - adding cold broth to risotto shocks the grains and ruins the creamy texture. Have a ladle ready.
2. Pat the chicken breasts dry and season both sides with 1/2 teaspoon of the salt and the black pepper. Heat the olive oil in a large deep skillet or Dutch oven over medium-high heat until shimmering. Sear the chicken 5-6 minutes per side without moving it, until deeply golden. It should release easily when the crust is formed; if it sticks, it is not ready to flip. Transfer to a plate and rest 5 minutes (resting keeps the juices in). Then slice across the grain into 1/2-inch strips. Check the thickest piece - 165 F and no pink.
3. Reduce the heat to medium. In the same pan with the chicken drippings, melt 1 tablespoon of the butter. Add the minced shallot and 1/2 teaspoon of the salt. Cook 2-3 minutes, stirring, until soft and translucent but not browned.
4. Add the arborio rice and stir 2 minutes until every grain is coated and the edges turn slightly translucent with a white dot in the center. This toasting step is called tostatura - it seals the grains so they release starch slowly and stay distinct. You will hear a faint crackling and smell a nutty aroma.
5. Pour in the white wine. It will sizzle and steam. Stir until the sharp alcohol smell disappears and the liquid is absorbed, about 2 minutes.
6. Now the rhythm of risotto: add the warm broth one ladle (about 1/2 cup) at a time, stirring frequently and letting each addition absorb before adding the next. Keep the heat at a steady medium so the rice bubbles gently - never a hard boil, never still. This takes 18-20 minutes. Start tasting at 16 minutes: the rice is done when it is creamy and tender with a slight bite at the center (al dente), flowing slowly when you shake the pan. You may not need all 5 cups - stop when the texture is right. Season with the remaining 1/2 teaspoon of salt.
7. Remove the pan from the heat. This next step is the mantecatura, the beating-in that makes risotto silky: add the cold butter cubes, the Parmesan, and the Dijon-cream mixture. Stir vigorously 1-2 minutes until the butter melts into a glossy sauce that waves when you tilt the pan - Italians call this all'onda, "like a wave." Stir in the tarragon.
8. Spoon the risotto into warm shallow bowls, fan the sliced chicken over the top, and finish with a little extra Parmesan and tarragon. Serve immediately - risotto waits for no one and stiffens within minutes. Storage: refrigerate up to 3 days (it will firm up). Reheat gently in a saucepan with a splash of broth, stirring, until creamy again; refresh with a spoonful of Dijon and Parmesan.

Common mistakes:
1. Adding all the broth at once or using cold broth. Risotto's creaminess comes from starch released gradually - one ladle at a time, broth kept simmering, 18-20 minutes of gentle bubbling.
2. Overcooking the rice to mush. Start tasting at 16 minutes and stop at al dente with a slight bite; carryover heat finishes it during the mantecatura.
3. Skipping the rest for the chicken or slicing it hot. The juices run out onto the cutting board instead of staying in the meat - 5 minutes of rest, then slice.

Title: Chicken Fajita Potatoes with Jalapeños
Ingredients:
2 lb Yukon Gold potatoes
3 tbsp olive oil, divided
1 1/2 tsp kosher salt, divided
1 1/2 lb boneless, skinless chicken breast, cut into 1/2-inch strips
2 tbsp chili powder
2 tsp ground cumin
2 tsp smoked paprika
2 tsp garlic powder
1 tsp onion powder
1 tsp dried oregano
1/2 tsp freshly ground black pepper
1/4 tsp cayenne pepper (use 1/2 tsp for extra heat)
3 bell peppers (mixed colors), cut into 1/2-inch strips
1 large yellow onion, cut into 1/2-inch strips
3 jalapenos, sliced into 1/4-inch rings (seeds in for heat, out for mild)
1 lime, cut into wedges
3/4 cup plain Greek yogurt, for serving
1/4 cup fresh cilantro, chopped, for serving
Steps:
1. Mise en place: Dice means small even cubes - cut the potatoes into 3/4-inch cubes (even size so they cook at the same rate). Slice means thin even pieces - cut the chicken breast into 1/2-inch strips across the grain, the bell peppers and onion into 1/2-inch strips, and the jalapenos into 1/4-inch rings. (Wash your hands after handling jalapenos and do not touch your face - the oils burn.) In a small bowl, mix the chili powder, cumin, smoked paprika, garlic powder, onion powder, oregano, black pepper, cayenne, and 1 teaspoon of the salt. This homemade fajita seasoning beats any packet. Cut the lime into wedges. Preheat the oven to 425 F and line a large rimmed baking sheet with foil.
2. Toss the potato cubes with 1 1/2 tablespoons of the olive oil and 1/2 teaspoon of the salt on the baking sheet. Spread in a single layer with space between cubes. Roast 20 minutes. They should be starting to crisp at the edges - shake the pan once halfway through.
3. While the potatoes roast, toss the chicken strips with the remaining 1 1/2 tablespoons of olive oil and ALL of the fajita seasoning, rubbing it into every strip with your hands. Let it sit 10 minutes - even this short rest lets the spices bloom into the meat.
4. Heat your largest skillet (cast iron is ideal) over HIGH heat until it just starts to smoke - about 3 minutes. A screaming-hot pan is the Tex-Mex secret: it sears the outside fast, giving you charred edges and juicy centers instead of pale, steamed chicken. Add half the chicken in a single layer. Let it sit undisturbed 2 minutes until browned underneath, then toss and cook 2-3 minutes more until cooked through. Remove to a plate. Repeat with the rest. Do not crowd - two batches, always.
5. In the same hot skillet, add the bell peppers, onion strips, and jalapeno rings. Sear 4-5 minutes, tossing only once or twice, until charred in spots but still crisp-tender. Fajita vegetables should have bite, not be soft. Squeeze half the lime over them.
6. Push the roasted potatoes (from the oven) into the skillet with the vegetables, or combine everything on the baking sheet. Return the chicken to the pan and toss 1 minute to marry the flavors. Cut the thickest chicken strip - 165 F inside and no pink.
7. Serve family-style from the skillet or in bowls: a base of crispy potatoes, piled with fajita chicken and peppers, a dollop of cool Greek yogurt, a shower of cilantro, and lime wedges for squeezing. The yogurt cools the jalapeno heat the way sour cream does, with more protein. Storage: refrigerate up to 4 days. Reheat in a 400 F oven or hot skillet to re-crisp the potatoes - the microwave makes them soggy.

Common mistakes:
1. Crowding the chicken into the pan. It steams in its own juice and never browns. Sear in two batches over high heat, in a single layer, 2 minutes undisturbed per side.
2. Cooking the peppers and onions until soft. Fajita vegetables should be charred outside and crisp-tender inside - 4-5 minutes, tossed only once or twice.
3. Cutting potatoes in uneven sizes. Big and small cubes on the same pan means some burn while others stay raw. Take the extra minute to cut them all 3/4 inch.

Title: Chicken Fried Rice
Ingredients:
1 3/4 lb boneless, skinless chicken breast
6 cups cooked long-grain white rice, cooked the day before and refrigerated uncovered (from about 2 cups dry rice)
4 large eggs
1 1/2 cups frozen peas and carrots (no need to thaw)
6 green onions
3 garlic cloves
4 tbsp low-sodium soy sauce, divided
1 tbsp toasted sesame oil
2 tbsp avocado oil (or another neutral high-heat oil), divided
1 tsp kosher salt, divided
1/2 tsp ground white pepper (black pepper works too)
Steps:
1. Mise en place (do ALL of this before the stove goes on): Cut the chicken into small dice (small cubes about 1/2 inch on each side). Pat the cubes dry with paper towels and put them in a bowl. Break up any hard clumps in the cold rice with your hands or a fork and leave it in a bowl at the counter -- cold, dry rice fries; wet rice steams. Crack the 4 eggs into a small bowl and beat them with a fork until no streaks remain. Mince the garlic (chop it very fine, almost a paste). Slice the green onions into thin rings, keeping the white bottoms and green tops in two separate piles. Measure the soy sauce, sesame oil, avocado oil, salt, and white pepper into small dishes. This dish cooks in under 15 minutes once the heat is on, so everything must be within arm's reach.
2. Heat your largest skillet or a wok over HIGH heat for 2 full minutes until it is smoking hot. (Restaurant wok burners are far hotter than home stoves; the trick at home is a ripping-hot pan, dry rice, and cooking in small batches so food fries instead of steams.) Add 1 tablespoon of the avocado oil and swirl it around.
3. Pour in the beaten eggs. They should sizzle and puff immediately. Let them sit 20 seconds, then scramble with a spatula, breaking them into small ribbons, 45 to 60 seconds total. They should look just set and pale gold, not browned. Scoop them onto a plate.
4. Add the remaining 1 tablespoon avocado oil to the hot pan. Add HALF the chicken in a single layer -- do not crowd it. Let it sit undisturbed for 90 seconds so it sears and browns, then stir-fry 2 to 3 minutes more until the pieces are golden on the edges and no pink shows when you cut one open. The internal temperature should reach 165 F. Scoop onto the plate with the eggs. Repeat with the remaining chicken. (Two batches keeps the pan hot; one crowded batch would steam the chicken gray.)
5. Drop the heat to medium-high. Add the white parts of the green onions and the minced garlic. Stir constantly for 30 seconds until fragrant -- garlic burns fast at this heat and turns bitter, so keep it moving. Add the frozen peas and carrots and stir-fry 2 minutes until they are hot and bright.
6. Push everything to the edges of the pan. Add the cold rice to the center and spread it into an even layer. Press it down with the spatula and LEAVE IT ALONE for 60 to 90 seconds -- you want the bottom to toast and pick up a few golden, slightly crispy spots. This is the home version of wok hei, the smoky char of restaurant fried rice. Then toss and stir 2 minutes, breaking up any remaining clumps, until every grain is hot and separate.
7. Drizzle 3 tablespoons of the soy sauce around the outer edge of the hot pan, not directly onto the rice. It will hiss and caramelize on the hot metal, giving a deeper, smokier flavor than pouring it on the rice. Toss everything together for 1 minute.
8. Return the chicken and eggs to the pan. Taste a grain of rice: add the last tablespoon of soy sauce only if it needs more salt, and sprinkle over the white pepper. Toss 1 more minute until everything is piping hot.
9. Turn the heat OFF. Drizzle the sesame oil over the top (it is a finishing oil -- heat kills its nutty aroma) and scatter the green onion tops over everything. Give one final gentle fold.
10. Serve: spoon into warm bowls. It is a complete meal on its own.
11. Storage: refrigerate leftovers in a sealed container within 2 hours; they keep 3 to 4 days. Reheat in a hot skillet with a teaspoon of oil (not the microwave) so the rice crisps again instead of going gummy; sprinkle a few drops of water over it as it reheats. Do not reheat more than once.

Common mistakes:
- Using fresh, warm rice. Fresh rice is too moist and turns to mush. Cook it the day before and refrigerate uncovered so the surface dries out. In a pinch, spread fresh rice on a sheet pan and refrigerate 2 hours.
- Crowding the pan. Too much food at once drops the temperature and everything steams. Cook the chicken in two batches and keep the rice in a thin layer.
- Adding the sesame oil during cooking. It is a finishing oil; high heat destroys its flavor. It always goes in off the heat at the very end.
- Overcooking the eggs. They get a second heating when they go back into the pan, so scramble them just until set -- pale and soft, not browned and rubbery.

Title: Chicken Katsu-Style Rice Bowls
Ingredients:
2 lb boneless, skinless chicken breast (4 large breasts)
2 cups short-grain white rice (sushi rice)
2 cups panko breadcrumbs (Japanese-style coarse crumbs)
2 large eggs
1/2 cup all-purpose flour
3 cups finely shredded green cabbage (about 1/2 small head)
1/3 cup tonkatsu sauce (store-bought; Bull-Dog brand is the classic)
1 cup neutral oil for frying (vegetable, canola, or avocado), plus 1 tsp for the cabbage
1 1/2 tsp kosher salt, divided
1/2 tsp black pepper
Lemon wedges, for serving (optional)
Steps:
1. Mise en place: Rinse the rice in a fine-mesh strainer under cold water, swishing with your hand, until the water runs mostly clear -- this washes off excess starch so the rice cooks up fluffy, not gummy. Put the rice and 2 1/4 cups water in a medium saucepan. Shred the cabbage: cut the cabbage half into thin ribbons (slice = thin, even pieces cut across the grain). Set up your breading station: put the flour on one large plate, beat the 2 eggs in a shallow bowl, and spread the panko on a second large plate. Keep a clean plate ready for the breaded cutlets.
2. Cook the rice: bring the saucepan to a boil over high heat, then immediately drop the heat to low, cover with a tight lid, and cook 15 minutes without peeking. Turn the heat off and let it rest, still covered, 10 minutes. Fluff with a fork. The grains should be tender, slightly sticky, and glossy.
3. While the rice cooks, prepare the chicken. Chicken katsu means the cutlets must be an even thickness or they cook unevenly. If a breast is thicker than 1/2 inch, butterfly it: lay your knife hand flat on top of the breast and slice horizontally through the middle, stopping 1/2 inch from the far edge, then open it like a book. Place each piece between two sheets of plastic wrap and pound with a meat mallet, rolling pin, or the bottom of a heavy pan until uniformly 1/2 inch thick. Season both sides of every cutlet with the salt and pepper.
4. Bread the cutlets, one at a time, using one hand for wet and one for dry to keep your fingers from getting caked: dredge in flour (coat fully, then shake off every bit of excess -- extra flour makes the coating slide off), dip in beaten egg (let the excess drip off), then press firmly into the panko, patting so the crumbs stick in a thick, even layer. Lay on the clean plate. Bread all cutlets before any frying starts.
5. Heat the 1 cup of oil in your largest heavy skillet over medium-high heat until it reaches 350 F. No thermometer? Drop in one panko crumb: it should sizzle immediately and float to the surface, turning golden in about 30 seconds. If it browns instantly, the oil is too hot; if it sinks quietly, it is too cool.
6. Fry 2 cutlets at a time (never crowd -- the temperature drops and the crust goes soggy). Fry 3 to 4 minutes per side, turning once, until deep golden brown. The crust should sound crisp and look evenly colored. Lift out with tongs or a slotted spatula and set on a wire rack set over a sheet pan -- a rack keeps the bottom crust crisp; a paper-towel-lined plate traps steam and softens it.
7. Check doneness: the thickest part of the cutlet must read 165 F on an instant-read thermometer. Between batches, skim out any dark crumbs from the oil with a slotted spoon so the next batch does not taste burnt, and let the oil come back to 350 F.
8. Rest the fried cutlets on the rack for 3 to 4 minutes. This is not optional -- the juices redistribute and the crust sets. Then slice each cutlet crosswise into 3/4-inch strips with a sharp knife, pressing straight down rather than sawing, so the crust stays attached.
9. Toss the shredded cabbage with the 1 teaspoon of oil and a pinch of salt (about 1/4 teaspoon). In Japan, katsu is always served with a mountain of crisp shredded cabbage -- it is not a garnish, it is part of the dish.
10. Serve: scoop rice into wide bowls, pile cabbage alongside, and fan the katsu strips over the top. Drizzle with tonkatsu sauce (start with 1 tablespoon per bowl and add more at the table) and add a lemon wedge if you like.
11. Storage: refrigerate leftover katsu and rice separately, up to 3 days. Reheat katsu in a 400 F oven or air fryer 8 to 10 minutes until crisp -- the microwave makes the crust rubbery. Rice reheats well sprinkled with water and covered in the microwave.

Common mistakes:
- Uneven chicken thickness. A breast that is 1 inch on one end and 1/2 inch on the other will be raw at the thick end or dry at the thin end by the time the crust is golden. Pound to a uniform 1/2 inch.
- Frying at the wrong temperature. Oil below 325 F soaks into the panko and makes it greasy; oil above 375 F burns the crust before the chicken cooks through. Hold 350 F and reheat between batches.
- Skipping the rest. Cutting into the cutlet straight out of the oil lets the juices flood out and softens the crust. Three to four minutes on a wire rack makes a real difference.
- Draining on paper towels. It seems tidy, but trapped steam is the enemy of crisp. A wire rack keeps air circulating under the crust.

Title: Chicken Marsala-Style Orzo
Ingredients:
2 lb boneless, skinless chicken breast
1/4 cup all-purpose flour, for dredging
2 cups orzo pasta (about 12 oz)
12 oz cremini mushrooms (baby bella)
1 shallot
3/4 cup dry Marsala wine (NOT sweet -- the bottle should say "dry" or "secco"; Marsala is a fortified wine from Sicily)
3 1/2 cups low-sodium chicken broth
2 tbsp unsalted butter
2 tbsp olive oil, divided
1/4 cup chopped fresh parsley
1 1/2 tsp kosher salt, divided
1/2 tsp black pepper
Steps:
1. Mise en place: Slice each chicken breast horizontally into cutlets about 1/2 inch thick (lay your palm flat on the breast and slice through the middle like opening a book). If any cutlet is thicker than 1/2 inch, pound it gently to even it out. Season both sides with 1 teaspoon of the salt and the pepper, then dredge lightly in the flour: coat each cutlet, then shake off ALL the excess -- you want a whisper of flour, not a coating. The flour gives the sear its golden color and later thickens the sauce. Slice the mushrooms about 1/4 inch thick. Mince the shallot (chop it very fine). Chop the parsley. Measure the wine and broth and set them by the stove.
2. Heat 1 tablespoon of the olive oil in a large, deep skillet or Dutch oven over medium-high heat until it shimmers. Sear the floured cutlets in two batches, 3 to 4 minutes per side, until deep golden brown. Do not move them for the first 2 minutes -- the crust needs contact time to form. They will NOT be cooked through yet; that is fine. Transfer to a plate. If the flour in the pan looks dark brown (not just golden), wipe the pan quickly with a paper towel before the next batch so the sauce does not taste burnt.
3. Drop the heat to medium. Add the remaining 1 tablespoon olive oil and the butter. When the butter foams, add the mushrooms in a single layer. Let them sit undisturbed 2 minutes so they brown, then stir and cook 3 to 4 minutes more until they have released their liquid and turned a rich brown. Browning the mushrooms -- not just softening them -- is where the sauce gets its deep, savory flavor. Add the minced shallot and cook 1 minute until softened and fragrant.
4. Pour in the Marsala wine. It will bubble furiously -- this is the alcohol burning off. Scrape the bottom of the pan with a wooden spoon to dissolve all the browned bits (this is called deglazing, and those bits are pure flavor). Let the wine simmer 2 to 3 minutes until it has reduced by about half and no longer smells sharply of alcohol.
5. Pour in the chicken broth and bring to a gentle boil. Stir in the orzo and the remaining 1/2 teaspoon salt. Cover, reduce the heat to medium-low, and simmer 10 minutes, stirring once halfway through so the orzo does not stick to the bottom. The orzo cooks directly in the Marsala-mushroom broth, absorbing it like a quick risotto.
6. Uncover and nestle the seared chicken cutlets into the orzo, spooning some orzo and sauce over them. Cover and simmer 3 to 4 minutes more, until the orzo is tender with a slight bite (al dente) and the thickest cutlet reads 165 F on an instant-read thermometer. If the pan looks dry, splash in 1/4 cup of water or broth -- the orzo keeps drinking liquid.
7. Turn off the heat. The sauce should lightly coat the orzo and pool a little in the pan. Shower with the chopped parsley and serve directly from the pan in shallow bowls, making sure everyone gets sauce.
8. Storage: refrigerate up to 3 days in a sealed container. The orzo will absorb the sauce overnight -- revive it when reheating with a splash of chicken broth in a covered skillet over medium-low heat, stirring gently, until hot. Microwave works in a pinch with added broth.

Common mistakes:
- Using sweet Marsala. Sweet Marsala (often labeled "dolce") makes the sauce cloying and dessert-like. Buy a bottle that says DRY Marsala -- it is in the wine aisle, not the vinegar aisle, and it keeps for months once opened.
- Skipping the flour dredge or leaving it too thick. No flour means a pale sear and a thin, watery sauce; too much flour makes the sauce gummy and pasty. A light dusting, shaken off well, is the target.
- Not browning the mushrooms. Mushrooms that are merely steamed soft taste flat and rubbery. Give them space in the pan and let them sit until genuinely brown before stirring.
- Overcooking the orzo. It goes from al dente to mushy in about 2 minutes. Start tasting at 9 minutes and pull the pan off the heat while it still has a slight bite -- it keeps cooking in the hot sauce.

Title: Chicken Milanesa with Parmesan Potatoes
Ingredients:
2 lb boneless, skinless chicken breast (4 large breasts)
1/4 cup all-purpose flour
3 large eggs
3 garlic cloves
3 tbsp chopped fresh parsley, plus more for serving
1 1/2 cups plain fine breadcrumbs (pan rallado style -- not Italian-seasoned)
1/2 cup finely grated Parmesan cheese, divided
2 lb Yukon Gold potatoes (about 4 medium)
3 tbsp olive oil, divided
1 lemon, cut into wedges
2 tsp kosher salt, divided, plus more for the potatoes
1 tsp black pepper
Steps:
1. Mise en place: Heat the oven to 425 F and put a large rimmed sheet pan in it to preheat (a hot pan gives the potatoes a head start on crisping). Cut the potatoes into wedges: halve each potato lengthwise, then cut each half into 3 or 4 long wedges about 3/4 inch thick at the wide end. Mince the garlic (chop it very fine). Chop the parsley. Grate the Parmesan if not pre-grated. Cut the lemon into 6 wedges. Set up the breading station: flour on one plate, the beaten eggs whisked with the minced garlic, chopped parsley, 1 teaspoon of the salt, and the pepper in a shallow bowl, and the breadcrumbs mixed with half the Parmesan on a second plate. In Argentina this garlicky, parsley-flecked egg wash is called the ligue -- it is the signature seasoning of a real milanesa.
2. Toss the potato wedges with 1 tablespoon of the olive oil and 1 teaspoon salt. Spread them on the hot sheet pan in a single layer with space between them. Roast 30 to 35 minutes, flipping once halfway, until deep golden and crisp at the edges. A fork should slide in easily.
3. While the potatoes roast, prepare the chicken. Authentic milanesa is pounded very thin -- about 1/4 inch. Butterfly any breast thicker than 1/2 inch (slice horizontally almost through, then open like a book), place between plastic wrap, and pound evenly to 1/4 inch. Thin cutlets cook in minutes and give the ideal crisp-coating-to-meat ratio. Season both sides with the remaining 1 teaspoon salt.
4. Bread the cutlets one at a time: dredge in flour and shake off the excess, dip in the egg ligue letting the excess drip back, then press firmly into the breadcrumb-Parmesan mixture, patting to build an even crust. Lay on a plate. When all are breaded, rest them 10 minutes at room temperature -- this sets the coating so it does not slide off in the oil.
5. Heat the remaining 2 tablespoons olive oil in your largest skillet over medium-high heat until it shimmers and a breadcrumb dropped in sizzles instantly (about 350 F). Fry 2 cutlets at a time, 2 to 3 minutes per side, until deep golden brown and crisp. Do not press them down and do not move them until you flip -- the crust needs undisturbed contact to set. Transfer to a wire rack set over a sheet pan (never paper towels -- steam softens the crust).
6. Check the thickest cutlet with an instant-read thermometer: it must read 165 F. Because the cutlets are so thin, color plus firmness is usually enough, but verify at least one.
7. When the potatoes have 5 minutes left, pull the pan out, sprinkle the remaining Parmesan over the wedges, and return to the oven so the cheese melts into a lacy, golden crust.
8. Serve: plate each milanesa with a pile of Parmesan potatoes, lemon wedges alongside, and a pinch of fresh parsley. In Buenos Aires, a squeeze of lemon over the cutlet is not optional -- it cuts the richness and brightens the whole plate.
9. Storage: refrigerate leftovers separately up to 3 days. Reheat milanesa on a rack in a 400 F oven 8 to 10 minutes to re-crisp; the microwave ruins the crust. Potatoes reheat well the same way.

Common mistakes:
- Pounding unevenly or not thin enough. Thick spots stay raw while thin spots overcook, and a thick cutlet needs so long in the oil that the crust burns. Take the time to get every cutlet to an even 1/4 inch.
- Seasoning only the meat. Argentine cooks season every station -- the egg ligue carries the garlic, parsley, salt, and pepper so the flavor is IN the crust, not just on the chicken. An unseasoned coating tastes like plain fried bread.
- Skipping the 10-minute rest after breading. A fresh, wet coating slides right off in hot oil. The short rest lets the egg glue set.
- Crowding the skillet. More than 2 cutlets drops the oil temperature, the breading absorbs oil instead of crisping, and you get greasy milanesa. Fry in batches and let the oil come back up to a sizzle between them.

Title: Chicken Moqueca-Style Rice
Ingredients:
2 lb boneless, skinless chicken breast
2 limes (1 juiced, 1 cut into wedges for serving)
4 garlic cloves, divided
2 tsp kosher salt, divided
2 cups long-grain white rice
2 tbsp olive oil, divided
1 large yellow onion
1 large red bell pepper
1 can (14.5 oz) diced tomatoes, drained
1 can (13.5 oz) full-fat coconut milk (shake the can well first)
1 tbsp achiote oil -- the home substitute for dende (red palm oil): warm 1 tbsp avocado oil with 1 tsp annatto seeds over low heat 3 minutes until the oil turns deep orange, then strain out the seeds. (Or use 1 tbsp olive oil plus 1/2 tsp sweet paprika.)
2 tsp sweet paprika
1/2 cup chopped fresh cilantro, plus whole leaves for serving
Steps:
1. Mise en place: Cut the chicken into 1 1/2-inch cubes (bigger than bite-size -- they shrink and must survive a 20-minute simmer). Put the cubes in a bowl with the juice of 1 lime, 2 minced garlic cloves (mince = chop very fine), and 1 teaspoon of the salt. Toss and refrigerate 15 minutes -- this quick lime marinade is classic Bahian seasoning and gently firms the chicken. Meanwhile, slice the onion into thin half-moons (slice = thin, even pieces): halve the onion top to bottom, then slice across. Slice the bell pepper into thin strips. Drain the diced tomatoes. Chop the cilantro. Make the achiote oil now if using annatto seeds. Measure the coconut milk, paprika, rice, and olive oil.
2. Start the rice Brazilian-style: heat 1 tablespoon of the olive oil in a medium saucepan over medium heat. Add the remaining 2 garlic cloves, minced, and cook 30 seconds until fragrant. Add the rice and stir 2 minutes until the grains look slightly translucent at the edges and smell toasty -- this is how rice is started all over Brazil and it keeps the grains separate. Add 3 cups water and the remaining 1 teaspoon salt, bring to a boil, then cover, drop the heat to low, and cook 15 minutes. Rest covered 5 minutes, then fluff.
3. While the rice cooks, build the moqueca in a large, wide pot or Dutch oven (a wide pot lets the steam escape so the stew stays rich, not watery). Drizzle in the remaining 1 tablespoon olive oil. Layer in this order: the sliced onion, then the bell pepper strips, then the drained tomatoes. Lift the chicken out of its marinade (discard the leftover marinade) and arrange the cubes over the vegetables in a single layer.
4. Pour the coconut milk evenly over everything. Drizzle the achiote oil over the top and sprinkle with the sweet paprika. The orange-red oil swirling on the coconut milk is the visual signature of a Bahian moqueca -- dende oil is traditional but nearly impossible to find outside Brazil, and the achiote oil gives the same sunset color.
5. Cover the pot and bring to a gentle simmer over medium heat -- you want lazy bubbles, not a rolling boil. Then reduce the heat to medium-low and cook, COVERED, 20 minutes. Do NOT stir: stirring breaks the chicken apart and clouds the broth. The layers steam in the coconut milk and everything cooks through undisturbed. The stew is done when the chicken reads 165 F inside and the peppers are silky-soft.
6. Uncover, scatter the chopped cilantro over the top, and squeeze the second lime's juice over everything (start with half the lime, taste, add more if you like). Taste the broth and add salt if needed.
7. Serve: spoon fluffy rice into wide bowls and ladle the moqueca -- chicken, vegetables, and plenty of the orange-gold broth -- over the top. Finish with whole cilantro leaves and lime wedges on the side.
8. Storage: refrigerate up to 3 days (coconut-milk stews keep well). Reheat gently in a covered pot over medium-low heat -- never a hard boil, which can split the coconut milk and toughen the chicken. Rice reheats best sprinkled with a little water and covered in the microwave.

Common mistakes:
- Boiling hard instead of simmering gently. A rolling boil shreds the chicken, turns the vegetables to mush, and can make the coconut milk separate into an oily layer. Lazy bubbles, lid on, 20 minutes.
- Stirring the pot. Every traditional moqueca recipe says the same thing: layer it, cover it, leave it alone. Stirring breaks the chicken cubes and muddies the beautiful layered broth.
- Skipping the lime marinade or the finishing lime. Lime juice at both the start and the end is what makes moqueca taste bright instead of heavy -- the rich coconut milk needs that acidity.
- Using light coconut milk or skipping the achiote oil. Light coconut milk makes a thin, watery broth, and without the red oil the dish loses its signature color and depth. Full-fat coconut milk and the quick achiote oil are worth it.

Title: Chicken, Olive & Tomato Orzo
Ingredients:
2 lb boneless, skinless chicken breast
2 tsp dried oregano, divided
2 cups orzo pasta (about 12 oz)
4 cups low-sodium chicken broth
1 1/2 pints cherry tomatoes (about 3 cups)
3/4 cup pitted Kalamata olives, halved
3 garlic cloves
2 tbsp olive oil
1/2 cup crumbled feta cheese
1 lemon
1 1/2 tsp kosher salt, divided
1/2 tsp black pepper
Steps:
1. Mise en place: Cut the chicken into 1-inch chunks (small cubes about 1 inch on each side). Pat dry and toss with 1 teaspoon of the oregano, 1 teaspoon of the salt, and the pepper. Halve the cherry tomatoes (slice each one through its middle). Halve the Kalamata olives lengthwise. Mince the garlic (chop it very fine). Crumble the feta if not pre-crumbled. Cut the lemon in half. Measure the orzo and broth and keep them by the stove.
2. Heat the olive oil in a large, deep skillet or Dutch oven over medium-high heat until it shimmers.
