Add the chicken in a single layer -- work in two batches if it crowds -- and brown 5 to 6 minutes, turning once, until golden on the outside. It does not need to be cooked through yet. You are building flavor on the surface; the orzo step finishes the cooking. Transfer to a plate.
3. Drop the heat to medium. Add the minced garlic and the remaining 1 teaspoon oregano; stir 30 seconds until fragrant. Add the dry orzo and stir 1 to 2 minutes until the grains are lightly toasted and smell nutty. Toasting the orzo first keeps each grain distinct instead of gummy.
4. Pour in the chicken broth -- it will steam and bubble. Scrape the bottom of the pan to release the browned bits from the chicken. Add the remaining 1/2 teaspoon salt and bring to a boil. Return the chicken (and any juices on the plate) to the pan.
5. Cover, reduce the heat to medium-low, and simmer 10 minutes, stirring once halfway through. The orzo absorbs the broth and turns creamy as its starch releases.
6. Uncover and stir in the halved tomatoes and olives. Cook 3 minutes more, uncovered, until the tomatoes just start to slump and release their juices but still hold their shape, the orzo is tender with a slight bite, and the chicken reads 165 F inside. If the pan looks dry before the orzo is tender, add 1/4 cup water.
7. Squeeze the juice of half the lemon over the pan, stir, and taste. Add more lemon or salt until it tastes bright and balanced -- the lemon is what lifts this from heavy to fresh. Cut the remaining half into wedges for the table.
8. Turn off the heat and shower the crumbled feta over the top. Let it sit 2 minutes so the feta softens slightly in the residual heat without fully melting. Serve in shallow bowls with lemon wedges.
9. Storage: refrigerate up to 3 days. The orzo drinks up liquid overnight, so reheat in a covered skillet over medium-low heat with a splash of water or broth, stirring gently. Add fresh feta after reheating rather than before -- reheated feta goes rubbery.

Common mistakes:
- Adding the tomatoes too early. Ten minutes of simmering turns cherry tomatoes into mush and dulls their fresh flavor. They go in for the last 3 minutes only, so they stay bright and just-burst.
- Not toasting the orzo. Skipping the 2-minute toast gives you soft, porridge-like orzo. The toast builds a nutty flavor and helps the grains stay separate.
- Forgetting the lemon at the end. Without acid, the olives and feta make the dish taste flat and salty. Taste after the first squeeze and add more until it tastes alive.
- Overcooking the chicken in step 2. The chunks finish cooking in the broth; if you cook them through during browning, they will be dry and tough by serving time. Brown the outside, then get them out.

Title: Chicken Parmesan Risotto
Ingredients:
2 lb boneless, skinless chicken breast (4 large breasts)
2 tbsp olive oil
2 cups arborio rice (risotto rice -- do not substitute long-grain rice)
1 yellow onion
6 cups low-sodium chicken broth
3/4 cup finely grated Parmesan cheese, plus more for serving
2 tbsp unsalted butter, cut into small pieces
1 1/2 cups marinara sauce (store-bought is fine)
1 cup shredded part-skim mozzarella
1/4 cup chopped fresh basil
1 1/2 tsp kosher salt, divided
1/2 tsp black pepper
Steps:
1. Mise en place: Dice the onion (cut into small cubes about 1/2 inch). Grate the Parmesan if not pre-grated. Chop the basil. Cut the butter into small pieces and keep it cold in the fridge -- cold butter is key for the creamy finish. Pour the broth into a separate saucepan and keep it at a bare simmer over low heat the entire time you cook the risotto; adding cold broth would shock the rice and ruin the creamy texture. Pat the chicken breasts dry and season both sides with 1 teaspoon of the salt and the pepper. Warm the marinara in a small saucepan over low heat.
2. Heat the olive oil in a large, wide, heavy pot or Dutch oven over medium-high heat until shimmering. Sear the chicken breasts 6 minutes per side without moving them, until deep golden brown. Transfer to a plate -- they should read 150 to 155 F now; they will finish cooking as they rest and under the broiler later. Tent loosely with foil and rest at least 5 minutes.
3. Pour off any burnt bits but leave the browned fond in the pot. Drop the heat to medium. Add the diced onion and cook 4 minutes, stirring, until soft and translucent. Add the arborio rice and stir constantly for 2 minutes. This step is called the tostatura: the grains should turn pearly-translucent at the edges with a white dot in the center and smell faintly nutty. It seals the grains so they release starch slowly -- the whole secret of creamy risotto.
4. Add one ladle (about 3/4 cup) of the hot broth. Stir with a wooden spoon, scraping the bottom. When the liquid is almost fully absorbed and the spoon leaves a brief trail on the bottom of the pot, add another ladle. Keep the heat at a steady, gentle bubble -- never a hard boil, never still. Continue ladle by ladle, stirring often, for 18 to 20 minutes. Taste at 18 minutes: the rice is done when it is tender with a slight bite in the center (al dente) and the overall texture flows like thick porridge. You may not need all 6 cups; stop adding broth when the texture is right.
5. Take the pot OFF the heat. This next step is the mantecatura, the Lombard technique that makes risotto glossy: beat in the cold butter pieces and the Parmesan, stirring vigorously until melted and the risotto looks creamy and shiny. It should spread slowly when you tilt the pot -- risotto should flow, not stand in a heap. Season with the remaining 1/2 teaspoon salt, taste, and adjust.
6. Slice the rested chicken breasts across the grain into 1/2-inch strips. Spoon the risotto into wide, shallow bowls. Fan the chicken slices over each bowl, spoon the warm marinara over the chicken, and scatter the mozzarella on top.
7. Set your oven broiler to HIGH and position a rack 6 inches from the element. Slide the bowls (only if they are broiler-safe; otherwise transfer to a sheet pan first) under the broiler for 1 to 2 minutes, watching constantly, until the mozzarella melts into gooey spots with a few browned edges. Do not walk away -- broilers turn cheese from melted to burnt in under a minute.
8. Finish each bowl with chopped basil and extra Parmesan. Serve immediately -- risotto waits for no one and starts to stiffen within minutes.
9. Storage: refrigerate up to 3 days. Risotto firms up cold; reheat in a saucepan over medium-low heat with a generous splash of broth, stirring until it loosens and turns creamy again. The microwave works with added broth, stirred halfway. Reheat the chicken gently so it does not dry out.

Common mistakes:
- Adding cold broth or all the broth at once. Cold broth stops the cooking and makes the rice gummy; dumping it all in boils the rice like pasta instead of coaxing out starch. Keep the broth simmering and add it one ladle at a time.
- Walking away during the 18 minutes. Risotto needs frequent stirring to release its starch evenly. Stir every minute or two, scraping the bottom so nothing sticks and scorches.
- Skipping the mantecatura or doing it over heat. Butter and Parmesan beaten in OFF the heat emulsify into a glossy sauce; over heat they can separate into a greasy slick.
- Overcooking to mush. Risotto should be al dente -- tender with a tiny bite -- and loose enough to flow. If it stands up in a stiff mound, it went too far; loosen with a splash of hot broth.

Title: Chicken Parm Pasta Bake
Ingredients:
2 lb boneless, skinless chicken breast
16 oz penne pasta (1 standard box)
3 cups marinara sauce (one 24-oz jar plus a little, or 3 cups homemade)
1 1/2 cups shredded part-skim mozzarella, divided
1/2 cup finely grated Parmesan cheese, divided
3/4 cup panko breadcrumbs
2 tsp Italian seasoning
2 tbsp olive oil
1 1/2 tsp kosher salt, divided, plus 1 tbsp for the pasta water
Steps:
1. Mise en place: Heat the oven to 400 F. Bring a large pot of water to a rolling boil and salt it generously (1 tablespoon -- the water should taste like the sea; this is the only chance to season the pasta itself). Cut the chicken into 1-inch cubes (small cubes about 1 inch on each side) and pat dry. Toss the cubes with the Italian seasoning and 1 teaspoon of the salt. Shred the mozzarella and grate the Parmesan if not pre-done. In a small bowl, mix the panko with half the Parmesan and 1 teaspoon of olive oil -- rubbing the oil into the crumbs with your fingers helps them brown evenly. Lightly oil a 9x13-inch baking dish.
2. Cook the penne in the boiling water for 2 minutes LESS than the package says for al dente. It will cook more in the oven, so undercooking now is essential -- fully cooked pasta turns to mush in the bake. Drain (do not rinse) and return to the pot.
3. While the pasta cooks, heat the remaining olive oil (about 1 tablespoon plus 2 teaspoons) in a large skillet over medium-high heat until shimmering. Brown the chicken cubes in a single layer, 6 to 7 minutes, turning once, until golden on the outside. They do not need to be cooked through -- the oven finishes them. If your skillet is small, brown in two batches so the chicken sears instead of steams.
4. Pour the marinara over the drained penne in the pot and add the browned chicken with all its juices. Add 1 cup of the mozzarella and half the remaining Parmesan. Toss everything together, then spread into the oiled baking dish in an even layer.
5. Sprinkle the remaining 1/2 cup mozzarella evenly over the top, then the remaining Parmesan, then the panko-Parmesan mixture in an even layer. The cheese goes under the crumbs so the crumbs crisp directly in the oven heat while the cheese melts beneath.
6. Bake uncovered 20 to 22 minutes, until the sauce bubbles vigorously around the edges, the panko is deep golden brown, and the center reads 165 F on an instant-read thermometer. If the top browns before the center is hot, tent loosely with foil for the last 5 minutes.
7. Rest 10 minutes before serving. This is not optional -- the bake needs time to set so it scoops in hearty portions instead of sliding apart into soup. The sauce thickens as it stands.
8. Serve: scoop generous portions into bowls with a big spoon, making sure everyone gets some of the crispy crumb topping.
9. Storage: refrigerate up to 4 days in a sealed container, or freeze up to 3 months (thaw overnight in the fridge). Reheat covered in a 350 F oven 20 minutes, then uncovered 5 minutes to re-crisp the top; add a spoonful of marinara if it looks dry. Single portions reheat well in the microwave with a damp paper towel over the top.

Common mistakes:
- Cooking the pasta fully before baking. Pasta that is already al dente becomes mushy after 20 minutes in hot sauce. Always pull it 2 minutes early.
- Skipping the rest. Cutting into the bake straight from the oven gives you a soupy slide instead of scoopable portions. Ten minutes lets the starches set and the sauce thickens.
- Uneven topping. Dumping the panko in clumps means some bites are bare and others are all crunch. Scatter it in a thin, even layer so every serving gets the crispy lid.
- A dry bake. If your marinara is very thick or you skimp on sauce, the pasta drinks it all and the bake turns stiff. The pasta should look generously saucy -- almost too saucy -- going into the oven.

Title: Chicken Pesto Orzo with Broccoli
Ingredients:
2 lb boneless, skinless chicken breast
2 cups orzo pasta (about 12 oz)
1 1/2 lb broccoli florets (about 2 large heads, cut into bite-size pieces)
1/3 cup finely grated Parmesan cheese, plus more for serving
1 lemon
2 tbsp olive oil
1 tsp kosher salt, divided, plus 1 tbsp for the pasta water
1/2 tsp black pepper
For the fresh pesto Genovese (makes about 3/4 cup):
2 cups packed fresh basil leaves (about 2 large bunches -- leaves only, no thick stems)
1/4 cup pine nuts
1/3 cup finely grated Parmigiano-Reggiano
2 tbsp finely grated pecorino Romano (Parmesan works if you cannot find it)
1/3 cup extra-virgin olive oil, plus more if needed
1 small garlic clove
1/2 tsp kosher salt
Steps:
1. Mise en place: Cut the chicken into bite-size pieces (about 1-inch cubes) and pat dry; season with 1/2 teaspoon of the salt and the pepper. Cut the broccoli into small, bite-size florets -- big chunks will not cook through in time. Pick the basil leaves off the stems and measure the pine nuts, cheeses, and olive oil for the pesto. Peel the garlic clove. Zest the lemon (grate only the yellow outer skin, not the bitter white pith underneath) and then cut it in half for juicing. Bring a large pot of water to a rolling boil and salt it with 1 tablespoon of salt.
2. Make the pesto Genovese -- the raw basil sauce of Liguria. Put the pine nuts, garlic, and 1/2 teaspoon salt in a food processor and pulse 5 to 6 times until coarsely ground. Add the basil leaves and pulse in short bursts -- 10 to 15 pulses -- scraping down the sides once, just until the basil breaks down into a coarse paste. Do NOT run the processor continuously: heat and over-processing turn basil dark and bitter. Add both cheeses and pulse twice to combine. With the processor running on low, drizzle in the 1/3 cup olive oil until you have a thick, spoonable, slightly textured sauce -- real pesto is never baby-food smooth. Taste and add salt if needed. Set aside. (If your kitchen is very warm, chill the processor bowl 10 minutes first; cold keeps the pesto bright green.)
3. Cook the orzo in the boiling salted water, stirring once at the start so it does not stick. After 6 minutes, add the broccoli florets to the same pot. Cook 3 minutes more -- the orzo should be tender with a slight bite and the broccoli bright green and just tender when pierced with a fork. Before draining, scoop out 1 cup of the starchy pasta water and set it aside (this liquid gold loosens the pesto into a sauce). Drain the orzo and broccoli together.
4. While the orzo cooks, heat the 2 tablespoons olive oil in a large skillet over medium-high heat until shimmering. Add the chicken in a single layer and cook 6 to 7 minutes, turning once, until golden on the outside and 165 F inside with no pink remaining. Transfer to a plate.
5. Return the drained orzo and broccoli to the warm (not hot) pot, OFF the heat. Add the pesto and 1/2 cup of the reserved pasta water. Toss gently but thoroughly -- the starchy water thins the pesto into a glossy sauce that coats every grain. This is the most important rule of pesto: NEVER cook it. Heat above a simmer destroys its fresh basil flavor and turns it dull olive-brown. The residual warmth of the pasta is all it needs. Add more pasta water a splash at a time until the orzo looks creamy and well coated.
6. Fold in the cooked chicken, the lemon zest, and a squeeze of lemon juice (start with half the lemon). Shower with the 1/3 cup Parmesan and toss once more. Taste: it should be bright, nutty, and savory. Add more lemon juice, salt, or Parmesan until it sings.
7. Serve: spoon into wide bowls and finish with extra Parmesan and a few basil leaves if you have them.
8. Storage: refrigerate up to 3 days. The pesto will darken a little overnight -- that is normal oxidation and it still tastes fine. Reheat gently in a skillet over medium-low heat with a splash of water, stirring just until warm; do not boil or blast it in the microwave on high, which kills the fresh pesto flavor. It is also excellent cold as a pasta salad the next day.

Common mistakes:
- Cooking the pesto. Even 30 seconds in a hot pan turns fresh pesto bitter and brown. It always goes into warm pasta OFF the heat, loosened with pasta water.
- Over-processing the basil. Running the food processor nonstop heats the leaves and makes the pesto dark and harsh. Short pulses, scrape once, stop while it is still slightly coarse.
- Forgetting to reserve pasta water. Without the starchy water, the pesto sits in clumps instead of becoming a silky sauce. Scoop out the cup BEFORE you drain -- you cannot get it back afterward.
- Overcooking the broccoli. Mushy, gray-green broccoli drags the whole dish down. Three minutes in the orzo water is enough -- it should be bright green with a little bite.

Title: Chicken with Tomato Olive Salsa
Ingredients:
2 lb boneless, skinless chicken breast (4 large breasts)
1 1/2 cups pearled farro (quick-cooking kind if you can find it)
1 1/2 pints cherry tomatoes (about 3 cups)
1/2 cup Castelvetrano olives, pitted and roughly chopped (the bright-green Sicilian olives; Kalamata work in a pinch)
2 tbsp capers, drained and roughly chopped
1 shallot
1/4 cup chopped fresh basil, plus whole leaves for serving
3 tbsp extra-virgin olive oil, divided
2 tbsp red wine vinegar
1 1/2 tsp kosher salt, divided, plus 1 tbsp for the farro water
1/2 tsp black pepper
Steps:
1. Mise en place: Bring a medium saucepan of water to a boil and salt it with 1 tablespoon of salt. Quarter the cherry tomatoes (cut each in half, then each half in half). Roughly chop the pitted olives and the drained capers -- you want chunky pieces, not a paste. Mince the shallot (chop it very fine). Chop the basil. Whisk together in a medium bowl: the tomatoes, olives, capers, minced shallot, basil, 2 tablespoons of the olive oil, the red wine vinegar, and 1/2 teaspoon of the salt. Set the salsa aside at room temperature -- 20 minutes of resting lets the flavors marry, and it should taste bright, briny, and punchy. Pound the chicken breasts to an even 3/4 inch: place between plastic wrap and pound the thick end down to match the thin end. Even thickness is the whole game for juicy chicken. Season both sides with the remaining 1 teaspoon salt and the pepper.
2. Add the farro to the boiling salted water, reduce to a steady simmer, and cook 25 to 30 minutes (15 to 20 if using quick-cooking pearled farro), until chewy-tender -- soft enough to eat comfortably but with a pleasant bite, never mushy. Drain well and return to the pot, covered, to steam 5 minutes.
3. While the farro cooks, heat the remaining 1 tablespoon olive oil in a large skillet over medium-high heat until it shimmers. Lay in the chicken breasts -- they should sizzle on contact. Sear 5 to 6 minutes per side without moving them, until deep golden brown. The chicken is done when the thickest part reads 165 F on an instant-read thermometer and the juices run clear.
4. Transfer the chicken to a clean plate and rest 5 to 10 minutes. Resting lets the juices redistribute; slice too soon and they flood the cutting board instead of staying in the meat. Then slice each breast across the grain into 1/2-inch strips.
5. Fluff the farro with a fork, taste, and add salt if needed. Spoon it into wide bowls or onto a platter. Fan the sliced chicken over the farro and spoon the tomato-olive salsa -- with all its briny juices -- generously over the top. Finish with whole basil leaves and a thread of your best olive oil if you have it.
6. Storage: refrigerate the chicken, farro, and salsa in separate containers up to 3 days (the salsa softens if stored on the chicken). Reheat chicken and farro in a covered skillet over medium-low heat with a splash of water, or in the microwave; serve the salsa at room temperature spooned over the top. The salsa itself keeps 4 days and is excellent on fish, eggs, or crusty bread.

Common mistakes:
- Slicing the chicken the second it leaves the pan. Five to ten minutes of rest is the difference between juicy slices and a dry breast sitting in a puddle. Tent loosely with foil -- do not wrap tightly or the crust steams soft.
- Uneven chicken thickness. An unpounded breast is twice as thick at one end; by the time the thick end hits 165 F, the thin end is overcooked and dry. Two minutes of pounding fixes it completely.
- Making the salsa at the last second or salting it too early. It needs about 20 minutes for the shallot to mellow and the juices to mingle -- but salt it right before that rest, not hours ahead, or the tomatoes go watery.
- Overcooking the farro. Farro goes from pleasantly chewy to blown-out mush quickly at the end. Start tasting 5 minutes before the package time and drain it the moment it is chewy-tender.

Title: Chili Garlic Shrimp with Bok Choy
Ingredients:
2 1/4 lb large shrimp, peeled and deveined, tails off
2 1/4 cups jasmine rice
3 cups water
1 1/2 lb baby bok choy
6 cloves garlic
1 tablespoon fresh ginger
3 green onions
3 tablespoons chili garlic sauce
3 tablespoons low-sodium soy sauce
2 tablespoons rice vinegar
1 tablespoon honey
2 tablespoons avocado oil, divided
1/2 teaspoon kosher salt, plus more for the rice
Steps:
1. Mise en place (get everything ready before you turn on any heat): Rinse the shrimp in a colander under cold water and pat them VERY dry with paper towels - dry shrimp sear instead of steam. Mince the garlic (a mince is a very fine chop - keep rocking the knife through the pile until the pieces are smaller than rice grains) and mince the ginger the same way. Slice the green onions into thin rings, keeping the white bottoms and green tops in separate piles. Halve each baby bok choy lengthwise through the root so the leaves stay attached. Measure the rice, water, chili garlic sauce, soy sauce, rice vinegar, and honey into small bowls. Stir the chili garlic sauce, soy sauce, rice vinegar, and honey together in one bowl - this is your stir-fry sauce.
2. Cook the rice: Put the rice, 3 cups water, and a pinch of salt in a medium saucepan. Bring to a boil over high heat, then immediately reduce to low, cover with a tight lid, and cook 15 minutes without lifting the lid. Remove from heat and let it stand, still covered, 5 minutes, then fluff with a fork. You will start the stir-fry while it stands.
3. Sear the bok choy: Heat 1 tablespoon of the oil in a large skillet or wok over medium-high heat until it shimmers and a drop of water dances. Lay the bok choy halves cut-side down in a single layer (cook in two batches if crowded). Sear undisturbed 2 minutes until the cut sides turn deep golden brown. Flip, add 3 tablespoons water, cover, and steam 1 minute - the leaves should be bright green and the stems tender-crisp, not limp. Sprinkle with the 1/2 teaspoon salt and transfer to a serving platter.
4. Stir-fry the aromatics and shrimp: Return the pan to medium-high heat and add the remaining 1 tablespoon oil. Add the garlic, ginger, and white parts of the green onions; stir constantly for 20 seconds until you smell a sharp, sweet fragrance - do not let the garlic turn brown or it will taste bitter. Add the shrimp in a single layer and cook 2 minutes without moving them, then flip and cook 1-2 minutes more until they curl into a C-shape and turn fully pink and opaque. (C = cooked, O = overcooked.)
5. Sauce and serve: Pour the sauce over the shrimp and toss 30 seconds until it bubbles and coats everything in a glossy glaze. Taste a shrimp - if you want more heat, add another teaspoon of chili garlic sauce. Spoon the shrimp and sauce over the rice and arrange the bok choy alongside. Scatter the green onion tops over everything.
6. Storage: Refrigerate leftovers in an airtight container up to 2 days. Reheat gently in a covered skillet over medium-low heat with a splash of water 2-3 minutes until just warm - the microwave makes shrimp rubbery. Rice reheats best sprinkled with a teaspoon of water and covered.
Common mistakes:
- Wet shrimp: If you skip patting the shrimp dry, they release water and steam gray instead of searing pink with golden edges. Dry them twice if needed.
- Burning the garlic: Garlic goes from fragrant to bitter and brown in under a minute over high heat. Add it right before the shrimp and keep it moving.
- Overcooked shrimp: Shrimp finish in 3-4 minutes total. Pull them the moment they curl into a C; an O-shape means they will be tough.

Title: Chili Lime Shrimp Noodle Bowls
Ingredients:
2 1/4 lb large shrimp, peeled and deveined
12 oz dried flat rice noodles
3 limes
3 tablespoons fish sauce
2 tablespoons sweet chili sauce
1 tablespoon granulated sugar
2 cloves garlic
1 teaspoon red pepper flakes (start with 1/2 teaspoon if you are heat-shy)
1 1/2 English cucumbers
3 medium carrots
1/3 cup roasted peanuts
3/4 cup fresh cilantro leaves
1 tablespoon avocado oil
1/2 teaspoon kosher salt
Steps:
1. Mise en place: Mince the garlic very fine (mince = pieces smaller than rice grains). Juice the limes into a small bowl - you want about 1/3 cup. Chop the peanuts into rough pieces. Pick the cilantro leaves off the tough stems. Peel the carrots. Cut the cucumber and carrots into matchsticks: first slice each into thin planks, stack the planks, then cut into thin sticks about 3 inches long and as thick as a match. Whisk together the lime juice, fish sauce, sweet chili sauce, sugar, garlic, and red pepper flakes until the sugar dissolves - taste it: it should be bright and tangy with a salty-sweet finish. If it makes you pucker, add 1 teaspoon more sugar.
2. Cook the noodles: Bring a large pot of water to a rolling boil. Add the rice noodles and cook 1 minute less than the package says (usually 4-6 minutes) - they should be tender but still a little chewy, since they soften a bit more in the dressing. Drain, rinse under cold water to stop the cooking, and shake very dry in the colander.
3. Cook the shrimp: Pat the shrimp dry with paper towels and toss with the salt. Heat the oil in a large skillet over medium-high heat until shimmering. Add the shrimp in a single layer and sear 2 minutes per side until pink, curled, and opaque in the center. Transfer to a bowl and toss with 2 tablespoons of the dressing while still warm - warm shrimp soak up flavor best.
4. Assemble the bowls: In a very large bowl, toss the noodles, cucumber, and carrots with the remaining dressing until every strand glistens. Divide among 6 bowls. Top each with shrimp, peanuts, and cilantro. Serve immediately with any extra lime wedges on the side.
5. Storage: This bowl is best eaten fresh - rice noodles turn gummy overnight. If you must store, keep the dressed noodles, shrimp, and vegetables in separate containers up to 1 day; refresh the noodles with a 30-second dip in hot water before eating.
Common mistakes:
- Overcooking the noodles: Rice noodles go from perfect to mush in under a minute. Start tasting a full minute before the package time and rinse them cold the moment they are tender.
- Too-sour dressing: Fish sauce and lime are both aggressive. The tablespoon of sugar is not optional - it balances the Thai sweet-sour-salty triangle. Taste and adjust before you pour.
- Crowding the shrimp: Shrimp packed together steam instead of sear. Cook in two batches if your skillet cannot hold them in one layer.

Title: Chipotle Beef & Black Bean Rice
Ingredients:
2 lb 93% lean ground beef
2 1/4 cups long-grain white rice
3 3/4 cups water, plus more as needed
2 (15-ounce) cans black beans
1 (28-ounce) can diced tomatoes
3 chipotle peppers in adobo sauce
2 tablespoons adobo sauce (from the can)
1 large yellow onion
3 cloves garlic
1 1/2 teaspoons ground cumin
1 teaspoon dried oregano
2 limes
1/3 cup chopped fresh cilantro
1 tablespoon avocado oil
1 1/2 teaspoons kosher salt, divided, plus more to taste
1/2 teaspoon black pepper
Steps:
1. Mise en place: Dice the onion - dice means small even cubes about 1/2 inch; cut the onion in half, make horizontal and vertical cuts, then slice across to release cubes. Mince the garlic very fine. Mince the chipotle peppers very fine (wash your hands well after - chipotle oil burns eyes). Measure the adobo sauce, cumin, oregano, salt, and pepper. Drain and rinse the black beans in a colander until the water runs clear. Juice 1 lime (about 2 tablespoons); cut the other into 6 wedges. Chop the cilantro.
2. Cook the rice: In a medium saucepan, combine the rice, 3 3/4 cups water, and 1/2 teaspoon of the salt. Bring to a boil over high heat, reduce to low, cover, and cook 18 minutes without peeking. Remove from heat, stand covered 5 minutes, then fluff and fold in the lime juice and half the cilantro. Cover to keep warm.
3. Brown the beef: Heat the oil in a large deep skillet or Dutch oven over medium-high heat until shimmering. Add the beef and onion together, breaking the beef into small crumbles with a wooden spoon. Cook 8-10 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the beef is deeply browned in spots and the onion is soft - browning, not graying, is where the flavor lives. Drain off any excess fat by tilting the pan and spooning it out.
4. Build the chipotle base: Stir in the garlic, minced chipotles, adobo sauce, cumin, oregano, the remaining 1 teaspoon salt, and the black pepper. Cook 1 minute, stirring, until the spices smell toasty and the paste coats the meat. Pour in the diced tomatoes with their juices and the rinsed beans. Bring to a simmer, then reduce to medium-low and cook 8-10 minutes, stirring occasionally, until thickened enough that a spoon leaves a trail. Taste - for more smoke and heat, stir in another teaspoon of adobo sauce; for more salt, add a pinch more kosher salt.
5. Serve: Spoon the cilantro-lime rice into 6 wide bowls and ladle the beef and beans over the top. Sprinkle with the remaining cilantro and serve lime wedges alongside. The long simmer guarantees the ground beef is well past the safe 160 F.
6. Storage: Refrigerate in airtight containers up to 4 days, or freeze the beef mixture up to 3 months. Reheat in a covered skillet over medium heat with a splash of water until steaming (165 F), or microwave 2-3 minutes, stirring halfway.
Common mistakes:
- Under-browning the beef: Gray, steamed beef tastes flat. Leave it alone for 2-3 minutes at a time so it actually browns, and use your biggest skillet so it is not crowded.
- Chipotle overload: Chipotles in adobo are potent; 3 peppers gives a solid medium heat. Taste before adding extra adobo sauce, and freeze leftover peppers from the can in a zip bag - they keep for months.
- Mushy rice: Lifting the lid during the 18 minutes lets steam escape and leaves the top layer crunchy. Set a timer and trust it.

Title: Cod & Tomato Orzo Skillet
Ingredients:
2 1/4 lb cod fillets (about 1 inch thick), skinless
2 1/4 cups orzo
1 (28-ounce) can diced tomatoes
3 1/2 cups low-sodium chicken broth
3 cloves garlic
1 tablespoon tomato paste
1 1/2 teaspoons dried oregano
3 cups baby spinach
1/3 cup crumbled feta cheese
2 tablespoons olive oil, divided
1 lemon
1 teaspoon kosher salt, divided, plus more to taste
1/2 teaspoon black pepper
Steps:
1. Mise en place: Mince the garlic very fine (mince = pieces smaller than rice grains). Measure the orzo, broth, tomatoes, tomato paste, and oregano into bowls. Cut the lemon in half - one half for juice, one half cut into 6 wedges for serving. Pat the cod fillets dry with paper towels and check for pin bones by running your fingertip over the surface; pull any you find with tweezers. Season both sides of the cod with 1/2 teaspoon of the salt and the black pepper.
2. Toast the orzo: Heat 1 tablespoon of the olive oil in a large deep skillet (with a lid) over medium heat. Add the garlic and tomato paste and stir 30 seconds until the garlic smells sweet and the paste darkens a shade - this toasting step deepens the tomato flavor. Add the orzo and oregano and stir 1 minute until the pasta looks lightly golden and smells nutty.
3. Simmer: Pour in the diced tomatoes with their juices and the broth, add the remaining 1/2 teaspoon salt, and stir. Bring to a boil over high heat, then reduce to medium-low, cover, and simmer 7 minutes, stirring once halfway so the orzo does not stick. The orzo should be just shy of tender with a little broth still visible.
4. Cook the fish: Lay the cod fillets on top of the orzo, nestling them in slightly. Drizzle the remaining 1 tablespoon olive oil over the fish, cover, and cook 8-10 minutes on medium-low until the fish is opaque and flakes easily when pressed with a fork - cod is done at 145 F. The thickest part should have no translucent center.
5. Finish and serve: Scatter the spinach around the fish, cover 1 minute until wilted, then squeeze the lemon half over everything. Crumble the feta over the top. Taste the orzo - add salt a pinch at a time until the tomato flavor pops. Serve in shallow bowls with lemon wedges.
6. Storage: Refrigerate up to 2 days. Reheat gently in a covered skillet over medium-low heat with a splash of broth until steaming - fish dries out fast, so warm it through, do not blast it.
Common mistakes:
- Soggy orzo: Too much liquid or too long a simmer turns orzo to mush. Keep the lid on, the heat at a gentle bubble, and check at 7 minutes - it finishes cooking with the fish.
- Overcooked cod: Cod goes from silky to dry in minutes. Start checking at 8 minutes; it is done when it flakes with gentle pressure, not when it falls apart on its own.
- Under-seasoning: Tomatoes and broth vary wildly in salt. Taste the orzo before serving and salt in pinches - the feta adds salt too, so season before the feta goes on.

Title: Cod with Tomato Olive Couscous
Ingredients:
2 1/4 lb cod fillets (about 1 inch thick), skinless
2 1/4 cups dry couscous
2 1/4 cups low-sodium chicken broth
1 1/2 pints cherry tomatoes
1/2 cup pitted green olives
1/2 red onion
4 cloves garlic
1 1/2 teaspoons ground cumin
1 1/2 teaspoons sweet paprika
1/2 teaspoon ground turmeric
3 tablespoons olive oil, divided
2 lemons
3 tablespoons chopped fresh parsley
3 tablespoons chopped fresh cilantro
1 teaspoon kosher salt, divided, plus more to taste
1/2 teaspoon black pepper
Steps:
1. Mise en place: Mince the garlic very fine. Halve the cherry tomatoes. Halve the olives. Dice the red onion into small 1/2-inch cubes (dice = small even cubes). Chop the parsley and cilantro. Cut 1 lemon in half for juice; cut the other into 6 wedges for serving. Pat the cod dry and check for pin bones. In a small bowl, mix the cumin, paprika, turmeric, 1/2 teaspoon of the salt, the black pepper, the minced garlic, the juice of half a lemon, and 1 tablespoon of the olive oil into a thick paste - this is a quick chermoula-style rub, the classic Moroccan seasoning for fish.
2. Season the cod: Rub the spice paste all over the cod fillets, coating every side. Set aside at room temperature 15 minutes while the oven heats - this short rest lets the spices bloom into the fish. Heat the oven to 425 F.
3. Roast: Toss the halved tomatoes and diced onion on a rimmed sheet pan with 1 tablespoon of the olive oil and a pinch of salt. Lay the cod fillets among the tomatoes. Roast 12-14 minutes until the tomatoes burst and slump and the cod is opaque and flakes easily - 145 F at the thickest point. The spice crust should look deep reddish-brown and smell warm and earthy.
4. Make the couscous: While the fish roasts, bring the broth to a boil in a medium saucepan. Stir in the couscous and the remaining 1/2 teaspoon salt, cover, remove from heat, and let stand 5 minutes - do not lift the lid. Fluff with a fork until no clumps remain. Fold in the roasted tomatoes and all their pan juices, the olives, the parsley, the cilantro, the juice of the remaining lemon half, and the last 1 tablespoon of olive oil. Taste and add salt a pinch at a time.
5. Serve: Spoon the couscous into 6 shallow bowls and lay a cod fillet on top of each. Serve with lemon wedges - a fresh squeeze at the table is the Moroccan way (preserved lemon is traditional, but fresh lemon keeps this weeknight-friendly).
6. Storage: Refrigerate up to 2 days. Reheat the couscous in a covered skillet with a splash of water and warm the fish gently alongside - or enjoy the leftovers cold as a grain salad.
Common mistakes:
- Dry couscous: If the broth is not at a full boil when the couscous goes in, the grains cook unevenly. Boil first, stir once, cover, and do not peek for 5 minutes.
- Over-roasted cod: Thin fillets finish closer to 12 minutes. Check at 12 - if the center still looks glassy and translucent, give it 2 more minutes.
- Skipping the spice rest: The rub needs those 15 minutes to penetrate; fish rubbed and roasted immediately tastes dusty on the outside and plain inside.

Title: Crab & Parmesan Orzo Bake
Ingredients:
1 1/2 lb lump crab meat
2 1/4 cups orzo
4 cups low-sodium chicken broth
1/2 cup heavy cream
1/2 cup dry white wine (such as Pinot Grigio)
3 cloves garlic
1 1/2 cups frozen peas
3/4 cup grated Parmesan cheese, divided
3/4 cup panko breadcrumbs
2 tablespoons butter
2 tablespoons olive oil
1 lemon
2 tablespoons chopped fresh parsley
1 teaspoon kosher salt, divided
1/2 teaspoon black pepper
Steps:
1. Mise en place: Heat the oven to 400 F. Mince the garlic very fine. Zest the lemon (grate just the yellow skin, not the bitter white pith underneath) and cut it in half for juice. Pick through the crab meat with your fingers, feeling for any hard bits of shell or cartilage - even good lump crab hides a few. Thaw the peas under warm running water in a colander and drain. Measure the orzo, broth, cream, wine, Parmesan, and panko. Toss the panko with 1/4 cup of the Parmesan in a small bowl.
2. Toast the orzo: Melt the butter with the olive oil in a large oven-safe skillet over medium heat. Add the garlic and orzo and stir 1-2 minutes until the garlic smells sweet and the orzo turns lightly golden - toasting keeps the pasta from going gummy in the oven.
3. Simmer: Pour in the wine and let it bubble 1 minute, scraping up the golden bits - most of the alcohol cooks off, leaving a bright flavor. Add the broth, cream, 1/2 teaspoon of the salt, and the black pepper. Bring to a boil, then reduce to a lively simmer and cook 8 minutes, stirring often so the orzo does not stick, until the pasta is just tender and the sauce has thickened to a creamy coating.
4. Assemble: Remove from heat. Gently fold in the peas, crab, lemon zest, juice of half the lemon, parsley, and the remaining 1/2 cup Parmesan - fold, do not stir hard, or the crab breaks into shreds. Taste and add the remaining salt a pinch at a time. Sprinkle the panko-Parmesan mixture evenly over the top.
5. Bake: Bake uncovered 15-18 minutes until the top is deep golden brown and the edges bubble. Let it rest 5 minutes - the sauce sets as it cools and the first scoop holds together. Serve with the remaining lemon half cut into wedges.
6. Storage: Refrigerate up to 2 days. Reheat covered at 350 F for 15 minutes with a splash of broth, or microwave individual portions - the panko topping will soften but the flavor holds.
Common mistakes:
- Rubbery crab: Crab is already cooked - it only needs to warm through. Folding it in off the heat keeps it sweet and tender; boiling it makes it tough.
- Skipping the shell check: One piece of shell ruins a bite. Run your fingers through the crab before it goes in, every time.
- Soggy topping: The panko must go on a surface that is already creamy-thick, not soupy, or it sinks. If your orzo looks loose after simmering, cook 2 more minutes before topping.

Title: Creamy Tuscan Chicken Pasta
Ingredients:
2 1/4 lb boneless, skinless chicken breasts
18 oz penne pasta
3/4 cup oil-packed sun-dried tomatoes, drained
4 1/2 cups baby spinach (about 5 oz)
5 cloves garlic
1 1/2 cups low-sodium chicken broth
3/4 cup heavy cream
1/2 cup grated Parmesan cheese
1 1/2 teaspoons Italian seasoning
1/2 teaspoon red pepper flakes
2 tablespoons olive oil
1 tablespoon butter
1 1/2 teaspoons kosher salt, divided
1/2 teaspoon black pepper
Steps:
1. Mise en place: Cut the chicken breasts into strips about 1/2 inch thick and 2 inches long - even thickness means even cooking. Mince the garlic very fine. Chop the sun-dried tomatoes into thin strips. Measure the broth, cream, Parmesan, Italian seasoning, and red pepper flakes. Put a large pot of generously salted water on to boil (it should taste like the sea - this is the only chance to season the pasta itself).
2. Cook the pasta: Boil the penne 1 minute less than the package says for al dente (firm to the bite with no raw white center). Before draining, scoop out 1 cup of the starchy pasta water and set it aside - this is liquid gold for fixing the sauce. Drain the pasta.
3. Sear the chicken: Pat the chicken strips dry, then toss with the Italian seasoning, 1 teaspoon of the salt, and the black pepper. Heat the olive oil in a large deep skillet over medium-high heat until shimmering. Add the chicken in a single layer and cook 5-6 minutes, turning once, until golden on both sides and the juices run clear - chicken is done at 165 F. Transfer to a plate; do not wash the skillet.
4. Build the sauce: Reduce the heat to medium. Melt the butter in the same skillet, add the garlic, sun-dried tomatoes, and red pepper flakes, and stir 1 minute until fragrant. Pour in the broth and cream, scraping up all the browned bits from the chicken - that is pure flavor. Simmer 4-5 minutes, stirring occasionally, until slightly thickened and it coats the back of a spoon.
5. Finish: Reduce the heat to low and stir in the Parmesan a handful at a time, letting each melt before adding more - this keeps the sauce smooth instead of grainy. Add the spinach and stir 1-2 minutes until just wilted. Return the chicken and the drained penne to the skillet and toss everything together. If the sauce is too thick, loosen it with splashes of the reserved pasta water. Taste and add the remaining 1/2 teaspoon salt if needed.
6. Serve and store: Serve in warm bowls with extra Parmesan on top. Refrigerate leftovers up to 3 days; reheat gently in a skillet over medium-low heat with a splash of cream or milk, stirring, until steaming - boiling a cream sauce can make it split.
Common mistakes:
- Curdled or grainy sauce: Two causes - heat too high when the cheese goes in, and adding all the Parmesan at once. Keep the heat low and add it gradually, stirring constantly.
- Dry chicken: Thin strips cook fast. If they go past 165 F they turn chalky - check the thickest strip with a thermometer and pull them at 160-165 F; they will coast a few degrees as they rest.
- Forgetting the pasta water: Without that starchy water, a thick sauce glues the penne together. Scoop it out BEFORE you drain - you cannot get it back.

Title: Dakgalbi-Style Chicken & Rice
Ingredients:
2 1/4 lb boneless, skinless chicken thighs
2 1/4 cups short-grain white rice
2 3/4 cups water, plus 1/2 cup more as needed
3 tablespoons gochujang (Korean chili paste)
1 1/2 tablespoons gochugaru (Korean chili flakes)
3 tablespoons low-sodium soy sauce
2 tablespoons honey
1 teaspoon Korean curry powder
5 cloves garlic
1 teaspoon grated fresh ginger
2 medium sweet potatoes (about 1 lb total)
3/4 head green cabbage (about 6 cups chopped)
1 large yellow onion
4 green onions
2 tablespoons avocado oil
1 teaspoon toasted sesame oil
1 teaspoon kosher salt
Steps:
1. Mise en place: Cut the chicken thighs into bite-size pieces about 1 1/2 inches - trim any big flaps of fat. Mince the garlic very fine; grate the ginger on the small holes of a box grater. In a large bowl, stir together the gochujang, gochugaru, soy sauce, honey, curry powder, garlic, ginger, and salt into a thick red paste. Add the chicken and mix with your hands (or a spoon) until every piece is coated. Cover and refrigerate at least 20 minutes, up to overnight - this marinate is the signature sweet-spicy Chuncheon flavor. Meanwhile, peel the sweet potatoes and slice into thin half-moons about 1/4 inch thick (thin = cooks through). Cut the cabbage into rough 2-inch chunks. Cut the onion into 1-inch chunks. Cut the green onions into 2-inch pieces.
2. Cook the rice: Put the rice in a medium saucepan with 2 3/4 cups water. Swirl and drain once to rinse. Bring to a boil over high heat, reduce to low, cover, and cook 15 minutes. Rest covered 10 minutes, then fluff. Short-grain rice should be slightly sticky - perfect for catching the sauce.
3. Sear the sweet potatoes: Heat the avocado oil in your largest skillet or a wok over medium-high heat until shimmering. Add the sweet potato slices in a single layer and cook 4-5 minutes, turning once, until they pick up golden edges. They will not be fully cooked - that is fine.
4. Cook the chicken and vegetables: Add the marinated chicken with all its marinade to the pan. Stir-fry 5-6 minutes, stirring often, until the chicken is mostly opaque and the sauce darkens and smells sweet and toasty. Add the cabbage and onion, pour in 1/4 cup of the extra water, and stir to combine. Reduce the heat to medium, cover, and cook 6-8 minutes, stirring twice, until the cabbage is wilted and tender and the sweet potatoes pierce easily with a fork. If the sauce looks dry or starts to stick, add water 2 tablespoons at a time. The chicken is done when the thickest piece reads 165 F and the juices run clear.
5. Finish and serve: Stir in the green onions and drizzle with the sesame oil. Taste - for more heat add 1 teaspoon more gochugaru; for more sweetness, 1 teaspoon more honey. Serve hot over the short-grain rice, spooning plenty of sauce over each bowl. In Chuncheon this is eaten family-style from the pan - set the skillet on a trivet and let everyone dig in.
6. Storage: Refrigerate up to 3 days. Reheat in a covered skillet over medium heat with a splash of water until steaming (165 F). The sauce thickens overnight; the water loosens it back up.
Common mistakes:
- Sweet potato chunks too thick: Thick pieces stay raw in the middle while everything else overcooks. Keep them 1/4 inch thin and they will finish with the cabbage.
- Burning the gochujang: The sugars in the marinade scorch if the pan is screaming hot and dry. Medium-high heat plus that splash of water keeps the sauce glossy, not bitter.
- Skipping the marinate: Even 20 minutes makes a difference - the salt and chili need time to season the chicken past the surface. Overnight is best if you can plan ahead.

Title: Dijon Pork with Parmesan Potatoes
Ingredients:
2 1/4 lb pork tenderloin
2 1/4 lb baby potatoes
1 1/2 lb green beans, trimmed
3 tablespoons Dijon mustard
1 1/2 tablespoons honey
3 cloves garlic
1 teaspoon dried thyme
1/3 cup grated Parmesan cheese
3 tablespoons olive oil, divided
1 1/2 teaspoons kosher salt, divided
3/4 teaspoon black pepper, divided
Steps:
1. Mise en place: Heat the oven to 425 F. Halve the baby potatoes (cut each through the middle so the flat side can sit on the pan). Trim the green beans - snap or cut off the stem ends. Mince the garlic very fine. In a small bowl, whisk together the Dijon mustard, honey, minced garlic, and thyme into a smooth glaze. Pat the pork tenderloin completely dry with paper towels and trim off the silverskin - that is the shiny, tough membrane on the surface; slide a thin knife under one end and peel it away, because it will not soften in cooking and makes the meat curl.
2. Roast the potatoes: Toss the halved potatoes on a large rimmed sheet pan with 2 tablespoons of the olive oil, 1 teaspoon of the salt, and 1/2 teaspoon of the pepper. Arrange them cut-side down in a single layer. Roast 15 minutes until the cut sides are golden and starting to crisp.
3. Sear the pork: While the potatoes roast, rub the pork all over with the remaining 1/2 teaspoon salt and 1/4 teaspoon pepper, then coat it evenly with the Dijon-honey glaze. Heat the remaining 1 tablespoon oil in a large oven-safe skillet over medium-high heat until shimmering. Sear the pork 4-5 minutes total, turning every minute or so, until browned on all sides. The glaze will caramelize - that is good - but if it starts to blacken, lower the heat slightly.
4. Finish in the oven: Transfer the seared pork to the sheet pan with the potatoes, pushing the potatoes aside to make room. Scatter the green beans around the pan, drizzle them with a little of the pan oil, and sprinkle with a pinch of salt. Roast 15-18 minutes until the pork reads 140-145 F on an instant-read thermometer in the thickest part and the potatoes are tender when pierced. The beans should be bright green with a few browned spots.
5. Rest and serve: Transfer the pork to a cutting board and rest 5 minutes - the temperature will coast to a juicy 145 F and the juices will redistribute so they do not flood the board. While it rests, toss the hot potatoes with the Parmesan so it melts into a savory crust. Slice the pork into 1/2-inch medallions and serve over the potatoes and green beans, spooning any pan juices over the top.
6. Storage: Refrigerate up to 3 days. Reheat slices gently in a covered skillet over medium-low heat with a splash of broth until just warm - pork tenderloin dries out if reheated hard. Do not microwave on high.
Common mistakes:
- Leaving the silverskin on: That silvery membrane shrinks in the heat and squeezes the tenderloin into a curved, unevenly cooked shape. Two minutes with a thin knife prevents it.
- Overcooking the pork: Tenderloin goes from juicy to chalky fast. Pull it at 140-145 F and rest it - carryover heat finishes the job. Anything past 155 F will be dry.
- Soggy potatoes: If the potatoes are crowded or piled up, they steam instead of crisp. Single layer, cut-side down, on a big pan - use two pans if needed.

Title: Garlic Beef & Green Onion Rice
Ingredients:
2 lb flank steak
2 1/4 cups jasmine rice
3 cups water
12 green onions
7 cloves garlic
1 tablespoon fresh ginger
4 tablespoons low-sodium soy sauce, divided
1 1/2 tablespoons oyster sauce
1 1/2 tablespoons cornstarch
1 teaspoon granulated sugar
2 tablespoons avocado oil, divided
1 teaspoon toasted sesame oil
1/2 teaspoon white pepper (or black pepper)
Steps:
1. Mise en place: This stir-fry cooks in minutes, so everything must be ready before the heat goes on. Slice the flank steak thin (about 1/4 inch) AGAINST the grain - look for the long muscle fibers running one direction and cut across them; this shortens the fibers and keeps the beef tender. Toss the beef with 1 tablespoon of the soy sauce, the cornstarch, and the sugar; the cornstarch coating is called velveting and protects the meat from the pan's heat so it stays silky. Mince the garlic very fine; mince the ginger the same way. Cut the green onions into 2-inch pieces, keeping the white and green parts in separate piles - the whites go in first, the greens at the end. Stir the remaining 3 tablespoons soy sauce, the oyster sauce, sesame oil, and white pepper together in a small bowl - this is your finishing sauce.
2. Cook the rice: Combine the rice, 3 cups water, and a pinch of salt in a medium saucepan. Bring to a boil over high heat, reduce to low, cover, and cook 15 minutes. Rest covered 5 minutes, then fluff.
3. Sear the beef: Heat 1 tablespoon of the avocado oil in a large skillet or wok over HIGH heat until it just starts to smoke. Add half the beef in a single layer and sear 1 minute without touching, flip, and sear 1 minute more - you want a deep brown crust with a still-pink center. Transfer to a plate. Repeat with the second half, adding a touch more oil if the pan looks dry. Do not crowd the pan - crowded beef steams gray instead of browning.
4. Stir-fry the aromatics: Reduce the heat to medium-high. Add the remaining 1 tablespoon oil, the garlic, ginger, and the white parts of the green onions. Stir-fry 30-45 seconds until intensely fragrant and the garlic is pale gold - not brown. Add the green parts of the green onions and toss 30 seconds until they turn bright green and just soften.
5. Combine: Return the beef and any juices to the pan. Pour in the finishing sauce and toss 30-45 seconds until the sauce bubbles, thickens slightly, and glazes every slice. Taste - add a splash more soy sauce if it needs salt. Serve immediately over the jasmine rice. The beef should be just cooked through with a rosy center; carryover heat finishes it.
6. Storage: Refrigerate up to 3 days. Reheat in a hot skillet for 1-2 minutes until steaming - the microwave turns the beef chewy. Add a splash of water if the sauce has thickened.
Common mistakes:
- Slicing with the grain: Long fibers make even thin beef chewy. Find the grain lines and cut across them - this single step matters more than any marinade.
- One crowded batch: Two pounds of beef will not sear in one go in a home skillet. Two quick batches give you a browned crust; one crowded batch gives you gray boiled meat.
- Walking away from the garlic: Minced garlic burns in under a minute over high heat and turns the whole dish bitter. Have the green onions ready to go in right behind it.

Title: Garlic Butter Chicken & Orzo
Ingredients:
- 2 lb boneless, skinless chicken breasts (about 3 large)
- 1 tsp kosher salt, plus more to taste
- 1/2 tsp black pepper
- 1 tsp garlic powder
- 1 tsp Italian seasoning
- 1 lb (about 2 3/4 cups) dry orzo
- 5 tbsp unsalted butter, divided
- 2 tbsp olive oil
- 6 cloves garlic, minced
- 2 tbsp fresh lemon juice (about 1 lemon)
- 1 1/2 cups chicken broth
- 1/2 cup heavy cream
- 1/2 cup freshly grated Parmesan, plus more for serving
- 5 oz baby spinach (about 5 packed cups)
- 1/4 cup chopped fresh parsley
Steps:
1. Mise en place: Dice the garlic — mince means chop it as fine as you can, into pieces smaller than a grain of rice. Cut the lemon in half and squeeze out 2 tbsp juice (pick out the seeds). Grate the Parmesan. Measure the orzo, broth, cream, butter, and oil and set them by the stove. Rinse the spinach and pat it mostly dry.

2. Even out the chicken. Lay each breast on the cutting board and cover with plastic wrap, then pound the thick end with a meat mallet, rolling pin, or the bottom of a heavy pan until the breast is an even 3/4-inch thickness all over. (Even thickness = even cooking; skip this and the thin end dries out before the thick end is done.)

3. Season the chicken on both sides with the salt, pepper, garlic powder, and Italian seasoning.

4. Heat the olive oil and 1 tbsp of the butter in a large deep skillet or Dutch oven over medium-high heat until the butter foams and the foam starts to settle, about 2 minutes.

5. Sear the chicken 5-6 minutes per side without moving it, until deep golden brown and it releases easily from the pan. The thickest part should read 165F on an instant-read thermometer. Transfer to a plate and tent loosely with foil — rest it at least 5 minutes so the juices redistribute.

6. Reduce the heat to medium. In the same pan, melt the remaining 4 tbsp butter. Add the garlic and cook 30 seconds, stirring, until fragrant but not brown — browned garlic turns bitter.

7. Add the orzo and stir 2 minutes until the edges look lightly toasted and smell nutty (this is tostatura — it keeps the orzo from going gummy).

8. Pour in the chicken broth and scrape up any browned bits from the bottom of the pan — that is pure flavor. Bring to a simmer, then reduce to medium-low, cover, and cook 10-12 minutes, stirring once halfway, until the orzo is tender with a slight bite and most of the liquid is absorbed.

9. Stir in the cream, Parmesan, lemon juice, and spinach. Cook 2 minutes, stirring, until the spinach wilts and the sauce turns glossy and coats the orzo. Taste and add up to 1/2 tsp more salt if needed.

10. Slice the rested chicken across the grain into 1/2-inch strips. (Across the grain means perpendicular to the lines you can see in the meat — it makes each bite tender instead of stringy.)

11. Serve: spoon the creamy orzo into wide bowls, fan the chicken slices over the top, and finish with parsley and extra Parmesan.

12. Storage: refrigerate leftovers in an airtight container up to 3 days. Reheat gently in a skillet over medium-low heat with a splash of broth or cream, stirring, until steaming — microwaving on high makes the chicken rubbery.

Common mistakes:
- Skipping the pounding step — uneven chicken cooks unevenly, dry outside and raw inside.
- Letting the garlic brown — 30 seconds is all it needs; brown garlic ruins the whole sauce.
- Overcooking the chicken — pull it at 165F and rest it; it will climb a couple more degrees on the plate.

Title: Garlic Butter Lobster Rice
Ingredients:
- 3 cups long-grain white rice
- 4 1/2 cups seafood stock or chicken broth
- 1 1/2 lb cooked lobster meat, cut into 1-inch chunks (look for claw and tail meat near the fish counter)
- 8 tbsp (1 stick) unsalted butter
- 8 cloves garlic, minced
- 1/4 cup dry sherry
- 2 tbsp fresh lemon juice, plus lemon wedges for serving
- 1 tsp lemon zest (the thin yellow outer peel, grated — stop before the white pith, which is bitter)
- 3 tbsp chopped fresh chives
- 2 tbsp chopped fresh parsley
- 1/2 tsp sweet paprika
- 1 tsp kosher salt, plus more to taste
Steps:
1. Mise en place: Cut the lobster meat into 1-inch chunks if it isn't already. Mince the garlic. Zest the lemon, then cut it in half and squeeze out 2 tbsp juice. Chop the chives and parsley. Rinse the rice in a fine-mesh strainer under cold water until the water runs mostly clear, then drain well — this removes excess starch so the rice stays fluffy.

2. Cook the rice: combine the rice, stock, and 1/2 tsp of the salt in a large pot. Bring to a boil over high heat, then reduce to low, cover tightly, and cook 18 minutes without lifting the lid. Turn off the heat and let it stand, still covered, 10 minutes. Then fluff with a fork.

3. While the rice rests, make the garlic butter: melt the butter in a large skillet over medium heat. When it foams, add the garlic and cook 45-60 seconds, stirring, until fragrant and just turning pale gold — not brown.

4. Add the sherry and simmer 1 minute to cook off the harsh alcohol edge. Stir in the lemon zest, paprika, and remaining 1/2 tsp salt.

5. Turn the heat to LOW. Add the lobster chunks and gently warm 2-3 minutes, spooning the butter over them, just until heated through. Lobster is already cooked — you are only warming it to about 140F. The moment it is hot to the touch, pull the pan off the heat. Overcooked lobster turns rubbery and tough in minutes.

6. Remove from the heat and stir in the lemon juice, chives, and parsley.

7. Serve: mound the rice in wide bowls and spoon the lobster with plenty of garlic butter over the top. Serve with lemon wedges.

8. Storage: refrigerate leftovers up to 2 days. Reheat VERY gently in a covered skillet over low heat with a splash of stock, just until steaming — or eat it cold over salad. Never microwave lobster on high; it will turn to rubber.

Common mistakes:
- Treating the lobster like raw seafood — it is already cooked, so high heat or long cooking is what makes it rubbery. Warm, don't cook.
- Browning the garlic — bitter garlic overwhelms the sweet lobster; pale gold is the limit.
- Skipping the rice rest — cutting it short gives you wet, sticky rice instead of fluffy grains.

Title: Garlic Butter Shrimp Orzo
Ingredients:
- 2 lb large shrimp (21/25 count), peeled and deveined
- 12 oz (about 2 cups) dry orzo
- 1 tsp kosher salt, plus more to taste
- 1/2 tsp black pepper
- 6 tbsp unsalted butter, divided
- 1 tbsp olive oil
- 6 cloves garlic, thinly sliced
- 1/2 tsp red pepper flakes
- 1 cup chicken broth
- 2 tbsp fresh lemon juice (about 1 lemon)
- 1/4 cup freshly grated Parmesan
- 8 oz cherry tomatoes, halved
- 1/4 cup chopped fresh parsley
Steps:
1. Mise en place: Pat the shrimp completely dry with paper towels — dry shrimp sear instead of steam. Slice the garlic into thin coins. Halve the cherry tomatoes. Chop the parsley. Cut the lemon and squeeze out the juice. Measure the orzo, broth, butter, and Parmesan and set them by the stove.

2. Season the shrimp with the salt and pepper.

3. Heat the olive oil and 1 tbsp of the butter in a large deep skillet over medium-high heat until the butter foams, about 2 minutes.

4. Sear the shrimp in a single layer, 1 1/2 to 2 minutes per side. They are done when they turn opaque pink-white and curl into a loose C shape. If they curl into a tight O, they are overcooked. Work in two batches if the pan is crowded — crowding makes them steam instead of sear. Transfer to a plate.

5. Reduce the heat to medium. Add 2 tbsp butter to the same pan, then the sliced garlic and red pepper flakes. Cook 1 minute, stirring, until the garlic is fragrant and just pale gold.

6. Add the orzo and stir 2 minutes until lightly toasted and nutty-smelling.

7. Pour in the chicken broth and scrape up the browned bits. Bring to a simmer, cover, and cook on medium-low 10-12 minutes, stirring once, until the orzo is tender and the liquid is mostly absorbed.

8. Stir in the remaining 3 tbsp butter, the lemon juice, and the Parmesan until the sauce turns glossy. Fold in the cherry tomatoes and cook 2 minutes until they just start to slump.

9. Return the shrimp and any juices to the pan. Toss 1 minute to warm through. Taste and add up to 1/2 tsp more salt.

10. Serve: spoon into wide bowls and shower with parsley and extra Parmesan.

11. Storage: refrigerate up to 2 days. Reheat in a skillet over medium-low with a splash of broth, just until steaming — the shrimp toughen if you blast them.

Common mistakes:
- Crowding the shrimp — they steam gray instead of searing pink; give them space or cook in batches.
- Cooking shrimp by the clock alone — go by the C-curl and opaque color; 30 extra seconds is the difference between snappy and rubbery.
- Adding the garlic over high heat — sliced garlic burns fast and turns the whole dish bitter.

Title: Garlic Chicken & Bok Choy
Ingredients:
For the velveting marinade:
- 1 3/4 lb boneless, skinless chicken breasts, sliced 1/4-inch thick
- 1 tbsp light soy sauce
- 1 tbsp Shaoxing wine (or dry sherry)
- 1 tbsp cornstarch
- 1 tbsp water
- 1 tbsp vegetable oil

For the stir-fry sauce:
- 1/4 cup chicken broth
- 2 tbsp oyster sauce
- 1 tbsp light soy sauce
- 1 tsp sugar
- 1 tbsp cornstarch
- 2 tbsp water

For the stir-fry:
- 2 lb baby bok choy
- 3 tbsp vegetable oil, divided
- 8 cloves garlic, roughly chopped
- 1 tbsp fresh ginger, minced
- 2 tsp toasted sesame oil
- 3 scallions, sliced
Steps:
1. Mise en place: Slice the chicken against the grain into 1/4-inch-thick pieces — against the grain means across the lines in the meat, which keeps each bite tender. Wash the bok choy carefully (grit hides between the leaves), drain completely, and cut each head in half lengthwise; quarter any large ones. Roughly chop the garlic into chunky pieces (bigger than minced — they should toast golden, not burn). Mince the ginger — grate it on a microplane or chop it as fine as you can. Slice the scallions. Stir the marinade ingredients, sauce ingredients, and keep everything by the stove. Stir-frying moves fast — you cannot stop to chop once the heat is on.

2. Velvet the chicken: toss the chicken slices with the soy sauce, Shaoxing wine, cornstarch, and water until every piece is coated, then drizzle in the 1 tbsp oil and toss again. Let it sit 15 minutes at room temperature. (Velveting is the classic Chinese technique that gives stir-fried meat its silky, tender bite — the cornstarch forms a thin protective coat so the chicken stays juicy over high heat.)

3. Heat 1 tbsp of the vegetable oil in a large wok or skillet over high heat until it shimmers and just starts to smoke.

4. Spread the chicken in a single layer. Let it sit undisturbed 30 seconds, then toss and stir-fry 2-3 minutes until just opaque and pale — it does not need to brown. Transfer immediately to a plate. It will finish cooking later; pulling it now keeps it tender. The chicken is done when the thickest piece reads 165F — check one now if unsure.

5. Add 1 tbsp oil to the same hot wok. Add the bok choy and stir-fry 2 minutes until the leaves wilt and the stems turn bright green and glossy but are still crisp at the core. Transfer to the plate with the chicken.

6. Add the last 1 tbsp oil. Add the garlic and ginger and stir-fry 30 seconds until fragrant — listen for the sizzle and watch for the garlic turning golden at the edges.

7. Pour in the stir-fry sauce (stir it first — the cornstarch settles). It will boil and thicken almost immediately, turning glossy, about 30-60 seconds.

8. Return the chicken and bok choy to the wok. Toss 1 minute until everything is coated and heated through. Drizzle with the sesame oil and toss once more.

9. Serve: spoon over steamed white rice and scatter the scallions over the top.

10. Storage: refrigerate up to 3 days. Reheat in a hot skillet for 1-2 minutes or microwave at 70% power — high heat makes the chicken chewy. The bok choy will soften on reheating but still tastes great.

Common mistakes:
- Skipping the velveting rest — the cornstarch coat is what keeps the chicken silky; without it the chicken seizes and turns chalky.
- Not drying the bok choy — wet leaves steam the wok and kill the sear; shake them dry in a colander.
- Stir-frying in a crowded pan — work in batches if needed; a crowded wok steams instead of sears.

Title: Garlic Cod & Potato Stew
Ingredients:
- 2 lb cod fillets (about 1 1/2 inches thick), cut into 2-inch chunks
- 2 lb Yukon Gold potatoes, peeled and sliced 1/4-inch thick
- 2 medium yellow onions, thinly sliced
- 3 large ripe tomatoes, sliced 1/4-inch thick
- 1 red bell pepper, sliced into strips
- 1 green bell pepper, sliced into strips
- 6 cloves garlic, thinly sliced
- 6 tbsp extra-virgin olive oil
- 1 cup dry white wine
- 1 cup fish stock, chicken broth, or water
- 2 bay leaves
- 1 tsp sweet paprika
- 1 1/2 tsp kosher salt, plus more to taste
- 1/2 tsp black pepper
- 1/4 cup chopped fresh parsley or cilantro
- Crusty bread, for serving
Steps:
1. Mise en place: Slice the potatoes into 1/4-inch rounds — even slices cook evenly. Slice the onions and tomatoes into 1/4-inch slices. Cut the peppers into strips. Slice the garlic thin. Cut the cod into 2-inch chunks and pat dry. Measure the oil, wine, and stock. This is a caldeirada, the Portuguese fisherman's stew — the whole method is layering everything raw in the pot and letting it simmer untouched, so have everything cut before you start.

2. Build the layers in a large Dutch oven or heavy pot with a lid. Start with a drizzle of olive oil, then layer in this order: half the potatoes, half the onions, half the tomatoes, half the peppers, half the garlic, then half the cod chunks. Sprinkle with half the salt, pepper, and paprika, and tuck in 1 bay leaf. Repeat with a second layer of everything, finishing with the cod on top.

3. Pour the wine, stock, and remaining olive oil evenly over the layers. Don't skimp on the oil — cooking the caldeirada in generous olive oil is what gives it its rich, traditional character.

4. Cover and bring to a bare simmer over medium heat — you want lazy bubbles, not a rolling boil. Then reduce to low and cook 35-40 minutes.

5. The golden rule of caldeirada: NEVER STIR. Stirring breaks the fish into mush. Instead, give the pot an occasional gentle shake or tilt to keep things from sticking. The layers protect the fish, and the wine, oil, and vegetable juices make the broth on their own.

6. Check at 35 minutes: the potatoes should be fork-tender (a fork slides in with no resistance) and the cod should flake easily and read 145F on a thermometer. If the potatoes need more time, give them 5-10 more minutes — the cod can take it.

7. Turn off the heat, taste the broth, and add salt if needed. Let it rest 5 minutes with the lid on.

8. Serve: bring the whole pot to the table, shower with parsley, and ladle into wide bowls with crusty bread standing by for the broth.

9. Storage: refrigerate up to 2 days. Reheat gently in a covered pot over low heat until steaming — boiling will shred the fish.

Common mistakes:
- Stirring the pot — this is THE caldeirada rule; one good stir turns the cod into fish porridge. Shake, don't stir.
- Boiling hard instead of simmering — aggressive heat breaks the fish and turns the potatoes to mush; keep it at a lazy bubble.
- Cutting the potatoes too thick — 1/4-inch slices cook through in the same time as the fish; thick chunks stay raw in the middle.

Note: the most traditional version uses salt cod (bacalhau) soaked overnight to desalt it. Fresh cod gives you the same layered, brothy stew in one evening — if you ever want the full traditional version, soak 2 lb salt cod in cold water 24 hours, changing the water 3 times, and use it exactly the same way (but halve the added salt).

Title: Garlic Lime Chicken Rice Bowls
Ingredients:
For the chicken:
- 2 lb boneless, skinless chicken thighs
- 6 cloves garlic, minced
- 1/4 cup fresh lime juice (about 3 limes)
- 2 tsp lime zest
- 1/4 cup olive oil
- 2 tsp ground cumin
- 2 tsp dried oregano
- 1 tsp chili powder
- 1 1/2 tsp kosher salt

For the bowls:
- 3 cups long-grain white rice
- 1 (15-oz) can black beans, drained and rinsed
- 1 1/2 cups frozen corn
- 2 medium tomatoes, diced
- 1/2 small red onion, diced
- 1 jalapeño, minced (remove the seeds for less heat)
- 1/4 cup chopped fresh cilantro, plus more for serving
- 1 large avocado, diced
- 2 oz cotija cheese, crumbled
- Lime wedges, for serving
Steps:
1. Mise en place: Mince the garlic. Zest the limes, then juice them. Dice the tomatoes, red onion, and jalapeño. Chop the cilantro. Dice the avocado — do this last so it doesn't brown. Rinse the rice until the water runs mostly clear.

2. Marinate the chicken: in a large bowl or zip-top bag, combine the garlic, lime juice, lime zest, olive oil, cumin, oregano, chili powder, and salt. Add the chicken thighs and turn to coat. Marinate 20 minutes at room temperature (or up to 4 hours in the fridge — but not longer, or the lime juice will start to "cook" the surface and make it mushy).

3. Cook the rice: combine the rice with 4 1/2 cups water and 1 tsp salt in a large pot. Bring to a boil, reduce to low, cover, and cook 18 minutes. Rest 10 minutes covered, then fluff with a fork and fold in half the cilantro.

4. Char the corn: heat a dry skillet over high heat until very hot. Add the frozen corn in a single layer and cook 4-5 minutes without stirring much, until blackened in spots and smelling toasty. Transfer to a bowl.

5. Make a quick pico: toss the diced tomatoes, red onion, jalapeño, remaining cilantro, a pinch of salt, and a squeeze of lime.

6. Heat the black beans in a small saucepan over medium-low heat with 1/4 cup water and a pinch of salt, 5 minutes, until steaming. Keep warm.

7. Sear the chicken: heat a large skillet or grill pan over medium-high heat. Remove the chicken from the marinade (let the excess drip off) and sear 5-6 minutes per side until deeply browned with charred edges and the thickest part reads 165F.

8. Rest the chicken 5 minutes on a cutting board, then slice across the grain into strips.

9. Assemble the bowls: rice first, then rows of sliced chicken, black beans, charred corn, pico de gallo, and avocado. Crumble cotija over everything, add lime wedges, and scatter extra cilantro.

10. Storage: refrigerate components separately up to 3 days (keep the avocado and pico separate — they don't keep well). Reheat the rice, beans, and chicken with a splash of water; assemble fresh with cold toppings.

Common mistakes:
- Marinating too long — past 4 hours the acid turns the chicken surface mushy instead of tender.
- Slicing with the grain — find the lines in the thigh meat and cut across them for tender bites.
- Dressing the avocado early — it browns fast; dice it right before serving and squeeze lime over it.

Title: Garlic Pork Tenderloin Risotto
Ingredients:
- 1 3/4 lb pork tenderloin, trimmed of silverskin
- 2 cups arborio rice
- 7 cups chicken stock
- 1/2 cup dry white wine
- 6 tbsp unsalted butter, cold, cut into pieces and divided
- 1 cup freshly grated Parmesan, plus more for serving
- 2 tbsp olive oil
- 1 large shallot (or 1 small onion), minced
- 6 cloves garlic, minced, divided
- 8 oz cremini mushrooms, sliced
- 2 tsp fresh thyme leaves (or 1/2 tsp dried)
- 1 1/2 tsp kosher salt, divided
- 1/2 tsp black pepper
Steps:
1. Mise en place: Trim the pork tenderloin — find the thin, shiny silverskin membrane and slide a knife under it to peel it off (it never softens in cooking). Mince the shallot and garlic. Slice the mushrooms. Grate the Parmesan. Measure the rice and wine. Pour the stock into a saucepan and keep it at a bare simmer over low heat the whole time — warm stock is non-negotiable for risotto; cold stock shocks the rice and turns it gummy.

2. Pat the pork completely dry with paper towels. Season all over with 1 tsp of the salt and the black pepper.

3. Sear the pork: heat 1 tbsp of the olive oil in a large oven-safe skillet over medium-high heat until shimmering. Sear the tenderloin 3-4 minutes per side, turning, until deep golden brown all over. The thickest part should read 145F on a thermometer.

4. Transfer the pork to a plate and rest it 10 minutes — resting lets the juices settle back into the meat instead of running out onto the cutting board. Do not skip this.

5. Meanwhile, start the risotto in a large deep skillet or Dutch oven: melt 2 tbsp of the butter with the remaining 1 tbsp olive oil over medium heat. Add the shallot and half the garlic and cook 3 minutes, stirring, until soft and translucent.

6. Add the thyme and the rice. Stir 2 minutes until every grain is coated and the edges of the grains turn translucent while the centers stay white — this is the tostatura (toasting), and it keeps the grains from blowing out into mush.

7. Pour in the wine. Stir until it is fully absorbed and the sharp alcohol smell cooks off, about 2 minutes.

8. Now add the warm stock one ladle (about 3/4 cup) at a time, stirring often and letting each addition absorb before adding the next. This takes 18-20 minutes. The rice is done when it is creamy and the grains are tender with a slight bite in the center (al dente) — you may not need all 7 cups; start tasting at 16 minutes.

9. While the risotto cooks, sauté the mushrooms: heat a separate skillet over medium-high heat with 1 tbsp butter until foaming. Add the mushrooms and remaining garlic and cook 5-6 minutes, stirring occasionally, until golden brown and their liquid has evaporated. Season with the remaining 1/2 tsp salt.

10. Fold the mushrooms into the finished risotto.

11. Mantecatura (the creamy finish): take the risotto OFF the heat. Beat in the remaining cold butter, a few pieces at a time, then the Parmesan, stirring vigorously until glossy. Proper risotto should be all'onda — "wavy" — meaning it ripples like thick waves when you shake the pan. If it is too thick, stir in a splash of warm stock.

12. Slice the rested pork across the grain into 1/2-inch medallions.

13. Serve: spoon the risotto into wide bowls, spread it with the back of the spoon, and fan the pork medallions over the top. Finish with extra Parmesan.

14. Storage: refrigerate up to 3 days. Risotto firms up cold — reheat in a saucepan over medium-low with a splash of stock, stirring, until creamy again. Reheat the pork gently; microwaving on high toughens it.

Common mistakes:
- Using cold or room-temperature stock — it stalls the cooking and makes the rice gummy. Keep it simmering.
- Rinsing the arborio — never rinse risotto rice; the surface starch is what makes it creamy.
- Skipping the pork rest — cutting too early spills all the juices onto the board and the meat eats dry.
- Overcooking past al dente — risotto keeps cooking off the heat; pull it when the centers still have a whisper of bite.

Title: Garlic Salmon Pasta Primavera
Ingredients:
- 2 lb salmon fillets (about 1 1/2 inches thick), cut into 6 portions, skin removed
- 1 lb fettuccine or linguine
- 3 tbsp olive oil, divided
- 2 tbsp unsalted butter
- 6 cloves garlic, thinly sliced
- 1/2 cup dry white wine
- 2 tbsp fresh lemon juice (about 1 lemon)
- 12 oz cherry tomatoes, halved
- 8 oz asparagus, tough ends snapped off, cut into 1 1/2-inch pieces
- 1 medium zucchini, halved lengthwise and sliced into half-moons
- 1 cup frozen peas
- 1/2 cup freshly grated Parmesan, plus more for serving
- 1/4 cup chopped fresh basil or parsley
- 1 1/2 tsp kosher salt, plus more for the pasta water
Steps:
1. Mise en place: Cut the salmon into 6 equal portions and pat them very dry. Slice the garlic into thin coins. Halve the cherry tomatoes. Snap the woody ends off the asparagus (bend each spear — it breaks naturally where the tough part starts) and cut into pieces. Slice the zucchini into half-moons. Squeeze the lemon. Chop the basil. Grate the Parmesan.

2. Bring a large pot of well-salted water to a rolling boil (it should taste like the sea — this is the only chance to season the pasta itself). Cook the fettuccine 1 minute less than the package says. Before draining, scoop out 1 cup of the starchy pasta water and save it — this is liquid gold for the sauce. Drain the pasta.

3. Season the salmon with 1 tsp of the salt and the pepper.

4. Heat 2 tbsp of the olive oil in a large skillet over medium-high heat until shimmering. Lay the salmon in presentation-side down and sear 4 minutes without moving, until deep golden and crisp.

5. Flip and cook 2-3 minutes more. It is done at 125-130F for medium — the center should still look slightly translucent and feel soft when pressed; it keeps cooking off the heat. Transfer to a plate.

6. Reduce the heat to medium. In the same skillet, add the butter and remaining 1 tbsp olive oil, then the sliced garlic. Cook 1 minute, stirring, until fragrant and pale gold.

7. Pour in the wine and lemon juice, scraping up the browned bits. Simmer 2 minutes until slightly reduced.

8. Add the asparagus and cook 3 minutes, then the zucchini and cook 2 minutes more. Add the tomatoes and peas and cook 2 minutes until the tomatoes slump and everything is bright and crisp-tender. Season with the remaining 1/2 tsp salt.

9. Add the drained pasta to the skillet with 1/2 cup of the reserved pasta water. Toss 1-2 minutes until the sauce turns glossy and clings to the noodles — add more pasta water a splash at a time if it looks dry. Toss in the Parmesan and half the basil.

10. Serve: twirl the pasta into wide bowls, set a salmon portion on top of each (or flake the salmon into large chunks over the pasta), and finish with the remaining basil and extra Parmesan.

11. Storage: refrigerate up to 2 days. Reheat gently in a skillet over medium-low with a splash of water, just until steaming — aggressive reheating overcooks the salmon.

Common mistakes:
- Cooking the salmon to 145F+ in the pan — it coasts past perfect; pull it at 125-130F and let carryover heat finish it.
- Forgetting to save pasta water — without it the sauce won't cling and the dish eats dry.
- Dumping all the vegetables in at once — asparagus needs a head start over zucchini and tomatoes, or half your veg is mush and half is raw.

Title: Garlic Shrimp & Tomato Rice
Ingredients:
- 2 lb large shell-on shrimp
- 2 1/2 cups long-grain white rice
- 1/4 cup olive oil
- 1 large yellow onion, diced
- 8 cloves garlic, minced
- 1 red bell pepper, diced
- 2 medium ripe tomatoes, diced
- 1 (28-oz) can crushed tomatoes
- 1/2 cup dry white wine
- 2 bay leaves
- 1 tsp sweet paprika
- 1/2 tsp piri-piri or red pepper flakes
- 1 tsp kosher salt, plus more to taste
- 1/4 cup chopped fresh cilantro
Steps:
1. Mise en place: Peel the shrimp, saving every shell and head in a bowl — the shells are the secret to the deep shrimp flavor in this dish. Devein the shrimp (run a paring knife along the back and pull out the dark vein). Dice the onion, bell pepper, and fresh tomatoes. Mince the garlic. Chop the cilantro. Measure the rice, oil, wine, and canned tomatoes.

2. Make the shrimp stock: put the shells in a pot with 5 cups of water. Bring to a boil, then simmer 15 minutes — the water will turn pink and smell intensely of shrimp. Strain through a fine-mesh strainer, pressing the shells to squeeze out every drop. You need about 4 1/2 cups; top up with water if short. Keep the stock warm over low heat — warm liquid keeps the rice cooking evenly.

3. Build the refogado (the Portuguese flavor base): heat the olive oil in a large Dutch oven over medium heat. Add the onion and bell pepper and cook 8 minutes, stirring, until soft and sweet-smelling.

4. Add the garlic, paprika, and piri-piri. Cook 1 minute, stirring, until fragrant — the paprika should bloom brick-red in the oil.
