5. Add the fresh diced tomatoes and cook 3 minutes until they start to break down. Pour in the crushed tomatoes and cook 5 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the sauce thickens slightly and turns a deep red.

6. Pour in the wine and simmer 2 minutes to cook off the alcohol.

7. Add the rice and stir 1 minute so every grain is coated in the red sauce.

8. Pour in the warm shrimp stock and add the bay leaves. Bring to a boil, then reduce to a steady simmer, cover, and cook 12 minutes. Do not stir — just let it bubble.

9. Uncover, nestle the shrimp into the rice, and give it one gentle stir. Cover and cook 5-7 minutes more, until the rice is tender and the shrimp are opaque and curled into a C. The dish should be soupy — this is arroz de camarão malandrinho, which literally means "naughty" rice, served brothy like a cross between rice and soup. If it looks dry, stir in 1/2 cup more warm water or stock.

10. Fish out the bay leaves. Stir in half the cilantro. Taste and add salt — up to 1 tsp more — until the broth sings.

11. Serve: ladle immediately into wide bowls, broth and all, and scatter the remaining cilantro over the top. This waits for no one — the rice keeps drinking the broth.

12. Storage: refrigerate up to 2 days. The rice will absorb the broth overnight — reheat in a pot over medium heat with 1/2 to 1 cup of water or stock, stirring, until soupy and steaming again.

Common mistakes:
- Throwing away the shells — the homemade shrimp stock is the entire soul of this dish; water or plain broth gives you a pale imitation.
- Adding the shrimp too early — they only need 5-7 minutes; earlier and they go rubbery before the rice is done.
- Cooking it dry — if it looks like pilaf, you've gone too far; malandrinho should glisten with broth in the bowl.

Title: Garlic Shrimp Bibimbap Bowls
Ingredients:
For the shrimp:
- 1 1/2 lb large shrimp, peeled and deveined
- 2 tbsp soy sauce
- 1 tbsp toasted sesame oil
- 4 cloves garlic, minced
- 1 tsp sugar

For the vegetables (namul):
- 10 oz baby spinach
- 12 oz bean sprouts
- 2 medium carrots, julienned (cut into thin matchsticks)
- 1 medium zucchini, julienned
- 6 oz shiitake mushrooms, sliced
- 3 tbsp toasted sesame oil, divided
- 2 tsp kosher salt, divided
- 2 cloves garlic, minced
- 1 tbsp toasted sesame seeds

For the gochujang sauce:
- 6 tbsp gochujang (Korean chili paste)
- 2 tbsp sugar
- 2 tbsp rice vinegar
- 1 tbsp toasted sesame oil
- 2 tbsp water
- 1 clove garlic, grated

For assembly:
- 2 cups short-grain white rice (makes about 6 cups cooked)
- 6 large eggs
- 2 tbsp vegetable oil
Steps:
1. Mise en place: This is a dish of many small parts, so get everything ready first. Peel and devein the shrimp. Julienne the carrots and zucchini — julienne means thin matchsticks about 2 inches long. Slice the shiitakes. Mince and grate the garlic. Rinse the spinach and bean sprouts. Whisk the gochujang sauce ingredients in a small bowl until smooth and set it on the table — everyone sauces their own bowl.

2. Cook the rice: rinse the short-grain rice until the water runs mostly clear, then cook with 2 1/2 cups water (rice cooker, or bring to a boil, reduce to low, cover 15 minutes, rest 10). Short-grain rice is slightly sticky — that stickiness is traditional and holds the bowl together. Keep it warm.

3. Marinate the shrimp: toss the shrimp with the soy sauce, sesame oil, garlic, and sugar. Set aside 10 minutes.

4. Blanch the spinach: bring a pot of salted water to a boil. Add the spinach and blanch 30 seconds — just until wilted and bright green. Drain, rinse under cold water to stop the cooking, then squeeze out as much water as you can with your hands (a fistful at a time). Toss with 1 tsp sesame oil, 1/2 tsp salt, and half the minced garlic.

5. Blanch the bean sprouts: in the same boiling water, cook the sprouts 3-4 minutes until tender-crisp. Drain, rinse cold, squeeze dry, and season the same way — 1 tsp sesame oil, 1/2 tsp salt, remaining minced garlic.

6. Sauté the remaining vegetables separately — this is the heart of bibimbap; each vegetable keeps its own flavor and color. Heat 1 tsp sesame oil in a skillet over medium-high heat. Sauté the carrots 1-2 minutes with a pinch of salt until tender-crisp; transfer to a plate. Repeat with the zucchini (2 minutes), then the mushrooms (3 minutes, until golden at the edges). A pinch of salt and a drizzle of sesame oil for each.

7. Sear the shrimp: heat 1 tbsp of the vegetable oil in the skillet over high heat until shimmering. Add the shrimp in a single layer and sear 1 1/2 to 2 minutes per side until opaque and curled into a C. Transfer to a plate.

8. Fry the eggs: heat the remaining 1 tbsp vegetable oil in a nonstick skillet over medium heat. Crack in the eggs and fry sunny-side up, 3-4 minutes, until the whites are fully set and the edges are lacy and crisp but the yolks are still runny. Season with a pinch of salt.

9. Assemble: divide the warm rice among 6 wide bowls. Arrange the spinach, sprouts, carrots, zucchini, and mushrooms in separate colorful sections over the rice, add a pile of shrimp, and crown each bowl with a fried egg. Sprinkle with sesame seeds.

10. Serve: set the gochujang sauce on the table and tell everyone to add a big spoonful and mix everything thoroughly before eating — the runny yolk, sauce, and rice become one glorious mess. That mixing is the whole point of bibimbap ("mixed rice").

11. Storage: refrigerate components separately up to 3 days (keep the fried eggs separate — fry fresh if you can). Reheat the rice and toppings in a skillet over medium heat; assemble with fresh sauce.

Common mistakes:
- Piling all the vegetables into the pan at once — they steam gray instead of staying bright and distinct; cook each separately, it only takes minutes.
- Not squeezing the blanched greens dry — watery spinach makes the whole bowl soggy.
- Overcooking the shrimp — they go from snappy to rubbery fast; pull them at the C-curl, opaque stage.
- Skimping on the sauce — bibimbap needs a generous spoonful per bowl; undressed, it's just rice and vegetables.

Note: classic bibimbap uses seasoned beef (bulgogi); shrimp is the twist here — it keeps the bowl lighter and cooks in minutes, and the sweet shrimp loves the spicy-sweet gochujang sauce.

Title: Garlic Shrimp Chimichurri Couscous
Ingredients:
- 1½ lb large shrimp, peeled and deveined (tails on or off)

For the chimichurri:
- 1 cup packed fresh flat-leaf parsley leaves (about 1 large bunch)
- 6 large garlic cloves, minced
- 1 tbsp dried oregano
- 1 tsp crushed red pepper flakes
- 1/3 cup red wine vinegar
- 1/2 cup extra-virgin olive oil
- 1 tsp kosher salt, plus more to taste — taste before serving and add up to 1/2 tsp more

For the couscous and shrimp:
- 2¼ cups dry couscous (about 13 oz)
- 2¼ cups water or chicken broth
- 2 tbsp extra-virgin olive oil, divided
- 6 large garlic cloves, thinly sliced
- 1 tsp ground cumin
- 2 tbsp fresh lemon juice (about 1 lemon), plus wedges for serving
- 1/2 tsp kosher salt
- 1/4 tsp freshly ground black pepper
Steps:
1. Mise en place: everything chopped, measured, and set out before any heat goes on. If your shrimp are not already peeled, peel them now: pull off the shell, then run a small knife down the back and rinse out the dark vein. Pat the shrimp very dry with paper towels. Thinly slice 6 garlic cloves (flat rounds about 1/8 inch thick). Mince the other 6 cloves (chop into pieces smaller than a grain of rice). Pull the parsley leaves from the stems and chop them fine. Juice the lemon. Measure the couscous, oil, vinegar, and spices into small bowls.

2. Make the chimichurri. In a medium bowl, combine the chopped parsley, minced garlic, dried oregano, red pepper flakes, red wine vinegar, and 1 tsp salt. Stir, then drizzle in the 1/2 cup olive oil while stirring. The sauce should look loose and spoonable, with visible bits of herb — not a smooth paste. Cover and let it rest at room temperature for at least 15 minutes so the flavors meld. (Chop by hand, not in a food processor: a processor turns it into pesto, and real Argentine chimichurri is chunky.)

3. Cook the couscous. Bring the 2¼ cups water or broth, 1 tbsp of the olive oil, and a pinch of salt to a rolling boil in a medium saucepan. Stir in the couscous, cover the pot, and take it off the heat. Let it stand 5 minutes. Uncover and fluff with a fork, breaking up any clumps — the grains should be separate, light, and steamy. Cover to keep warm.

4. Sear the shrimp. Heat the remaining 1 tbsp olive oil in a large skillet over medium-high heat until it shimmers. Season the shrimp with the 1/2 tsp salt and the black pepper. Lay the shrimp in a single layer — you should hear a confident sizzle. Cook 90 seconds without moving them, then flip and cook 60-90 seconds more, until pink with golden edges and opaque all the way through. In the last 30 seconds, scatter in the sliced garlic and the cumin and stir; the garlic should smell toasty and turn pale gold, not brown. Squeeze the lemon juice over everything and take the pan off the heat. (Shrimp are done when they curl into a loose C shape; a tight O means overcooked.)

5. Taste the chimichurri and add more salt if it needs it, up to 1/2 tsp more. Spoon the couscous into wide bowls, top with the shrimp, and spoon 2-3 tbsp of chimichurri over each serving. Serve with lemon wedges.

6. Storage and reheating: refrigerate leftovers in an airtight container up to 3 days. Reheat the shrimp very gently — 30-60 seconds in the microwave at 50% power, or 1 minute in a skillet over medium-low — just until warm, or they turn rubbery. Reheat the couscous with a splash of water, covered, in the microwave 1-2 minutes, then fluff. Leftover chimichurri keeps 1 week refrigerated; let it come to room temperature before serving so the oil loosens.

Common mistakes:
- Crowding the shrimp in the pan: they steam instead of sear. Cook in two batches if needed.
- Letting the sliced garlic go past pale gold: brown garlic tastes bitter.
- Pureeing the chimichurri: hand-chopped and chunky is the authentic texture.

Title: Garlic Shrimp Couscous
Ingredients:
- 1½ lb large shrimp, peeled and deveined
- 2½ cups dry couscous
- 2½ cups hot chicken broth
- 3 tbsp extra-virgin olive oil, divided
- 1 large yellow onion, diced
- 1 red bell pepper, diced
- 4 garlic cloves, minced
- 1 large tomato, diced
- 1½ tsp ground cumin
- 1½ tsp sweet paprika
- 1 tsp ground turmeric
- 1/2 tsp ground cinnamon
- Big pinch of saffron threads (optional)
- 1 cup frozen peas
- 1/4 cup chopped fresh parsley
- 2 tbsp fresh lemon juice (about 1 lemon)
- 1 tsp kosher salt, plus more to taste — taste before serving and add up to 1/2 tsp more
Steps:
1. Mise en place: everything chopped, measured, and set out before any heat goes on. Dice the onion (cut into small 1/4-inch cubes). Dice the bell pepper and the tomato the same size. Mince the garlic (chop into pieces smaller than a grain of rice). Measure all the spices into one small bowl. Pat the shrimp very dry with paper towels — dry shrimp sear; wet shrimp steam. Heat the chicken broth in a saucepan until steaming and keep it hot.

2. Prep the couscous. Put the dry couscous in a large bowl and toss it with 1 tbsp of the olive oil, rubbing the grains between your fingers so each one is lightly coated — this is the Moroccan home-cook trick for separate, fluffy grains. Pour the hot broth over the couscous, stir once, cover tightly, and let stand 5 minutes. Uncover and fluff with a fork, gently breaking up any lumps with your fingertips. Cover to keep warm. (The fully traditional method steams the grains three times over a simmering stew; this hot-broth method gives you a weeknight version with the same North African spice character.)

3. Build the base. Heat the remaining 2 tbsp olive oil in a large deep skillet or Dutch oven over medium heat. Add the onion and cook 5 minutes, stirring, until soft and translucent. Add the bell pepper and cook 3 minutes more. Stir in the garlic and all the spices (cumin, paprika, turmeric, cinnamon, saffron); cook 30-60 seconds, stirring constantly, until the spices smell deeply fragrant and the oil turns golden-orange. Add the diced tomato and 1 tsp salt; cook 2 minutes, until the tomato melts into a thick, saucy base.

4. Cook the shrimp. Raise the heat to medium-high. Add the shrimp in a single layer and cook 2 minutes per side, until pink, opaque, and curled into a loose C. Stir in the frozen peas and cook 1 minute, just until heated through.

5. Combine. Fold the fluffed couscous into the skillet and toss everything together so the grains soak up the spiced sauce. Stir in the lemon juice and parsley. Taste and add more salt if needed, up to 1/2 tsp more.

6. Serve in wide bowls with extra lemon wedges on the side.

7. Storage and reheating: refrigerate in an airtight container up to 3 days. Reheat with a splash of water, covered, in the microwave 2 minutes or in a skillet over medium heat, stirring, until steaming.

Common mistakes:
- Adding the shrimp before the vegetables are done: they overcook while you wait. Shrimp go in last and cook fast.
- Skipping the spice-toasting step: raw spices taste dusty; 30-60 seconds in hot oil wakes them up.
- Guessing the broth amount: measure it. Too much liquid makes gluey couscous.

Title: Garlic Shrimp Paella
Ingredients:
- 1½ lb large shrimp, peeled and deveined
- 2½ cups short-grain paella rice (bomba or arborio)
- 5 cups fish or seafood stock
- 1/4 cup extra-virgin olive oil
- 1 large yellow onion, finely diced
- 1 red bell pepper, diced
- 6 garlic cloves, minced
- 1 cup grated fresh tomato (about 2 large tomatoes, grated on a box grater)
- 2 tsp sweet smoked paprika
- 1/2 tsp saffron threads
- 1 cup frozen peas
- 1/2 cup dry white wine
- 2 tsp kosher salt, plus more to taste
- Lemon wedges and chopped fresh parsley, for serving
Steps:
1. Mise en place: everything chopped, measured, and set out before any heat goes on. Finely dice the onion (cut into small 1/4-inch cubes). Dice the bell pepper. Mince the garlic (chop into pieces smaller than a grain of rice). Grate the tomatoes on the large holes of a box grater, discarding the skins — you want a pulpy puree. Pour the stock into a saucepan and keep it at a bare simmer the whole time; crumble the saffron into a small cup with 1/4 cup of the hot stock to bloom. Pat the shrimp dry.

2. Sear the shrimp. Heat 1 tbsp of the olive oil in a paella pan or your widest skillet over medium-high heat until shimmering. Sear the shrimp 1 minute per side — just until the outsides turn pink; they will finish cooking in the rice. Remove to a plate.

3. Make the sofrito. In the same pan over medium heat, add the remaining oil, the onion, and the bell pepper. Cook 8-10 minutes, stirring, until completely soft and sweet. Stir in the garlic and cook 30 seconds. Add the grated tomato and the smoked paprika; cook 10-12 minutes, stirring regularly, until the mixture is dark, thick, and jammy, and you can see the oil starting to glisten at the edges — that separation is the sign the sofrito is done.

4. Toast the rice. Stir the rice into the sofrito and cook 2 minutes, stirring, until the grains turn translucent around the edges. Pour in the white wine and let it bubble away for 1 minute, scraping the bottom.

5. Add the stock. Pour in the remaining hot stock plus the saffron liquid and the 2 tsp salt. Shake the pan gently to level the rice into an even layer. From this moment on, do not stir the rice — stirring is what prevents the crispy bottom from forming. Bring to a lively simmer.

6. Cook the paella. Cook 6 minutes over medium-high heat, then reduce to medium-low and cook 12 minutes more. When the grains start to peek above the liquid, scatter the peas over the top and nestle the shrimp into the rice. Taste a grain from just below the surface; it should be al dente with a tiny bite.

7. Make the socarrat. When the liquid is nearly gone, listen: the sound changes from bubbling to a faint crackle. Raise the heat to high for 60-90 seconds, until you smell toasty, nutty rice. Do not walk away — it goes from golden to burnt fast. You are caramelizing the bottom layer into the prized crispy crust called socarrat.

8. Rest. Take the pan off the heat, cover with foil, and rest 5-10 minutes so the top layer of rice finishes steaming.

9. Serve straight from the pan with lemon wedges and a shower of chopped parsley.

10. Storage and reheating: refrigerate up to 2 days. Reheat covered in a skillet over medium-low heat with a splash of stock until steaming. (The socarrat will not survive reheating — that is normal; it is a fresh-pan pleasure.)

Common mistakes:
- Stirring after the stock goes in: no stir means socarrat; stirring means risotto.
- Adding cold stock: it shocks the rice and ruins the texture. Keep it simmering.
- Leaving the pan during the socarrat step: 90 seconds of inattention turns prized crust into bitter charcoal.

Title: Garlic Shrimp Rice Bowls
Ingredients:
- 1½ lb large shrimp, peeled and deveined, tails on (shell-on, deveined shrimp are the most authentic shrimp-truck style; peeled is easier to eat)
- 3 tbsp rice flour (or mochiko)
- 1 tbsp cornstarch
- 1 tbsp paprika
- 2 tsp kosher salt
- 1/2 tsp cayenne pepper (optional, for heat)
- 1/2 tsp freshly ground black pepper
- 6 tbsp unsalted butter
- 2 tbsp olive oil, divided
- 1/3 cup minced garlic (about 12 cloves)
- 1 lemon, cut into wedges
- 4 green onions, thinly sliced
- 2½ cups dry long-grain white rice (about 7½ cups cooked), cooked and kept hot
Steps:
1. Mise en place: everything chopped, measured, and set out before any heat goes on. Get the rice cooking first: rinse 2½ cups rice, combine with 3¾ cups water in a pot, bring to a boil, stir once, cover, and cook on low 15 minutes; rest 10 minutes off the heat, then fluff. Mince the garlic (chop into pieces smaller than a grain of rice). Slice the green onions into thin rings. Cut the lemon into wedges. Pat the shrimp extremely dry with paper towels — this is the most important step for a crispy coating. In a large bowl, whisk together the rice flour, cornstarch, paprika, salt, cayenne, and black pepper.

2. Make the garlic butter. Melt the butter in a large skillet over medium-low heat. Add the minced garlic and cook 3-4 minutes, stirring often, until the garlic is pale gold and smells sweet and nutty. Do not let it go brown — browned garlic turns bitter and will ruin the sauce. Scrape the garlic butter into a bowl and set aside. Wipe out the skillet.

3. Dredge the shrimp. Toss the dry shrimp in the flour-spice mixture until every shrimp is lightly and evenly coated. Shake off the excess.

4. Sear the shrimp. Heat 1 tbsp of the olive oil in the skillet over medium-high heat until shimmering. Add half the shrimp in a single layer — you should hear a strong sizzle. Cook 2 minutes per side without fussing, until golden-crisp at the edges, pink, and opaque. Transfer to a plate and repeat with the remaining 1 tbsp oil and shrimp.

5. Finish. Return all the shrimp to the skillet over medium-low heat. Pour the garlic butter over them and toss for 60 seconds, until every shrimp is glossy and coated.

6. Serve. Spoon hot rice into bowls, pile on the shrimp, and drizzle the extra garlic butter from the pan over the rice — that butter-soaked rice is the whole point. Squeeze lemon over everything and scatter the green onions on top.

7. Storage and reheating: refrigerate up to 3 days. The garlic butter will solidify in the fridge; that is fine, it melts on reheating. Warm gently in a skillet over medium-low heat just until hot, or the shrimp get tough.

Common mistakes:
- Skipping the pat-dry: wet shrimp shed the coating and steam instead of crisping.
- Browning the garlic past pale gold: it goes from sweet to bitter in under a minute, so watch it.
- Crowding the pan: shrimp need space to crisp. Two batches, always.

Title: Garlic Shrimp Yakimeshi
Ingredients:
- 1¼ lb medium shrimp, peeled and deveined
- 6 cups cooked day-old short-grain white rice (from about 2½ cups dry), chilled
- 3 large eggs, beaten
- 3 tbsp neutral oil (canola or vegetable), divided
- 1 tsp toasted sesame oil
- 3 tbsp soy sauce
- 1 tbsp mirin
- 1 tbsp sake
- 6 garlic cloves, thinly sliced
- 1 tbsp grated fresh ginger
- 4 green onions, thinly sliced (whites and greens separated)
- 1/2 cup frozen peas
- 1 tsp kosher salt
- 1/2 tsp white pepper
Steps:
1. Mise en place: everything chopped, measured, and set out before any heat goes on. The rice MUST be cold and at least a day old — spread freshly cooked rice on a sheet pan and chill it uncovered for 1 hour if you forgot to cook it yesterday. Warm, fresh rice turns to mush in the pan. Thinly slice the garlic (flat rounds about 1/8 inch). Grate the ginger on the fine holes of a box grater. Slice the green onions and keep the white and green parts in separate piles. Beat the eggs in a small bowl. Measure the soy sauce, mirin, and sake together in a cup.

2. Scramble the eggs. Heat a wok or your largest skillet over high heat until a drop of water dances and evaporates. Add 1 tbsp of the neutral oil and swirl. Pour in the beaten eggs; let them set 30 seconds, then scramble into soft pieces. Remove to a plate — they should be just cooked, still tender.

3. Sear the shrimp. Add another 1 tbsp oil to the hot wok. Add the shrimp in a single layer and sear 90 seconds per side, until pink and opaque with lightly browned edges. Remove to the plate with the eggs.

4. Bloom the aromatics. Add the last 1 tbsp oil. Stir-fry the sliced garlic, grated ginger, and the white parts of the green onions for 30 seconds, until fragrant and the garlic is pale gold. Add the frozen peas and stir-fry 1 minute.

5. Fry the rice. Add all the cold rice, breaking up any clumps with your spatula. Press the rice against the hot pan, then toss — repeat for 3-4 minutes. You want to hear a steady sizzle and smell something nutty; a few grains should turn lightly golden. Drizzle the soy sauce mixture around the hot edge of the pan (it will sizzle and caramelize on contact) and toss everything to coat.

6. Finish. Return the eggs and shrimp to the wok. Season with the salt and white pepper and toss 1 minute. Take off the heat, drizzle with the sesame oil, and toss in the green onion tops.

7. Serve immediately in warm bowls. Yakimeshi waits for no one — it is best in the first 10 minutes.

8. Storage and reheating: refrigerate up to 3 days. Reheat in a hot skillet with a tiny drizzle of oil, tossing, until steaming — the microwave makes fried rice gummy.

Common mistakes:
- Using fresh, warm rice: the number-one cause of mushy fried rice. Cold and dry is the rule.
- Drowning it in soy sauce: yakimeshi is lightly seasoned, not dark and salty. Measure the 3 tbsp.
- Overcrowding the pan: if the rice piles up and steams instead of sizzling, fry it in two batches.

Title: Ginger Beef & Edamame Rice
Ingredients:
- 1¼ lb flank steak
- 2 cups frozen shelled edamame, thawed
- 2½ cups dry short-grain white rice

For the ginger marinade:
- 3 tbsp soy sauce
- 2 tbsp mirin
- 2 tbsp sake
- 2 tbsp grated fresh ginger (about a 2-inch piece)
- 3 garlic cloves, minced
- 1 tbsp brown sugar

To finish:
- 1 tbsp neutral oil (canola or vegetable)
- 1 tsp toasted sesame oil
- 4 green onions, thinly sliced
- 1 tbsp toasted sesame seeds
Steps:
1. Mise en place: everything chopped, measured, and set out before any heat goes on. Get the rice cooking: rinse 2½ cups short-grain rice, combine with 3 cups water in a pot, bring to a boil, stir once, cover, cook on low 15 minutes, rest 10 minutes, fluff. Slice the flank steak: look for the long lines (the grain) running through the meat and cut ACROSS them into thin strips about 1/4 inch thick — cutting against the grain is what keeps flank steak tender. Grate the ginger and mince the garlic. Whisk all the marinade ingredients in a bowl, add the beef strips, and marinate 15 minutes at room temperature (up to 30 minutes; no longer or the texture softens too much).

2. Sear the beef. Heat a large skillet or wok over high heat until a drop of water sizzles violently. Add the 1 tbsp neutral oil and swirl. Lift the beef out of the marinade with tongs, letting the excess drip off (reserve the marinade in the bowl). Sear the beef in a single layer — work in two batches — 60-90 seconds per side, until the edges are deeply browned. Remove to a plate. Thin strips cook fast; pull them while the centers still show a hint of pink. (If the beef is gray and swimming in liquid, the pan was crowded or not hot enough.)

3. Make the pan sauce. Pour the reserved marinade into the hot pan — it will bubble furiously. Boil 1-2 minutes, stirring, until slightly thickened and syrupy. This step is mandatory: the marinade touched raw beef, so it must come to a full boil to be safe.

4. Finish. Return the beef to the pan along with the thawed edamame. Toss 1 minute, just until the edamame are hot and everything is glossy and coated.

5. Serve over hot rice. Drizzle with the sesame oil and scatter the green onions and sesame seeds over each bowl.

6. Storage and reheating: refrigerate up to 3 days. Reheat in a skillet over medium-high heat with a splash of water, tossing, just until steaming — thin beef strips go tough if reheated twice.

Common mistakes:
- Slicing with the grain: flank steak cut the wrong way is chewy no matter how perfectly you cook it. Find the lines, cut across them.
- Skipping the marinade boil: raw-beef marinade must hit a rolling boil before it becomes sauce.
- Overcooking the strips: 60-90 seconds per side is enough. They finish in the hot sauce.

Title: Ginger Chicken & Bok Choy Rice
Ingredients:
- 1½ lb boneless, skinless chicken breasts
- 1½ lb baby bok choy
- 2½ cups dry jasmine rice
- 6 cups chicken broth
- 1/4 cup sliced fresh ginger (about a 3-inch piece, cut into coins)
- 6 scallions, cut into 3-inch pieces, plus more sliced for garnish

For the ginger-scallion oil:
- 1/2 cup neutral oil (canola or vegetable)
- 6 scallions, finely minced
- 3 tbsp grated fresh ginger
- 1 tsp kosher salt
- 1 tsp sugar
- 1 tsp rice vinegar

To serve:
- 1 cucumber, thinly sliced
- Soy sauce (optional)
Steps:
1. Mise en place: everything chopped, measured, and set out before any heat goes on. Slice the ginger into coins about 1/8 inch thick. Cut 6 scallions into 3-inch pieces; finely mince 6 more scallions for the sauce. Grate the ginger for the sauce on the fine holes of a box grater. Trim the root ends off the bok choy and rinse the leaves well — grit hides between them. Rinse the rice in a fine-mesh strainer until the water runs mostly clear. Slice the cucumber.

2. Poach the chicken. In a large pot, combine the 6 cups chicken broth, the sliced ginger, and the 3-inch scallion pieces. Bring to a boil over high heat. Add the chicken breasts, return to the barest simmer — small lazy bubbles, not a rolling boil — and cook 12-15 minutes, until the thickest part reads 165F on an instant-read thermometer. (A hard boil makes chicken tough and stringy; gentle is the whole secret.) Lift the chicken to a plate and rest 5 minutes. Keep the broth at a low simmer — you need it for the rice and the bok choy.

3. Make the ginger-scallion oil. While the chicken poaches, put the minced scallions, grated ginger, salt, and sugar in a heatproof bowl. Heat the 1/2 cup neutral oil in a small saucepan until it shimmers and just begins to smoke. Carefully pour the hot oil over the scallion mixture — it will sizzle violently, so stand back. Stir in the rice vinegar. This sizzling oil is what blooms the raw ginger and scallion into the silky, punchy sauce Hainan chicken rice is famous for.

4. Cook the rice in the poaching broth. Measure 3¾ cups of the hot poaching broth into a medium pot, add the rinsed rice and 1 tbsp of the ginger-scallion oil, and stir once. Bring to a boil, cover, reduce to low, and cook 15 minutes. Rest 10 minutes off the heat, then fluff with a fork. The rice should be fragrant, glossy, and faintly gingery.

5. Blanch the bok choy. Bring the remaining simmering broth back up and add the bok choy. Cook 2-3 minutes, until the leaves are bright green and wilted and the white stems are tender-crisp when pierced with a knife. Lift out with tongs.

6. Slice the chicken across the grain into 1/2-inch slices.

7. Serve. Spoon rice into bowls. Fan the sliced chicken over the rice, lay bok choy alongside, and spoon about 2 tbsp of ginger-scallion oil over each serving. Add cucumber slices on the side and pass soy sauce for anyone who wants it.

8. Storage and reheating: store rice, chicken, bok choy, and oil in separate airtight containers up to 3 days. Reheat the rice with a splash of broth, covered, in the microwave. Warm the chicken gently — 60-90 seconds at 50% power — or it dries out. The ginger-scallion oil keeps 1 week refrigerated; the oil will firm up, so let it sit at room temperature 15 minutes before serving.

Common mistakes:
- Boiling the chicken hard: a rolling boil squeezes the juices out and gives you dry, stringy meat. Bare simmer only.
- Pouring lukewarm oil over the scallions: the oil must be shimmering-hot or you get flat, raw-tasting sauce instead of the signature sizzle-bloomed flavor.
- Skipping the rest: slice too soon and the juices run out onto the cutting board instead of staying in the meat.

Title: Ginger Pork Donburi
Ingredients:
- 1¼ lb pork tenderloin
- 2½ cups dry short-grain white rice

For the donburi sauce:
- 2 cups water
- 2 tsp instant dashi granules
- 1/4 cup soy sauce
- 3 tbsp mirin
- 2 tbsp sake
- 2 tbsp sugar
- 2 tbsp grated fresh ginger

For the topping:
- 1 large yellow onion, thinly sliced
- 4 large eggs, lightly beaten
- 1 tbsp neutral oil (canola or vegetable)
- 2 green onions, thinly sliced
- 1 tsp toasted sesame seeds
- Beni shoga (pickled red ginger), optional, for serving
Steps:
1. Mise en place: everything chopped, measured, and set out before any heat goes on. Get the rice cooking: rinse 2½ cups short-grain rice, combine with 3 cups water, bring to a boil, stir once, cover, cook on low 15 minutes, rest 10 minutes, fluff. Cut the pork tenderloin into 1/2-inch medallions, then cut each medallion into bite-size strips. Slice the onion into thin half-moons about 1/4 inch thick (cut the onion in half top to bottom, then slice across). Beat the eggs lightly in a bowl — you want visible streaks of white and yolk, not a uniform yellow. Grate the ginger. Dissolve the dashi granules in the hot water, then stir in the soy sauce, mirin, sake, sugar, and grated ginger.

2. Sear the pork. Heat the 1 tbsp oil in a large skillet over medium-high heat until shimmering. Add the pork in a single layer and sear 2 minutes per side, until golden-brown at the edges. Check the thickest piece with a thermometer: 145F. Remove to a plate. (Tenderloin is lean — a minute too long and it dries out, so watch it.)

3. Simmer the onion. In the same skillet, pour in the donburi sauce and add the sliced onion. Simmer over medium heat 4-5 minutes, until the onion is completely soft, sweet, and translucent and the sauce smells savory-sweet.

4. Return the pork to the pan and simmer 2 minutes, turning the pieces so they soak up the sauce.

5. Set the egg. Drizzle the beaten egg in ribbons over the pork and onion — pour slowly in a spiral so it lands in strands, not one sheet. Cover the skillet and cook 1-2 minutes, until the egg is just set but still glossy on top. Do not stir or scramble; you want silky ribbons of egg, the hallmark of a real donburi topping.

6. Serve. Fill deep bowls with hot rice. Slide the pork, onion, egg, and a generous spoonful of sauce over the rice — donburi should be glossy and juicy, the sauce soaking slightly into the top of the rice, but not swimming. Garnish with green onions, sesame seeds, and beni shoga if using.

7. Storage and reheating: refrigerate up to 3 days. Reheat covered in a skillet over medium-low heat with a splash of water until steaming. The egg will firm up a bit — that is unavoidable and still delicious.

Common mistakes:
- Scrambling the egg: stirred egg is a different dish. Drizzle, cover, and leave it alone for silky ribbons.
- Cutting the pork too thick: 1/2-inch pieces stay tender; thick chunks turn chewy in the simmer.
- Flooding the bowl: you want the rice glossy with sauce, not soup. Spoon, do not pour.

Title: Gochujang Beef Bowls
Ingredients:
- 1¼ lb 93% lean ground beef
- 2½ cups dry jasmine rice

For the gochujang sauce:
- 1/4 cup gochujang (Korean fermented chili paste)
- 3 tbsp soy sauce
- 2 tbsp honey
- 1 tbsp brown sugar
- 1 tbsp rice vinegar
- 2 tsp toasted sesame oil
- 4 garlic cloves, minced
- 1 tbsp grated fresh ginger

For the bowls:
- 1 tbsp neutral oil (canola or vegetable)
- 1 cup shredded carrots
- 1 cucumber, thinly sliced
- 6 large eggs
- 4 green onions, thinly sliced
- 1 tbsp toasted sesame seeds
Steps:
1. Mise en place: everything chopped, measured, and set out before any heat goes on. Get the rice cooking: rinse 2½ cups jasmine rice, combine with 3¾ cups water, bring to a boil, stir once, cover, cook on low 15 minutes, rest 10 minutes, fluff. Whisk all the sauce ingredients in a small bowl until smooth. Mince the garlic (chop into pieces smaller than a grain of rice) and grate the ginger. Shred the carrots on the large holes of a box grater. Thinly slice the cucumber and the green onions.

2. Brown the beef. Heat a large skillet over medium-high heat until a drop of water sizzles hard. Add the ground beef and break it into crumbles with a wooden spoon. Now leave it alone: let it sit undisturbed 2-3 minutes so it develops a deep brown crust, then break and turn, repeating for 6-8 minutes total, until no pink remains and the crumbles are well browned. (Constant stirring steams the meat gray; patience browns it.) The beef is done at 160F. If more than a spoonful of fat pools in the pan, tilt and spoon it off.

3. Sauce it. Stir the garlic and ginger into the beef and cook 30 seconds until fragrant. Pour in the gochujang sauce and stir to coat. Reduce the heat to medium and simmer 2-3 minutes, stirring, until the sauce thickens, turns glossy, and clings to every crumble. Taste: this is the moment to balance it. Too fiery? Add another teaspoon of honey. Too sweet or flat? Add another teaspoon of gochujang. Gochujang brands vary wildly in heat, so trust your tongue, not the recipe.

4. Fry the eggs. Heat the 1 tbsp neutral oil in a nonstick skillet over medium heat. Crack in the eggs and cook 2-3 minutes sunny-side up, until the whites are fully set and the yolks are still runny — the runny yolk becomes a second sauce for the bowl. Season with a pinch of salt. (Prefer set yolks? Cover the pan for the last minute.)

5. Assemble. Spoon rice into bowls. Top with a generous scoop of gochujang beef, a handful of shredded carrots, and cucumber slices. Crown each bowl with a fried egg, then scatter green onions and sesame seeds over everything.

6. Storage and reheating: refrigerate the beef and rice up to 4 days in airtight containers; keep cucumbers and carrots separate so they stay crisp. Reheat the beef in a skillet over medium heat with a splash of water until steaming. Fry the eggs fresh — reheated fried eggs are rubbery; leftovers keep 2 days.

Common mistakes:
- Stirring the beef constantly: you get gray steamed crumbles instead of browned, flavorful ones. Let it sit.
- Letting the sugary sauce scorch: once the sauce goes in, keep it at a gentle simmer and keep it moving.
- Skipping the taste-and-adjust: gochujang heat varies by brand, so the honey-to-heat balance must be tuned by tasting.

Title: Gochujang Salmon Rice Bowls
Ingredients:
- 1½ lb salmon fillet, skin removed, cut into 6 portions
- 2½ cups dry jasmine rice

For the gochujang glaze:
- 1/4 cup gochujang (Korean fermented chili paste)
- 2 tbsp honey
- 2 tbsp soy sauce
- 1 tbsp toasted sesame oil
- 1 tbsp rice vinegar
- 3 garlic cloves, minced
- 1 tbsp grated fresh ginger

For the bowls:
- 1 tbsp neutral oil (canola or vegetable)
- 1 ripe avocado, sliced
- 1 cucumber, thinly sliced
- 4 green onions, thinly sliced
- 1 tbsp toasted sesame seeds
- Lime wedges
Steps:
1. Mise en place: everything chopped, measured, and set out before any heat goes on. Get the rice cooking: rinse 2½ cups jasmine rice, combine with 3¾ cups water, bring to a boil, stir once, cover, cook on low 15 minutes, rest 10 minutes, fluff. Whisk all the glaze ingredients in a small bowl. Spoon 3 tbsp of the glaze into a separate small bowl and set aside for drizzling — this keeps the serving sauce free of raw-fish contact. Cut the salmon into 6 even portions and pat them very dry with paper towels. Slice the avocado, cucumber, and green onions. Cut the lime into wedges.

2. Glaze the salmon. Brush the salmon portions generously on all sides with the main batch of glaze (not the reserved drizzle portion).

3. Cook the salmon — pick one method. Skillet: heat the 1 tbsp neutral oil in a large skillet over medium-high heat until shimmering. Sear the salmon 3 minutes per side, until the glaze caramelizes to a deep amber and the center reads 125-130F for medium. Oven: arrange on a foil-lined sheet pan and bake at 425F for 10-12 minutes, until 125-130F at the thickest point. Either way, watch the color: the honey and gochujang sugars go from beautifully caramelized to burnt quickly, so medium-high heat, not maximum.

4. Rest the salmon 2 minutes. The temperature will coast up a few degrees and the juices will settle.

5. Assemble. Spoon rice into bowls. Set a salmon portion on each, then arrange avocado and cucumber alongside. Drizzle with the reserved glaze, scatter green onions and sesame seeds, and add lime wedges.

6. Serve with extra lime for squeezing — the acidity is what keeps the rich salmon and sweet heat in balance.

7. Storage and reheating: refrigerate up to 3 days. Reheat gently — microwave at 50% power in 30-second bursts just until warm, or the salmon dries out. Slice the avocado fresh; it does not keep.

Common mistakes:
- Burning the glaze: honey plus high heat equals charcoal. Medium-high, watchful eyes, deep amber — not black.
- Overcooking the salmon: pull it at 125-130F. At 145F+ it is dry, and no glaze can save it.
- Double-dipping the brush: glaze that touched raw fish must never go back on the finished bowl. That is why you reserved the drizzle portion first.

Title: Grilled Steak with Tomato Chimichurri Rice
Ingredients:
- 2 1/2 lb sirloin steak, about 1 1/2 inches thick
- 1 tsp kosher salt, plus more to taste
- 1/2 tsp black pepper
- 1 tbsp olive oil (for the grill)

For the tomato rice:
- 2 1/2 cups long-grain white rice
- 2 tbsp olive oil
- 1 small yellow onion, finely diced
- 2 tbsp tomato paste
- 3 3/4 cups chicken broth
- 1 tsp kosher salt

For the tomato chimichurri:
- 1 pint cherry tomatoes (about 12 oz)
- 1 1/2 cups packed fresh flat-leaf parsley leaves (about 2 bunches)
- 4 garlic cloves, minced
- 2 tsp dried oregano
- 1/2 tsp red pepper flakes
- 3 tbsp red wine vinegar
- 1/3 cup extra-virgin olive oil
- 1 tsp kosher salt, plus more to taste - taste the sauce before serving and add up to 1/2 tsp more
Steps:
1. Mise en place: Pat the steak very dry with paper towels and season both sides with the salt and pepper. Let it sit at room temperature for 30 minutes (cold steak sears unevenly). Finely chop the parsley (cut off the thick stems first, then rock your knife through the leaves until fine). Mince the garlic (chop into tiny pieces). Dice the onion (cut into small 1/4-inch cubes). Measure everything else and set it out. Preheat your grill or grill pan to high heat, 450-500F.

2. Make the chimichurri: In a medium bowl, stir together the chopped parsley, garlic, oregano, red pepper flakes, red wine vinegar, and salt. Pour in the olive oil and stir. Set aside for at least 15 minutes so the flavors meld. Taste and add salt up to 1/2 tsp more if it tastes flat.

3. Start the tomato rice: Heat 2 tbsp olive oil in a large pot over medium heat. Add the diced onion and cook 4-5 minutes, stirring, until soft and translucent. Stir in the tomato paste and cook 1-2 minutes until it darkens to a brick-red color and smells sweet. Add the rice and stir for 1 minute to coat every grain. Pour in the chicken broth and add the salt. Bring to a boil, then reduce to low heat, cover with a tight lid, and cook 15 minutes without lifting the lid. Remove from heat and rest, still covered, 10 minutes. Fluff with a fork.

4. Blister the tomatoes: Heat a large dry skillet over high heat with 1 tsp of the grill olive oil. Add the cherry tomatoes in a single layer. Cook 3-4 minutes without moving them, until the skins char and split and some tomatoes burst. Shake the pan once or twice. Season with a pinch of salt and set aside.

5. Grill the steak: Oil the hot grill grates with the remaining olive oil (use tongs and a folded paper towel). Lay the steak on the grill and cook 4-5 minutes per side for medium-rare, until deep char marks form and the steak feels firm but springy when pressed. Check with a thermometer: 130-135F for medium-rare.

6. Rest the steak: Move it to a cutting board, tent loosely with foil, and rest 8-10 minutes. This lets the juices redistribute; cutting too soon spills them onto the board.

7. Finish and plate: Fold the blistered tomatoes into the chimichurri. Slice the steak thinly against the grain (look for the lines running through the meat and cut across them). Spoon the tomato rice into wide bowls, fan the steak slices over the top, and spoon the tomato chimichurri generously over everything.

8. Storage and reheating: Refrigerate leftovers in separate containers up to 4 days. Reheat rice with a splash of water, covered, in the microwave. Warm steak slices gently in a skillet over medium-low heat just until heated through so they stay pink inside.

Common mistakes:
- Slicing with the grain makes even good steak chewy - always cut across the lines.
- Skipping the rest lets all the juice run out onto the cutting board.
- Drowning the steak in chimichurri; it is a spoon-over condiment, not a marinade bath.
- Lifting the rice lid during cooking releases the steam and gives gummy, uneven rice.

Title: Herbes de Provence Chicken & Potatoes
Ingredients:
- 1 whole chicken, about 4 1/2 lb, giblets removed
- 2 tsp kosher salt, plus more to taste
- 1 tsp black pepper

For the herb butter:
- 6 tbsp unsalted butter, softened at room temperature
- 2 tbsp herbes de Provence
- 4 garlic cloves, minced
- 1 tsp lemon zest (about 1 lemon)

- 1 lemon, quartered
- 3 lb Yukon Gold potatoes, cut into 1 1/2-inch chunks
- 2 tbsp olive oil
- 4 sprigs fresh thyme (optional)
Steps:
1. Mise en place: Take the chicken out of the refrigerator 45 minutes before cooking so it loses its chill and roasts evenly. Remove the giblets from the cavity (check both ends). Pat the chicken VERY dry inside and out with paper towels - dry skin is the secret to crisp, golden skin. Cut the potatoes into 1 1/2-inch chunks (roughly the size of a golf ball). Mince the garlic. Zest the lemon (grate only the yellow outer peel, not the bitter white pith). Quarter the zested lemon. Preheat the oven to 425F with the rack in the middle position.

2. Make the herb butter: In a small bowl, mash the softened butter with the herbes de Provence, minced garlic, lemon zest, 1 tsp of the salt, and 1/2 tsp of the pepper until evenly mixed. It should smell fragrant and look speckled with herbs.

3. Season the chicken: Sprinkle 1 tsp salt inside the cavity. Stuff the lemon quarters inside. Gently slide your fingers under the skin over the breast to loosen it without tearing. Push about half the herb butter under the skin, spreading it over the breast meat. Rub the remaining butter all over the outside of the bird. Tie the legs together with kitchen twine and tuck the wing tips under the body.

4. Prepare the potatoes: Toss the potato chunks with the olive oil, the remaining salt, and pepper. Spread them in a single layer in a large roasting pan. Set the chicken on top of the potatoes (or nestle it in the center with potatoes around it).

5. Roast: Put the pan in the 425F oven and roast 1 hour 15 minutes to 1 hour 30 minutes, until the skin is deep golden brown and crisp, the juices run clear when you pierce the thigh, and a thermometer in the thickest part of the thigh (not touching bone) reads 165F. If the skin browns too fast, tent loosely with foil for the last 20 minutes.

6. Rest: Transfer the chicken to a cutting board, tent loosely with foil, and rest 15-20 minutes. Do not skip this - the juices need time to settle back into the meat.

7. Carve and serve: Cut through the skin between each leg and the breast, then press to pop the hip joint and separate the legs. Slice the breast meat off the bone in thick slices. Arrange on a platter with the roasted potatoes and spoon the pan juices over everything.

8. Storage and reheating: Refrigerate up to 4 days. Reheat covered at 325F with a splash of chicken broth until steaming, about 20 minutes. Save the carcass for stock.

Common mistakes:
- Wet skin never crisps - pat the bird thoroughly dry, inside and out.
- Skipping the rest gives you dry breast meat and juice all over the board.
- Roasting straight from the fridge cooks the outside before the inside is done.
- Under-salting: a whole bird needs the full 2 tsp of salt to taste seasoned.

Title: Korean Beef & Potato Bowls
Ingredients:
- 3 cups long-grain white rice (for serving)
- 2 lb Yukon Gold or russet potatoes, peeled and cut into 1-inch cubes
- 1 lb ground beef (90% lean)
- 4 green onions, thinly sliced (white and green parts separated)
- 6 garlic cloves, minced
- 1 jalapeño, thinly sliced (optional, for heat)
- 1/2 cup soy sauce
- 3 tbsp sugar
- 1 tbsp toasted sesame oil
- 1 1/2 cups water
- 1 tbsp toasted sesame seeds
Steps:
1. Mise en place: Peel the potatoes and cut into 1-inch cubes (about the size of dice). Mince the garlic. Slice the green onions, keeping the white bottoms and green tops in separate piles. Slice the jalapeño if using. Measure the soy sauce, sugar, sesame oil, and water. Start the rice in a rice cooker or pot so it is ready when the beef and potatoes finish.

2. Brown the beef: Heat a large heavy pot or Dutch oven over medium-high heat. Add the ground beef and cook 5-6 minutes, breaking it into small crumbles with a wooden spoon, until no pink remains and the edges are browned and sizzling. The beef should reach 160F.

3. Build the flavor base: Stir in the minced garlic, the white parts of the green onions, and the jalapeño. Cook 1 minute until fragrant. Pour in the soy sauce, sprinkle in the sugar, and drizzle in the sesame oil. Stir for 30 seconds until the sugar starts to dissolve.

4. Braise the potatoes: Add the potato cubes and the water. Stir to coat. Bring to a rolling boil, then reduce to a steady simmer over medium heat. Cook 12-15 minutes, stirring gently every few minutes, until the potatoes are fork-tender and the sauce has reduced to a glossy glaze that coats everything. The liquid should be mostly gone, not soupy.

5. Finish: Taste a potato - it should be savory-sweet and tender all the way through. Sprinkle the green onion tops and sesame seeds over the top.

6. Serve: Spoon over bowls of hot steamed rice, making sure each bowl gets plenty of the glazed sauce.

7. Storage and reheating: Refrigerate up to 4 days. The sauce thickens as it sits; reheat in a pot over medium heat with a splash of water, stirring gently so the potatoes do not break apart.

Common mistakes:
- Cutting the potatoes too small turns them to mush before the sauce reduces - keep them a full inch.
- Serving it soupy: let the liquid cook down until it glazes the potatoes.
- Adding the sesame oil at the very start can make it taste bitter; it goes in with the sauce.
- Stirring aggressively breaks the tender potatoes into the sauce.

Title: Lemon Chicken Couscous Bowls
Ingredients:
- 2 1/2 lb boneless, skinless chicken thighs
- 2 tsp kosher salt, plus more to taste
- 1 tsp black pepper
- 2 tbsp olive oil

For the tagine:
- 1 large yellow onion, thinly sliced
- 4 garlic cloves, minced
- 1 tbsp grated fresh ginger
- 1 tsp ground turmeric
- 1 tsp ground cumin
- 1/2 tsp ground cinnamon
- 1/4 tsp cayenne pepper (optional)
- 1 1/2 cups chicken broth
- 1 large preserved lemon, pulp removed and rind thinly sliced (about 2 oz; find them in the Middle Eastern aisle, or substitute 2 tbsp fresh lemon juice plus 1 tsp zest)
- 3/4 cup pitted green olives (such as Castelvetrano)
- 1/2 cup chopped fresh cilantro, plus more for serving
- 1/4 cup chopped fresh parsley

For the couscous:
- 2 1/2 cups dry couscous
- 2 1/2 cups boiling water or chicken broth
- 2 tbsp olive oil or butter
- 1 tsp kosher salt
Steps:
1. Mise en place: Pat the chicken thighs dry and season with the salt and pepper. Thinly slice the onion (cut into thin half-moons). Mince the garlic. Grate the ginger (peel the knobby skin first, then grate on the small holes). Remove the pulp from the preserved lemon (scoop out the soft interior with a spoon) and slice the rind into thin strips. Pit the olives if needed. Chop the cilantro and parsley. Measure the spices into one small bowl so they are ready.

2. Sear the chicken: Heat the olive oil in a large Dutch oven over medium-high heat until shimmering. Sear the chicken thighs 4-5 minutes per side until deep golden brown. Work in two batches so the pan is not crowded. Set the chicken aside on a plate.

3. Soften the onion: Reduce the heat to medium. Add the sliced onion to the same pot and cook 8-10 minutes, stirring, until soft and golden at the edges. Add the garlic, ginger, turmeric, cumin, cinnamon, and cayenne. Stir 1 minute until very fragrant - the spices should smell toasty, not raw.

4. Braise: Pour in the chicken broth and scrape up all the browned bits from the bottom of the pot. Return the chicken to the pot. Bring to a gentle simmer, cover, and cook 30 minutes, turning the chicken once halfway through.

5. Finish the tagine: Stir in the preserved lemon strips and the olives. Simmer uncovered 10-15 minutes more, until the sauce thickens enough to coat a spoon and the chicken is fall-apart tender. Thighs are best around 175F. Stir in the cilantro and parsley. Taste and add salt only if needed - the preserved lemon and olives are already salty.

6. Make the couscous: While the tagine finishes, put the dry couscous, salt, and olive oil in a large heatproof bowl. Pour the boiling water over it, stir once, cover tightly, and let stand 5 minutes without peeking. Uncover and fluff with a fork until the grains separate.

7. Serve: Spoon couscous into wide bowls, top with chicken thighs and plenty of sauce, and shower with extra cilantro.

8. Storage and reheating: Refrigerate up to 4 days, stored separately from the couscous. This dish tastes even better the next day. Reheat gently on the stove with a splash of water.

Common mistakes:
- Using fresh lemon instead of preserved lemon makes the sauce harsh and one-dimensional; preserved lemon is mellow and floral.
- Adding the olives at the start turns them mushy and gray - they go in at the end.
- Peeking at the couscous before 5 minutes lets the steam escape and leaves gummy clumps.
- Skipping the sear gives you pale chicken and a thin-tasting sauce.

Title: Lemon Garlic Salmon Risotto
Ingredients:
- 1 1/2 lb salmon fillet, skin on, cut into 6 portions
- 1 tsp kosher salt, plus more to taste
- 1/2 tsp black pepper
- 2 tbsp olive oil

For the risotto:
- 6 to 7 cups chicken broth, kept hot
- 2 tbsp olive oil
- 1 medium yellow onion, finely diced
- 4 garlic cloves, minced
- 2 cups arborio rice (do not rinse)
- 1/2 cup dry white wine (such as Pinot Grigio)
- 1 tbsp lemon zest (about 2 lemons)
- 3 tbsp fresh lemon juice
- 4 tbsp cold unsalted butter, cubed
- 3/4 cup grated Parmesan, plus more for serving
- 1/4 cup chopped fresh parsley
Steps:
1. Mise en place: Pour the chicken broth into a saucepan and keep it at a bare simmer over low heat the entire time you cook - hot stock is non-negotiable for risotto. Dice the onion (cut into small 1/4-inch cubes). Mince the garlic. Zest the lemons (grate only the yellow peel), then juice them. Cut the cold butter into cubes and keep it refrigerated until the end. Grate the Parmesan. Pat the salmon portions dry and season with the salt and pepper. Measure the rice - do NOT rinse it; the surface starch is what makes risotto creamy.

2. Sear the salmon: Heat 2 tbsp olive oil in a large skillet over medium-high heat until shimmering. Lay the salmon portions skin-side down and press gently for 10 seconds so the skin stays flat. Cook 4-5 minutes without moving until the skin is crisp and the flesh has turned opaque about two-thirds of the way up. Flip and cook 1-2 minutes more. The salmon is done at 125-130F for medium - it should flake easily but still look slightly translucent in the very center. Set aside on a warm plate.

3. Soften the aromatics: In a large heavy pot or Dutch oven, heat 2 tbsp olive oil over medium heat. Add the diced onion and cook 4-5 minutes until soft and translucent. Add the garlic and cook 30 seconds until fragrant.

4. Toast the rice (tostatura): Add the arborio rice and stir constantly for 2 minutes. The grains should turn pearly at the edges with a white dot in the center, and smell faintly nutty. This step keeps the grains distinct instead of mushy.

5. Deglaze: Pour in the white wine. It will hiss and steam. Stir until the wine is almost completely absorbed and the sharp alcohol smell cooks off, about 2 minutes.

6. Add stock ladle by ladle: Add 1 cup of hot broth and stir fairly often (you do not need to stir nonstop, but do not walk away). When the liquid is mostly absorbed and the rice looks creamy, add another cup. Repeat for 18-20 minutes total. Taste at 18 minutes: the rice should be tender with a slight bite in the center (al dente). You may not need all the broth; stop when it is creamy and flowing, not stiff.

7. Finish with lemon and mantecatura: Stir in the lemon zest and lemon juice. Remove the pot from the heat. Add the cold butter cubes and the Parmesan and beat vigorously with a wooden spoon for 1 minute until glossy and creamy. This off-heat beating is called mantecatura and it is what makes risotto silky. Let it rest 2 minutes. Taste and add salt if needed.

8. Serve: Spoon the risotto into warm shallow bowls. Lay a salmon portion on top of each, letting it flake slightly into the rice. Shower with parsley and extra Parmesan.

9. Storage and reheating: Refrigerate up to 2 days. Risotto firms up cold; reheat gently in a pot with a splash of broth, stirring, until creamy again. Do not microwave the salmon to rubber - warm it separately and gently.

Common mistakes:
- Adding cold or room-temperature stock stalls the cooking and makes gummy risotto - keep it simmering.
- Rinsing the rice washes away the starch that creates the creamy texture.
- Adding the lemon juice early in the cooking makes it taste bitter; it goes in at the end.
- Cooking the salmon IN the risotto overcooks it into dry flakes - cook it separately.

Title: Lemon Salmon & Olive Potatoes
Ingredients:
- 3 lb Yukon Gold potatoes, peeled and cut into wedges
- 1/2 cup extra-virgin olive oil
- 1/2 cup fresh lemon juice (about 3 lemons)
- 1 cup water or chicken broth
- 4 garlic cloves, minced
- 1 tbsp dried oregano, plus more for serving
- 2 tsp kosher salt, plus more to taste
- 1 tsp black pepper
- 1 cup Kalamata olives, pitted
- 2 lb salmon fillet, cut into 6 portions
- Lemon wedges and chopped fresh parsley, for serving
Steps:
1. Mise en place: Preheat the oven to 400F. Peel the potatoes and cut each into 6-8 long wedges (like thick steak fries). Mince the garlic. Juice the lemons. Pit the olives if needed. Pat the salmon portions dry. In a large roasting pan, whisk together the olive oil, lemon juice, water, garlic, oregano, salt, and pepper.

2. Roast the potatoes: Add the potato wedges to the pan and turn them until every piece is coated in the lemony oil. Spread in a single layer with a little space between pieces - crowding steams them instead of crisping them. Roast 30 minutes, then turn each wedge over with tongs.

3. Add the olives and salmon: Scatter the olives around the potatoes. Season the salmon portions with salt, pepper, and a pinch of oregano, drizzle with a spoonful of the pan juices, and nestle them among the potatoes. Do not let the salmon sit in the lemon juice longer than 15 minutes total - the acid starts to "cook" the flesh like ceviche.

4. Finish roasting: Roast 12-15 minutes more, until the potatoes are golden with crisp edges and tender inside (a knife slides in easily) and the salmon is just opaque and flakes with a fork. The salmon is done at 125-130F for medium. The pan liquid should be mostly absorbed into a glossy lemony sauce.

5. Rest and serve: Let the pan rest 5 minutes. Transfer potatoes, olives, and salmon to a platter or plates, spoon the pan sauce over everything, and finish with lemon wedges, parsley, and an extra pinch of oregano.

6. Storage and reheating: Refrigerate up to 3 days. Reheat in a 350F oven until warmed through, about 12 minutes; the microwave makes the potatoes soggy and the salmon rubbery.

Common mistakes:
- Crowding the pan gives you steamed, pale potatoes instead of crisp, golden ones - use two pans if needed.
- Letting the salmon marinate in lemon juice too long turns the outside mushy and chalky.
- Waiting for the salmon to "look done" all the way through in the oven means it is overdone on the plate - pull it at 125-130F and let carryover heat finish it.
- Skipping the mid-roast turn leaves one side of every potato pale.

Title: Lemongrass Chicken Rice Bowls
Ingredients:
- 3 cups jasmine rice (for serving)
- 2 1/2 lb boneless, skinless chicken thighs, cut into 1-inch pieces

For the marinade:
- 4 stalks lemongrass, tough outer layers removed, finely minced (about 1/2 cup)
- 4 garlic cloves, minced
- 2 Thai bird chiles, thinly sliced (or 1/2 tsp red pepper flakes)
- 3 tbsp fish sauce
- 2 tbsp sugar
- 1 tbsp neutral oil (such as avocado oil)

For the bowls:
- 3 tbsp neutral oil, divided
- 1/2 cup water
- 1 cucumber, thinly sliced
- 1/2 cup fresh cilantro leaves
- 4 green onions, thinly sliced
- Lime wedges, for serving
Steps:
1. Mise en place: Trim the woody base off each lemongrass stalk and peel away the tough outer layers until you reach the pale, tender core. Bruise it with the flat of your knife, slice it into thin rings, then mince very fine - woody chunks are unpleasant to chew, so take your time here. Mince the garlic. Slice the chiles. Cut the chicken into 1-inch pieces (about the size of a large grape). Slice the cucumber and green onions. Start the jasmine rice.

2. Marinate: In a large bowl, toss the chicken with the minced lemongrass, garlic, chiles, fish sauce, sugar, and 1 tbsp oil. Mix well so every piece is coated. Let stand at room temperature for 30 minutes (or refrigerate up to overnight for deeper flavor).

3. Sear the chicken: Heat a large wok or heavy skillet over high heat until it just starts to smoke. Add 1 1/2 tbsp oil and swirl. Add HALF the chicken in a single layer - crowding steams the meat instead of searing it. Cook 5-6 minutes, turning once, until charred at the edges and cooked through to 165F. Transfer to a plate and repeat with the remaining chicken and oil.

4. Make the glaze: Return all the chicken to the hot pan. Pour in the 1/2 cup water and scrape up the browned bits. Simmer 3-4 minutes, stirring, until the liquid reduces to a sticky, glossy glaze that coats the chicken. The kitchen should smell intensely of lemongrass and caramelized fish sauce.

5. Build the bowls: Spoon hot jasmine rice into bowls. Pile the glazed lemongrass chicken over the rice. Fan cucumber slices alongside, then shower with cilantro, green onions, and a squeeze of lime.

6. Storage and reheating: Refrigerate up to 4 days. Reheat in a skillet over medium heat with a splash of water to loosen the glaze, or microwave covered.

Common mistakes:
- Crowding the pan gives you gray, steamed chicken with no char - sear in two batches.
- Using the tough green tops of the lemongrass leaves woody fibers in the dish; only the pale tender base is edible.
- Cranking the heat to maximum after adding the sugar burns it bitter - keep it at medium-high once the chicken is seared.
- Skipping the water-and-reduce step leaves the chicken dry; the glaze is the whole point.

Title: Lemongrass Pork Rice Plates
Ingredients:
- 3 cups jasmine rice (broken rice if you can find it at an Asian market - that is the Saigon original)
- 2 1/2 lb boneless pork chops, about 3/4 inch thick

For the marinade:
- 3 stalks lemongrass, tough outer layers removed, finely minced
- 4 garlic cloves, minced
- 1/4 cup fish sauce
- 2 tbsp soy sauce
- 1/4 cup sugar
- 2 tbsp neutral oil (such as avocado oil)

For the nuoc cham (dipping sauce):
- 1/4 cup fish sauce
- 1/4 cup water
- 3 tbsp sugar
- 2 tbsp fresh lime juice
- 1 garlic clove, minced
- 1 Thai chile, thinly sliced

For the quick pickles:
- 1 cup julienned carrot
- 1 cup julienned daikon radish (or use all carrot)
- 1/2 cup rice vinegar
- 1/2 cup water
- 2 tbsp sugar
- 1 tsp kosher salt

For serving:
- 1/4 cup neutral oil
- 6 green onions, thinly sliced
- 1 cucumber, thinly sliced
- Fresh cilantro sprigs
Steps:
1. Mise en place: Mince the lemongrass (use only the pale tender core, minced very fine). Mince the garlic. Julienne the carrot and daikon (cut into thin matchsticks). Slice the green onions and cucumber. Make the marinade and the pickles before anything else, since the pork needs marinating time.

2. Marinate the pork: In a large bowl or zip-top bag, combine the lemongrass, garlic, fish sauce, soy sauce, sugar, and oil. Add the pork chops and massage the marinade into the meat. Refrigerate at least 2 hours, or overnight for the deepest flavor.

3. Make the nuoc cham: Whisk the fish sauce, water, sugar, lime juice, garlic, and chile in a small bowl until the sugar dissolves completely. Taste - it should be a bold balance of salty, sweet, and sour. Adjust with a squeeze more lime if it tastes flat. Set aside at room temperature.

4. Quick-pickle the vegetables: In a bowl, whisk the rice vinegar, water, sugar, and salt until dissolved. Add the carrot and daikon matchsticks, press them under the liquid, and let stand at least 30 minutes. Drain before serving.

5. Cook the rice: Rinse the jasmine rice until the water runs mostly clear, then cook in a rice cooker or pot (3 cups rice to 3 1/2 cups water). Keep warm.

6. Grill the pork: Pound the chops lightly to an even 3/4-inch thickness so they cook evenly. Heat a grill, grill pan, or broiler to medium-high heat. Grill the chops 5-6 minutes per side until nicely charred at the edges and the internal temperature reads 145F. Watch closely - the sugar in the marinade burns fast over high heat. If flare-ups happen, move the chops to a cooler spot.

7. Rest and slice: Transfer the pork to a cutting board and rest 3 minutes. Slice thinly across the grain.

8. Make the scallion oil: Heat the 1/4 cup oil in a small pan until shimmering (not smoking). Put the sliced green onions in a heatproof bowl with a pinch of salt and pour the hot oil over them. They will sizzle and turn vivid green.

9. Plate Saigon-style: Mound rice on each plate. Arrange sliced pork beside it. Add a tangle of drained pickles, cucumber slices, and cilantro. Drizzle a spoonful of scallion oil over the rice. Serve the nuoc cham in small bowls on the side for spooning over everything.

10. Storage and reheating: Refrigerate pork, rice, and pickles separately up to 4 days. Reheat pork gently in a covered skillet over medium-low heat with a splash of water so it stays juicy. The pickles keep 2 weeks.

Common mistakes:
- Blasting sugary marinated pork over maximum heat chars it black before the inside cooks - medium-high with attention is right.
- Skipping the rest lets the juices escape and leaves dry pork.
- Forgetting to dissolve the sugar in the nuoc cham leaves gritty sauce - whisk until completely clear.
- Serving the pork unsliced: thin slices across the grain are what make each bite tender.

Title: Miso Butter Cod & Bok Choy
Ingredients:
- 2 1/2 cups jasmine rice (for serving)
- 2 1/2 lb cod fillets, 1 to 1 1/2 inches thick, cut into 6 portions
- 1 tsp kosher salt

For the miso butter glaze:
- 1/3 cup white miso paste
- 3 tbsp unsalted butter, softened
- 2 tbsp mirin (sweet Japanese rice wine)
- 1 tbsp sugar

For the bok choy:
- 2 lb baby bok choy, halved lengthwise
- 1 tbsp neutral oil (such as avocado oil)
- 3 garlic cloves, thinly sliced
- 2 tbsp water
- 1 tsp soy sauce
- 1 tsp toasted sesame seeds (optional)
Steps:
1. Mise en place: Preheat the oven to 400F and line a sheet pan with foil (miso drips burn onto bare pans). Pat the cod portions very dry with paper towels and season lightly with the salt. Halve the bok choy lengthwise through the core so the leaves stay attached. Thinly slice the garlic. Whisk the miso, softened butter, mirin, and sugar in a small bowl until completely smooth. Start the jasmine rice.

2. Glaze the cod - thinly: Spread a THIN, even layer of the miso butter over the top and sides of each fillet. A thick coat will burn before the fish cooks through; you want a film, not a frosting. Choose fillets at least 1 inch thick - thin tail pieces dry out before the glaze caramelizes.

3. Bake: Arrange the fillets on the prepared pan with space between them. Bake 10-12 minutes, until the fish is nearly opaque all the way through and flakes gently when nudged with a fork.

4. Broil - and do not walk away: Switch the oven to broil on high. Broil the cod 1-2 minutes, watching it every second, until the glaze bubbles and turns deep golden with a few caramelized spots. The sugars in the miso and mirin go from caramelized to burnt in under a minute. The fish is done when it reaches 145F in the thickest part and flakes easily.

5. Sauté the bok choy: While the cod bakes, heat 1 tbsp oil in a large skillet over medium-high heat. Add the garlic and cook 30 seconds until fragrant but not brown. Add the bok choy cut-side down in a single layer. Cook 2 minutes until the cut sides are golden. Add the water, cover, and steam 2-3 minutes until the stems are tender-crisp and the leaves are bright green and wilted. Splash with the soy sauce and toss.

6. Serve: Spoon jasmine rice into bowls. Arrange the bok choy beside the rice, lay a glazed cod fillet on top, and sprinkle with sesame seeds if using.

7. Storage and reheating: Refrigerate up to 3 days. Reheat gently in a 300F oven, covered with foil, until just warmed through - high heat makes cod rubbery and the glaze bitter.

Common mistakes:
- A thick layer of miso glaze burns to bitter black before the fish is done - thin film only.
- Walking away during the 1-2 minute broil; miso sugars caramelize and then burn almost instantly.
- Using thin fillets: they overcook and dry out before the glaze gets its golden color.
- Overcooking the bok choy until olive-drab and mushy - it should stay bright green with bite in the stems.

Title: Miso Chicken & Zucchini Rice
Ingredients:
- 3 cups jasmine rice (for serving)
- 2 lb boneless, skinless chicken breasts

For the miso glaze:
- 1/4 cup white miso paste
- 2 tbsp unsalted butter, softened
- 1 tbsp mirin (sweet Japanese rice wine)
- 1 tbsp soy sauce
- 1 tsp grated fresh ginger

- 1 1/2 lb zucchini, halved lengthwise and cut into 1/2-inch half-moons
- 1 tbsp neutral oil (such as avocado oil)
- 1 tsp toasted sesame oil (optional, for finishing)
- 2 green onions, thinly sliced
- 1 tsp toasted sesame seeds
Steps:
1. Mise en place: Start the jasmine rice. Whisk the miso, softened butter, mirin, soy sauce, and grated ginger in a small bowl until smooth. Cut the zucchini into half-moons (slice the zucchini in half lengthwise, then cut across into 1/2-inch pieces). Slice the green onions. Pound the chicken breasts to an even 3/4-inch thickness (cover with plastic wrap and pound the thick end down) so they cook evenly. Pat dry and season lightly with salt.

2. Sear the chicken: Heat 1 tbsp neutral oil in a large skillet over medium-high heat until shimmering. Add the chicken and sear 5-6 minutes per side without moving it, until deep golden brown. The chicken should reach about 160F at this point.

3. Glaze - only at the end: Brush the miso glaze generously over the tops of the chicken pieces. Cook 1-2 minutes more, turning once, until the glaze bubbles and caramelizes in spots and the chicken reaches 165F in the thickest part. Miso is full of sugar and burns fast, which is why the glaze goes on last, never at the start.

4. Rest: Transfer the chicken to a plate and rest 5 minutes. Do not wipe out the skillet - those caramelized bits flavor the zucchini.

5. Sauté the zucchini: Return the skillet to medium-high heat. Add the zucchini in a single layer (work in two batches if needed) and cook 4-5 minutes, turning once, until golden-brown on the cut sides and crisp-tender - a knife should meet slight resistance. Season with a pinch of salt. Drizzle with the sesame oil if using.

6. Serve: Slice the rested chicken across the grain. Spoon jasmine rice into bowls, arrange zucchini over the rice, fan the sliced chicken on top, and drizzle with any glaze left in the skillet. Finish with green onions and sesame seeds.

7. Storage and reheating: Refrigerate up to 4 days. Reheat gently in a covered skillet over medium-low heat with a splash of water; the microwave can toughen the chicken.

Common mistakes:
- Brushing the miso glaze on at the start burns it to bitter black long before the chicken cooks through.
- Skipping the pounding leaves you with a dry thin end and a raw thick end.
- Crowding the zucchini steams it into a soggy pile - give each piece contact with the pan.
- Overcooking the chicken breasts past 165F; carryover heat takes them the rest of the way during the rest.

Title: Orange-Ginger Chicken & Broccoli
Ingredients:
- 1 3/4 lb boneless, skinless chicken thighs, cut into 1-inch pieces

For the velveting marinade:
- 2 tbsp soy sauce
- 1 tbsp Shaoxing wine (or dry sherry)
- 1 tbsp cornstarch
- 1 tbsp water

For the orange-ginger sauce:
- 1 cup fresh orange juice (about 3 large oranges)
- 1 tbsp orange zest (from 1 large orange)
- 1/4 cup soy sauce
- 3 tbsp honey
- 2 tbsp rice vinegar
- 1 tbsp cornstarch
- 1 tbsp fresh ginger, grated (about a 1-inch piece)
- 2 garlic cloves, minced
- 1/2 tsp red pepper flakes

For cooking and serving:
- 1 1/2 lb broccoli florets (about 8 cups)
- 1 1/2 cups jasmine rice, dry
- 3 tbsp neutral oil (such as avocado or canola), divided
- 2 tsp toasted sesame oil
- 1 tsp sesame seeds
- 2 green onions, thinly sliced
- 1 tsp kosher salt, plus more to taste - taste the sauce before serving and add up to 1/2 tsp more
Steps:
1. Mise en place (get everything ready before any heat goes on). Dice nothing here, but do this prep: Cut the chicken thighs into 1-inch pieces (about the size of a walnut). Cut the broccoli into bite-size florets (little tree shapes, stems trimmed short). Mince the garlic (chop into tiny pieces). Grate the ginger on the small holes of a box grater until you have 1 tbsp. Zest the orange (scrape just the orange part of the peel with a grater, not the white pith) and squeeze 1 cup of juice. Measure the rice, the oil, and everything for the sauce. Slice the green onions thinly into little rings.

2. Velvet the chicken. In a medium bowl, whisk the 2 tbsp soy sauce, Shaoxing wine, 1 tbsp cornstarch, and 1 tbsp water until smooth. Add the chicken pieces and toss until every piece is coated in a thin slippery glaze. Set aside for 15 minutes at room temperature. (Velveting is the classic Chinese technique that gives stir-fried meat its silky, tender texture.)

3. Make the sauce. In a separate bowl or large measuring cup, whisk together the orange juice, orange zest, 1/4 cup soy sauce, honey, rice vinegar, 1 tbsp cornstarch, ginger, garlic, and red pepper flakes until the cornstarch disappears. Set it by the stove - stir-frying moves fast and you will want it within arm's reach.

4. Cook the rice. Rinse the rice in a fine-mesh strainer under cold water until the water runs mostly clear. Put it in a medium saucepan with 2 1/4 cups water and 1/2 tsp of the kosher salt. Bring to a boil over high heat, then drop the heat to low, cover with a tight lid, and cook 15 minutes without lifting the lid. Turn off the heat and let it stand, covered, 10 minutes, then fluff with a fork.

5. Sear the broccoli. Heat 1 tbsp of the neutral oil in a large wok or 12-inch skillet over high heat until it shimmers and just starts to smoke. Add the broccoli in a single layer (work in two batches if needed) and let it sit undisturbed 2 minutes so the edges char. Stir-fry 3-4 minutes more, tossing every minute, until bright green with browned spots and crisp-tender when you bite a stem. Sprinkle with 1/4 tsp salt, transfer to a plate, and set aside.

6. Sear the chicken. Add the remaining 2 tbsp neutral oil to the same hot pan. Lift the chicken out of its marinade with tongs (leave the thin coating on the meat; discard any pooled liquid in the bowl). Add the chicken in a single layer - do not crowd, or it will steam instead of sear. Cook undisturbed 3-4 minutes until deep golden brown on the bottom, then flip and cook 3-4 minutes more until the other side is golden and the thickest piece reads 165F on an instant-read thermometer.

7. Sauce it. Give the orange-ginger sauce a quick re-whisk (the cornstarch settles) and pour it over the chicken. It will bubble and sizzle immediately. Return the broccoli to the pan. Cook over medium-high heat 2-3 minutes, tossing constantly, until the sauce turns glossy and thick enough to coat the back of a spoon and cling to the chicken. Taste and add up to 1/2 tsp more salt if you like.

8. Finish and serve. Drizzle the toasted sesame oil over everything and toss once. Spoon the rice into wide bowls, pile the chicken and broccoli over it, and shower with the sliced green onions and sesame seeds. Serve right away while the sauce is glossy and the broccoli still has bite.

9. Storage and reheating. Cool leftovers within 2 hours, then refrigerate in an airtight container up to 4 days. Reheat in a skillet over medium heat with a splash of water (2-3 tbsp) for 4-5 minutes, stirring, until steaming hot - the microwave makes the broccoli rubbery. Freeze up to 2 months; thaw overnight in the fridge.

Common mistakes:
- Crowding the chicken in the pan - pieces steam instead of sear. Cook in two batches if your pan is smaller than 12 inches.
- Skipping the sauce re-whisk - cornstarch sinks to the bottom and the sauce turns lumpy instead of glossy.
- Bottled orange juice concentrate - it is too sweet and flat; fresh-squeezed juice is what makes the glaze bright.

Title: Parmesan Cod & Pea Risotto
Ingredients:
- 1 3/4 lb cod fillets, cut into 2-inch chunks (about 12 pieces)
- 2 cups Arborio rice (do not rinse it - the starch on the grains is what makes risotto creamy)
- 7 cups chicken stock (or light fish stock)
- 1/2 cup dry white wine
- 1 large yellow onion, finely diced (cut into small 1/4-inch cubes)
- 2 tbsp olive oil
- 2 tbsp unsalted butter
- 2 cups frozen peas
- 1 cup freshly grated Parmesan cheese (about 3 1/2 oz)
- 3 tbsp cold unsalted butter, cut into small cubes
- 1 tsp lemon zest
- 2 tbsp fresh parsley, chopped
- 2 tbsp fresh lemon juice
- 1 1/2 tsp kosher salt, plus more to taste - taste before serving and add up to 1/2 tsp more
- 1/2 tsp black pepper
Steps:
1. Mise en place. Pour the stock into a medium saucepan and bring it to a gentle simmer over medium heat, then keep it barely simmering with the lid ajar for the whole cook - adding warm stock to the rice is essential. Dice the onion into 1/4-inch cubes. Cut the cod into 2-inch chunks and pat them very dry with paper towels; season them with 1/2 tsp of the salt and the black pepper. Zest the lemon, chop the parsley, grate the Parmesan, and cube the cold butter (keep the butter cold in the fridge until the end). Measure the rice, wine, peas, and olive oil and set everything by the stove.

2. Sweat the onion. Heat the olive oil and 2 tbsp butter in a wide, heavy pot or Dutch oven over medium heat until the butter melts and foams. Add the onion and 1/2 tsp salt and cook 6-8 minutes, stirring often, until soft, sweet-smelling, and translucent but not browned.

3. Tostatura (toasting the rice). Add the Arborio rice to the pot and stir with a wooden spoon so every grain is coated in the fat. Cook 2-3 minutes, stirring constantly, until the grains look pearly and the edges turn translucent with a tiny white dot still visible in the center, and you hear a faint crackling. Do not let the rice brown.

4. Deglaze with wine. Pour in the white wine. It will hiss and steam - stir and scrape the bottom of the pot until the wine is almost completely absorbed and the sharp alcohol smell fades, about 1-2 minutes.

5. Ladle by ladle. Now the patient part: add warm stock one ladle (about 3/4 cup) at a time. After each addition, stir frequently - not frantically, just a slow steady sweep every 30 seconds or so - and wait until the liquid is nearly absorbed before adding the next ladle. You will see the grains release starch and the liquid turn creamy. Keep the heat at a steady gentle simmer; if the stock vanishes in seconds, turn the heat down. Continue 18-20 minutes.

6. Peas and the final ladles. When the rice has been cooking about 15 minutes and is close but still firm in the center, stir in the frozen peas with the next ladle of stock. Keep going until the rice is al dente - tender with the faintest bite in the center - about 20-22 minutes total. You may not need all the stock; stop when the texture is right. The finished risotto should be loose and creamy, flowing slowly when you tilt the pot (Italians call this "all'onda," like a wave), not stiff like oatmeal.

7. Fold in the cod. Gently nestle the seasoned cod chunks into the hot risotto, pushing them just under the surface. Cover the pot and let it stand OFF the heat for 4-5 minutes. The trapped steam finishes cooking the fish delicately - it should be opaque and flake easily, reaching 145F inside. Do not stir at this stage or the fish will break apart.

8. Mantecatura (the creamy finish). Uncover, pull the pot off the burner, and add the cold butter cubes, the grated Parmesan, the lemon zest, and the lemon juice. Beat vigorously with a wooden spoon for a full minute until the butter and cheese melt into the starch and the risotto turns glossy and silky. This step must happen off the heat or the cheese goes stringy. Taste and add up to 1/2 tsp more salt.

9. Serve immediately. Spoon into warm shallow bowls, scatter the parsley over each, and serve at once. Risotto waits for no one - it stiffens within minutes. If it tightens on the way to the table, stir in a splash of warm stock.

10. Storage and reheating. Risotto is at its best the moment it is made, but leftovers keep in the fridge up to 3 days in an airtight container. Reheat gently in a saucepan over medium-low heat with a splash of stock, stirring, until hot and creamy again. Do not freeze - the rice turns grainy. To reuse leftovers, shape cold risotto into balls, coat in breadcrumbs, and pan-fry into arancini.

Common mistakes:
- Adding cold stock to the rice - it shocks the grains and the risotto cooks unevenly. Keep the stock at a bare simmer the whole time.
- Rinsing the Arborio rice - you wash away the surface starch that creates the creaminess.
- Adding the Parmesan over the heat - the cheese seizes and turns stringy instead of melting into silk.
- Overcooking the cod - it only needs the covered rest; simmering it in the pot turns it to mush.

Title: Parmesan Trout with Pea Orzo
Ingredients:
