- 6 skin-on trout fillets, about 5-6 oz each
- 12 oz orzo pasta, dry
- 1 1/2 cups frozen peas
- 3/4 cup freshly grated Parmesan cheese (about 2 1/2 oz)
- 3 tbsp unsalted butter
- 2 tbsp olive oil, divided
- 3 garlic cloves, minced (chopped into tiny pieces)
- 2 tbsp fresh lemon juice (about 1 lemon)
- 2 tbsp fresh parsley, chopped
- 1 1/2 tsp kosher salt, plus more to taste - taste the orzo before serving and add up to 1/2 tsp more
- 1/2 tsp black pepper
Steps:
1. Mise en place. Fill a large pot with water, salt it generously (it should taste like the sea), and set it over high heat to boil. Mince the garlic into tiny pieces. Chop the parsley. Grate the Parmesan. Cut the lemon in half and squeeze 2 tbsp of juice. Pat the trout fillets very dry on both sides with paper towels - dry skin is what crisps. Measure the orzo, peas, butter, and oil and set everything by the stove.

2. Cook the orzo and peas. When the water is at a rolling boil, add the orzo and stir once so it does not stick. Cook 7 minutes, then stir in the frozen peas and cook 2 minutes more, until the orzo is tender with a slight bite and the peas are bright green. Before draining, scoop out 1/2 cup of the starchy pasta water into a mug and set it aside. Drain the rest.

3. Make the pea orzo. Return the drained orzo and peas to the warm pot (off the heat). Add the butter, 1 tbsp of the olive oil, the minced garlic, and the grated Parmesan. Toss with a wooden spoon, splashing in the reserved pasta water a little at a time, until the cheese melts into a light glossy coating on every grain. Stir in the lemon juice and half the parsley. Taste and add up to 1/2 tsp more salt. Cover to keep warm.

4. Crisp the trout. Heat the remaining 1 tbsp olive oil in a large nonstick or cast-iron skillet over medium-high heat until it shimmers. Season the trout flesh side with 1 tsp salt and the pepper. Lay the fillets in the pan SKIN SIDE DOWN, pressing each one flat with a spatula for 10 seconds so the skin makes full contact. Cook undisturbed 4-5 minutes - you will hear a steady sizzle and see the flesh turning opaque from the bottom up. The skin should be deep golden and crisp, and it will release easily from the pan when it is ready.

5. Flip and finish. Turn the fillets over carefully and cook just 1-2 minutes on the flesh side, until the thickest part is opaque all the way through and reads 145F on an instant-read thermometer. Squeeze the lemon juice over the fish in the pan - it will sizzle - then lift the fillets out.

6. Serve. Spoon the pea orzo into shallow bowls, lay a trout fillet on top skin side UP (so the crispy skin stays crisp), and scatter with the remaining parsley. Serve immediately with extra lemon wedges if you like.

7. Storage and reheating. Refrigerate leftovers separately in airtight containers up to 2 days. Reheat the orzo in a skillet over medium heat with a splash of water until hot. Warm the trout gently in a 300F oven for 8-10 minutes - the microwave makes it rubbery. Do not freeze.

Common mistakes:
- Wet fish going into the pan - moisture steams the skin and it never crisps. Pat it truly dry.
- Flipping the fillets early - if the skin sticks, it is not ready. Wait until it releases on its own.
- Putting the fillet skin side down on the plate - the steam trapped underneath softens that beautiful crisp skin.

Title: Patagonian Trout with Crispy Potatoes
Ingredients:
- 6 skin-on trout fillets, about 6 oz each
- 2 1/2 lb small Yukon Gold potatoes, scrubbed and halved (quartered if large)
- 1/4 cup olive oil, divided
- 2 tbsp unsalted butter
- 1 large lemon, half cut into wedges and half juiced
- 3 garlic cloves, thinly sliced (cut into thin coins)
- 2 tbsp fresh parsley, chopped
- 1 tsp smoked paprika (optional, for the potatoes)
- 2 tsp kosher salt, plus more to taste - taste a potato before serving and add up to 1/2 tsp more
- 1/2 tsp black pepper
Steps:
1. Mise en place. Heat the oven to 425F and put a large rimmed sheet pan inside to preheat (a hot pan starts the crisping instantly). Scrub the potatoes and cut them in half - you want flat cut sides to press against the hot pan. Slice the garlic into thin coins. Chop the parsley. Cut the lemon: juice one half into a small bowl, cut the other half into wedges. Pat the trout fillets completely dry with paper towels and set them on a plate in the fridge, uncovered, while you start the potatoes - cold dry skin crisps best.

2. Parboil the potatoes. Put the potatoes in a large pot, cover with cold water by an inch, and add 1 tbsp salt. Bring to a boil over high heat and cook 10-12 minutes, until a knife slides in with just a little resistance - tender at the edges but still firm in the middle. Drain well in a colander and let them steam-dry 2 minutes, shaking the colander once or twice. Rough, dry surfaces turn the crispiest.

3. Roast until crisp. Carefully pull the hot sheet pan from the oven. Pour 3 tbsp of the olive oil onto it and tilt to coat. Arrange the potatoes cut side down in a single layer - you should hear a satisfying sizzle. Sprinkle with 1 tsp salt, the pepper, and the smoked paprika if using. Roast 35-40 minutes, flipping once halfway through, until deep golden brown and shatteringly crisp on the cut sides and fork-tender inside.

4. Score and season the trout. While the potatoes roast, take the trout out of the fridge. With a sharp knife, make 3-4 shallow diagonal slashes through the skin of each fillet, just into the skin and not into the flesh - this keeps the skin from curling and lets it render evenly. Season both sides with the remaining 1 tsp salt.

5. Sear the trout, skin down. Heat the remaining 1 tbsp olive oil in a large skillet (cast iron is ideal) over medium-high heat until it shimmers. Lay the fillets in skin side down and press each flat with a spatula for 10 seconds. Cook undisturbed 5-6 minutes. You will hear a strong sizzle that slowly quiets as the fat renders out; the skin should be deep golden and crisp, and the flesh will have turned opaque about three-quarters of the way up the side of the fillet.

6. Flip and make the lemon-herb butter. Flip the fillets and cook 1 minute more on the flesh side, until the thickest part reads 145F. Remove the fish to a warm plate, skin side up. Drop the heat to medium, add the butter and sliced garlic to the same pan, and swirl 1-2 minutes until the garlic turns pale gold and smells nutty - do not let it brown dark or it turns bitter. Squeeze in the lemon juice (it will bubble), swirl once, and pull off the heat. Stir in the parsley.

7. Serve. Pile the crispy potatoes onto a platter or plates, lay the trout fillets skin side up on top, and spoon the warm lemon-herb garlic butter over everything. Serve the lemon wedges alongside. In Patagonia this fish is treated simply - the crisp skin and the lemon butter are the whole point.

8. Storage and reheating. Refrigerate leftovers in an airtight container up to 2 days. Reheat the potatoes in a 425F oven for 10 minutes to re-crisp; warm the trout gently in a 300F oven 8-10 minutes. The microwave makes both soggy. Do not freeze.

Common mistakes:
- Starting the potatoes on a cold pan - the cut sides steam instead of sear, and you lose the crunch.
- Moving the trout while the skin sears - every touch cools the pan and softens the skin. Lay it down and leave it alone.
- Burning the garlic in the butter - pale gold is perfect; dark brown is bitter. Pull it off the heat the moment it turns.

Title: Picanha-Style Steak Rice Bowls
Ingredients:
- 2 1/2 lb picanha (top sirloin cap) with the fat cap intact
- 2 tbsp coarse kosher salt (or coarse sea salt)
- 1 1/2 cups long-grain white rice, dry

For the vinagrete (Brazilian tomato-onion relish):
- 2 medium tomatoes, diced (cut into 1/2-inch cubes)
- 1/2 small red onion, finely diced
- 1/2 green bell pepper, finely diced
- 1/4 cup olive oil
- 3 tbsp red wine vinegar
- 1/4 cup fresh cilantro or flat-leaf parsley, chopped
- 1 tsp kosher salt, plus more to taste - taste before serving and add up to 1/2 tsp more
Steps:
1. Mise en place. Take the picanha out of the fridge 30-40 minutes before cooking so it loses its chill. Dice the tomatoes into 1/2-inch cubes for the vinagrete. Finely dice the red onion and green bell pepper. Chop the cilantro or parsley. Measure the rice, vinegar, and oil.

2. Score the fat cap. Pat the picanha dry with paper towels. With a sharp knife, cut a crosshatch (diamond) pattern into the thick white fat cap, cutting about 1/2 inch deep - stay inside the fat and do not cut into the meat. Scoring lets the fat render and crisp instead of shrinking and curling. Rub the entire piece, fat cap and all, generously with the 2 tbsp coarse salt.

3. Cook the rice. Rinse the rice until the water runs mostly clear. Put it in a saucepan with 2 1/4 cups water and 1/2 tsp salt. Bring to a boil, drop to low, cover tightly, and cook 15 minutes. Rest covered 10 minutes off the heat, then fluff.

4. Make the vinagrete. Stir the tomatoes, onion, bell pepper, olive oil, red wine vinegar, cilantro, and 1 tsp salt in a bowl. Taste and add up to 1/2 tsp more salt - it should be bright, juicy, and well seasoned. Set aside at room temperature so the flavors marry.

5. Grill the picanha. Heat a grill to medium-high (about 400-450F). Place the picanha FAT SIDE DOWN directly over the heat and cook 4-5 minutes, until the fat is golden, rendered, and lightly crisped. Flip and sear the meat sides 4-5 minutes per side for medium-rare, until the thickest part reads 130-135F on an instant-read thermometer. (No grill? Sear fat side down in a screaming-hot cast-iron skillet 5 minutes, then finish in a 400F oven 10-15 minutes to 130-135F.) Expect flare-ups from the dripping fat - keep the meat moving and never walk away.

6. Rest and slice. Transfer to a cutting board and rest 10 full minutes - the juices redistribute and the meat stays juicy instead of flooding the board. Slice AGAINST the grain into thin strips (look for the lines of the muscle fibers and cut across them). If you slice with the grain, even this tender cut eats chewy.

7. Build the bowls. Spoon rice into wide bowls, fan the sliced picanha over it, and spoon the vinagrete - with its juices - generously over the top. Serve immediately.

A note on the cut: true picanha is the top sirloin cap with its fat cap left whole. It is rare in American supermarkets, so ask your butcher for "top sirloin cap" or "coulotte" with the fat cap on - most can cut one with a day's notice. If you truly cannot find it, use a well-marbled top sirloin steak (no fat cap) and add 1 tbsp of olive oil to the pan; it will be delicious but will not render that signature crispy fat.

8. Storage and reheating. Refrigerate leftovers in airtight containers up to 3 days; keep the vinagrete separate. Reheat steak gently in a 275F oven 10-12 minutes to warm without overcooking, or eat it cold over salad - it is excellent both ways. Reheat rice with a splash of water. Freeze the steak (not the vinagrete) up to 2 months.

Common mistakes:
- Trimming off the fat cap - that fat is the flavor and the basting; cook with it on and trim on your plate if you prefer.
- Slicing with the grain - picanha sliced wrong eats tough even when cooked perfectly. Find the grain lines and cut across them.
- Skipping the rest - cutting too soon spills all the juices onto the board instead of keeping them in the meat.

Title: Pork & Broccoli Garlic Rice
Ingredients:
- 1 3/4 lb pork tenderloin, sliced into thin 1/4-inch medallions
- 1 1/4 lb broccoli florets (about 6 cups)

For the velveting marinade:
- 1 tbsp soy sauce
- 1 tbsp Shaoxing wine (or dry sherry)
- 1 tbsp cornstarch

For the garlic rice:
- 2 cups jasmine rice, dry
- 6 garlic cloves, thinly sliced (cut into thin coins)
- 2 tbsp neutral oil (such as avocado or canola)

For the stir-fry sauce and finish:
- 2 tbsp soy sauce
- 2 tbsp oyster sauce
- 1 tbsp fresh ginger, grated (about a 1-inch piece)
- 1 tsp toasted sesame oil
- 3 green onions, sliced into 1-inch pieces
- 1 tsp kosher salt, plus more to taste - taste before serving and add up to 1/2 tsp more
Steps:
1. Mise en place. Slice the pork tenderloin into thin 1/4-inch medallions (put it in the freezer 20 minutes first and the knife glides through). Cut the broccoli into bite-size florets. Slice the garlic into thin coins. Grate the ginger. Slice the green onions into 1-inch pieces. Whisk the 2 tbsp soy sauce and oyster sauce in a small bowl. Measure the rice, oil, and sesame oil and set everything by the stove.

2. Velvet the pork. In a bowl, toss the pork medallions with the 1 tbsp soy sauce, Shaoxing wine, and cornstarch until each piece is coated in a thin glaze. Set aside 15 minutes at room temperature. This classic Chinese step keeps the lean tenderloin silky instead of dry.

3. Cook the rice. Rinse the rice until the water runs mostly clear. Cook in a saucepan with 3 cups water and 1/2 tsp salt: boil, drop to low, cover 15 minutes, rest 10 minutes off the heat, then fluff.

4. Fry the garlic. Heat the 2 tbsp neutral oil in a large wok or 12-inch skillet over medium heat. Add the sliced garlic and cook 2-3 minutes, stirring constantly, until pale gold and fragrant - pull it before it browns dark, or it turns bitter. Scoop the garlic out with a slotted spoon onto a paper towel, leaving the garlicky oil in the pan.

5. Turn it into garlic rice. Add the cooked rice to the garlicky oil in the pan. Stir-fry 3-4 minutes over medium-high heat, breaking up any clumps, until the grains are coated and smell toasty. Fold in the fried garlic coins and 1/2 tsp of the salt. Transfer to a serving bowl and cover to keep warm.

6. Sear the broccoli. Wipe the pan, add 1 tbsp fresh neutral oil, and heat over high heat until shimmering. Add the broccoli and 2 tbsp water, cover immediately, and steam 2 minutes. Uncover and stir-fry 2-3 minutes more until bright green, charred at the edges, and crisp-tender. Season with 1/4 tsp salt and transfer to a plate.

7. Sear the pork. Add the remaining 1 tbsp oil to the hot pan. Lift the pork from its marinade with tongs (discard pooled liquid). Sear in a single layer 2-3 minutes per side until golden and the thickest medallion reads 145F. Add the ginger and stir-fry 30 seconds until fragrant.

8. Bring it together. Return the broccoli to the pan, pour in the soy-oyster sauce mixture, and toss over high heat 1-2 minutes until everything is glazed and the sauce clings. Drizzle with the sesame oil, toss in the green onions, taste, and add up to 1/2 tsp more salt. Serve over the garlic rice immediately.

9. Storage and reheating. Refrigerate in an airtight container up to 4 days. Reheat in a skillet over medium heat with a splash of water until steaming; the microwave is fine for the rice portion. Freeze up to 2 months.

Common mistakes:
- Slicing the pork thick - tenderloin seizes up if overcooked; thin medallions cook in minutes and stay tender.
- Burning the garlic coins - they go from pale gold to bitter in seconds. Stir constantly and pull them early.
- Adding the sauce to a cool pan - the sauce should hit a hot pan and glaze in a minute or two, not pool and make everything soggy.

Title: Pork & Jalapeño Tacos
Ingredients:
- 1 3/4 lb ground pork
- 12 corn tortillas (6-inch)
- 3 jalapenos, sliced into thin rings (remove the seeds and white ribs for milder heat)
- 1 large yellow onion, diced (cut into small 1/4-inch cubes)
- 1 tbsp neutral oil (such as avocado or canola)
- 1 tbsp chili powder
- 2 tsp ground cumin
- 1 tsp dried oregano (Mexican oregano if you can find it)
- 1 tsp garlic powder
- 2 limes, cut into wedges
- 1/2 cup fresh cilantro, chopped
- 2 tsp kosher salt, plus more to taste - taste the pork before serving and add up to 1/2 tsp more
Steps:
1. Mise en place. Dice the onion into 1/4-inch cubes. Slice the jalapenos into thin rings - wear gloves or wash your hands right after, and do not touch your eyes. Cut the limes into wedges. Chop the cilantro. Measure the oil and stir the chili powder, cumin, oregano, garlic powder, and 2 tsp salt together in a small bowl so the spice mix is ready to go. Stack the tortillas and wrap them in a clean kitchen towel or foil.

2. Brown the pork. Heat the oil in a large skillet over medium-high heat until shimmering. Add the ground pork and break it into small crumbles with a wooden spoon. Cook 6-8 minutes, stirring and breaking it up, until browned all over with crispy edges. If a lot of fat pools in the pan, spoon most of it out, leaving about 1 tbsp.

3. Add the vegetables and spices. Stir in the diced onion and jalapeno rings and cook 3-4 minutes until the onion softens and the jalapenos smell spicy-sweet. Sprinkle the spice mix over everything and stir 1-2 minutes more, until the spices smell toasty and coat the meat. The pork should reach 160F inside. Taste and add up to 1/2 tsp more salt.

4. Warm the tortillas. While the pork finishes, warm the tortillas: lay them directly over a gas burner flame 15-20 seconds per side until lightly charred and pliable, or heat a dry skillet over medium-high heat and warm each 30 seconds per side. Stack them in the towel or foil as you go so they stay soft and steamy.

5. Assemble and serve. Double up the tortillas (two per taco - this is the taqueria way, and it keeps them from falling apart). Spoon the pork and jalapeno mixture down the center, top with cilantro, and serve with lime wedges for squeezing over. Serve immediately while the tortillas are warm.

6. Storage and reheating. Refrigerate the pork mixture in an airtight container up to 4 days; store tortillas separately in a zip-top bag. Reheat the pork in a skillet over medium heat with a splash of water until steaming, and warm fresh tortillas - reheated tortillas turn stiff. Freeze the pork mixture up to 3 months.

Common mistakes:
- Skipping the spice toast - raw spices taste dusty; that 1-2 minute stir in the hot pan wakes them up.
- Serving on a single cold tortilla - corn tortillas tear and crack unless doubled and properly warmed.
- Leaving all the jalapeno seeds in - the seeds and white ribs hold most of the heat. Remove them if you want flavor without fire.

Title: Pork Albondigas with Saffron Rice
Ingredients:
For the albondigas (Spanish meatballs):
- 1 1/2 lb ground pork
- 1 large egg, lightly beaten
- 1/2 cup plain breadcrumbs
- 1/4 cup whole milk
- 1/2 small yellow onion, very finely minced
- 2 garlic cloves, minced (chopped into tiny pieces)
- 1/4 cup fresh parsley, chopped
- 1 tsp smoked paprika
- 1/2 tsp ground cumin
- 1 1/2 tsp kosher salt, plus more to taste - taste the sauce before serving and add up to 1/2 tsp more
- 1/2 tsp black pepper

For the tomato sauce:
- 2 tbsp olive oil
- 1 large yellow onion, diced (cut into small 1/4-inch cubes)
- 3 garlic cloves, minced
- 1 can (28 oz) crushed tomatoes
- 1 tsp smoked paprika
- 1 bay leaf
- 1/2 tsp sugar

For the saffron rice:
- 1 1/2 cups long-grain white rice, dry
- 1/2 tsp saffron threads
- 3 cups chicken stock, warmed
- 1 tbsp olive oil
- 1 small yellow onion, finely diced
- 1/2 tsp kosher salt
Steps:
1. Mise en place. Put the breadcrumbs and milk in a large bowl and let them soak 5 minutes - this panade (soaked crumbs) is what keeps the meatballs tender. Meanwhile, very finely mince the half onion for the meatballs (tiny pieces so they melt in). Mince all 5 garlic cloves. Dice the large onion and the small onion into 1/4-inch cubes. Chop the parsley. Measure the rice, warm the stock in a saucepan until steamy (not boiling), and crumble the saffron threads into it to bloom - the stock will turn golden within minutes. Open the tomato can. Beat the egg in a small bowl.

2. Mix the meatballs gently. To the soaked breadcrumbs add the ground pork, beaten egg, minced half-onion, 2 minced garlic cloves, parsley, 1 tsp smoked paprika, cumin, 1 1/2 tsp salt, and pepper. Mix with your hands just until everything is combined - stop the moment it looks uniform. Overmixing squeezes out the juices and makes tough meatballs.

3. Roll small meatballs. With damp hands, roll the mixture into walnut-size balls, about 1 inch across - you should get about 30. Spanish albondigas are small, closer to a large marble than an Italian meatball. Set them on a plate.

4. Brown the meatballs. Heat the 2 tbsp olive oil in a large deep skillet or Dutch oven over medium-high heat until shimmering. Brown the meatballs in two batches, 5-6 minutes per batch, turning gently so they color on most sides. They do not need to cook through - just get a golden crust. Transfer to a plate.

5. Build the sauce. In the same pan over medium heat, add the diced large onion and cook 5-6 minutes, stirring, until soft and sweet. Add the 3 minced garlic cloves, 1 tsp smoked paprika, and the bay leaf and cook 1 minute until fragrant. Pour in the crushed tomatoes, add the sugar and 1/2 tsp salt, and bring to a lively simmer, scraping up the browned bits from the meatballs - that is pure flavor.

6. Simmer. Nestle the browned meatballs into the sauce, reduce the heat to low, and cover. Simmer gently 20 minutes, stirring once or twice, until the sauce thickens and the meatballs are cooked through - cut one open to check there is no pink, or confirm 160F inside. Fish out the bay leaf. Taste and add up to 1/2 tsp more salt.

7. Cook the saffron rice. While the meatballs simmer, heat the 1 tbsp olive oil in a medium saucepan over medium heat. Add the diced small onion and 1/2 tsp salt and cook 4-5 minutes until soft. Add the rice and stir 2 minutes until the grains are coated and smell faintly toasty. Pour in the warm saffron stock (it should be golden), bring to a boil, then drop to low, cover tightly, and cook 15 minutes. Rest 10 minutes off the heat, then fluff - the grains should be separate and sunset-gold.

8. Serve. Spoon the saffron rice into shallow bowls, ladle the albondigas and plenty of tomato sauce over the top, and scatter with a little extra parsley. Serve immediately.

9. Storage and reheating. Refrigerate in airtight containers up to 4 days - like most braised dishes, the albondigas taste even better the next day. Reheat gently in a saucepan over medium-low heat with a splash of water until steaming. Freeze up to 3 months; thaw overnight in the fridge.

Common mistakes:
- Overmixing the meat mixture - mix just until combined or the meatballs turn dense and rubbery.
- Making the meatballs too big - walnut-size cooks through in the simmer; golf-ball size stays raw in the middle.
- Skipping the saffron bloom - dry saffron tossed into the pot gives pale, uneven rice. Ten minutes in warm stock unlocks the color and aroma.

Title: Pork Carnitas Potato Bowls
Ingredients:
For the carnitas:
- 2 1/2 lb boneless pork shoulder (Boston butt), cut into 3-inch chunks
- 1 large orange, halved
- 1 large white onion, quartered
- 6 garlic cloves, smashed (press flat with the side of a knife)
- 2 bay leaves
- 1 tbsp kosher salt, plus more to taste - taste the shredded pork before serving and add up to 1 tsp more
- 2 tsp ground cumin
- 1 tsp dried oregano
- 2 cups chicken broth

For the crispy potatoes:
- 2 lb Yukon Gold potatoes, cut into 1-inch cubes
- 2 tbsp olive oil
- 1 tsp kosher salt
- 1/2 tsp black pepper

For crisping and serving:
- 3 tbsp neutral oil (such as avocado or canola)
- 1/2 cup fresh cilantro, chopped
- 1/2 white onion, finely diced
- 2 limes, cut into wedges
Steps:
1. Mise en place. Cut the pork shoulder into 3-inch chunks (about the size of a deck of cards) - big pieces stay juicy through the long cook. Smash the garlic cloves flat with the side of your knife. Quarter the onion. Halve the orange. Measure the broth, salt, cumin, and oregano. Cut the potatoes into 1-inch cubes and dice the half onion for topping. Chop the cilantro and cut the limes into wedges.

A note on authenticity: true Michoacan carnitas are made in a cazo (a big copper pot) where pork confits slowly in its own rendered fat and lard. Most home kitchens do not have a cazo or gallons of lard, so this version braises the pork until melting-tender, then crisps the edges under the broiler - same tender-inside, crisp-edged spirit, honestly adapted for a Dutch oven.

2. Season and braise. Heat the oven to 300F. Pat the pork chunks dry and rub them all over with the salt, cumin, and oregano. Set a large Dutch oven over medium-high heat and sear the pork in two batches, 3-4 minutes per side, until browned - this crust is where the deep flavor comes from. Return all the pork to the pot. Squeeze the orange halves over the meat and drop them in, peels and all. Add the quartered onion, smashed garlic, bay leaves, and chicken broth - the liquid should come about halfway up the pork.

3. Slow-cook until melting. Cover with the lid and slide into the 300F oven for 2 1/2 to 3 hours, until the pork shreds easily when you press it with a fork and the largest chunk reads at least 195F inside - carnitas are done well past the 145F chop temperature; this is fork-tender territory. Let the pot cool 15 minutes, then lift the pork out with a slotted spoon onto a cutting board. Fish out and discard the orange peels, bay leaves, onion, and garlic.

4. Roast the potatoes. While the pork braises (about 45 minutes before it is done), heat the oven to 425F - you can use a second oven or wait until the pork comes out and raise the temperature. Toss the potato cubes on a rimmed sheet pan with the olive oil, 1 tsp salt, and pepper in a single layer. Roast 30-35 minutes, flipping once, until deep golden and crisp at the edges and fluffy inside.

5. Crisp the carnitas. Shred the pork into bite-size pieces with two forks, keeping some chunky bits. Spread it in a single layer on a clean rimmed sheet pan and drizzle with the 3 tbsp neutral oil and 1/2 cup of the reserved braising liquid. Broil 4-6 inches from the heat for 5-8 minutes, until the edges are browned and crackly - watch closely, as broilers turn on you fast. Toss once and broil 2-3 minutes more. Taste and add up to 1 tsp more salt.

6. Build the bowls. Spoon the crispy potatoes into wide bowls, pile the carnitas alongside, and top with the diced onion, cilantro, and a generous squeeze of lime. Serve immediately while the edges are still crackling.

7. Storage and reheating. Refrigerate in airtight containers up to 4 days; store toppings separately. Reheat the carnitas in a hot skillet over medium-high heat 4-5 minutes until the edges re-crisp - the microwave makes them steamy and soft. Reheat potatoes in a 425F oven 10 minutes. Freeze the carnitas up to 3 months.

Common mistakes:
- Cutting the pork too small - little cubes dry out over the long braise. Keep the chunks big.
- Shredding before the pork is ready - if it resists the fork, give it another 30 minutes. Carnitas cannot be rushed.
- Walking away from the broiler - the line between crisp-edged and burnt is about ninety seconds. Stay and watch.

Title: Pork Chops with Garlic Lyonnaise Potatoes
Ingredients:
- 6 boneless pork chops, about 8 oz each and 1 inch thick
- 2 1/2 lb Yukon Gold or russet potatoes, peeled
- 2 large yellow onions, halved and thinly sliced (cut into thin half-moons)
- 5 tbsp unsalted butter, divided
- 1 tbsp olive oil
- 4 garlic cloves, minced (chopped into tiny pieces)
- 1/4 cup fresh parsley, chopped
- 2 tsp kosher salt, plus more to taste - taste the potatoes before serving and add up to 1/2 tsp more
- 1 tsp black pepper
- 1 tsp dried thyme (optional)
Steps:
1. Mise en place. Peel the potatoes. Halve the onions and slice them into thin half-moons. Mince the garlic. Chop the parsley. Pat the pork chops very dry with paper towels - dry meat sears instead of steams. Take the chops out of the fridge 20-30 minutes before cooking so they lose their chill and cook evenly.

2. Parboil the potatoes. Put the whole peeled potatoes in a large pot, cover with cold salted water, and bring to a boil over high heat. Cook 10-12 minutes, until a knife goes in with some resistance - firm, not fully tender. Drain and let them cool 5 minutes, then slice into 1/4-inch rounds. (True Lyonnaise potatoes are always boiled before frying; raw slices would burn outside before cooking through.)

3. Fry the potatoes golden. Melt 3 tbsp of the butter in a large skillet (12-inch) over medium heat until it foams. Add the potato slices in as close to a single layer as you can - work in two batches if needed. Cook 5-6 minutes undisturbed until the bottoms are golden brown, then flip and cook 5-6 minutes more until golden on both sides and tender when pierced. Season with 1 tsp salt and 1/2 tsp pepper as they cook. Transfer to a plate.

4. Soften the onions separately. In a second skillet (or the same one, wiped out), melt the remaining 2 tbsp butter over medium heat. Add the sliced onions and 1/2 tsp salt and cook 8-10 minutes, stirring often, until pale gold, soft, and sweet - not dark and caramelized, just gently golden. Add the minced garlic and cook 1 minute more until fragrant.

5. Combine, Lyonnaise-style. Return the potatoes to the onion pan, toss gently so the onions thread through the golden slices, and cook 2-3 minutes together so the flavors marry. Taste and add up to 1/2 tsp more salt. Keep warm over the lowest heat while you cook the chops. (There is no "Lyonnaise sauce" - in Lyon, "a la lyonnaise" simply means cooked with onions.)

6. Sear the pork chops. Season the chops on both sides with the remaining 1/2 tsp salt, 1/2 tsp pepper, and the thyme if using. Heat the olive oil in a large skillet over medium-high heat until it shimmers. Sear the chops 4-5 minutes per side without moving them, until deep golden brown with a crisp crust. The thickest part should read 145F on an instant-read thermometer - a hint of blush inside is perfect and safe.

7. Rest and serve. Transfer the chops to a plate and rest 5 minutes - the juices settle back into the meat instead of running out on the first cut. Spoon a generous bed of the Lyonnaise potatoes onto each plate, lay a pork chop on top, and scatter with the chopped parsley. Serve immediately.

8. Storage and reheating. Refrigerate leftovers in airtight containers up to 3 days. Reheat the chops gently in a 300F oven 10-12 minutes to avoid drying them out; warm the potatoes in a hot skillet with a knob of butter to re-crisp. Do not freeze - the potatoes turn mealy.

Common mistakes:
- Frying raw potato slices - they brown on the outside while staying hard inside. The parboil is the whole trick.
- Crowding the potato pan - slices steam instead of browning. Give them room or work in batches.
- Skipping the rest on the chops - cutting immediately spills the juices; five minutes keeps them juicy.

Title: Pork Chops with Salsa Criolla Rice
Ingredients:
2 lb boneless pork chops, 1-inch thick (about 6 chops)
1 tbsp kosher salt, divided (start with 1 tbsp; add more to taste at the end)
1 tsp black pepper, freshly ground
2 tbsp olive oil, for searing
2 cups long-grain white rice, uncooked
3 cups water, for the rice
1 large red bell pepper, finely diced (dice = cut into small even cubes about 1/2 inch)
1 large white onion, finely diced
2 large tomatoes, seeded and finely diced
4 cloves garlic, minced (mince = chop very fine)
1/2 cup extra-virgin olive oil, for the salsa
1/3 cup red wine vinegar, for the salsa
1/2 cup water, for the salsa
1 tsp dried oregano
1/2 tsp crushed red pepper flakes (start with 1/2 tsp; add up to 1 tsp for more heat)
1/4 cup fresh parsley, chopped
Steps:
1. Mise en place: everything chopped, measured, and set out before any heat goes on. Dice (cut into small even cubes about 1/2 inch) the red bell pepper, white onion, and tomatoes. Mince (chop very fine) the garlic. Chop the parsley. Measure the rice, water, olive oil, vinegar, oregano, and red pepper flakes. Pat the pork chops dry with paper towels and season both sides with the salt and pepper.
2. Make the salsa criolla: in a medium bowl, combine the diced bell pepper, onion, tomatoes, and minced garlic. Add the 1/2 cup olive oil, red wine vinegar, 1/2 cup water, oregano, red pepper flakes, parsley, and 1 tsp of the salt. Stir well. Taste and add more salt or vinegar until it is bright and tangy. Set aside for at least 15 minutes so the flavors meld. (Authentic salsa criolla is a raw onion-and-pepper condiment dressed with oil and vinegar, served over grilled meat in Argentina -- do not cook it.)
3. Cook the rice: in a medium saucepan, combine the rice, 3 cups water, and 1 tsp salt. Bring to a boil over high heat, stir once, reduce the heat to low, cover with a tight lid, and cook 15 minutes without lifting the lid. Remove from the heat and rest, covered, 10 minutes. Fluff with a fork -- the grains should be separate and tender.
4. Sear the pork chops: heat the 2 tbsp olive oil in a large heavy skillet over medium-high heat until the oil shimmers and moves easily. Lay the chops in the pan -- you should hear a loud sizzle. Cook 4 to 5 minutes per side without moving them, until deep golden brown. Check with a meat thermometer: pork is done at 145 F. If the chops are very thick, lower the heat to medium and cook a few minutes more.
5. Rest and serve: transfer the chops to a plate and rest 5 minutes so the juices stay in the meat. Spoon the rice onto plates, place a chop alongside, and spoon a generous scoop of salsa criolla over the rice and the chop.
6. Storage and reheating: store leftovers in an airtight container in the refrigerator up to 3 days, with the salsa criolla in a separate jar. Reheat the chops gently in a 325 F oven 10 to 12 minutes until warmed through; warm the rice with a splash of water. Serve the salsa at room temperature.
Common mistakes: Overcooking the chops -- pork dries out fast past 145 F, so use a thermometer and pull them at 140-145 F. Lifting the lid while the rice steams -- it lets the steam escape and the rice turns gummy. Skipping the salsa rest -- the vinegar needs 15 minutes to soften the raw onion, or it tastes harsh. Pan too hot for the sear -- if the oil smokes heavily, lower to medium-high so the crust browns instead of charring.

Title: Pork Egg Fried Rice
Ingredients:
6 cups cooked long-grain rice, day-old and cold (from 2 cups uncooked rice)
1 lb pork loin or tenderloin, cut into 1/2-inch cubes
6 large eggs, beaten in a bowl
1 cup frozen peas, thawed
1 cup frozen corn kernels, thawed
4 green onions, thinly sliced (slice = cut into thin flat pieces), white and green parts kept separate
3 tbsp neutral oil (vegetable or canola), divided
3 tbsp light soy sauce (start with 3 tbsp; add up to 4 tbsp to taste)
1 tbsp Shaoxing wine or dry sherry, optional
1 tsp kosher salt, divided (start with 1 tsp; adjust at the end)
1/2 tsp black pepper
Steps:
1. Mise en place: everything ready before the wok gets hot. Beat the eggs in a bowl. Cut the pork into 1/2-inch cubes. Slice the green onions (cut into thin flat pieces), keeping the white and green parts separate. Measure the peas, corn, oil, soy sauce, and seasonings. Have the cold rice at hand -- cold, day-old rice fries up separate and loose instead of mushy.
2. Scramble the eggs: heat a wok or large skillet over medium-high heat. Add 1 tbsp oil and swirl to coat. Pour in the beaten eggs. Let them set 15 to 20 seconds, then push and break them into small soft pieces with a spatula, about 1 minute total. Transfer to a plate. (They should look just set and glossy, not browned.)
3. Sear the pork: add 1 tbsp oil to the same pan. Add the pork cubes in a single layer. Cook 4 to 5 minutes over medium-high heat, turning, until browned on the outside and cooked through -- no pink inside; small cubes finish in this time. Remove to the plate with the eggs.
4. Fry the rice: add the remaining 1 tbsp oil. Add the white parts of the green onions and stir-fry 30 seconds until fragrant. Add the cold rice, breaking up any clumps with the spatula. Spread it out and let it sit untouched 1 minute to toast, then toss. Fry 3 to 4 minutes until the grains are hot and a little toasty at the edges.
5. Combine and season: return the eggs and pork to the pan along with the peas and corn. Drizzle the soy sauce and Shaoxing wine around the edge of the hot pan, then toss everything 2 minutes. Season with the salt and pepper, taste, and add a splash more soy sauce only if it needs it. Fold in the green parts of the green onions.
6. Serve immediately in warm bowls. (Yangzhou-style fried rice is light and delicate -- it should taste of toasted rice and egg, not heavy soy sauce.)
7. Storage and reheating: refrigerate in an airtight container up to 3 days. Reheat in a skillet over medium-high heat 4 to 5 minutes with a teaspoon of oil until steaming hot throughout.
Common mistakes: Using fresh hot rice -- it turns gummy; spread cooked rice on a tray and refrigerate uncovered at least 4 hours or overnight. Crowding the pan -- a too-full wok steams instead of frying; cook in two batches if your pan is small. Overcooking the eggs -- they finish in the hot rice at the end, so pull them soft. Too much soy sauce -- Yangzhou fried rice is pale and mild; season lightly and taste before adding more.

Title: Pork Kofta Rice Bowls
Ingredients:
2 lb ground pork (85 percent lean)
1 large egg
1/2 cup plain breadcrumbs
1 medium onion, grated on a box grater (keep the juice)
4 cloves garlic, minced (mince = chop very fine)
1/2 cup fresh parsley, finely chopped
2 tbsp ground cumin
1 tbsp sweet paprika
1 tbsp dried mint
2 tsp ground coriander
2 tsp dried oregano
2 tsp kosher salt, divided (start with 2 tsp; adjust at the end)
1 tsp black pepper
2 cups long-grain rice, uncooked
3 cups water, for the rice
2 tbsp olive oil, for cooking
1 cup plain Greek yogurt
2 tbsp lemon juice
1 large cucumber, diced (dice = cut into small even cubes about 1/2 inch)
2 large tomatoes, diced
1/2 red onion, thinly sliced (slice = cut into thin flat pieces)
Steps:
1. Mise en place: everything ready before cooking. Grate the onion (keep the juice -- it keeps the kofta moist). Mince (chop very fine) the garlic. Finely chop the parsley. Dice (cut into small even cubes about 1/2 inch) the cucumber and tomatoes. Thinly slice (cut into thin flat pieces) the red onion. Measure all the spices and breadcrumbs.
2. Mix the kofta: in a large bowl, combine the ground pork, egg, breadcrumbs, grated onion with its juice, garlic, parsley, cumin, paprika, dried mint, coriander, oregano, salt, and pepper. Mix with your hands just until everything is evenly distributed -- stop as soon as it comes together. Overmixing makes dense, tough kofta.
3. Shape: wet your hands lightly. Divide the mixture into 12 equal portions and roll each into an oval about 3 inches long and 1 inch thick. Set on a plate.
4. Cook the rice: in a saucepan, combine the rice, 3 cups water, and 1 tsp salt. Bring to a boil over high heat, stir once, reduce to low, cover, and cook 15 minutes without lifting the lid. Rest, covered, 10 minutes off the heat. Fluff with a fork.
5. Cook the kofta: heat the olive oil in a large skillet over medium heat. Cook the kofta 4 to 5 minutes per side, turning once or twice, until deeply browned and firm to the touch. Check with a thermometer: ground pork must reach 160 F inside. Rest 3 minutes.
6. Make the yogurt sauce: stir together the Greek yogurt, lemon juice, and a pinch of salt.
7. Assemble the bowls: divide the rice among 6 bowls. Top each with 2 kofta, a spoonful of cucumber, tomato, and red onion, and a generous dollop of yogurt sauce.
8. Storage and reheating: store the kofta and rice separately in airtight containers up to 3 days (yogurt sauce keeps 4 days). Reheat the kofta in a 350 F oven 10 minutes or until steaming hot; warm the rice with a splash of water.
Common mistakes: Overmixing the meat -- mix only until combined or the kofta turn rubbery. Squeezing the grated onion dry -- its juice keeps the kofta juicy. Undercooking -- ground pork must hit 160 F inside, not just look brown outside. Cooking on too-high heat -- medium heat browns the spices without burning them; scorched cumin tastes bitter.

Title: Pork Meatballs with Parmesan Orzo
Ingredients:
2 lb ground pork
1 large egg
1 cup plain breadcrumbs
1/2 cup grated Parmesan cheese, for the meatballs, plus 1/2 cup for the orzo
1/2 cup fresh parsley, finely chopped
4 cloves garlic, minced (mince = chop very fine), divided
1 tsp dried oregano
1 tsp dried basil
2 tsp kosher salt, divided (start with 2 tsp; adjust at the end)
1 tsp black pepper
2 tbsp olive oil, for the sauce
1 medium onion, diced (dice = cut into small even cubes about 1/2 inch)
1 can (28 oz) crushed tomatoes
2 1/2 cups orzo pasta, uncooked
3 tbsp butter
2 tbsp lemon juice (from 1 lemon)
1/4 cup fresh basil leaves, torn
Steps:
1. Mise en place: everything chopped, measured, and set out first. Mince (chop very fine) the garlic. Chop the parsley. Dice (cut into small even cubes about 1/2 inch) the onion. Grate the Parmesan. Tear the basil. Juice the lemon. Measure the breadcrumbs, orzo, butter, and tomatoes. Heat the oven to 425 F.
2. Make the meatball mixture: in a large bowl, combine the ground pork, egg, breadcrumbs, 1/2 cup Parmesan, parsley, half the garlic, oregano, basil, 1 tsp salt, and the pepper. Mix with your hands just until combined -- no more.
3. Roll and bake: roll into 24 golf-ball-size meatballs (about 1 1/2 inches), using loose hands. Place on a rimmed baking sheet. Bake 18 to 20 minutes, turning once halfway, until browned and firm. They should reach 160 F inside.
4. Make the sauce: while the meatballs bake, heat the olive oil in a large skillet over medium heat. Cook the onion 4 to 5 minutes until soft and translucent. Add the remaining garlic and cook 30 seconds until fragrant. Pour in the crushed tomatoes and 1/2 tsp salt. Simmer 10 minutes, stirring occasionally, until slightly thickened. Nestle the baked meatballs into the sauce and simmer 5 minutes more.
5. Cook the orzo: bring a large pot of salted water to a rolling boil. Cook the orzo 8 to 9 minutes until al dente (tender with a slight bite). Drain, reserving 1/2 cup of the pasta water. Return to the pot and toss with the butter, lemon juice, remaining 1/2 cup Parmesan, and a splash of pasta water until creamy. Season with salt to taste.
6. Serve: spoon the lemony Parmesan orzo into bowls, top with meatballs and sauce, and finish with the torn basil.
7. Storage and reheating: refrigerate up to 3 days in airtight containers. Reheat the meatballs and sauce in a saucepan over medium heat until bubbling; revive the orzo with a splash of water and a knob of butter.
Common mistakes: Packing the meatballs too tight -- loose hands give tender meatballs. Skipping the reserved pasta water -- its starch is what makes the orzo creamy, not just the butter. Overcooking the orzo -- pull it at al dente since it keeps cooking in the hot pan. Not salting the pasta water -- bland water makes bland orzo; it should taste like the sea.

Title: Pork Ragu with Parmesan Polenta
Ingredients:
2 1/2 lb pork shoulder, cut into 2-inch chunks (trim very large fat caps but leave some)
2 tbsp olive oil
2 tsp kosher salt, divided (start with 2 tsp; adjust at the end)
1 tsp black pepper
1 large onion, diced (dice = cut into small even cubes about 1/2 inch)
2 medium carrots, diced
2 ribs celery, diced
4 cloves garlic, minced (mince = chop very fine)
1 cup dry white wine
2 tbsp tomato paste
1 can (28 oz) crushed tomatoes
2 bay leaves
1 cup whole milk, for the ragu
2 cups coarse polenta (cornmeal), dry
4 cups water, for the polenta
2 cups whole milk, for the polenta
4 tbsp butter
1 cup grated Parmesan cheese
2 tbsp fresh parsley, chopped, for serving
Steps:
1. Mise en place: everything ready before heat goes on. Cut the pork into 2-inch chunks. Dice (cut into small even cubes about 1/2 inch) the onion, carrots, and celery -- this trio is the soffritto, the aromatic base of northern Italian ragus. Mince (chop very fine) the garlic. Measure the wine, tomato paste, tomatoes, milk, polenta, butter, and Parmesan. Heat the oven to 325 F.
2. Brown the pork: pat the pork chunks dry. Heat the olive oil in a large heavy Dutch oven over medium-high heat until shimmering. Season the pork with 1 tsp salt and the pepper. Brown the chunks in two batches, 3 to 4 minutes per side, until deep brown all over -- you should hear a steady sizzle. Set the browned pork on a plate. (Browning builds the deep flavor of the sauce; do not skip it.)
3. Build the soffritto: in the same pot, add the onion, carrots, and celery. Cook over medium heat 6 to 8 minutes, stirring, until soft and golden at the edges. Add the garlic and tomato paste; cook 2 minutes, stirring, until the paste darkens to brick red and smells sweet.
4. Deglaze and braise: pour in the white wine and scrape up all the browned bits from the bottom -- that is pure flavor. Add the crushed tomatoes, bay leaves, and 1 tsp salt. Return the pork to the pot with any juices. Bring to a gentle simmer, cover, and move to the oven. Braise 2 1/2 to 3 hours, stirring once halfway, until the pork falls apart when pressed with a spoon. During the last 30 minutes, stir in the 1 cup milk and leave the lid ajar -- milk is the classic northern Italian finish that mellows and enriches the sauce.
5. Shred: remove the bay leaves. Use two forks to shred the pork into the sauce. Taste and adjust salt. Keep warm over low heat.
6. Make the polenta: bring the 4 cups water and 2 cups milk to a boil in a large pot over medium-high heat, then reduce to a gentle simmer. Rain in the polenta slowly while whisking constantly to prevent lumps. Switch to a wooden spoon and cook 30 to 40 minutes, stirring often, until thick and creamy and the grains feel tender on the tongue. Stir in the butter and Parmesan until melted. Season with salt.
7. Serve: spoon creamy polenta into warm bowls, ladle the ragu over the top, and finish with parsley and extra Parmesan.
8. Storage and reheating: refrigerate up to 4 days. Reheat the ragu in a saucepan over medium-low heat, adding a splash of water if thick. Polenta firms up when cold -- reheat with a splash of milk, whisking smooth.
Common mistakes: Rushing the braise -- the pork needs the full 2 1/2 hours to turn tender; undercooked shoulder is chewy. Dumping the polenta in all at once -- it clumps; rain it in slowly while whisking. Scorching the polenta -- stir often on low heat or it burns on the bottom. Serving it bland -- both the ragu and the polenta need generous salt; taste at the end and adjust.

Title: Pork Tenderloin with Lime Potatoes
Ingredients:
3 lb pork tenderloin (about 2 tenderloins)
1 cup fresh orange juice (about 3 oranges)
1/3 cup fresh lime juice (about 3 limes), plus 1 lime cut into wedges
8 cloves garlic, smashed (hit once with the flat of the knife so each clove breaks open)
1 tsp ground cumin
1 tsp dried oregano
1/3 cup olive oil, for the marinade, plus a glug for searing
2 tsp kosher salt, divided (start with 2 tsp; adjust at the end)
1 tsp black pepper
3 lb baby potatoes, halved
1/4 cup fresh cilantro, chopped
Steps:
1. Mise en place: everything ready first. Squeeze the orange and lime juice. Smash (hit once with the flat of the knife so each clove breaks open) the garlic. Halve the potatoes. Chop the cilantro. Measure the cumin, oregano, olive oil, salt, and pepper. Heat the oven to 425 F.
2. Make the mojo marinade: in a bowl, whisk the orange juice, lime juice, smashed garlic, cumin, oregano, 1/3 cup olive oil, 1 tsp salt, and the pepper. (Mojo is Cuba's garlic-citrus marinade -- bright, garlicky, and sour.) Place the tenderloins in a large zip-top bag, pour in two-thirds of the mojo, seal, and marinate in the refrigerator 30 minutes to 2 hours. Reserve the remaining third in the fridge for the potatoes -- never reuse marinade that touched raw pork.
3. Sear and roast the pork: remove the pork from the marinade and pat dry (discard the used marinade). Heat a glug of olive oil in a large oven-safe skillet over medium-high heat until shimmering. Sear the tenderloins 2 to 3 minutes per side until golden brown. Transfer the skillet to the oven and roast 15 to 18 minutes, until a meat thermometer reads 145 F in the thickest part. Rest 10 minutes on a cutting board, then slice into 1/2-inch medallions.
4. Roast the lime potatoes: toss the halved potatoes with the reserved clean mojo, 1 tbsp olive oil, and 1 tsp salt on a rimmed baking sheet, spread in a single layer. Roast at 425 F for 30 to 35 minutes, turning once halfway, until crisp-edged and golden and a fork slides in easily. Squeeze the lime wedges over them and sprinkle with cilantro.
5. Serve the sliced pork over the lime potatoes with any pan juices spooned over.
6. Storage and reheating: refrigerate up to 3 days. Slice leftover pork cold for sandwiches, or warm gently in a 300 F oven 10 minutes; crisp the potatoes in a hot oven.
Common mistakes: Reusing the marinade the raw pork sat in -- always reserve a separate clean portion before the meat goes in. Overcooking tenderloin -- it dries out fast; pull it at exactly 145 F. Cutting too soon -- skipping the rest lets the juices run out. Roasting wet, crowded potatoes -- pat them dry and give them space on the pan, or they steam instead of crisping.

Title: Provencal Cod with Tomato & Olives
Ingredients:
2 1/2 lb cod fillets, about 1 1/2 inches thick
3 tbsp olive oil, divided
1 large onion, sliced into thin half-rounds (slice = cut into thin flat pieces)
4 cloves garlic, minced (mince = chop very fine)
2 cans (14.5 oz each) diced tomatoes
1 cup kalamata olives, halved
2 tbsp capers, drained
1 tsp herbes de Provence
1/2 tsp crushed red pepper flakes (start with 1/2 tsp; add up to 1 tsp for more heat)
2 tsp kosher salt, divided (start with 2 tsp; adjust at the end)
1 tsp black pepper
2 tbsp lemon juice
1/4 cup fresh parsley, chopped
Steps:
1. Mise en place: everything ready before cooking. Slice (cut into thin flat pieces) the onion into thin half-rounds. Mince (chop very fine) the garlic. Halve the olives. Chop the parsley. Open the cans of tomatoes. Juice the lemon. Pat the cod fillets very dry with paper towels -- dry fish sears instead of steaming.
2. Start the sauce: heat 2 tbsp olive oil in a large deep skillet over medium heat until it shimmers. Add the onion and cook 4 to 5 minutes until soft and translucent. Add the garlic, herbes de Provence, and red pepper flakes; cook 1 minute until fragrant.
3. Simmer the tomatoes: pour in the diced tomatoes with their juices, the olives, capers, 1 tsp salt, and the pepper. Bring to a lively simmer and cook 10 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the sauce thickens slightly and tastes rich and briny.
4. Nestle in the cod: season the cod with 1 tsp salt and drizzle with the remaining 1 tbsp olive oil. Nestle the fillets into the bubbling sauce, spooning a little sauce over the tops. Cover and cook 6 to 8 minutes, until the fish flakes easily with a fork and is opaque all the way through -- internal temperature 145 F.
5. Finish: remove from the heat, squeeze the lemon juice over everything, and sprinkle with parsley. Taste the sauce and adjust salt.
6. Serve in shallow bowls with the sauce spooned over. Crusty bread for soaking up the sauce is strongly recommended.
7. Storage and reheating: refrigerate up to 2 days. Reheat gently in a covered saucepan over low heat until just warmed through -- microwaving makes fish rubbery.
Common mistakes: Cooking the cod too long -- check at 6 minutes; overcooked cod turns dry and falls apart. Watery sauce -- let the tomatoes simmer the full 10 minutes before the fish goes in. Forgetting to pat the fish dry -- wet cod releases water and thins the sauce. Skimping on the lemon -- the bright acidity is what makes the Provencal flavors sing.

Title: Salmon Couscous with Cucumber & Olives
Ingredients:
2 lb salmon fillets, skin-on, cut into 6 portions
2 tsp kosher salt, divided (start with 2 tsp; adjust at the end)
1 tsp black pepper
1 tsp dried oregano
2 tbsp olive oil, divided
2 cups couscous, uncooked
2 cups chicken or vegetable broth
1 large cucumber, diced (dice = cut into small even cubes about 1/2 inch)
1 pint cherry tomatoes, halved
1 cup kalamata olives, halved
1/2 red onion, thinly sliced (slice = cut into thin flat pieces)
4 oz feta cheese, crumbled
1/4 cup olive oil, for the dressing
3 tbsp lemon juice
1/4 cup fresh dill, chopped (or 1 tbsp dried dill)
Steps:
1. Mise en place: everything chopped, measured, and set out first. Dice (cut into small even cubes about 1/2 inch) the cucumber. Halve the cherry tomatoes and olives. Thinly slice (cut into thin flat pieces) the red onion. Crumble the feta. Chop the dill. Juice the lemon. Measure the couscous and broth. Pat the salmon dry.
2. Make the couscous: bring the broth to a boil in a medium saucepan. Stir in the couscous and 1/2 tsp salt, cover, and remove from the heat. Let stand 5 minutes. Fluff with a fork -- the grains should be separate and tender. Drizzle with 1 tbsp olive oil and fluff again. Set aside.
3. Season the salmon: rub the salmon with the remaining 1 tbsp olive oil. Season with 1 tsp salt, the pepper, and the oregano.
4. Sear the salmon: heat a large skillet over medium-high heat until a drop of water sizzles. Place the salmon skin-side down -- it should sizzle loudly. Cook 5 to 6 minutes without moving until the skin is crisp and the fish is opaque about two-thirds up the side. (For extra-crisp skin, press down lightly with a spatula for the first 30 seconds.) Flip and cook 1 to 2 minutes more. Salmon is done at 145 F inside, or when it flakes gently with a fork.
5. Toss the salad: in a large bowl, combine the warm couscous, cucumber, tomatoes, olives, red onion, feta, 1/4 cup olive oil, lemon juice, dill, and 1/2 tsp salt. Toss and taste -- add more lemon or salt until bright.
6. Serve the couscous salad in bowls with a salmon fillet on top, skin-side up so it stays crisp.
7. Storage and reheating: store the salad and salmon separately up to 2 days. Eat the salad cold or at room temperature; warm the salmon gently in a 300 F oven 8 minutes to protect its texture.
Common mistakes: Mushy couscous -- do not cook it on the heat; off the heat, covered, exactly 5 minutes. Flipping the salmon too soon -- if it sticks, the skin is not crisp yet; wait until it releases. Dressing cold couscous -- toss the dressing while the couscous is still warm so it soaks in flavor. Overcooking salmon -- 145 F max; it keeps cooking as it rests.

Title: Salmon Teriyaki with Bok Choy
Ingredients:
2 lb salmon fillets, cut into 6 portions
1/2 cup low-sodium soy sauce
1/2 cup mirin (sweet Japanese cooking wine)
1/4 cup packed brown sugar
1 tbsp fresh ginger, grated
2 cloves garlic, minced (mince = chop very fine)
1 tsp cornstarch mixed with 1 tbsp cold water (stir until smooth -- a smooth slurry keeps the sauce from lumping)
2 lb baby bok choy, halved lengthwise
1 tbsp toasted sesame oil
1 tbsp neutral oil (vegetable or canola)
2 cups long-grain rice, uncooked
3 cups water, for the rice
2 tbsp sesame seeds, toasted, for garnish
3 green onions, thinly sliced (slice = cut into thin flat pieces)
Steps:
1. Mise en place: everything ready before heat goes on. Grate the ginger. Mince (chop very fine) the garlic. Halve the bok choy lengthwise. Slice (cut into thin flat pieces) the green onions. Measure the soy sauce, mirin, brown sugar, oils, rice, and sesame seeds. Stir the cornstarch with the cold water until smooth. Pat the salmon dry.
2. Cook the rice: in a saucepan, combine the rice, 3 cups water, and 1 tsp salt. Bring to a boil over high heat, stir once, reduce to low, cover, and cook 15 minutes without lifting the lid. Rest, covered, 10 minutes off the heat. Fluff with a fork.
3. Make the teriyaki sauce: in a small saucepan over medium heat, combine the soy sauce, mirin, brown sugar, ginger, and garlic. Bring to a gentle simmer, stirring, until the sugar dissolves. Whisk in the cornstarch slurry and simmer 1 to 2 minutes until the sauce thickens enough to coat the back of a spoon -- it should look glossy. Set aside.
4. Sear the salmon: heat the neutral oil in a large skillet over medium-high heat until shimmering. Place the salmon skin-side down and cook 5 minutes until the skin crisps. Flip, brush the tops generously with teriyaki sauce, and cook 1 to 2 minutes more until 145 F inside. Transfer to a plate and brush with a little more sauce.
5. Wilt the bok choy: in the same skillet over medium-high heat, add the sesame oil. Add the bok choy cut-side down in a single layer and sear 2 minutes until the cut sides are golden. Flip, add 1/4 cup water, cover, and steam 2 to 3 minutes until the stems are tender-crisp and bright green.
6. Serve over rice: divide the rice among bowls, top with salmon and bok choy, spoon over extra teriyaki sauce, and garnish with sesame seeds and green onions.
7. Storage and reheating: refrigerate up to 2 days. Reheat the salmon gently in a 300 F oven 8 minutes; warm the bok choy and rice with a splash of water.
Common mistakes: Boiling the teriyaki sauce hard -- it turns bitter and over-reduces; keep it at a gentle simmer. Adding cornstarch to hot liquid directly -- it lumps; always stir it into cold water first. Overcrowding the bok choy -- give it a single layer or it steams soggy instead of searing. Microwaving the salmon to reheat -- it goes dry and fishy; use the low oven.

Title: Salmon with Lemon Butter Orzo
Ingredients:
2 lb salmon fillets, cut into 6 portions
2 tsp kosher salt, divided (start with 2 tsp; adjust at the end)
1 tsp black pepper
2 tbsp olive oil, divided
2 cups orzo pasta, uncooked
6 tbsp butter (3/4 stick)
4 cloves garlic, minced (mince = chop very fine)
1/4 cup lemon juice (about 2 lemons), plus lemon wedges for serving
1 tsp lemon zest
1/2 cup grated Parmesan cheese
1 bunch asparagus, tough ends trimmed, cut into 2-inch pieces
1/4 cup fresh parsley, chopped
Steps:
1. Mise en place: everything ready first. Mince (chop very fine) the garlic. Zest and juice the lemons. Grate the Parmesan. Chop the parsley. Trim the tough ends off the asparagus and cut into 2-inch pieces. Measure the orzo and butter. Pat the salmon dry and season with 1 tsp salt and the pepper.
2. Start the orzo: bring a large pot of generously salted water to a rolling boil. Cook the orzo 6 minutes, then add the asparagus pieces and cook 2 to 3 minutes more, until the orzo is al dente (tender with a slight bite) and the asparagus is bright green and tender-crisp. Drain, reserving 1 cup of the pasta water.
3. Make the lemon butter sauce: in the same pot over medium heat, melt the butter. Add the garlic and cook 1 minute until fragrant and just turning golden -- do not let it brown. Stir in the lemon juice, lemon zest, and 1/2 cup of the reserved pasta water. Bring to a gentle simmer.
4. Finish the orzo: return the drained orzo and asparagus to the pot. Add the Parmesan and toss 2 minutes until creamy and glossy, adding splashes of pasta water as needed. Stir in half the parsley. Taste and adjust salt.
5. Sear the salmon: heat 1 tbsp olive oil in a large skillet over medium-high heat until shimmering. Cook the salmon skin-side down 5 minutes until crisp, flip, and cook 1 to 2 minutes more until 145 F inside and the flesh flakes gently.
6. Serve the orzo in bowls with a salmon fillet on top, skin-side up so the skin stays crisp, spooning extra lemon butter sauce over. Garnish with the remaining parsley and serve with lemon wedges.
7. Storage and reheating: refrigerate up to 2 days. Reheat the orzo in a saucepan over low heat with a splash of water to loosen; warm the salmon in a 300 F oven 8 minutes.
Common mistakes: Overcooking the garlic -- browned garlic tastes bitter; pull it at pale gold. Skipping the reserved pasta water -- its starch is what turns butter and lemon into a silky sauce. Overcooking the orzo -- it keeps absorbing sauce in the pot, so pull it a minute early. Plating the salmon skin-side down -- the crisp skin goes soggy; keep it on top.

Title: Salmon with Rice, Peas & Garlic
Ingredients:
2 lb salmon fillets, cut into 6 portions
2 tsp kosher salt, divided (start with 2 tsp; adjust at the end)
1 tsp black pepper
2 tbsp olive oil
2 cups long-grain rice, uncooked
3 cups water, for the rice
2 cups frozen peas, thawed (run under warm water first)
6 cloves garlic, minced (mince = chop very fine)
3 tbsp butter
2 tbsp lemon juice
1/4 cup fresh parsley, chopped
Lemon wedges, for serving
Steps:
1. Mise en place: everything ready before heat goes on. Mince (chop very fine) the garlic. Chop the parsley. Juice the lemon. Thaw the peas under warm water. Measure the rice, water, butter, and oil. Pat the salmon dry and season with 1 tsp salt and the pepper.
2. Cook the rice: in a medium saucepan, combine the rice, 3 cups water, and 1/2 tsp salt. Bring to a boil over high heat, stir once, reduce to low, cover, and cook 15 minutes without lifting the lid. Rest, covered, 10 minutes off the heat. Fluff with a fork.
3. Sear the salmon: heat the olive oil in a large skillet over medium-high heat until shimmering. Place the salmon skin-side down -- it should sizzle. Cook 5 minutes without moving until the skin is crisp, flip, and cook 1 to 2 minutes more until 145 F inside. Transfer to a plate.
4. Make the garlic butter peas: in the same skillet over medium heat, melt the butter. Add the garlic and cook 1 minute until fragrant and pale gold -- do not brown it. Add the peas and 1/2 tsp salt; cook 3 to 4 minutes, stirring, until the peas are bright green and heated through. Stir in the lemon juice and parsley.
5. Serve the rice in bowls, top with the garlic butter peas, and lay a salmon fillet on top. Serve with lemon wedges.
6. Storage and reheating: refrigerate up to 2 days. Warm the rice and peas with a splash of water; warm the salmon gently in a 300 F oven 8 minutes.
Common mistakes: Burning the garlic -- it goes bitter fast; keep the heat at medium and pull it at pale gold. Overcooking the salmon -- check at the low end of the time range; it firms up as it rests. Soggy rice -- never lift the lid during the 15-minute cook or the 10-minute rest. Using still-frozen peas -- they drop the pan temperature and turn mushy before they heat through; thaw them under warm water first.

Title: Salsa Verde Cod Tacos
Ingredients:
2 lb cod fillets, skinless, cut into strips about 3 inches long and 1 inch wide, patted very dry
1.5 cups all-purpose flour, divided (1 cup for the batter, 0.5 cup for dredging)
0.5 cup cornstarch
1 tbsp baking powder
2 tsp kosher salt, divided
1 tsp ground cumin
1 tsp smoked paprika
1 cup cold Mexican lager beer (keep it ice cold; do not open until batter time)
1 large egg, lightly beaten
5 cups avocado oil, for frying (about 2 inches deep in a heavy skillet)
18 small corn tortillas (6-inch)
4 cups shredded green cabbage
0.5 cup Mexican crema (or sour cream)
0.25 cup mayonnaise
1 tbsp fresh lime juice, plus extra lime wedges for serving
1.5 cups salsa verde (tomatillo salsa)
0.75 cup crumbled cotija cheese
0.5 cup chopped fresh cilantro
Steps:
1. Mise en place (get everything ready before any heat goes on): Cut the cod into strips about 3 inches long and 1 inch wide, then pat them dry with paper towels — dry fish grips batter better. Shred the cabbage into thin strips (shred = cut into long thin strips). Chop the cilantro (chop = cut into rough small pieces). Juice the lime. Slice limes into wedges. Set out the flour, cornstarch, baking powder, salt, cumin, paprika, egg, and beer near the stove. Make the lime crema: whisk the crema, mayonnaise, lime juice, and 0.5 tsp of the salt in a small bowl. Toss the cabbage with 2 tbsp of that crema mixture in a large bowl to make the slaw; keep the rest of the crema in the fridge for drizzling later.
2. Set a large heavy skillet (cast iron is best) over medium-high heat and pour in the avocado oil, about 2 inches deep. Heat the oil to 360F, checked with a kitchen thermometer. No thermometer? Dip a wooden spoon handle in the oil — if bubbles form vigorously around the wood, the oil is ready. If it smokes, it is too hot; slide the pan off the burner for a minute.
3. While the oil heats, whisk together the 1 cup of flour, cornstarch, baking powder, 1 tsp of the salt, cumin, and paprika in a large bowl. In a second bowl, whisk the cold beer with the beaten egg. Pour the wet mix into the dry mix and whisk just until smooth — a few small lumps are fine. The batter should be a little thinner than pancake batter. Keep it cold; if your kitchen is warm, set the batter bowl over a larger bowl of ice.
4. Season the fish strips with the remaining 1 tsp of salt. Put the 0.5 cup of flour for dredging on a plate. Working with one strip at a time, roll it in the flour and shake off the excess, dip it into the batter letting the extra drip off, and lay it gently into the hot oil, away from you so no oil splashes. Fry 4 to 5 pieces at a time — crowding drops the oil temperature and makes soggy batter.
5. Fry for 3 to 4 minutes total, turning once with tongs, until the coating is deep golden brown, puffed, and very crispy — it should sound loud and crackly. Lift each piece onto a wire rack set over a baking sheet (not paper towels; the rack keeps the bottom crisp) and sprinkle with a pinch of salt while hot. The cod should flake easily and read 145F at the thickest point. Let the oil come back to 360F between batches.
6. While the last batch fries, warm the tortillas: heat a dry skillet over medium-high heat and warm each tortilla 30 to 45 seconds per side until soft, pliable, and lightly charred in spots. Stack them in a clean kitchen towel to keep them warm.
7. Assemble: lay a warm tortilla flat, add a small handful of slaw, 2 pieces of crispy cod, a spoonful of salsa verde, a drizzle of the lime crema, a sprinkle of cotija and cilantro, and a squeeze of lime. Serve right away while the fish is crackling.
8. Storage and reheating: fried fish is best eaten fresh. Refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours in a covered container for up to 2 days. Reheat in a 400F oven on a wire rack for 8 to 10 minutes until crisp again — never microwave fried fish, which turns the batter rubbery. Slaw keeps 2 days in the fridge.
Common mistakes:
- Oil too cool (under 340F): the batter soaks up oil and turns greasy instead of crisp — use a thermometer and wait for 360F between batches.
- Warm batter: warm beer makes a flat, heavy coating — keep the beer ice cold until the moment you whisk it in.
- Wet fish: damp strips make the batter slide off — pat the cod thoroughly dry before dredging.
- Overcooking the cod: past 145F it goes dry and chalky — check the temperature at the thickest strip.

Title: Scallop Tomato Risotto
Ingredients:
1.5 cups arborio rice
2 lb large dry sea scallops (U-15/U-20), side muscle removed, patted very dry
6 cups low-sodium chicken or vegetable broth
1.5 cups crushed tomatoes
1 large yellow onion, diced (cut into small even cubes about 1/2 inch)
4 garlic cloves, minced (chopped very fine)
0.5 cup dry white wine, such as pinot grigio or sauvignon blanc
4 tbsp unsalted butter, divided
3 tbsp olive oil, divided
1 cup finely grated Parmesan cheese
0.5 cup chopped fresh basil or flat-leaf parsley
1 tbsp fresh lemon juice, plus the zest of 1 lemon
1.5 tsp kosher salt, divided, plus more as needed
0.75 tsp black pepper, divided
Steps:
1. Mise en place: Dice the onion (dice = cut into small even cubes about 1/2 inch). Mince the garlic (mince = chop very fine). Grate the Parmesan. Chop the basil or parsley. Zest and juice the lemon. Pull the tough side muscle off each scallop (it is the small flap on the edge; it just peels off) and pat the scallops very dry with paper towels — dry scallops are the secret to a golden sear. Pour the broth into a saucepan and keep it warm over low heat; cold broth cools the pan and stalls the risotto.
2. Heat 1 tbsp of the butter and 1 tbsp of the olive oil in a wide, heavy pan or Dutch oven over high heat until the butter foams and just starts to brown. Working in two batches so the scallops do not steam each other, lay the scallops in a single layer with space between them and sear 1.5 to 2 minutes per side without moving them, until each side has a deep golden-brown crust. The center should be opaque and just firm to the touch (translucent center = not done yet). Season with 0.5 tsp of the salt and 0.25 tsp of the pepper as they cook. Move the scallops to a plate; they will finish in the hot risotto later.
3. Reduce the heat to medium. In the same pan, add 1 tbsp of the olive oil and the diced onion with the remaining 1 tsp of salt. Cook 5 to 7 minutes, stirring often, until the onion is soft, translucent, and sweet-smelling — not browned. Add the garlic and cook 30 seconds more, until fragrant.
4. Stir in the arborio rice and toast it for 2 minutes, stirring constantly, until the edges of the grains look translucent and they smell faintly nutty (this step is called the tostatura; it keeps the grains distinct). Pour in the white wine and stir until it has almost completely evaporated and the pan no longer smells sharp and boozy, about 1 minute.
5. Stir in the crushed tomatoes and one ladle (about 0.75 cup) of the warm broth. Simmer gently, stirring every minute or two, until most of the liquid is absorbed. Keep adding warm broth one ladle at a time, stirring and waiting for absorption before adding the next. After 18 to 22 minutes, taste a grain: it should be tender with a tiny bite at the center (al dente) and the mixture should look creamy, flowing like thick porridge — risotto should spread slowly when you shake the pan (the Italian ideal, all'onda, "like a wave"). You may not need every drop of broth.
6. Off the heat, stir in the remaining 2 tbsp of butter, the Parmesan, the lemon zest and lemon juice, and 0.25 tsp of the pepper. Taste and add more salt if it needs it. Fold the seared scallops into the risotto and let it sit 2 minutes — the residual heat warms them through without overcooking.
7. Serve: spoon into warm bowls, top with the chopped basil or parsley, and finish with a thread of olive oil. Serve immediately — risotto waits for no one and thickens as it stands.
8. Storage and reheating: refrigerate within 2 hours for up to 2 days. To reheat, warm gently in a saucepan over low heat with a splash of broth, stirring until creamy again — the microwave makes it gummy. Leftover risotto makes excellent crisped risotto cakes in a hot oiled skillet.
Common mistakes:
- Cold or added-all-at-once broth: it shocks the starch and the risotto turns gluey or chalky — keep the broth at a bare simmer and add it ladle by ladle.
- Crowding the scallops: they steam instead of searing and never get a crust — sear in two batches with space between each scallop, and pat them dry first.
- Overcooking the rice: mushy risotto has no bite — start tasting at 18 minutes and stop at tender-with-a-tiny-core.

Title: Seared Trout with Tomato Olive Rice
Ingredients:
2 lb rainbow trout fillets (6 fillets, about 5 to 6 oz each), skin on or off
2 cups long-grain white rice
1 can (14.5 oz) diced tomatoes with their juices
1 cup pitted Kalamata olives, halved (slice = cut into thin flat pieces)
1 large yellow onion, diced (cut into small even cubes about 1/2 inch)
4 garlic cloves, minced (chopped very fine)
3 cups low-sodium chicken broth
4 tbsp olive oil, divided
1.5 tsp smoked paprika (pimenton dulce), divided
0.25 tsp saffron threads, crumbled (optional; or 0.5 tsp turmeric for color)
1 lemon, cut into wedges
0.5 cup chopped fresh flat-leaf parsley
1.75 tsp kosher salt, divided
0.75 tsp black pepper
Steps:
1. Mise en place: Dice the onion (dice = cut into small even cubes about 1/2 inch). Mince the garlic (mince = chop very fine). Halve the olives (slice = cut into thin flat pieces). Chop the parsley. Cut the lemon into wedges. Check the trout for bones: run a fingertip along the thickest part and pull any pin bones you feel with tweezers or clean pliers. Pat the fillets dry — dry skin crisps, wet skin steams. If using saffron, crumble the threads into 2 tbsp of hot water and let them soak while you cook.
2. Heat 2 tbsp of the olive oil in a large heavy pot or Dutch oven over medium heat. Add the onion and 1 tsp of the salt and cook 6 to 8 minutes, stirring often, until soft and translucent with lightly golden edges. Add the garlic and 1 tsp of the smoked paprika; stir 30 seconds until it smells toasty and sweet — do not let the paprika burn or it turns bitter.
3. Stir in the rice and toast 1 minute, coating every grain in the flavored oil. Pour in the diced tomatoes with their juices, the olives, the saffron soaking liquid (or the turmeric), and the chicken broth. Stir once, bring to a boil, then reduce to a gentle simmer and cover.
4. Cook the rice undisturbed for 18 minutes — do not lift the lid and do not stir, which makes rice gummy. Then turn off the heat and let it rest, still covered, for 10 minutes. The resting time finishes the grains and lets the steam settle. Fluff with a fork; every grain should be tender and separate, tinted golden from the tomato and saffron, studded with olives.
5. While the rice rests, sear the trout. Season the fillets with the remaining 0.75 tsp of salt, the remaining 0.5 tsp of smoked paprika, and the black pepper. Heat the remaining 2 tbsp of olive oil in a large skillet over medium-high heat until it shimmers and flows easily. Lay the fillets skin-side down (or presentation-side down if skinless), pressing gently with a spatula for 10 seconds so they do not curl.
6. Sear 4 to 5 minutes on the first side without moving them — the skin should be crisp and deep golden, and the flesh will have turned opaque about two-thirds of the way up. Flip carefully and cook 2 to 3 minutes more, until the thickest part flakes with a fork and reads 145F. Move to a plate and let the fish rest 2 minutes.
7. Serve: spoon the tomato olive rice into shallow bowls, lay a trout fillet on top, scatter with parsley, and finish with a squeeze of lemon. Andalusia-style — simple, bright, and unhurried.
8. Storage and reheating: refrigerate within 2 hours for up to 2 days. Reheat the fish gently in a 300F oven for 10 minutes so it does not dry out; warm the rice in a covered saucepan with a splash of broth. Do not microwave the trout — it goes rubbery.
Common mistakes:
- Stirring or peeking at the rice: it releases starch and turns sticky instead of fluffy — cover and leave it alone for the full 18 minutes plus the 10-minute rest.
- Moving the fish too soon: the skin sticks and tears — it releases from the pan by itself once it is properly crisped.
- Burning the paprika: it scorches in seconds — add it with the garlic and keep everything moving for just 30 seconds.

Title: Sesame-Free Tuna Poke Bowls
Ingredients:
2 lb sushi-grade ahi tuna, cut into 3/4-inch cubes
3 cups short-grain white rice, rinsed well
3 cups water, for cooking rice
1 tsp kosher salt, for the rice water
0.5 cup low-sodium soy sauce
2 tbsp rice vinegar
1 tbsp honey
1 tbsp avocado oil (this recipe is sesame-free; we skip sesame oil and sesame seeds entirely)
1 tbsp fresh ginger, grated
4 green onions, thinly sliced (slice = cut into thin flat pieces)
1 tsp crushed red pepper flakes (start with 0.5 tsp if you like it mild)
2 ripe avocados, diced
2 cups diced fresh mango
1 English cucumber, thinly sliced
0.5 cup roasted macadamia nuts, coarsely crushed
4 cups shredded red cabbage
0.25 cup chopped fresh cilantro
1 lime, cut into wedges
Steps:
1. Mise en place and food safety first: poke uses RAW fish, so buy tuna labeled sushi-grade or sashimi-grade from a trusted fish market, keep it in the coldest part of the fridge (under 40F) until the moment you cook, and keep everything — cut board, knife, bowl — cold and clean. If the tuna smells fishy instead of fresh and ocean-clean, do not use it. Cube the tuna into 3/4-inch pieces and return it to the fridge immediately. Rinse the rice in a fine-mesh strainer until the water runs clear. Grate the ginger. Thinly slice the green onions (slice = cut into thin flat pieces). Dice the avocados and mango. Thinly slice the cucumber. Shred the red cabbage. Chop the cilantro. Crush the macadamia nuts with the bottom of a pan. Cut the lime into wedges.
2. Cook the rice: combine the rinsed rice, 3 cups of water, and the salt in a medium saucepan. Bring to a boil over high heat, then reduce to the lowest simmer, cover tightly, and cook 15 minutes without lifting the lid. Turn off the heat and rest 10 minutes. Fluff with a fork or rice paddle. Short-grain rice should be plump, slightly sticky, and glossy. Let it cool to warm (not hot) — spread it on a tray for 10 minutes if you are in a hurry.
3. Make the poke sauce: in a large bowl, whisk the soy sauce, rice vinegar, honey, avocado oil, grated ginger, and red pepper flakes until the honey dissolves. Taste it — you want salty, tangy, and a little sweet, with gentle heat. Add more honey or pepper flakes to adjust.
4. Take the tuna out of the fridge and add the cold cubes to the sauce along with half of the sliced green onions. Toss gently with a spoon — do not stir hard or the cubes break apart. Cover and marinate in the fridge for 10 to 15 minutes, no longer (the acid starts to "cook" the fish and change its texture if left too long).
5. Build the bowls: spoon warm rice into 6 wide bowls. Arrange the marinated tuna over the rice, spooning the extra sauce over the top. Fan the avocado, mango, cucumber, and red cabbage alongside the tuna. Finish with the crushed macadamia nuts (your sesame-free crunch), the remaining green onions, cilantro, and a lime wedge.
6. Serve immediately while the tuna is still cold and the rice is warm. Eat poke the day it is made — raw fish should never sit out more than 2 hours, and any leftovers must be refrigerated and eaten within 24 hours.
7. Storage: this dish does not keep well. Leftover tuna can be refrigerated in a covered container and eaten the next day, but the texture is best fresh. Do not freeze raw poke tuna.
Common mistakes:
- Using fish that is not sushi-grade: raw fish carries food-safety risk — buy from a reputable fish counter and ask for sushi-grade ahi, keeping it ice cold until serving.
- Over-marinating: after 15 minutes the tuna turns chalky at the edges — keep it to 10 to 15 minutes in the fridge.
- Hot rice under raw fish: it warms the tuna and dulls its flavor — cool the rice to just warm before building bowls.
- Adding sesame: this recipe is intentionally sesame-free (macadamia nuts give the richness and crunch) — double-check any store-bought sauces for hidden sesame oil.

Title: Shaking Beef Tomato Rice
Ingredients:
2.5 lb top sirloin, cut into 1-inch cubes
3 tbsp oyster sauce
2 tbsp fish sauce
2 tbsp low-sodium soy sauce
1 tbsp granulated sugar
5 garlic cloves, minced (chopped very fine), divided
1 tsp black pepper
3 tbsp avocado oil (or another neutral high-heat oil), divided
2 tbsp unsalted butter, divided
1 large red onion, cut into thin wedges (slice = cut into thin flat pieces)
5 cups cooked jasmine rice, day-old and chilled (start with about 1.75 cups dry rice)
2 tbsp tomato paste
1 tbsp fish sauce (for the rice)
2 tsp chicken bouillon powder (or 1 crumbled bouillon cube)
2 large eggs, beaten
1 bunch watercress (or 4 cups mixed salad greens)
2 ripe tomatoes, cut into wedges
1 cucumber, thinly sliced (slice = cut into thin flat pieces)
2 tbsp fresh lime juice (about 2 limes)
1 tsp kosher salt
1 tsp black pepper (for the lime-pepper dip)
Steps:
1. Mise en place: Cut the sirloin into 1-inch cubes — even cubes cook evenly. Mince the garlic (mince = chop very fine). Cut the red onion into thin wedges. Slice the cucumber into thin pieces (slice = cut into thin flat pieces). Cut the tomatoes into wedges. Juice the limes. Beat the eggs. If you do not have day-old rice, spread freshly cooked jasmine rice on a tray and refrigerate it uncovered for at least 30 minutes — dry, cold rice fries up fluffy instead of gummy.
