2. Marinate the beef: in a large bowl, toss the beef cubes with the oyster sauce, fish sauce, soy sauce, sugar, 4 of the minced garlic cloves, and the 1 tsp of black pepper. Let it marinate at room temperature for 15 minutes (or refrigerate up to 8 hours for deeper flavor — bring it back to room temperature for 20 minutes before cooking so it sears instead of steams).
3. Make the lime-pepper dipping sauce: stir the lime juice, kosher salt, and the second 1 tsp of black pepper in a small bowl until the salt mostly dissolves. Set aside — this bright, peppery dip is the signature finish of bo luc lac.
4. Make the tomato rice: heat 1 tbsp of the avocado oil in a large skillet or wok over medium heat. Add the beaten eggs and scramble 1 to 2 minutes until just set in soft curds; move to a plate. Add another 1 tbsp of oil and the remaining 1 minced garlic clove; cook 1 minute until fragrant and pale gold. Add the tomato paste and cook 1 minute, stirring, until it darkens to a brick red and smells sweet — cooking the paste raw-tomato taste out. Add the cold rice, breaking up any clumps with a spatula, then the fish sauce and bouillon powder. Toss 3 to 4 minutes until every grain is rosy and the rice is hot through. Fold the scrambled egg back in. Keep warm.
5. Sear the beef: wipe the skillet clean and heat the remaining 1 tbsp of oil over HIGH heat until it shimmers and just starts to smoke. Add HALF the beef cubes in a single layer with space between them — crowding is the enemy of a crust. Leave them alone for 2 minutes until deeply browned on one side, then shake the pan (the dish's namesake "luc lac" shaking) or flip the cubes and sear 1 to 2 minutes more. You want a charred crust and a pink center, about 130 to 135F — medium-rare. Move to a plate and repeat with the second half.
6. With the heat still on, add 1 tbsp of butter to the empty pan and the red onion wedges; toss 1 to 2 minutes until they soften slightly but keep a bite. Return all the beef to the pan, add the remaining 1 tbsp of butter, and toss everything for 30 seconds so the cubes gloss with sauce. The beef needs a 5-minute rest — the juices settle back in and it stays juicy.
7. Serve: pile the tomato rice on a platter, arrange the watercress, tomato wedges, and cucumber alongside, and spoon the shaking beef over the top. Serve the lime-pepper dip on the side for each person to dip or drizzle.
8. Storage and reheating: refrigerate within 2 hours for up to 3 days. Reheat the beef gently in a hot skillet for 2 minutes — just until warm — since it is already medium-rare and will overcook if blasted. Warm the rice in a covered skillet with a splash of water. The salad greens are best fresh.
Common mistakes:
- Crowding the pan: the beef steams gray instead of searing — cook in two batches with space between cubes, on the highest heat your stove gives.
- Cooking past medium-rare: 1-inch cubes go from juicy to tough in a minute — sear fast, rest 5 minutes, and trust the pink center.
- Fresh, wet rice for the tomato rice: it clumps and steams — day-old cold rice (or chilled spread-out fresh rice) fries up separate and fluffy.

Title: Shrimp & Broccoli Couscous
Ingredients:
2 lb large shrimp (21/25), peeled and deveined, tails removed
2 cups dry instant couscous
2.25 cups low-sodium chicken broth
6 cups broccoli florets (about 1.5 lb), cut into bite-size pieces
2 tsp ground cumin
1.5 tsp ground coriander
1 tsp ground turmeric
1 tsp sweet paprika
0.5 tsp ground cinnamon
0.5 tsp cayenne pepper (optional; start with 0.25 tsp for gentle heat)
4 tbsp olive oil, divided
3 tbsp unsalted butter, divided
1 large yellow onion, diced (cut into small even cubes about 1/2 inch)
4 garlic cloves, minced (chopped very fine)
1.5 tsp kosher salt, divided
0.5 cup golden raisins
0.33 cup sliced almonds, toasted
0.5 cup chopped fresh cilantro
0.25 cup chopped fresh mint
1 lemon, cut into wedges
Steps:
1. Mise en place: Dice the onion (dice = cut into small even cubes about 1/2 inch). Mince the garlic (mince = chop very fine). Cut the broccoli into bite-size florets (small enough to eat in one bite). Chop the cilantro and mint. Cut the lemon into wedges. Measure all the spices into one small bowl — cumin, coriander, turmeric, paprika, cinnamon, and cayenne — so they go in together. Pat the shrimp dry; dry shrimp sears instead of steams.
2. Cook the broccoli: bring a large pot of salted water to a rolling boil and blanch the broccoli for 2 minutes, until bright green and just tender when pierced with a fork — it should still have bite. Drain and immediately run under cold water (or plunge into ice water) to lock in the color. Set aside.
3. Make the couscous: in a saucepan, bring the chicken broth, 1 tbsp of the butter, and 0.75 tsp of the salt to a boil. Take the pan OFF the heat, pour in the couscous, stir once, and cover tightly. Let it sit undisturbed for 5 minutes — the grains swell and absorb every drop. Then uncover and fluff with a fork, breaking up any clumps by raking the tines through the grains (never mash with a spoon, which crushes them). Stir in 1 tbsp of butter while the couscous is hot. Authentic Moroccan couscous is triple-steamed in a couscoussier, which takes an hour; this 5-minute method gives the same fluffy spirit in a weeknight kitchen.
4. Heat 2 tbsp of the olive oil in a large deep skillet over medium-high heat until shimmering. Add the shrimp in a single layer, season with 0.5 tsp of the salt and all the spice mix, and cook 2 minutes per side without moving them — they are done when curled into a loose C, pink, and opaque all the way through. An overcooked shrimp curls into a tight O. Move to a plate.
5. In the same skillet, heat the remaining 2 tbsp of olive oil over medium heat. Add the onion and remaining 0.25 tsp of salt; cook 5 minutes until soft and golden at the edges. Add the garlic and cook 30 seconds until fragrant. Add the broccoli and raisins; toss 2 minutes until the broccoli is hot and glossy with the spiced oil.
6. Add the fluffed couscous to the skillet and toss everything together 1 minute. Fold in the shrimp, the toasted almonds, cilantro, and mint. Taste and add more salt or a squeeze of lemon until it sings — lemon wakes up all the warm spices.
7. Serve: mound the couscous in a wide serving bowl or platter, scatter a few extra almonds and herbs on top, and pass lemon wedges. Traditionally it is mounded into a cone — a fun, authentic touch.
8. Storage and reheating: refrigerate within 2 hours for up to 3 days. Reheat in a covered skillet over medium heat with a splash of broth for 5 minutes, stirring once, until steaming — the microwave dries out shrimp. The couscous also makes a great cold lunch straight from the fridge.
Common mistakes:
- Skipping the fluff: unfluffed couscous sits in a dense cake — rake it with a fork the moment it comes off the heat, twice if needed.
- Overcooking the shrimp: rubbery shrimp ruin the dish — 2 minutes per side is plenty; pull them when they form a loose C.
- Using unsalted cooking water or broth for the couscous: the grains taste bland from the inside — always salt the liquid.

Title: Shrimp & Tomato Orzo
Ingredients:
1 lb dry orzo
2 lb large shrimp (21/25), peeled and deveined
2 cans (14.5 oz each) crushed tomatoes
0.5 cup extra-virgin olive oil, divided
1 large red onion, diced (cut into small even cubes about 1/2 inch)
4 garlic cloves, minced (chopped very fine)
1 tbsp dried oregano
0.5 tsp crushed red pepper flakes (start with 0.25 tsp for gentle heat)
6 oz feta cheese, crumbled
0.5 cup pitted Kalamata olives, halved (slice = cut into thin flat pieces)
0.5 cup chopped fresh flat-leaf parsley
1 lemon, cut into wedges
1.5 tsp kosher salt, divided
0.75 tsp black pepper
Steps:
1. Mise en place: Dice the red onion (dice = cut into small even cubes about 1/2 inch). Mince the garlic (mince = chop very fine). Halve the olives (slice = cut into thin flat pieces). Chop the parsley. Crumble the feta. Cut the lemon into wedges. Pat the shrimp very dry. Position an oven rack 6 inches from the broiler and heat the broiler to high — you will finish the dish under it, Greek taverna style.
2. Cook the orzo: bring a large pot of well-salted water to a rolling boil and cook the orzo 1 to 2 minutes LESS than the package says for al dente — it will finish in the sauce. Drain, reserving 1 cup of the pasta water, and toss the orzo with 1 tbsp of the olive oil so it does not stick.
3. Sear the shrimp: heat 2 tbsp of the olive oil in a large oven-safe skillet over medium-high heat until shimmering. Add the shrimp in a single layer with 0.5 tsp of the salt and 0.25 tsp of the pepper; cook 1 to 2 minutes per side until just pink and curled. They will finish under the broiler, so pull them early — still slightly translucent in the very center is perfect. Move to a plate.
4. Build the tomato sauce (garides saganaki style): in the same skillet over medium heat, add 2 tbsp of the olive oil and the red onion with 0.5 tsp of the salt; cook 5 minutes until soft and sweet. Add the garlic, oregano, and red pepper flakes; cook 30 seconds until fragrant. Pour in the crushed tomatoes and simmer 8 to 10 minutes, stirring often, until the sauce thickens enough that a spoon leaves a brief trail — it should look rich and glossy, not watery. Season with the remaining 0.5 tsp of salt and 0.5 tsp of pepper; taste and adjust.
5. Fold the drained orzo and the olives into the sauce, adding splashes of the reserved pasta water until the orzo is glossy and saucy but not soupy. Nestle the shrimp into the orzo, then crumble the feta evenly over the top.
6. Slide the skillet under the broiler for 2 to 3 minutes, until the feta softens and turns golden at the edges and the sauce bubbles at the corners. Watch it closely — broilers go from golden to burnt fast. Let it rest 3 minutes so the sauce settles.
7. Serve: drizzle with the remaining olive oil (about 3 tbsp), scatter the parsley, and pass lemon wedges for squeezing over each bowl. Crusty bread for the sauce is very Greek and very encouraged.
8. Storage and reheating: refrigerate within 2 hours for up to 3 days. Reheat in a covered skillet over medium-low heat with a splash of water for 6 to 8 minutes until steaming — the feta re-melts into the sauce. The microwave works in a pinch but the feta gets rubbery.
Common mistakes:
- Overcooking the orzo in the pot: it goes mushy in the sauce — pull it 1 to 2 minutes early; it finishes in the tomato sauce.
- Cooking the shrimp twice as long: sear briefly on the stove because the broiler finishes them — fully cooked shrimp plus broiler time equals rubber.
- Walking away from the broiler: feta browns in seconds and burns just as fast — stay at the oven and watch.

Title: Shrimp Enchilada Rice Bake
Ingredients:
2 lb large shrimp (21/25), peeled, deveined, and cut into thirds
4 cups cooked long-grain white rice (from about 1.25 cups dry)
2 cans (10 oz each) red enchilada sauce
2 cups shredded Monterey Jack cheese, divided
1 cup shredded sharp cheddar cheese
1 can (15 oz) black beans, drained and rinsed
1 can (4.25 oz) diced green chiles
1 large yellow onion, diced (cut into small even cubes about 1/2 inch)
2 garlic cloves, minced (chopped very fine)
2 tbsp olive oil
1 tsp ground cumin
1 tsp chili powder
1.25 tsp kosher salt, divided
0.5 cup sour cream, for serving
0.5 cup chopped fresh cilantro
1 fresh jalapeno, thinly sliced (optional, for serving)
Steps:
1. Mise en place: Preheat the oven to 375F. If the rice is not already cooked, start it first — 1.25 cups of dry rice simmered in 2.5 cups of salted water for 15 minutes, then rested 10 minutes, makes about 4 cups. Dice the onion (dice = cut into small even cubes about 1/2 inch). Mince the garlic (mince = chop very fine). Cut the shrimp into thirds so the pieces are bite-size. Drain and rinse the black beans. Shred the cheeses if not pre-shredded. Chop the cilantro. Thinly slice the jalapeno if using. Lightly oil a 9x13-inch baking dish.
2. Heat the olive oil in a large skillet over medium-high heat. Add the onion and 0.5 tsp of the salt; cook 5 minutes, stirring, until soft and golden at the edges. Add the garlic, cumin, and chili powder; cook 30 seconds until the spices smell toasty.
3. Add the shrimp pieces, the remaining 0.75 tsp of salt, and the diced green chiles. Cook 2 to 3 minutes, stirring, just until the shrimp turn pink and curl — they will finish in the oven, so pull them slightly underdone.
4. Stir in the enchilada sauce, black beans, and the cooked rice. Fold everything together until the rice is evenly coated. Fold in 1 cup of the Monterey Jack until just starting to melt. Taste and add more salt if it needs it — the sauce brands vary in saltiness.
5. Spread the mixture evenly into the prepared baking dish. Sprinkle the remaining 1 cup of Monterey Jack and the cheddar evenly over the top.
6. Bake 20 to 25 minutes, until the cheese is melted, golden in spots, and the edges bubble vigorously. The center should be steaming hot (165F on an instant-read thermometer) and the shrimp fully pink and opaque. If the cheese needs more color, broil 1 to 2 minutes at the end — watch closely.
7. Rest 10 minutes out of the oven so the bake sets and is easier to serve. Top with dollops of sour cream, the cilantro, and jalapeno slices. Serve straight from the dish.
8. Storage and reheating: refrigerate within 2 hours for up to 3 days. Reheat covered with foil in a 350F oven for 20 minutes, or microwave single portions 2 to 3 minutes until steaming. It also freezes well for up to 2 months — thaw overnight in the fridge before reheating.
Common mistakes:
- Fully cooking the shrimp on the stove: they turn rubbery in the oven — pull them when just pink, still slightly underdone.
- Skipping the rest: cutting in immediately makes a soupy scoop — 10 minutes lets the cheese and rice set.
- Dry rice in the bake: day-old dry rice soaks up the sauce perfectly; if your rice is fresh and wet, use a touch less enchilada sauce.

Title: Shrimp Jalapeño Tacos
Ingredients:
2 lb large shrimp (21/25), peeled and deveined
3 fresh jalapenos, thinly sliced into rounds (slice = cut into thin flat pieces)
1 cup sour cream
1 fresh jalapeno, minced (mince = chop very fine)
2 tbsp fresh lime juice, plus lime wedges for serving
2 tbsp unsalted butter
1 tbsp olive oil
3 garlic cloves, minced (chopped very fine)
1 tsp ground cumin
1 tsp chili powder
0.75 tsp kosher salt
18 small corn tortillas (6-inch)
3 cups shredded green cabbage
1 ripe avocado, sliced
0.5 cup chopped fresh cilantro
Steps:
1. Mise en place: Thinly slice 3 jalapenos into rounds (slice = cut into thin flat pieces) — wear gloves or wash your hands well after, and do not touch your eyes. Mince the remaining jalapeno (mince = chop very fine) for the crema. Mince the garlic. Juice the limes. Shred the cabbage. Slice the avocado just before serving so it does not brown. Chop the cilantro. Pat the shrimp dry. Stir the crema: whisk the sour cream, minced jalapeno, lime juice, and a pinch of the salt in a bowl. Taste — for more heat, add some of the jalapeno seeds; for less, leave them out. Keep it chilled.
2. Warm the tortillas: heat a dry skillet over medium-high heat and warm each tortilla 30 to 45 seconds per side until soft, pliable, and lightly charred in spots. Stack them in a clean kitchen towel so they stay warm and do not crack when folded.
3. Heat the butter and olive oil in a large skillet over medium-high heat until the butter melts and foams. Add the shrimp in a single layer along with the cumin, chili powder, and the 0.75 tsp of salt. Cook 2 minutes, then flip and scatter the jalapeno rounds over the shrimp. Cook 1 to 2 minutes more, until the shrimp are pink, curled into a loose C, and opaque — the jalapeno rounds should be bright green and just softened. Add the garlic in the last 30 seconds, stirring, until fragrant (garlic burns fast, so it goes in last).
4. The shrimp are done when they read 145F at the thickest point or are opaque all the way through. Squeeze half a lime over the pan and toss.
5. Assemble: on each warm tortilla, lay a small handful of cabbage, 3 to 4 shrimp, a few softened jalapeno rounds, avocado slices, a drizzle of jalapeno-lime crema, and a sprinkle of cilantro. Serve with lime wedges for squeezing.
6. Storage and reheating: refrigerate leftover shrimp within 2 hours for up to 2 days. Reheat gently in a covered skillet over medium-low heat for 3 to 4 minutes with a splash of water — just until warm — since shrimp toughen quickly. Keep the crema chilled and use within 3 days. Tortillas rewarm in a dry skillet.
Common mistakes:
- Adding the garlic too early: minced garlic burns in under a minute over high heat and turns bitter — stir it in for only the final 30 seconds.
- Overcooking the shrimp: tight-O curls are rubbery — pull them at a loose C, pink and just opaque.
- Cold, stiff tortillas: they crack when folded — warm them in a dry skillet and keep them wrapped in a towel until serving.

Title: Shrimp Pomodoro Risotto
Ingredients:
1.5 cups arborio rice
2 lb large shrimp (21/25), peeled and deveined
1 can (28 oz) crushed tomatoes
6 cups low-sodium chicken or vegetable broth, kept warm
1 large yellow onion, diced (cut into small even cubes about 1/2 inch)
4 garlic cloves, minced (chopped very fine)
0.5 cup dry white wine
4 tbsp unsalted butter, divided
3 tbsp olive oil, divided
0.75 cup finely grated Parmesan cheese
0.5 cup torn fresh basil leaves
0.5 tsp crushed red pepper flakes (optional; start with 0.25 tsp for gentle heat)
1 tbsp fresh lemon juice
1.5 tsp kosher salt, divided
0.75 tsp black pepper
Steps:
1. Mise en place: Dice the onion (dice = cut into small even cubes about 1/2 inch). Mince the garlic (mince = chop very fine). Grate the Parmesan. Tear the basil leaves. Juice the lemon. Pat the shrimp very dry. Pour the broth into a saucepan and keep it at a bare simmer over low heat — warm broth keeps the risotto cooking steadily; cold broth stalls it and makes the rice gummy.
2. Heat 2 tbsp of the olive oil in a wide, heavy pan or Dutch oven over medium-high heat until shimmering. Season the shrimp with 0.5 tsp of the salt and 0.25 tsp of the pepper. Sear in a single layer 1 to 2 minutes per side, just until pink and curled into a loose C — pull them slightly underdone (still a hint translucent at the thickest point) because they will finish in the hot risotto. Move to a plate.
3. Reduce the heat to medium. In the same pan, add the remaining 1 tbsp of olive oil and the onion with 0.5 tsp of the salt. Cook 5 to 7 minutes, stirring often, until soft, translucent, and sweet — not browned. Add the garlic and red pepper flakes; cook 30 seconds until fragrant.
4. Stir in the arborio rice and toast 2 minutes, stirring constantly, until the grain edges look translucent and smell faintly nutty. Pour in the wine and stir until it has nearly evaporated and the sharp boozy smell is gone, about 1 minute.
5. Pour in the crushed tomatoes and stir to coat the rice. Add one ladle (about 0.75 cup) of warm broth and simmer gently, stirring every minute or two, until most of the liquid is absorbed. Keep adding broth one ladle at a time, stirring and waiting for absorption. After 18 to 22 minutes total, taste a grain: it should be tender with a tiny bite at the center, and the whole pan should look creamy and flow slowly when shaken — never stiff or soupy.
6. Off the heat, stir in the remaining 2 tbsp of butter, the Parmesan, and the lemon juice. Fold in the seared shrimp and let it sit 2 minutes — the residual heat finishes the shrimp gently so they stay plump. Taste and add the remaining 0.5 tsp of salt and 0.5 tsp of pepper, or more to your liking.
7. Serve: spoon into warm bowls and shower with the torn basil. A true pomodoro risotto glistens — finish with a thin thread of olive oil if you like.
8. Storage and reheating: refrigerate within 2 hours for up to 2 days. Reheat gently in a saucepan over low heat with a splash of broth, stirring until creamy again. Like all risotto, it is best fresh and thickens as it stands, so do not over-reduce on the stove.
Common mistakes:
- Adding cold broth: it drops the pan temperature and the starch seizes — keep the broth at a bare simmer the whole time.
- Cooking the shrimp fully on the stove: they finish in the risotto's residual heat, so sear them just underdone — pink outside, a whisper translucent inside.
- Serving too thick: risotto should ripple and spread when the bowl is shaken — if it stands in a stiff mound, stir in another splash of warm broth.

Title: Soy Garlic Chicken & Edamame
Ingredients:
3 lb boneless, skinless chicken thighs, cut into 1.5-inch pieces
0.5 cup low-sodium soy sauce
0.25 cup packed brown sugar (or 3 tbsp honey)
6 garlic cloves, minced (chopped very fine)
1 tbsp fresh ginger, grated
2 tbsp rice vinegar
1 tbsp toasted sesame oil
3 tbsp avocado oil (or another neutral oil), divided
2 cups frozen shelled edamame, thawed
4 green onions, thinly sliced (slice = cut into thin flat pieces)
1 tbsp sesame seeds (optional, for garnish)
4 cups cooked white rice, for serving
0.5 tsp black pepper
Steps:
1. Mise en place: Cut the chicken thighs into 1.5-inch pieces — even pieces cook evenly. Mince the garlic (mince = chop very fine). Grate the ginger. Thinly slice the green onions (slice = cut into thin flat pieces). Thaw the edamame by running it under warm water in a strainer, then drain well. In a large bowl, whisk the soy sauce, brown sugar, garlic, ginger, rice vinegar, and sesame oil until the sugar dissolves — this is both the marinade and the glaze.
2. Add the chicken pieces to the marinade and toss to coat every piece. Marinate 15 minutes at room temperature (or refrigerate up to 8 hours for deeper flavor — set it out 20 minutes before cooking so the cold chicken does not cool the pan). Keep the marinade bowl — you will use it next. (Food-safety rule: marinade that touched raw chicken must be boiled a full 2 minutes before it becomes sauce — that happens in step 5, so do not taste it raw.)
3. Lift the chicken out of the marinade, letting the excess drip off, and set the marinade bowl aside — you will use it next. Heat 1.5 tbsp of the avocado oil in a large heavy skillet over medium-high heat until shimmering. Add HALF the chicken in a single layer with space between pieces and sear 3 to 4 minutes per side without moving, until deep golden-brown with caramelized edges. The chicken should read 165F at the thickest piece and the juices should run clear. Move to a plate and repeat with the remaining 1.5 tbsp of oil and the second half.
4. Return all the chicken to the skillet. Pour in the reserved marinade from the bowl (the rice vinegar is already in it) and bring everything to a vigorous boil and cook 2 to 3 minutes, tossing, until the sauce thickens into a glossy glaze that coats the chicken. Boiling the marinade for a full 2 minutes makes it safe after touching raw chicken — do not skip this. If it gets too thick, splash in 1 to 2 tbsp of water.
5. Add the thawed edamame to the pan and toss 2 minutes, just until the edamame is hot and bright green. Taste the glaze — for more tang add a squeeze of lime or a splash more rice vinegar; for more sweetness, a pinch more brown sugar.
6. Serve: spoon the cooked white rice into 6 bowls, pile the glazed chicken and edamame over it, spoon over the extra glaze from the pan, and finish with the sliced green onions and sesame seeds.
7. Storage and reheating: refrigerate within 2 hours for up to 4 days. Reheat in a covered skillet over medium heat with a splash of water for 5 to 6 minutes, or microwave 2 to 3 minutes, until steaming (165F). The glaze re-melts beautifully.
Common mistakes:
- Reusing raw marinade without boiling: marinade that touched raw chicken must boil a full 2 minutes to be safe — never drizzle it on as a finishing sauce straight from the bowl.
- Crowding the chicken: it steams instead of searing and the glaze never caramelizes — cook in two batches with space between pieces.
- Burning the glaze: sugar scorches fast once the sauce thickens — keep it at a steady boil, keep tossing, and pull it the moment it coats the chicken.

Title: Soy Garlic Pork & Zucchini
Ingredients:
1.5 lb pork tenderloin, trimmed of silverskin and sliced into 1/4-inch medallions
3 medium zucchini (about 1.5 lb), halved lengthwise and sliced into 1/4-inch half-moons
6 tbsp soy sauce
3 tbsp honey
6 cloves garlic, minced
1 tbsp rice vinegar
1 tsp red pepper flakes (start here; add more at the end if you want more heat)
2 tbsp toasted sesame oil
2 tbsp avocado oil, divided
4 green onions, sliced thin on a diagonal
1 tbsp sesame seeds
Steps:
1. Mise en place (get everything ready before the heat goes on): Pat the pork very dry with paper towels (dry meat browns; wet meat steams). Slice the pork into medallions about 1/4 inch thick. Slice each zucchini in half lengthwise, then cut into half-moon slices about 1/4 inch thick (slice = cut into thin flat pieces). Mince the garlic (mince = chop very fine, almost a paste). Slice the green onions thin on a diagonal. In a small bowl, stir together the soy sauce, honey, rice vinegar, and red pepper flakes - this is your glaze. Set the sesame oil, avocado oil, and sesame seeds by the stove.
2. Sear the pork: Heat a large skillet over medium-high heat. Add 1 tablespoon avocado oil and wait until it shimmers and flows easily. Lay half the pork medallions in a single layer with space between them. Do not touch for 2 minutes - they should sizzle loudly and develop a golden-brown crust. Flip and cook 1 to 2 minutes more, until no pink remains and the center reads 145F on an instant-read thermometer. Transfer to a plate. Repeat with the remaining 1 tablespoon oil and pork.
3. Cook the zucchini: In the same hot skillet, add the zucchini slices. Cook 3 to 4 minutes, stirring only occasionally, until the edges are browned and the zucchini is bright green and just tender with a little bite left. It will smell sweet and nutty.
4. Glaze: Return the pork and any juices to the pan. Add the minced garlic and stir 30 seconds until fragrant (do not let it brown or it turns bitter). Pour in the soy-honey glaze. Toss everything 1 to 2 minutes until the sauce thickens slightly, turns glossy, and coats every piece.
5. Finish: Take the pan off the heat. Drizzle with the toasted sesame oil and toss with half the green onions and half the sesame seeds. Taste a piece: add 1 teaspoon more honey if you want it sweeter, or 1 teaspoon more vinegar if you want it brighter.
6. Serve: Spoon the pork and zucchini over steamed rice if you like, making sure everyone gets some of the pan glaze. Top with the remaining green onions and sesame seeds. Serve hot.
7. Storage and reheating: Refrigerate leftovers in an airtight container up to 4 days. Reheat in a skillet over medium heat with a splash of water, 3 to 4 minutes, until steaming. The zucchini will be softer the next day but still tasty.
Common mistakes: (1) Crowding the pan - the pork steams instead of searing and never browns; cook in two batches. (2) Overcooking the zucchini - it goes mushy fast; pull it while it still has a little bite. (3) Adding the honey glaze too early - honey burns over high heat; add it at the end and toss just until glossy.

Title: Spanish Pork & Crispy Potatoes
Ingredients:
2.5 lb Yukon Gold potatoes, scrubbed and cut into 3/4-inch cubes
1.75 lb boneless pork loin, cut into 1-inch-thick chops (about 6 pieces)
5 tbsp olive oil, divided
2 tsp smoked paprika (pimenton), divided
1 tsp dried oregano
5 cloves garlic, minced
1 tbsp sherry vinegar (or red wine vinegar)
1.5 tsp kosher salt, divided
1 tsp black pepper
1/4 cup fresh parsley, chopped
Steps:
1. Mise en place: Preheat the oven to 425F with a rack in the middle. Dice the potatoes into even 3/4-inch cubes (dice = cut into small even cubes; even size means even cooking). Pat the pork chops very dry and season both sides with 1 teaspoon salt, the black pepper, oregano, and 1 teaspoon of the smoked paprika. Mince the garlic (mince = chop very fine). Chop the parsley. Measure the oils, vinegar, and remaining spices into small bowls.
2. Roast the potatoes: Toss the potato cubes with 2 tablespoons olive oil, the remaining 1/2 teaspoon salt, and the remaining 1 teaspoon smoked paprika until evenly coated. Spread in a single layer on a large rimmed sheet pan with space between pieces. Roast 35 to 40 minutes, flipping once halfway with a spatula, until deep golden with crisp, crunchy edges. They should sound crisp when tapped with the spatula.
3. Sear the pork: While the potatoes roast, heat a large skillet over medium-high heat with 2 tablespoons olive oil until shimmering. Lay in the pork chops without crowding. Sear 3 to 4 minutes per side without moving them, until deeply golden-brown. Check the thickest chop with an instant-read thermometer - pull at 145F. Transfer to a plate and tent loosely with foil; rest 5 minutes so the juices redistribute instead of running out.
4. Make the pan drizzle: Return the same skillet to medium heat. Add the remaining 1 tablespoon olive oil and the garlic; stir 30 seconds until fragrant and just turning golden (not brown). Splash in the sherry vinegar and scrape the bottom of the pan with a wooden spoon to dissolve all the browned bits, about 1 minute, until it smells sharp and savory.
5. Serve: Slice the rested pork against the grain into 1/2-inch slices (look for the lines running through the meat and cut across them - this keeps every bite tender). Pile the crispy potatoes on plates, fan the pork over them, spoon the garlic-vinegar pan drippings over everything, and shower with chopped parsley. Serve hot.
6. Storage and reheating: Refrigerate up to 3 to 4 days. Re-crisp the potatoes in a 425F oven for 10 to 12 minutes - do not microwave them or they go soggy. Warm the pork in a skillet over medium heat with a splash of water until it reaches 145F.
Common mistakes: (1) Piling the potatoes up - they steam instead of crisping; give every cube its own space on the pan. (2) Slicing the pork with the grain - it turns chewy; always cut across the visible lines in the meat. (3) Skipping the rest - cut too soon and the juices run all over the plate instead of staying in the meat.

Title: Spicy Beef & Zucchini Rice
Ingredients:
2.5 cups jasmine rice, rinsed
1.5 lb ground beef (85/15)
2 medium zucchini (about 1 lb), cut into 1/2-inch dice
3 tbsp gochujang (Korean fermented chili paste; start with 2 tbsp if you are heat-shy)
3 tbsp soy sauce
1 tbsp brown sugar (start here; add 1 tsp more at the end if you want it sweeter)
2 tbsp toasted sesame oil
4 cloves garlic, minced
1 tbsp fresh ginger, minced
1 tbsp avocado oil
4 green onions, sliced
1 tbsp sesame seeds
Steps:
1. Mise en place: Rinse the rice in a fine-mesh strainer until the water runs mostly clear. Start the rice now: combine with 3 3/4 cups water in a pot, bring to a boil, cover, reduce to low, and cook 15 minutes; then rest 10 minutes off the heat with the lid on. Dice the zucchini into 1/2-inch cubes (dice = cut into small even cubes about 1/2 inch). Mince the garlic and ginger (mince = chop very fine). Slice the green onions. In a small bowl, stir together the gochujang, soy sauce, and brown sugar.
2. Brown the beef: Heat a large skillet over medium-high heat with the avocado oil until shimmering. Add the ground beef and break it into crumbles with a wooden spoon. Cook 6 to 8 minutes, stirring occasionally, until no pink remains and the edges are crispy and browned. It should smell deeply savory. Tilt the pan and spoon off the excess fat, leaving about 1 tablespoon in the pan.
3. Season: Stir in the garlic and ginger; cook 30 seconds until fragrant. Pour in the gochujang mixture and stir 1 to 2 minutes until the beef is glossy, brick-red, and evenly coated.
4. Add the zucchini: Push the beef to the edges of the pan and add the zucchini to the center. Cook 3 to 4 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the zucchini is bright green and just tender with a little bite - it keeps cooking in the hot beef, so err on the firm side.
5. Finish: Take the pan off the heat. Drizzle with the toasted sesame oil and fold in half the green onions and half the sesame seeds. Taste: for more heat add gochujang 1 teaspoon at a time; for more sweetness add brown sugar 1 teaspoon at a time.
6. Serve: Fluff the rice with a fork. Bowl up generous scoops of rice, top with the spicy beef and zucchini, and finish with the remaining green onions and sesame seeds. Serve hot.
7. Storage and reheating: Store the beef mixture and rice in separate airtight containers in the fridge up to 4 days. Reheat the beef in a skillet over medium heat 4 to 5 minutes until steaming. Reheat rice in the microwave with a damp paper towel laid over it.
Common mistakes: (1) Not draining the fat - the sauce turns greasy; spoon off all but about a tablespoon. (2) Cooking the zucchini to mush - it keeps softening off the heat, so pull it while still a little firm. (3) Tasting the gochujang heat straight from the jar - it mellows once mixed with the beef and rice, so season at the end.

Title: Spicy Pork Bulgogi Bowls
Ingredients:
2 lb pork shoulder, placed in the freezer 30 minutes before slicing
1/3 cup gochujang (Korean fermented chili paste)
3 tbsp soy sauce
2 tbsp sugar (start here; add 1 tsp more at the end if you want it sweeter)
2 tbsp toasted sesame oil
5 cloves garlic, minced
1 tbsp fresh ginger, grated
1/2 yellow onion, grated on a box grater
2 tbsp mirin (or 1 tbsp rice vinegar mixed with 1 tbsp water)
1 tsp gochugaru or red pepper flakes (optional, for extra heat)
2.5 cups jasmine rice, rinsed
2 large carrots, peeled and cut into thin matchsticks
1 English cucumber, sliced into thin half-moons
1 tbsp avocado oil, plus more between batches if the pan looks dry
4 green onions, sliced
1 tbsp sesame seeds
Steps:
1. Mise en place: Put the pork shoulder in the freezer for 30 minutes - firmer meat slices much thinner. Rinse the rice and start it cooking (2.5 cups rice with 3 3/4 cups water; boil, cover, low 15 minutes, rest 10 minutes off heat). In a large bowl, whisk together the gochujang, soy sauce, sugar, sesame oil, garlic, ginger, grated onion, mirin, and gochugaru. Mince the garlic (mince = chop very fine). Cut the carrots into thin matchstick sticks (julienne = thin sticks about 2 inches long). Slice the cucumber into thin half-moons. Slice the green onions.
2. Slice and marinate: Remove the firm pork from the freezer. Slice it as thin as you can - about 1/8 inch - cutting against the grain (across the visible lines in the meat). Toss the slices in the marinade until every piece is coated. Cover and refrigerate at least 30 minutes, or up to 8 hours for deeper flavor.
3. Sear in batches: Heat a large skillet or wok over HIGH heat with 1 tablespoon avocado oil until it just starts to smoke. Add one-third of the pork in a single layer - pieces should not touch. Do not move them for 2 minutes; the edges should char and caramelize. Flip and cook 2 to 3 minutes more until cooked through with no pink (thin slices cook fast; spot-check that the thickest piece reads 145F). Transfer to a plate. Repeat with the remaining pork, adding a drizzle more oil between batches if the pan looks dry.
4. Warm through: Return all the pork to the hot pan for 30 seconds, tossing, just to warm it through and recoat it in the pan juices. Take off the heat.
5. Build the bowls: Fluff the rice. Divide among 6 bowls: a scoop of rice, a pile of spicy pork, matchstick carrots, and cucumber half-moons. Drizzle a spoonful of the pan juices over each bowl. Top with green onions and sesame seeds. Serve hot.
6. Storage and reheating: Refrigerate the pork separate from the vegetables up to 4 days. Reheat the pork in a ripping-hot skillet 2 to 3 minutes (the microwave makes thin pork rubbery). Slice fresh cucumber and carrots when serving leftovers.
Common mistakes: (1) Slicing the pork thick - thick slices stay chewy; the brief freeze is what makes thin slicing possible. (2) Crowding the pan - the pork steams in its own juices and the marinade never caramelizes; cook in three batches. (3) Timid heat - bulgogi needs high heat for those charred, crispy edges.

Title: Steak au Poivre with Parmesan Mash
Ingredients:
3 lb Yukon Gold or russet potatoes, peeled and cut into 1.5-inch chunks
4 tbsp unsalted butter, divided
1 cup whole milk, warmed
1 cup Parmesan cheese, finely grated (about 3 oz), plus extra for serving
6 sirloin steaks, 8 oz each and 1 to 1.25 inches thick
3 tbsp whole black peppercorns, coarsely crushed
2 tbsp avocado oil
1 large shallot, minced
1/3 cup brandy or cognac
1 cup beef stock
1 cup heavy cream
1 tsp Dijon mustard
2 tsp kosher salt, plus more to taste
Steps:
1. Mise en place: Take the steaks out of the fridge 30 minutes before cooking so they cook evenly. Peel the potatoes and cut into 1.5-inch chunks; drop them into a pot of cold salted water. Crush the peppercorns coarsely - put them in a zip-top bag and smash with the bottom of a heavy pan until cracked into rough pieces (not powder; fine pepper burns and turns bitter). Grate the Parmesan. Warm the milk in the microwave until steamy, about 90 seconds. Mince the shallot (mince = chop very fine). Measure the brandy, beef stock, and cream into separate cups. Pat the steaks VERY dry with paper towels, season both sides generously with salt, then press the crushed peppercorns firmly onto both sides of each steak.
2. Cook the potatoes: Bring the pot to a boil over high heat, then reduce to a steady simmer. Cook 15 to 18 minutes, until a fork slides into a chunk with zero resistance. Drain well in a colander, then return the potatoes to the hot empty pot for 1 minute, shaking gently, to steam off surface water (dry potatoes make fluffy mash).
3. Mash: Mash the potatoes with a potato masher until smooth. Stir in 3 tablespoons of the butter and the warm milk until creamy. Fold in the grated Parmesan and season with salt to taste. Cover the pot and keep warm on the lowest heat.
4. Sear the steaks: Heat a large heavy skillet over medium-high heat with the avocado oil until it just starts to smoke. Lay the steaks in without crowding - they should sizzle hard on contact. Do not move them for 3 to 4 minutes, until a deep brown crust forms. Flip once and cook 3 to 4 minutes more for medium-rare (130 to 135F on an instant-read thermometer). For rare, go 2 to 3 minutes per side (120 to 125F); for medium, 5 to 6 minutes per side (135 to 145F). Transfer to a warm plate, tent loosely with foil, and rest 5 to 10 minutes.
5. Start the pan sauce: Pour off any excess fat from the skillet, leaving the browned bits. Set over medium heat, add the remaining 1 tablespoon butter and the shallot; cook 1 minute until softened.
6. Add the brandy SAFELY: Pull the pan OFF the heat. Pour in the brandy away from any open flame - never pour from the bottle near the stove. Return the pan to medium heat and let it bubble 1 minute, scraping the bottom with a wooden spoon to dissolve the browned bits. If it flames, stay calm: pull the pan off the heat and let the flame burn out on its own. The alcohol smell should cook off, leaving a sweet, oaky aroma.
7. Finish the sauce: Pour in the beef stock and simmer 3 to 4 minutes until reduced by half. Stir in the heavy cream and Dijon mustard; simmer 2 to 3 minutes more, until the sauce thickly coats the back of a spoon. Taste and add salt if needed - the sauce should be peppery, creamy, and savory.
8. Serve: Spoon a swoosh of Parmesan mash onto each plate, set a steak beside it (whole or sliced), and ladle the au poivre sauce generously over the steak. Sprinkle a little extra Parmesan over the mash. Serve immediately.
9. Storage and reheating: Refrigerate steak and sauce in separate containers up to 3 days. Reheat steak gently in a 250F oven for 15 to 20 minutes until warmed to about 120F inside - this keeps it pink instead of turning it gray. Warm the sauce over low heat, whisking, adding a splash of cream if it got too thick. Reheat the mash in the microwave with a splash of milk, stirring halfway.
Common mistakes: (1) Wet steaks - surface moisture kills the crust; pat them very dry before the pepper goes on. (2) Pouring brandy over an open flame or straight from the bottle - always pull the pan off the heat first. (3) Finely ground pepper - it scorches and tastes acrid; use coarse-crushed peppercorns. (4) Skipping the rest - the steak keeps cooking gently and the juices settle back into the meat.

Title: Tomato Beef Rice Bowls
Ingredients:
2.5 cups jasmine rice, rinsed
1.5 lb flank steak, sliced 1/4-inch thin against the grain
2 tbsp soy sauce, plus 2 tbsp more for the sauce
1 tbsp Shaoxing wine (or dry sherry)
1 tbsp cornstarch, plus 2 tsp more for the slurry
1 tsp toasted sesame oil
1 tsp sugar, plus 2 tbsp more for the sauce
1/2 tsp baking soda (tenderizer - no need to rinse at this small amount)
1/3 cup ketchup
1 tbsp tomato paste
1/2 cup water or beef stock
2 tbsp cold water (for the slurry)
3 large ripe tomatoes, cut into wedges
1 large onion, cut into wedges
3 cloves garlic, minced
1 tbsp fresh ginger, minced
3 tbsp avocado oil, divided
1/2 tsp white pepper
2 green onions, sliced
Steps:
1. Mise en place: Rinse the rice and start it cooking (2.5 cups rice with 3 3/4 cups water; boil, cover, low 15 minutes, rest 10 minutes off heat). Look at the flank steak and find the long lines running through the meat - slice ACROSS those lines (against the grain) into 1/4-inch thin strips; this is what keeps flank steak tender. Toss the beef with 2 tablespoons soy sauce, the Shaoxing wine, 1 tablespoon cornstarch, the sesame oil, 1 teaspoon sugar, and the baking soda; rest 15 minutes. Cut the tomatoes and onion into wedges. Mince the garlic and ginger (mince = chop very fine). In a bowl, stir together the ketchup, remaining 2 tablespoons soy sauce, remaining 2 tablespoons sugar, tomato paste, and the water or stock - this is your sauce. In a separate tiny bowl, stir the remaining 2 teaspoons cornstarch with the 2 tablespoons cold water until smooth - this is your slurry. Slice the green onions.
2. Sear the beef: Heat a wok or large skillet over HIGH heat with 1 tablespoon avocado oil until smoking. Add half the beef in a single layer; sear 1 to 2 minutes per side until browned but still a little pink inside. Remove to a plate. Repeat with 1 tablespoon oil and the remaining beef. Do not fully cook it now - it finishes in the sauce.
3. Build the base: In the same pan over medium-high heat, add the remaining 1 tablespoon oil and the onion wedges. Cook 2 minutes until the edges char slightly. Add the garlic and ginger; stir 30 seconds until fragrant.
4. Tomatoes and sauce: Add the tomato wedges; cook 2 to 3 minutes, stirring gently, until they start to slump and release their juice. Pour in the sauce mixture and bring to a bubbling simmer. It should smell sweet, tangy, and savory.
5. Thicken: Give the slurry a quick re-stir (cornstarch sinks to the bottom), then drizzle it into the bubbling sauce while stirring. In about 30 seconds the sauce will turn glossy and thick enough to coat a spoon.
6. Finish: Return the beef with any collected juices to the pan. Toss 1 minute just to heat through - any longer and the beef toughens. Take off the heat. Sprinkle with the white pepper and green onions. Taste the sauce: add 1 teaspoon more sugar if too sharp, or 1 teaspoon more soy sauce if too sweet.
7. Serve: Fluff the rice and divide among bowls. Spoon the tomato beef and plenty of glossy sauce over each bowl. Serve hot.
8. Storage and reheating: Refrigerate up to 4 days. Reheat in a skillet over medium heat with a splash of water, 4 to 5 minutes, until steaming.
Common mistakes: (1) Slicing with the grain - flank steak becomes shoe leather; always cut across the visible lines. (2) Overcooking the beef in the sauce - it only needs 1 minute to warm through after searing. (3) Forgetting to re-stir the slurry - the cornstarch settles and the sauce will not thicken evenly.

Title: Tomato Braised Pork with Rice
Ingredients:
2.5 lb boneless pork shoulder, cut into 2-inch chunks
2 tbsp olive oil
1 large onion, diced
2 carrots, peeled and diced
2 celery stalks, diced
5 cloves garlic, minced
2 tbsp tomato paste
1 cup dry red wine (Chianti or similar - cook with one you would drink)
1 (28 oz) can San Marzano tomatoes, crushed by hand
1 cup chicken stock
2 sprigs fresh rosemary
2 bay leaves
1 tsp dried oregano
1/2 tsp red pepper flakes (start here for gentle heat; add more at the end if you want it spicier)
2 tsp kosher salt, plus more to taste
1 tsp black pepper
3 cups long-grain rice, rinsed
Steps:
1. Mise en place: Preheat the oven to 325F with a rack in the lower middle. Cut the pork into 2-inch chunks, pat very dry with paper towels, and season all over with the salt and black pepper. Dice the onion, carrots, and celery into roughly 1/2-inch pieces (dice = cut into small even cubes about 1/2 inch). Mince the garlic (mince = chop very fine). Open the tomato can and crush the tomatoes by hand into a bowl, letting the juices run through your fingers. Measure the tomato paste, wine, and stock. Tie the rosemary sprigs together with kitchen twine if you have it, so they are easy to fish out later.
2. Sear the pork: Heat a large Dutch oven over medium-high heat with the olive oil until shimmering. Brown the pork in 2 to 3 batches - 3 to 4 minutes per side, deep golden on at least two sides. Do not crowd the pot; crowded meat steams instead of browning. Transfer each batch to a plate. That dark fond stuck to the pot bottom is pure flavor - leave it there.
3. Soften the vegetables: In the same pot over medium heat, add the onion, carrots, and celery with a pinch of salt. Cook 6 to 8 minutes, stirring occasionally, until softened and the onion is translucent. Add the garlic and tomato paste; stir constantly 2 minutes until the paste darkens to brick red and smells sweet and caramelized (raw tomato paste tastes tinny).
4. Deglaze: Pour in the red wine. Scrape the bottom of the pot hard with a wooden spoon to dissolve every browned bit. Let it simmer 3 minutes until slightly reduced and the sharp alcohol smell mellows.
5. Braise: Stir in the crushed tomatoes, chicken stock, rosemary, bay leaves, oregano, and red pepper flakes. Return the pork with any collected juices to the pot. The liquid should nearly cover the meat - add a splash of water if a lot of pork is exposed. Bring to a gentle simmer on the stove (a lazy bubble or two, not a rolling boil).
6. Into the oven: Cover with the lid and transfer to the oven. Braise 2 to 2 1/2 hours, giving it one stir halfway through, until the pork shreds easily when pressed with a fork and the sauce is thick and brick-red.
7. Cook the rice: About 30 minutes before the pork is done, cook the rice (3 cups rice with 4 1/2 cups water; boil, cover, low 15 minutes, rest 10 minutes off heat).
8. Finish the sauce: Remove the pot from the oven. Fish out the rosemary stems and bay leaves. Tilt the pot and spoon off any large pools of fat from the surface if you like. Taste: add salt confidently (a big pot needs it), a pinch of sugar 1 teaspoon at a time if the tomatoes taste too acidic, or a small splash of red wine vinegar if the sauce tastes flat.
9. Serve: Fluff the rice and mound it in wide bowls. Ladle over big chunks of pork and plenty of sauce. Serve hot. This dish is even better the next day.
10. Storage and reheating: Refrigerate up to 5 days; freeze up to 3 months. Reheat covered in a 325F oven for 25 to 30 minutes, or on the stove over low heat with a splash of water, stirring, until bubbling throughout.
Common mistakes: (1) Skipping the sear - those browned crusts are where the deep, meaty flavor comes from; pale pork makes pale sauce. (2) Boiling instead of braising - keep it at a lazy bubble; hard boiling squeezes moisture out and toughens the meat. (3) Under-seasoning - a big pot of braise needs more salt than you think; taste at the end and adjust.

Title: Tomato Coconut Cod Stew
Ingredients:
2.5 lb cod fillets, cut into 2-inch chunks
Juice of 2 limes
2 tsp kosher salt, divided
1 tsp black pepper
2 tbsp dende (Brazilian red palm oil) - or substitute 2 tbsp olive oil plus 1 tsp sweet paprika for the golden color
2 tbsp olive oil
1 large onion, thinly sliced
4 cloves garlic, minced
1 red bell pepper, thinly sliced
1 yellow bell pepper, thinly sliced
3 large ripe tomatoes, sliced into rounds
1 (13.5 oz) can full-fat coconut milk, shaken well
1 cup fish or chicken stock
1/2 cup fresh cilantro, chopped, plus more for serving
Lime wedges, for serving
3 cups long-grain rice, rinsed
Steps:
1. Mise en place: Cut the cod into 2-inch chunks. Toss gently in a bowl with the lime juice, 1 teaspoon of the salt, and the black pepper; refrigerate 15 minutes (the lime lightly firms the fish so it holds together). Thinly slice the onion and both bell peppers (slice = cut into thin flat pieces). Slice the tomatoes into rounds about 1/4 inch thick. Mince the garlic (mince = chop very fine). Chop the cilantro. Shake the coconut milk can hard so the cream and liquid recombine. Rinse the rice and start it cooking (3 cups rice with 4 1/2 cups water; boil, cover, low 15 minutes, rest 10 minutes off heat).
2. Soften the aromatics: Heat a large Dutch oven or deep skillet over medium heat. Add the olive oil and the dende (or the olive oil-paprika substitute) and warm until shimmering and fragrant - dende smells nutty and earthy. Add the onion and cook 4 to 5 minutes until soft and translucent. Add the garlic and stir 30 seconds until fragrant.
3. Layer - do not stir after this: Arrange half the tomato rounds over the onions. Add half the sliced peppers, then half the fish chunks in a single layer, then half the cilantro and a pinch of salt. Repeat with the remaining tomatoes, peppers, fish, cilantro, and salt. Layering (instead of stirring) is the traditional moqueca method - it keeps the fish in beautiful whole pieces.
4. Add the liquid: Pour the coconut milk and the stock evenly over everything. Bring to a gentle simmer over medium heat - you want small bubbles around the edges, never a rolling boil. Boiling can split the coconut milk and shred the fish.
5. Simmer: Cover, reduce the heat to low, and simmer 12 to 15 minutes. The fish is done when it is opaque all the way through, flakes easily with a fork, and reads 145F in the thickest piece. If you need to move things, shake the pan gently instead of stirring.
6. Taste and serve: Taste the golden broth - add more salt, a squeeze of lime, or another drizzle of dende until it sings. Ladle into wide bowls over rice, spooning plenty of broth over each serving. Top with fresh cilantro and serve with lime wedges.
7. Storage and reheating: Refrigerate up to 3 days - fish stews do not keep long. Reheat gently on the stove over low heat until just steaming; never boil or the fish falls apart. This stew does not freeze well (the coconut milk separates when thawed).
Common mistakes: (1) Boiling the stew - coconut milk can curdle and the cod disintegrates; keep it at a bare simmer. (2) Stirring - breaks the fish into shreds; layer the ingredients and leave them alone. (3) Overcooking - cod goes from perfect to mushy fast; start checking at 12 minutes.

Title: Tomato Saffron Cod with Rice
Ingredients:
2.5 lb cod fillets, cut into 2-inch chunks
1/2 tsp saffron threads
1/2 cup dry white wine, warmed
4 tbsp olive oil, divided
1 large onion, diced
1 red bell pepper, diced
5 cloves garlic, minced
1 tsp smoked paprika
1 (28 oz) can crushed tomatoes
1 cup fish or vegetable stock
2 bay leaves
1/2 cup fresh parsley, chopped
1 lemon, cut into wedges
1.5 tsp kosher salt, plus more to taste
1/2 tsp black pepper
2.5 cups long-grain rice, rinsed
Steps:
1. Mise en place: Warm the white wine until just steamy (microwave about 20 seconds - not boiling). Crumble the saffron threads into it and let steep 15 minutes until the wine turns deep gold - this blooming step pulls the color and honey-like aroma out of the saffron; cold liquid will not do it. Cut the cod into 2-inch chunks. Dice the onion and bell pepper into 1/2-inch pieces (dice = cut into small even cubes about 1/2 inch). Mince the garlic (mince = chop very fine). Chop the parsley. Cut the lemon into wedges. Rinse the rice and start it cooking (2.5 cups rice with 3 3/4 cups water; boil, cover, low 15 minutes, rest 10 minutes off heat).
2. Build the sofrito: Heat a large deep skillet or Dutch oven over medium heat with 3 tablespoons of the olive oil. Add the onion and bell pepper with a pinch of salt. Cook 6 to 8 minutes, stirring occasionally, until soft, sweet-smelling, and just starting to turn golden at the edges. Add the garlic and smoked paprika; stir 1 minute until fragrant and rust-colored.
3. Bloom and simmer: Pour in the saffron wine, scraping the bottom of the pan with a wooden spoon. Simmer 2 minutes. Add the crushed tomatoes, stock, bay leaves, salt, and black pepper. Bring to a gentle simmer and cook 12 to 15 minutes, until slightly thickened and the raw, tinny tomato edge is gone. Taste for salt - the sauce should be savory with a floral saffron perfume.
4. Poach the cod: Nestle the cod chunks into the sauce in a single layer and spoon a little sauce over each piece. Cover and simmer gently 8 to 10 minutes. The fish is done when opaque all the way through, flakes easily with a fork, and reads 145F in the thickest piece. Do not stir - lift sauce over the fish with a spoon if a piece looks dry on top.
5. Finish: Take off the heat. Fish out the bay leaves. Drizzle with the remaining 1 tablespoon olive oil and shower with the chopped parsley.
6. Serve: Fluff the rice and divide among wide bowls. Set the cod over the rice and ladle plenty of the saffron-tomato sauce around it. Serve with lemon wedges for squeezing over the top.
7. Storage and reheating: Refrigerate up to 3 days. Reheat gently over low heat until just steaming. The sauce freezes well up to 2 months (freeze sauce alone for best texture - the fish softens on thawing).
Common mistakes: (1) Adding saffron straight to the pot - it needs to steep in warm liquid first or you get pale sauce and wasted saffron. (2) Boiling the fish - a hard bubble turns cod to mush; keep the simmer gentle. (3) Overcooking - start checking at 8 minutes; carryover heat finishes the job off the burner.

Title: Turkey-Free Beef Moussaka Bowls
Ingredients:
2 large eggplants (about 2.5 lb), cut into 1-inch cubes
3 tbsp olive oil, divided
1.5 lb ground beef (85/15)
1 large onion, diced
4 cloves garlic, minced
2 tbsp tomato paste
1 (14.5 oz) can diced tomatoes
1/2 cup dry red wine (or beef stock)
1.5 tsp dried oregano
1/2 tsp ground cinnamon
1/4 tsp ground nutmeg, plus 1/4 tsp more for the bechamel
1 bay leaf
2 tsp kosher salt, divided, plus more to taste
3 tbsp unsalted butter
3 tbsp all-purpose flour
2 cups whole milk, warmed
1/2 cup Parmesan cheese, grated
1 large egg yolk
1/4 tsp white pepper
2 cups long-grain rice, rinsed
1/4 cup fresh parsley, chopped, for serving
Steps:
1. Mise en place: Preheat the oven to 425F with a rack in the middle. Cut the eggplant into 1-inch cubes and toss on a large rimmed sheet pan with 2 tablespoons olive oil and 1 teaspoon salt, spread in a single layer. Dice the onion (dice = cut into small even cubes about 1/2 inch). Mince the garlic (mince = chop very fine). Grate the Parmesan. Warm the milk until steamy in the microwave, about 2 minutes - warm milk is the secret to lump-free bechamel. Rinse the rice and start it cooking (2 cups rice with 3 cups water; boil, cover, low 15 minutes, rest 10 minutes off heat).
2. Roast the eggplant: Roast 25 to 30 minutes, flipping once halfway, until the cubes are golden-brown with caramelized edges and creamy inside. Pale, firm cubes are underdone - you want real color. Set aside.
3. Brown the beef: Heat a large skillet over medium-high heat with the remaining 1 tablespoon olive oil. Add the ground beef and break into crumbles; cook 6 to 8 minutes until no pink remains and the edges brown. Tilt and spoon off the excess fat.
4. Build the moussaka sauce: Add the onion to the beef and cook 5 minutes until soft. Add the garlic and stir 30 seconds until fragrant. Stir in the tomato paste and cook 2 minutes until it darkens. Pour in the red wine and scrape up all the browned bits; simmer 2 minutes. Add the diced tomatoes, oregano, cinnamon, 1/4 teaspoon nutmeg, bay leaf, and the remaining 1 teaspoon salt. Simmer 15 to 20 minutes, stirring occasionally, until thick - a spoon dragged across the bottom should leave a trail. Fish out the bay leaf. Taste: the cinnamon should whisper in the background, not shout.
5. Make the bechamel: In a medium saucepan over medium heat, melt the butter. Whisk in the flour and cook 2 minutes, stirring constantly, until it smells toasty like pie crust (raw flour tastes pasty). Slowly pour in the warm milk a little at a time, whisking constantly - go slow or it lumps. Bring to a gentle simmer and cook 3 to 4 minutes, stirring, until thick enough to coat the back of a spoon. Take off the heat. Whisk in the Parmesan, the remaining 1/4 teaspoon nutmeg, the white pepper, and salt to taste. Then whisk in the egg yolk quickly and thoroughly - it enriches the sauce without scrambling.
6. Assemble the bowls: Fluff the rice. Divide among 6 bowls: rice, a scoop of roasted eggplant, a generous ladle of the beef sauce, and a big spoonful of warm bechamel over the top. Sprinkle with chopped parsley. Serve hot.
7. Storage and reheating: Refrigerate the components in separate containers up to 4 days. Reheat the sauce and eggplant in a 350F oven for 15 minutes; warm the bechamel over low heat, whisking, with a splash of milk if it thickened too much. Assembled bowls reheat fine in the microwave.
Common mistakes: (1) Watery eggplant - if you pull it before it is truly golden, it weeps in the bowl; roast until caramelized. (2) Cold milk into the roux - it seizes into lumps; warm the milk first and add it slowly. (3) Heavy hand with cinnamon - 1/2 teaspoon is the moussaka signature; more turns the sauce toward dessert.

Title: Turmeric Fish with Dill Rice
Ingredients:
2.5 lb cod fillets (or halibut), cut into 1.5-inch chunks
2 tbsp ground turmeric
3 tbsp fish sauce
2 tbsp sugar
1/2 cup plain whole-milk yogurt
4 cloves garlic, minced
2 tbsp fresh galangal, grated (traditional; or substitute fresh ginger)
2 tbsp avocado oil, plus 4 tbsp more for frying
1 tsp kosher salt
1/2 tsp black pepper
2 tbsp cornstarch
2 large bunches fresh dill (about 4 oz), cut into 2-inch lengths
8 green onions, cut into 2-inch lengths
1/2 cup roasted peanuts, roughly chopped
3 cups jasmine rice, rinsed
1/4 cup fish sauce (for the dipping sauce)
1/4 cup warm water (for the dipping sauce)
2 tbsp sugar (for the dipping sauce)
Juice of 2 limes
2 cloves garlic, minced (for the dipping sauce)
1 Thai chili, minced (start with half if you are heat-shy)
Steps:
1. Mise en place: This Hanoi classic (cha ca la vong) traditionally uses catfish and is served over rice noodles with pungent fermented shrimp paste - here we adapt it to easy-to-find cod, jasmine rice, and a friendlier fish-sauce-lime dip. Cut the fish into 1.5-inch chunks. In a large GLASS or stainless-steel bowl (turmeric permanently stains plastic), whisk the turmeric, 3 tablespoons fish sauce, 2 tablespoons sugar, yogurt, garlic, grated galangal or ginger, 2 tablespoons avocado oil, salt, and pepper. Add the fish and turn gently to coat every piece. Cover and refrigerate 30 minutes (up to 2 hours). Rinse the rice and start it cooking (3 cups rice with 4 1/2 cups water; boil, cover, low 15 minutes, rest 10 minutes off heat). Cut the dill and green onions into 2-inch lengths. Roughly chop the peanuts. Stir the dipping-sauce ingredients (1/4 cup fish sauce, warm water, 2 tablespoons sugar, lime juice, garlic, chili) in a small bowl until the sugar dissolves.
2. Coat the fish: Lift the fish pieces from the marinade, letting the excess drip off. Dust lightly with the cornstarch on all sides and shake off the extra - you want a whisper of coating, not a batter. Discard the leftover marinade.
3. Fry in batches: Heat a large heavy skillet over medium-high heat with 2 tablespoons of the frying oil until shimmering. Add half the fish in a single layer with space between pieces. Cook 2 to 3 minutes per side until deep golden at the edges and opaque in the center (145F inside). Transfer to a plate. Repeat with the remaining 2 tablespoons oil and fish.
4. Wilt the herbs: In the same skillet over medium-high heat with 1 teaspoon of oil, add the green onions and dill. Toss 30 to 60 seconds, just until bright green and slightly wilted - they should still look fresh and smell intensely fragrant, not cooked down.
5. Combine: Return the fish to the pan and toss gently for 30 seconds to warm everything through. Take off the heat.
6. Serve: Fluff the rice and divide among bowls. Top with the turmeric fish, the wilted dill and green onions, and a scatter of chopped peanuts. Pass the dipping sauce for drizzling over each bowl. Serve hot and eat right away - this dish waits for no one.
7. Storage and reheating: Refrigerate the fish separate from the rice up to 3 days. Reheat the fish in a hot skillet 2 to 3 minutes (the microwave makes it rubbery). The dipping sauce keeps 1 week refrigerated.
Common mistakes: (1) Marinating in a plastic container - turmeric stains it bright yellow forever; use glass or metal. (2) Wilting the dill to death - 60 seconds maximum; it should stay bright green and perfumed. (3) Crowding the fry - the pieces steam and the light coating never crisps; cook in two batches.
